question: In 490 BC, 10,000 Athenians ran downhill to crush a Persian invasion force at which plain?
answer: Marathon
choices: Marathon
Salamis
Thermopylae
Plataea
context: Miltiades led the charge. The runner Pheidippides died bringing word back to Athens — the 26.2-mile race honors his run.

question: The 300 Spartans who held the pass against Xerxes' invasion were led by which king?
answer: Leonidas
choices: Leonidas
Agesilaus
Pausanias
Cleomenes
context: Thermopylae, 480 BC. Spartans + Thespians + Thebans fought to the last to delay Persia. Salamis followed weeks later.

question: Themistocles lured Xerxes' fleet into a narrow strait in 480 BC and crushed it at:
answer: Salamis
choices: Salamis
Marathon
Mycale
Lade
context: Themistocles had spent silver from new mines to build 200 triremes. Xerxes watched from a throne on shore as his navy burned.

question: Convicted of corrupting Athens' youth in 399 BC, Socrates was sentenced to die by drinking what?
answer: Hemlock
choices: Hemlock
Wine and opium
Belladonna
Wormwood
context: He could have escaped — Crito had bribed the guards. He refused. Plato's Phaedo records his final hours discussing the soul.

question: Told that whoever untied the Gordian Knot would rule Asia, Alexander the Great solved it how?
answer: Cut it with his sword
choices: Cut it with his sword
Wove it tighter then cut
Burned the rope
Soaked it in oil
context: Phrygia, 333 BC. The oracle's prophecy had stood for centuries. Alexander conquered the Persian Empire within four years.

question: Leaping from his bath shouting 'Eureka!', Archimedes had discovered the principle of:
answer: Displacement
choices: Displacement
Magnetism
Refraction
Capillary action
context: King Hiero had asked whether a goldsmith cheated him. Archimedes' bath solved it — and founded fluid statics.

question: Drawing circles in the sand at the fall of Syracuse in 212 BC, Archimedes was killed by:
answer: A Roman soldier
choices: A Roman soldier
A falling column
An assassin's arrow
Plague
context: 'Do not disturb my circles' is his alleged last line. General Marcellus had ordered him spared.

question: Around 240 BC, Eratosthenes measured the Earth's circumference using shadows in two Egyptian cities. He was off by what?
answer: Less than 2%
choices: Less than 2%
About 25%
Nearly half
An order of magnitude
context: He compared shadow angles at Syene and Alexandria. Library of Alexandria's chief librarian — a polymath called 'Beta' for second-best at everything.

question: Legend says Pythagoreans drowned one of their own, Hippasus, for revealing what mathematical scandal?
answer: Irrational numbers
choices: Irrational numbers
The fifth element
A divine ratio
The infinite series
context: Their cult held that all was rational ratio. The square root of 2, which could not be written as a fraction, broke the doctrine.

question: The Greek writer who traveled the known world recording stories of Persia, Egypt and Scythia is called the father of:
answer: History
choices: History
Geography
Anthropology
Biography
context: 5th-century BC. His Histories explained the Persian Wars. Cicero gave him the title; later critics also called him the father of lies.

question: Plato founded a school in a grove outside Athens that gave its name to all later schools. What was it called?
answer: The Academy
choices: The Academy
The Lyceum
The Stoa
The Garden
context: Founded c. 387 BC near the shrine of Akademos. It ran for nine centuries until Justinian closed it in 529 AD.

question: From 343 BC, Aristotle personally tutored which future world-conqueror at the Macedonian court?
answer: Alexander the Great
choices: Alexander the Great
Pyrrhus of Epirus
Antiochus III
Ptolemy I
context: King Philip II hired him. Alexander reportedly slept with Homer and a dagger under his pillow — Aristotle's edition of the Iliad.

question: Stranded deep in Persia in 401 BC, 10,000 Greek mercenaries fought their way home. The march was recorded by:
answer: Xenophon
choices: Xenophon
Thucydides
Polybius
Plutarch
context: His Anabasis tells the march. 'Thalassa! Thalassa!' the troops cried — 'The sea! The sea!' — when they reached the Black Sea.

question: The Greek poet credited with the Iliad and the Odyssey, composed orally and only later written down, is:
answer: Homer
choices: Homer
Hesiod
Pindar
Aeschylus
context: Probably 8th century BC. Whether one poet or many, the poems set the moral imagination of Greece — Achilles, Odysseus, Hector.

question: Greek physicians for over two millennia have sworn the medical oath named after which figure?
answer: Hippocrates
choices: Hippocrates
Galen
Asclepius
Praxagoras
context: Cos, 5th century BC. The oath bans abortion and euthanasia in its original form. 'First, do no harm' is its enduring summary.

question: Carrying a lantern through Athens in broad daylight, Diogenes the Cynic claimed to be searching for what?
answer: An honest man
choices: An honest man
The lost soul of Greece
Truth itself
A real philosopher
context: He lived in a barrel. Asked by Alexander the Great what he wanted, he replied: 'Stand out of my sunlight.'

question: Made dictator of Rome in 458 BC to save the army, Cincinnatus resigned 16 days later and returned to:
answer: His plow
choices: His plow
His legal practice
His vineyard
The Senate floor
context: Two terms as dictator, twice resigning. George Washington consciously echoed him — the Society of the Cincinnati is named in his honor.

question: In 218 BC, Hannibal crossed the Alps into Italy with what unusual cargo?
answer: War elephants
choices: War elephants
Greek fire
Captured eagles
Slingers from Crete
context: 37 elephants set out; few survived the crossing. He campaigned in Italy 16 years and never lost a major battle there.

question: At Cannae in 216 BC, Hannibal destroyed a Roman army of 86,000 using a tactic still studied today:
answer: Double envelopment
choices: Double envelopment
Oblique order
Refused flank
Phalanx square
context: A weak center bowed inward; the wings swung shut. Schlieffen's WWI plan and Norman Schwarzkopf's Desert Storm both cited it.

question: In 202 BC at Zama, Hannibal was finally defeated in Africa by which Roman general?
answer: Scipio Africanus
choices: Scipio Africanus
Fabius Maximus
Marcellus
Flamininus
context: Scipio had studied Hannibal's tactics for 16 years. He used Numidian cavalry — once Carthage's strength — to crush Carthage's army.

question: After the Third Punic War in 146 BC, Roman legend says Carthage was destroyed and its fields:
answer: Sown with salt
choices: Sown with salt
Burned to ash
Plowed under
Left to wolves
context: The salt legend is likely 19th-century invention; the destruction was real. Cato had ended every Senate speech: 'Carthago delenda est.'

question: The Thracian gladiator who led 70,000 escaped slaves against Rome in 73 BC was:
answer: Spartacus
choices: Spartacus
Vercingetorix
Arminius
Mithridates
context: He defeated nine Roman armies before Crassus cornered him. 6,000 captives were crucified along the Appian Way.

question: Crossing the Rubicon in 49 BC, Julius Caesar reportedly said:
answer: The die is cast
choices: The die is cast
Veni, vidi, vici
Et tu, Brute
Beware the Ides
context: 'Alea iacta est.' The Rubicon was the legal boundary into Italy proper. Crossing with his legion meant civil war.

question: On the Ides of March 44 BC, Julius Caesar was assassinated by senators in:
answer: The Theatre of Pompey
choices: The Theatre of Pompey
The Senate House
The Forum
His own villa
context: 23 wounds. Brutus among the killers. Caesar reportedly pulled his toga over his head when he saw him — Suetonius' account.

question: At Actium in 31 BC, Octavian's fleet crushed the navy of Antony and Cleopatra to end Rome's:
answer: Civil wars
choices: Civil wars
Punic Wars
Social War
Italian War
context: Cleopatra fled; Antony followed. Both later killed themselves in Egypt. Octavian became Augustus — Rome's first emperor.

question: After Actium, Octavian took a new name that meant 'revered' and became Rome's first:
answer: Emperor
choices: Emperor
Tribune
Censor
Pontifex Maximus
context: 27 BC: the Senate granted him the name Augustus. The Pax Romana — two centuries of peace — began with his reign.

question: Nero blamed which group for the Great Fire of Rome in 64 AD?
answer: Christians
choices: Christians
Jews
Gauls
Praetorian guards
context: Tacitus describes Christians wrapped in animal skins and torn apart, or burned as living torches. Peter and Paul probably died in the persecutions that followed.

question: The eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD buried Pompeii and killed which Roman naturalist?
answer: Pliny the Elder
choices: Pliny the Elder
Seneca the Younger
Tacitus the Annalist
Suetonius Tranquillus
context: He sailed toward the cloud to rescue people and to observe it. His nephew Pliny the Younger wrote the eyewitness letters that named the cloud type.

question: To mark the northern limit of Roman Britain, Emperor Hadrian built around 122 AD a:
answer: 73-mile stone wall
choices: 73-mile stone wall
Series of forts along the Thames
Fortified river barge fleet
Chain of signal towers
context: Garrisoned for nearly three centuries. Sections still stand in Northumberland. Hadrian's response to barbarian raids was containment, not conquest.

question: The Stoic emperor who wrote private philosophical notes to himself between 170 and 180 AD was:
answer: Marcus Aurelius
choices: Marcus Aurelius
Septimius Severus
Antoninus Pius
Trajan
context: The Meditations were never meant for publication. He campaigned against Germanic tribes on the Danube while writing them in Greek.

question: Before the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in 312 AD, Constantine reportedly saw a vision of:
answer: A cross in the sky
choices: A cross in the sky
An eagle with snakes
A flaming sword
A pillar of fire
context: 'In hoc signo vinces' — by this sign you will conquer. He won, became sole emperor, and legalized Christianity the next year by the Edict of Milan.

question: In 410 AD, the city of Rome itself was sacked for the first time in 800 years by:
answer: The Visigoths under Alaric
choices: The Visigoths under Alaric
The Huns under Attila
The Vandals under Gaiseric
The Ostrogoths under Theodoric
context: Jerome wept in Bethlehem when he heard. Augustine answered the pagan charge that Christianity caused it by writing The City of God.

question: The Hun warlord stopped at Chalons in 451 AD by Roman-Visigoth forces was:
answer: Attila
choices: Attila
Genseric
Alaric
Odoacer
context: Called 'the Scourge of God.' He turned back from Italy the next year after meeting Pope Leo I — legend gave Leo the credit.

question: The traditional date for the fall of the Western Roman Empire is 476 AD, when the Germanic chief Odoacer deposed:
answer: Romulus Augustulus
choices: Romulus Augustulus
Honorius
Valentinian III
Majorian
context: A boy emperor with the ironic name of Rome's founder and her first emperor. The Eastern Empire continued from Constantinople for 1,000 more years.

question: The Roman senator whose orations against Mark Antony got him executed in 43 BC was:
answer: Cicero
choices: Cicero
Cato the Younger
Brutus
Cassius
context: Antony had his head and hands nailed to the Senate rostra. His wife Fulvia stabbed his tongue with a hairpin. His letters survived to teach Latin to Europe.

question: Ordered by Nero in 65 AD to kill himself for an alleged plot, the Stoic philosopher who opened his veins was:
answer: Seneca
choices: Seneca
Epictetus
Lucan
Persius
context: His tutor turned victim. Tacitus describes him dictating to scribes as he bled. His Letters to Lucilius remain a Stoic foundation text.

question: Knocked from his horse on the road to Damascus around 34 AD by a blinding light, Saul of Tarsus became:
answer: The apostle Paul
choices: The apostle Paul
Mark the Evangelist
Stephen the Martyr
Barnabas of Cyprus
context: He had been hunting Christians. The vision turned the persecutor into the missionary who carried the gospel from Jerusalem to Rome.

question: The North African bishop who wrote the Confessions in 397 AD and later The City of God was:
answer: Augustine of Hippo
choices: Augustine of Hippo
Ambrose of Milan
Jerome of Bethlehem
John Chrysostom
context: Restless youth, Manichee, then a garden in Milan: 'Take up and read.' He became the most influential theologian in Western Christianity.

question: Around 530 AD, a monk at Monte Cassino wrote a rule for monastic life that shaped Western monasticism. He was:
answer: Benedict of Nursia
choices: Benedict of Nursia
Anthony of Egypt
Bernard of Clairvaux
Francis of Assisi
context: 'Ora et labora' — pray and work. Benedictine houses preserved manuscripts through the Dark Ages and seeded universities later.

question: The Byzantine emperor who codified Roman law in the 530s as the Corpus Juris Civilis was:
answer: Justinian
choices: Justinian
Heraclius
Basil II
Constantine V
context: His legal compilation is the root of European civil law. He also built the Hagia Sophia and tried to reconquer the Western Empire.

question: Built in Constantinople between 532 and 537 under Justinian, the great domed church was named:
answer: Hagia Sophia
choices: Hagia Sophia
Hagia Triada
Hagia Eirene
Saint Mark's
context: 'Holy Wisdom.' Justinian on first entering reportedly cried: 'Solomon, I have surpassed thee!' It became a mosque in 1453 and a museum in 1935.

question: At Tours in 732 AD, the Frankish leader who stopped the Muslim advance into Europe was:
answer: Charles Martel
choices: Charles Martel
Pepin the Short
Charlemagne
Clovis I
context: 'Martel' means hammer. His grandson Charlemagne built the empire that became the Holy Roman Empire. Gibbon saw Tours as Europe's hinge.

question: On Christmas Day 800 AD, Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne as:
answer: Emperor of the Romans
choices: Emperor of the Romans
King of Italy
Defender of the Faith
Vicar of Christ
context: Charlemagne claimed afterward he had not expected it. The act revived the Western imperial title and reshaped relations between papacy and crown.

question: In 793 AD, Viking raiders shocked Europe by attacking and looting the monastery on which English island?
answer: Lindisfarne
choices: Lindisfarne
Iona
Jarrow
Wearmouth
context: Alcuin wrote: 'Never before has such terror appeared in Britain.' The Viking Age had begun. Within a century Vikings ruled half of England.

question: In 1077, Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV stood barefoot in the snow for three days at Canossa to beg forgiveness from:
answer: Pope Gregory VII
choices: Pope Gregory VII
Pope Urban II
Pope Innocent III
Pope Leo IX
context: The Investiture Controversy. Henry had been excommunicated. Gregory absolved him — then the fight resumed and Henry drove Gregory into exile.

question: The First Crusade, called by Pope Urban II at Clermont in 1095, captured Jerusalem in:
context: Three years of marching, plague, and battle. The crusaders massacred Jerusalem's Muslim and Jewish defenders. The Crusader Kingdom lasted 88 years.

question: Jerusalem was retaken by Muslim forces in 1187 by the Kurdish-born sultan:
answer: Saladin
choices: Saladin
Baibars
Suleiman
Mehmed II
context: At the Battle of Hattin he destroyed the Crusader army. Even his Christian enemies praised his chivalry. Dante placed him in Limbo with the virtuous pagans.

question: On a meadow at Runnymede in 1215, King John of England was forced by his barons to seal:
answer: Magna Carta
choices: Magna Carta
The Forest Charter
The Provisions
The Settlement Act
context: Article 39: no free man imprisoned 'except by lawful judgment of his peers.' The seed of due process. John repudiated it within months but died the next year.

question: The 13th-century Dominican friar who synthesized Aristotle with Christian theology in the Summa Theologica was:
answer: Thomas Aquinas
choices: Thomas Aquinas
Bonaventure
Duns Scotus
Albertus Magnus
context: Called 'the Dumb Ox' as a student for his silent bulk. Late in life he stopped writing after a mystical experience: 'All I have written seems like straw.'

question: The Florentine poet who in exile wrote The Divine Comedy, taking readers through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise, was:
answer: Dante Alighieri
choices: Dante Alighieri
Francesco Petrarch
Giovanni Boccaccio
Torquato Tasso
context: Banished from Florence 1302; never returned. He placed his enemies in Hell. The Comedy founded modern Italian literature.

question: Arriving in Europe in 1347 on Genoese ships from Crimea, the bubonic plague killed roughly what share of Europe?
answer: One-third
choices: One-third
One-tenth
One-half
Three-quarters
context: 25-30 million dead in four years. Boccaccio set the Decameron in plague-time Florence. Wages rose; serfdom weakened; the medieval world cracked.

question: In 1429, a 17-year-old French peasant girl lifted the English siege of Orleans claiming heavenly voices. She was:
answer: Joan of Arc
choices: Joan of Arc
Catherine of Siena
Hildegard of Bingen
Margery Kempe
context: She crowned Charles VII at Reims, was captured, sold to the English, and burned for heresy at Rouen in 1431. Canonized 1920.

question: Around 1450 in Mainz, the German goldsmith who developed movable-type printing was:
answer: Johannes Gutenberg
choices: Johannes Gutenberg
William Caxton
Aldus Manutius
Christophe Plantin
context: His 42-line Bible is the era's masterpiece. Movable type made Luther's Reformation possible 70 years later — and the Scientific Revolution after that.

question: Constantinople fell in 1453 to Ottoman cannon under which sultan?
answer: Mehmed II
choices: Mehmed II
Suleiman I
Selim I
Bayezid II
context: His giant Orban cannon battered the Theodosian walls. Emperor Constantine XI died in the breach. A 1,000-year empire ended; Greek scholars fled to Italy.

question: The 14th-century English poet who wrote the Canterbury Tales, a portrait of medieval pilgrims, was:
answer: Geoffrey Chaucer
choices: Geoffrey Chaucer
John Gower
William Langland
Thomas Malory
context: Customs officer, diplomat, poet. The tales — left unfinished at his death in 1400 — fixed Middle English as a literary language.

question: The 15th-century Florentine banking dynasty that funded Brunelleschi, Donatello, Botticelli and Michelangelo was the:
answer: Medici
choices: Medici
Strozzi
Pazzi
Acciaiuoli
context: Cosimo and his grandson Lorenzo the Magnificent ran the city. Three Medici became popes. The bank financed half of Europe before it collapsed.

question: The 1436 dome of Florence Cathedral, then the largest since antiquity, was engineered by:
answer: Filippo Brunelleschi
choices: Filippo Brunelleschi
Leon Battista Alberti
Andrea del Verrocchio
Lorenzo Ghiberti
context: 138 feet across, built without flying buttresses. He invented the herringbone brick pattern and a hoisting machine for it.

question: The Renaissance polymath whose notebooks contained flying machines, anatomical studies and the Mona Lisa was:
answer: Leonardo da Vinci
choices: Leonardo da Vinci
Albrecht Durer
Raphael
Andrea Mantegna
context: Left-handed mirror writing. Patron-hopped from Milan to Florence to France. He carried the Mona Lisa with him until he died at Francis I's court in 1519.

question: Between 1508 and 1512, Michelangelo painted the ceiling of which papal chapel for Julius II?
answer: The Sistine Chapel
choices: The Sistine Chapel
Saint Peter's Basilica
Santa Maria del Fiore
San Giovanni in Laterano
context: He worked lying on scaffolding. He insisted he was a sculptor, not a painter. Twenty years later he returned to paint the Last Judgment on the altar wall.

question: The 1511 Vatican fresco depicting Plato and Aristotle surrounded by philosophers was painted by:
answer: Raphael
choices: Raphael
Michelangelo
Botticelli
Titian
context: He included Leonardo as Plato, Michelangelo brooding on the steps as Heraclitus, and himself in the corner. Raphael died at 37 on Good Friday 1520.

question: The Florentine diplomat who in 1513, exiled and tortured, wrote a manual on power for the Medici was:
answer: Niccolo Machiavelli
choices: Niccolo Machiavelli
Francesco Guicciardini
Baldassare Castiglione
Pico della Mirandola
context: The Prince urges effectiveness over piety. The book got him no Medici job. It became one of the most influential — and feared — political texts ever written.

question: On October 12, 1492, Christopher Columbus made landfall on a Caribbean island sponsored by:
answer: Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain
choices: Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain
John II of Portugal
Henry VII of England
Charles VIII of France
context: He died believing he had reached the Indies. His four voyages opened the Columbian Exchange — and the conquest of the Americas.

question: The Portuguese captain who sailed for Spain and led the first circumnavigation, dying in the Philippines in 1521, was:
answer: Ferdinand Magellan
choices: Ferdinand Magellan
Vasco da Gama
Juan Sebastian Elcano
Bartolomeu Dias
context: Killed by Lapu-Lapu's men on Mactan. Elcano brought one ship home in 1522 — 18 men of the original 270. They had proved the world was round and far larger than imagined.

question: The Spanish conquistador who toppled the Aztec empire of Montezuma II by 1521 was:
answer: Hernan Cortes
choices: Hernan Cortes
Francisco Pizarro
Vasco Nunez de Balboa
Pedro de Alvarado
context: He burned his ships at Veracruz. Smallpox killed more Aztecs than Spanish steel did. Tenochtitlan became Mexico City.

question: The Spanish conquistador who captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa and toppled Peru by 1533 was:
answer: Francisco Pizarro
choices: Francisco Pizarro
Hernan Cortes
Pedro de Valdivia
Diego de Almagro
context: 168 Spaniards seized an empire of millions. Atahualpa filled a room with gold for ransom; Pizarro garroted him anyway.

question: On October 31, 1517, the German monk who nailed 95 theses to a Wittenberg church door was:
answer: Martin Luther
choices: Martin Luther
Philip Melanchthon
Ulrich Zwingli
Andreas Karlstadt
context: The protest was against indulgences. Within five years Tetzel was disgraced, Luther was outlawed, and the Reformation had split Christendom.

question: At the Diet of Worms in 1521, ordered to recant, Luther reportedly answered:
answer: Here I stand, I can do no other
choices: Here I stand, I can do no other
I appeal to a free council
God forgive me, Amen
Do with me what you will
context: He left under safe-conduct; Frederick the Wise then 'kidnapped' him to Wartburg Castle, where he translated the New Testament into German in eleven weeks.

question: In 1534, an English king broke with Rome to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon. He was:
answer: Henry VIII
choices: Henry VIII
Henry VII
Edward VI
James I
context: Six wives: divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived. He kept the doctrine Catholic but the church English — and seized the monasteries.

question: The Frenchman who turned Geneva into a Protestant city-state in the 1540s, teaching predestination, was:
answer: John Calvin
choices: John Calvin
Theodore Beza
John Knox
Heinrich Bullinger
context: His Institutes of the Christian Religion became Reformed theology's foundation. Knox carried it to Scotland; Puritans carried it to New England.

question: Wounded by a cannonball in 1521 and converted during recovery, the Spanish soldier who founded the Jesuits in 1540 was:
answer: Ignatius of Loyola
choices: Ignatius of Loyola
Francis Xavier
Robert Bellarmine
Peter Canisius
context: His Spiritual Exercises trained the order. Within a century Jesuits were teaching in Lima, Beijing and Goa. They became the Counter-Reformation's vanguard.

question: Refusing to acknowledge Henry VIII as head of the Church of England, the author of Utopia was beheaded in 1535. He was:
answer: Thomas More
choices: Thomas More
Cardinal Wolsey
Thomas Cromwell
John Fisher
context: 'The king's good servant, but God's first.' Erasmus' close friend. Canonized in 1935. His daughter Margaret recovered his head from London Bridge.

question: The 1588 Spanish Armada sent against England by Philip II was defeated under Queen:
answer: Elizabeth I
choices: Elizabeth I
Mary I
Anne
Victoria
context: Drake harried them in the Channel. A 'Protestant wind' wrecked the rest off Scotland and Ireland. Elizabeth at Tilbury: 'I have the heart and stomach of a king.'

question: The 1648 treaty that ended the Thirty Years War and established state sovereignty as a principle was the Peace of:
answer: Westphalia
choices: Westphalia
Augsburg
Utrecht
Vienna
context: Germany lost 4-8 million dead. The treaty fixed cuius regio, eius religio and is taken as the birth of the modern state system.

question: In January 1649, an English king was tried, convicted of treason and beheaded on a scaffold at Whitehall. He was:
answer: Charles I
choices: Charles I
Charles II
James I
James II
context: The only English monarch ever executed. Cromwell signed the warrant. 'I go from a corruptible to an incorruptible Crown,' Charles said. Eleven years of republic followed.

question: The 1688 Glorious Revolution placed William of Orange and his wife on the English throne in place of:
answer: James II
choices: James II
Charles II
James I
Edward VI
context: James fled to France. Parliament invited William and Mary on terms set out in the 1689 Bill of Rights — limited monarchy, parliamentary supremacy, no Catholic king.

question: Published on his deathbed in 1543, the work proposing a sun-centered solar system was written by:
answer: Nicolaus Copernicus
choices: Nicolaus Copernicus
Tycho Brahe
Johannes Kepler
Galileo Galilei
context: De Revolutionibus Orbium Coelestium. He delayed publication for decades, fearing church reaction. Legend says he saw the printed book the day he died.

question: Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe lost the bridge of his nose in 1566 in a duel with a fellow student over what?
answer: A mathematics dispute
choices: A mathematics dispute
A woman
A political quarrel
A horse race
context: He wore a metal nose for the rest of his life. He built the observatory Uraniborg on the island of Hven and produced the era's most precise observations.

question: The three laws of planetary motion — ellipses, equal areas, harmonics — were formulated by:
answer: Johannes Kepler
choices: Johannes Kepler
Tycho Brahe
Galileo
Newton
context: He used Tycho's data on Mars. The ellipse law overthrew 2,000 years of circular-orbit cosmology. He also defended his mother in her witch trial.

question: In 1610 Galileo used his telescope to discover four moons orbiting which planet?
answer: Jupiter
choices: Jupiter
Saturn
Mars
Venus
context: Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto — the Galilean moons. The discovery proved that not everything orbits Earth. He named them for Medici patrons.

question: In 1633 the Roman Inquisition forced Galileo to recant the claim that:
answer: The Earth moves around the Sun
choices: The Earth moves around the Sun
The universe is infinite
Comets are not omens
Tides come from the moon
context: He spent his last nine years under house arrest near Florence. Legend has him muttering 'Eppur si muove' — and yet it moves. He went blind before he died in 1642.

question: The French philosopher who in 1637 reasoned his way to 'I think, therefore I am' was:
answer: Rene Descartes
choices: Rene Descartes
Blaise Pascal
Pierre Gassendi
Nicolas Malebranche
context: Cogito ergo sum. He set Western philosophy on its modern footing. He died in Stockholm in 1650 — Queen Christina insisted on 5 AM lessons in the cold.

question: The 1687 work setting out three laws of motion and universal gravitation was the Principia of:
answer: Isaac Newton
choices: Isaac Newton
Edmond Halley
Robert Hooke
Christiaan Huygens
context: Halley paid for printing. The book unified earth and sky under one mathematics. Newton later ran the Royal Mint and hanged counterfeiters.

question: Sheltering from plague at Woolsthorpe in 1666, Newton famously watched what fall?
answer: An apple
choices: An apple
A plum
A pear
A walnut
context: Voltaire heard the story from Newton's niece. Whether literal or polished, the 'plague years' were when he formulated gravity, calculus and optics.

question: Locked in a calculus priority dispute with Newton, the German polymath who died in 1716 with only his secretary at the funeral was:
answer: Gottfried Leibniz
choices: Gottfried Leibniz
Christian Wolff
Samuel Pufendorf
Christian Thomasius
context: His notation — dx, dy, the integral sign — is the one mathematicians still use. Newton's faction had hounded him out of favor.

question: The Anglo-Irish scientist whose 1661 Sceptical Chymist helped found modern chemistry was:
answer: Robert Boyle
choices: Robert Boyle
Isaac Newton
Joseph Priestley
John Dalton
context: He attacked alchemical 'elements' and demanded experimental method. Boyle's law on gas volume and pressure followed in 1662.

question: The English physician who in 1628 demonstrated that blood circulates through the body was:
answer: William Harvey
choices: William Harvey
Andreas Vesalius
Michael Servetus
Marcello Malpighi
context: His De Motu Cordis ended 1,400 years of Galen's theory. His practice shrank — many thought him mad — but the proofs stood.

question: The French prodigy who in 1642, aged 19, built a mechanical adding machine for his tax-collector father was:
answer: Blaise Pascal
choices: Blaise Pascal
Rene Descartes
Pierre de Fermat
Christiaan Huygens

context: He escaped; British Major John Andre, his contact, was hanged as a spy. Arnold's name in America became synonymous with traitor. He died in London in 1801.

Boston

Edmund Randolph

context: He was 36 — the most prepared man in the room. The notes weren't published until after his death in 1836. He later co-wrote The Federalist and the Bill of Rights.

Court testimony

George Mason
John Hancock
context: Published under the pen name 'Publius.' Hamilton wrote 51, Madison 29, Jay 5. They remain the most influential commentary on the American constitutional order.

Washington DC

context: Their feud over a national bank, a national debt, and France versus Britain split American politics into the first parties: Federalists and Democratic-Republicans.

Western state admission
Commerce with Britain

Quasi-War Plot
context: American slogan: 'Millions for defense but not one cent for tribute.' President John Adams kept the country out of full war with France, costing him the 1800 election.

context: It was decided in the House on the 36th ballot after Aaron Burr refused to concede. Adams left Washington at dawn rather than attend Jefferson's inauguration.

choices: John Marshall

$150 million
$1.5 billion
context: Roughly 3 cents an acre. Jefferson worried it was unconstitutional but did it anyway. The deal doubled the country. Napoleon needed money for European war.

answer: William Clark

John Colter
Stephen Long
context: Their Shoshone guide and translator was Sacagawea. They covered 8,000 miles. Lewis died mysteriously on the Natchez Trace in 1809 — likely suicide.

choices: James Madison
Thomas Jefferson
John Quincy Adams
James Monroe
context: Impressment of US sailors, British support for tribes, war hawks in Congress. The war ended in a draw at the Treaty of Ghent — but launched Jackson, Harrison and a stronger national identity.

answer: George Washington
choices: George Washington

John Adams
James Madison
context: Gilbert Stuart's Lansdowne portrait. She cut it from the frame as British soldiers approached. The White House, Capitol and Treasury all burned. A hurricane the next day damaged the British.

Andrew Jackson
Henry Clay
Daniel Webster
context: He watched from a British ship. The flag still flew at dawn. The poem was set to a British drinking song. It became the national anthem only in 1931.

The British had captured Washington
Florida had been ceded
Texas had revolted
context: Treaty of Ghent: December 24, 1814. News was crossing the Atlantic. Jackson lost 71 men; the British 2,000. The victory made him a national hero.

question: The 1823 doctrine warning European powers against further colonization in the Americas was articulated by President:
answer: James Monroe

James Madison
John Quincy Adams
Andrew Jackson
context: His Secretary of State John Quincy Adams wrote most of it. Britain quietly supported it with the Royal Navy. The doctrine guided US foreign policy for over a century.

The Mason-Dixon line
The Ohio River
context: Henry Clay's deal. Jefferson called it 'a fire bell in the night.' The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 repealed it and helped trigger the Civil War.

answer: John Quincy Adams

Henry Clay
William Crawford
Daniel Webster
context: Jackson believed his wife Rachel was killed by election slander. He took office in grief. His inaugural mob nearly destroyed the White House.

question: The forced 1838 removal of the Cherokee Nation along which thousands died is called the:

choices: Trail of Tears
Long Walk
Long March
Removal Road
context: Roughly 4,000 dead of about 16,000 marched. Authorized by Jackson's 1830 Indian Removal Act; Chief Justice Marshall had ruled against it; Jackson reportedly said: 'Let him enforce it.'

answer: Santa Anna's Mexican army
choices: Santa Anna's Mexican army
Comanche raiders
Apache war bands
Texas Rangers in mutiny
context: 187 defenders, no survivors among the fighting men. Travis drew a line in the sand. Six weeks later Sam Houston defeated Santa Anna at San Jacinto, shouting 'Remember the Alamo!'

question: The 1840s phrase 'manifest destiny,' justifying westward expansion, was coined by journalist:
answer: John O'Sullivan
choices: John O'Sullivan
Horace Greeley
Frederick Douglass
James Gordon Bennett
context: 1845. He argued it was America's destiny 'to overspread the continent.' The phrase rationalized the Mexican War and the seizure of California and the Southwest.

Texas only, no more
Baja and Sonora coast

context: $15 million paid. Future Civil War officers — Grant, Lee, Sherman, Jackson — learned their trade. Grant later called it 'the most unjust war ever waged.'

answer: American River
choices: American River

San Joaquin River
Yuba River
context: James Marshall found gold flakes. Within a year 80,000 'forty-niners' poured west. San Francisco grew from 1,000 to 25,000 in two years. California became a state in 1850.

context: Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott organized it. Frederick Douglass attended and supported the demand for women's suffrage. It took 72 more years for the 19th Amendment.

Plessy v. Ferguson

Ableman v. Booth
context: Chief Justice Roger Taney wrote the opinion. It struck down the Missouri Compromise. Lincoln campaigned against it. The 13th and 14th Amendments overturned it after the war.

Henry Ward Beecher

James Buchanan
John Breckinridge

context: Four candidates, sectional split. He took no Southern state. Within weeks of his election, South Carolina seceded. Six more states followed before he took office.

Antietam
Murfreesboro

Ypres
context: Paris taxis ferried French reserves to the front. Joffre committed everything. The Schlieffen Plan failed; both sides dug trenches; the Western Front would not move much for four years.

question: In August 1914, German generals Hindenburg and Ludendorff destroyed two Russian armies in East Prussia at:
answer: Tannenberg
choices: Tannenberg
Masurian Lakes
Gumbinnen
Lodz
context: The Russian general Samsonov shot himself in the woods. 92,000 prisoners taken. Hindenburg would later be a Field Marshal, then president of Weimar Germany.

question: Winston Churchill's failed 1915 attempt to seize the Dardanelles ended in evacuation from:
answer: Gallipoli
choices: Gallipoli
Salonika
Smyrna
Lemnos
context: ANZAC troops — Australians and New Zealanders — fought their own war. 130,000 dead on both sides. Mustafa Kemal Ataturk made his name defending the heights. Churchill resigned.

question: From February to December 1916, the longest battle of WWI was at the French fortress of:
answer: Verdun
choices: Verdun
Reims
Belfort
Toul
context: Petain coined 'They shall not pass.' About 700,000 casualties on both sides. The forts were ground to powder; many remains were never recovered.

question: On July 1, 1916, the British suffered roughly 57,000 casualties — the bloodiest day in their army's history — on the:
answer: Somme
choices: Somme
Aisne
Marne
Yser
context: 20,000 dead. Walking pace, full pack, into machine guns. The five-month battle gained six miles. The 'Pals' battalions — friends from one town — were wiped out.

question: The 1917 battle of mud and slaughter near Ypres is also called by what name?
answer: Passchendaele
choices: Passchendaele
Cambrai
Caporetto
Vimy
context: Heavy rain turned shell-cratered ground to liquid. Men drowned in mud. About 500,000 casualties total for a village barely captured.

question: In May-June 1940, 338,000 Allied soldiers escaped from northern France via small boats from:
answer: Dunkirk
choices: Dunkirk
Calais
Boulogne
Cherbourg
context: Operation Dynamo. Churchill called it 'a miracle of deliverance.' The British army was saved; equipment was lost. Hitler had paused his panzers, a decision still debated.

question: From July to October 1940, the RAF defeated Goering's Luftwaffe in the Battle of:
answer: Britain
choices: Britain
Kent
London
the Channel
context: Churchill: 'Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few.' Spitfires and Hurricanes broke the air assault. Invasion was postponed indefinitely.

question: In October-November 1942, Montgomery defeated Rommel in Egypt at the second battle of:
answer: El Alamein
choices: El Alamein
Tobruk
Gazala
Mersa Matruh
context: Churchill called it 'the end of the beginning.' German tanks ran out of fuel. The Afrika Korps' long retreat ended six months later in Tunisia with surrender.

question: The German Sixth Army surrendered in February 1943 at which Soviet city on the Volga?
answer: Stalingrad
choices: Stalingrad
Voronezh
Saratov
Astrakhan
context: Five months of street fighting. About 1 million Soviet casualties; 91,000 German prisoners taken. Field Marshal Paulus surrendered. Of his men, fewer than 6,000 ever returned home.

question: The largest tank battle in history was fought in July 1943 between Germans and Soviets at:
answer: Kursk
choices: Kursk
Belgorod
Orel
Voronezh
context: Six thousand tanks engaged. Hitler had delayed for new Tiger and Panther production. The Soviets dug in 25 miles deep. The Wehrmacht never mounted a strategic offensive in the east again.

question: In June 1942, US carrier aircraft sank four Japanese fleet carriers in roughly six minutes at:
answer: Midway
choices: Midway
Coral Sea
Santa Cruz
Eastern Solomons
context: Codebreakers had read Japanese plans. Dive bombers caught the carriers refueling planes on deck. The Pacific War turned on a single morning.

question: Beginning in August 1942, the first US ground offensive in the Pacific was on which Solomon island?
answer: Guadalcanal
choices: Guadalcanal
Tulagi
Bougainville
New Britain
context: Six months of land, sea and air fighting. Henderson Field was the prize. The Marines coined 'Tokyo Express' and 'Iron Bottom Sound.' Japan finally evacuated in February 1943.

question: The June 6, 1944 D-Day landings hit five beaches on the coast of:
answer: Normandy
choices: Normandy
Brittany
Calais
Picardy
context: Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno, Sword. Omaha nearly failed. About 4,400 Allied dead on the first day. Within two months Paris was liberated.

question: The June 1944 Soviet offensive that destroyed Army Group Center on the Eastern Front was named for which Russian hero?
answer: General Bagration
choices: General Bagration
Marshal Kutuzov
Admiral Ushakov
General Suvorov
context: Stalin timed it for D-Day. 17 German divisions annihilated, 50,000 prisoners marched through Moscow. The Wehrmacht's worst defeat of the war.

question: In September 1944, Montgomery's airborne attempt to leap the Rhine ended in failure at the Dutch town of:
answer: Arnhem
choices: Arnhem
Eindhoven
Nijmegen
Wesel
context: 'A bridge too far.' British paratroopers expected light resistance; SS panzer divisions were refitting nearby. About 8,000 lost. The war went on into 1945.

question: In December 1944, the 101st Airborne held a Belgian crossroads town in the Battle of the Bulge. The town was:
answer: Bastogne
choices: Bastogne
Malmedy
Sankt Vith
Houffalize
context: Surrounded. Asked to surrender, General McAuliffe replied: 'Nuts!' Patton's Third Army turned 90 degrees and broke through within a week.

question: From February to March 1945, US Marines took an eight-square-mile Pacific island at the cost of nearly 7,000 dead. It was:
answer: Iwo Jima
choices: Iwo Jima
Okinawa
Tarawa
Peleliu
context: 26,000 American casualties; over 18,000 Japanese dead. Mount Suribachi's flag-raising photo by Joe Rosenthal became the era's icon. Three of the six men in the picture died on Iwo.

question: The largest amphibious operation of the Pacific War, April-June 1945, was on the island of:
answer: Okinawa
choices: Okinawa
Iwo Jima
Saipan
Luzon
context: About 12,000 American dead, 100,000 Japanese, perhaps 100,000 civilians. Kamikazes sank or damaged hundreds of ships. The toll shaped Truman's decision on the atom bombs.

question: In September 1950, MacArthur's amphibious landing far behind North Korean lines was at the port of:
answer: Inchon
choices: Inchon
Pusan
Wonsan
Hungnam
context: Tides at Inchon are among the world's most extreme. Most planners said impossible. MacArthur insisted; the landing cut off the North Korean army. Seoul was retaken within two weeks.

question: In late 1950, US Marines fought their way out of a Chinese encirclement at the:
answer: Chosin Reservoir
choices: Chosin Reservoir
Yalu River
Imjin River
Heartbreak Ridge
context: 30 below zero. 30,000 men against ten Chinese divisions. 'We are not retreating — we are advancing in a different direction.' One of the legendary Marine actions.

question: The 1954 defeat that ended French Indochina was at the besieged valley of:
answer: Dien Bien Phu
choices: Dien Bien Phu
Lang Son Pass
Cao Bang Pass
Na San Camp
context: Vo Nguyen Giap dragged artillery up the surrounding hills. The French parachute reinforcements were thrown into a closing trap. The Geneva Conference followed; America inherited the war.

question: In June 1967, Israel destroyed the air forces of Egypt, Jordan and Syria — and tripled in size — in a war lasting:
answer: Six days
choices: Six days
Sixty days
Six weeks
Six months
context: Pre-emptive strike at dawn on June 5. Gaza, Sinai, West Bank, Golan all taken. The Old City of Jerusalem reunited under Israeli control for the first time in 19 centuries.

question: On October 6, 1973, Egypt and Syria launched a surprise attack against Israel on the Jewish high holiday of:
answer: Yom Kippur
choices: Yom Kippur
Passover
Rosh Hashanah
Sukkot
context: Israel reeled, then counter-attacked. Sharon crossed the Suez Canal. A ceasefire under US and Soviet pressure stopped it. The war led to the 1978 Camp David peace.

question: In 1982, Margaret Thatcher dispatched a naval task force 8,000 miles south to retake the:
answer: Falkland Islands
choices: Falkland Islands
South Georgia
Tristan da Cunha
Ascension Island
context: Argentina had invaded April 2. British forces retook the capital Port Stanley on June 14. About 900 dead total. The war saved Thatcher's premiership and toppled Argentina's junta.

question: The 1991 Desert Storm ground campaign liberated Kuwait from Iraq in roughly:
answer: 100 hours
choices: 100 hours
100 days
10 days
10 hours
context: Schwarzkopf's 'left hook' through the desert avoided the dug-in Iraqi defenses. Coalition fatalities were under 300. Saddam remained in power for another 12 years.

question: On October 3-4, 1993, an American raid in the Somali capital of Mogadishu ended in 18 dead Rangers and Delta operators. The book by Mark Bowden is titled:
answer: Black Hawk Down
choices: Black Hawk Down
Path of the Warrior
The Long Night
Day of Battle
context: Two US helicopters shot down. Pilot Mike Durant captured and later released. The Clinton administration soon pulled out of Somalia. The episode shaped a generation of US policy.

question: The 2004 US Marine assault on insurgent-held streets of Iraq was at:
answer: Fallujah
choices: Fallujah
Mosul
Tikrit
Najaf
context: The April and November battles were two of the heaviest Marine actions since Hue 1968. Hundreds of US dead and wounded. The Anbar Awakening followed in 2007.

question: In December 2001, US-led forces nearly cornered Osama bin Laden in mountains of eastern Afghanistan at:
answer: Tora Bora
choices: Tora Bora
Kandahar
Mazar-i-Sharif
Khost
context: Reliance on Afghan tribal forces let him slip into Pakistan. He was killed there a decade later by SEAL Team Six. Tora Bora became a watchword for missed chances.

question: The October 1777 surrender of British General Burgoyne at Saratoga is called the turning point of which war?
answer: The American Revolution
choices: The American Revolution
The French and Indian War
The War of 1812
Queen Anne's War
context: Burgoyne had marched south from Canada; Gates and Arnold trapped him. France soon allied openly with the Americans. Without it the Revolution might have starved.

question: At the surrender at Yorktown in 1781, British bands reportedly played a tune called:
answer: The World Turned Upside Down
choices: The World Turned Upside Down
The British Grenadiers' March
The Marlborough Field Tune
The Drum and Fife Recall
context: Anecdote may be apocryphal but captures the moment. Cornwallis claimed illness and sent O'Hara to give up his sword. Britain effectively quit the war.

question: The three-day Pennsylvania battle of July 1-3, 1863 — the turning point of the American Civil War in the East — was at:
answer: Gettysburg
choices: Gettysburg
Antietam
Chancellorsville
Fredericksburg
context: Meade in command only days; Lee invading the North. About 51,000 casualties. Pickett's Charge on day three ended any hope of Confederate victory in the East.

question: The 47-day siege that gave the Union control of the Mississippi River ended on July 4, 1863 with the surrender of:
answer: Vicksburg
choices: Vicksburg
Port Hudson
Memphis
Natchez
context: 30,000 Confederates capitulated. Grant's relentless campaign across Mississippi made his reputation. Lincoln finally had a general willing to win.

question: On April 9, 1865, Lee surrendered to Grant in the parlor of Wilmer McLean's home at:
answer: Appomattox Court House
choices: Appomattox Court House
Petersburg Junction
Sailor's Creek
Five Forks
context: McLean's previous home had been on the first Bull Run battlefield. He famously said the war 'began in my front yard and ended in my parlor.' Grant offered generous terms.

question: On September 20, 1792, French revolutionary armies stopped Prussia at the artillery duel of:
answer: Valmy
choices: Valmy
Jemappes
Fleurus
Hondschoote
context: Goethe witnessed it. 'Here and today begins a new era in the history of the world,' he said. The Republic was proclaimed the next day; Louis XVI's days were numbered.

question: The First Punic War (264-241 BC), Rome's first war with Carthage, was decided primarily on which element?
answer: On the sea
choices: On the sea
On Sicily's plains
In the Po valley
On Spain's coast
context: Rome had no fleet at the start. They built one from a captured Carthaginian ship as model, learning by doing. Sea power won the war. Sicily became Rome's first province.

question: The first major Civil War battle in July 1861, where Washington picnickers expected an easy Union win, was at:
answer: First Bull Run
choices: First Bull Run
Ball's Bluff
Wilson's Creek
Big Bethel
context: Confederate Thomas Jackson stood 'like a stone wall,' winning his nickname. Federal troops fled back to Washington. Both sides realized this would be a long war.

question: The bloodiest single day in American history — about 23,000 casualties — was September 17, 1862 at:
answer: Antietam
choices: Antietam
Gettysburg
Shiloh
Chickamauga
context: Lee's first invasion of the North stopped. McClellan failed to follow up. Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation five days later, changing the war's meaning.

question: In September 1863, Confederate Braxton Bragg won a costly tactical victory at the Tennessee creek of:
answer: Chickamauga
choices: Chickamauga
Stones River
Lookout Mountain
Missionary Ridge
context: George Thomas's stand prevented total Union rout. He earned the nickname 'Rock of Chickamauga.' Bragg failed to follow up; two months later he lost Chattanooga.

question: Beginning May 5, 1864, Grant's Overland Campaign opened with tangled woodland fighting in Virginia at the:
answer: Wilderness
choices: Wilderness
North Anna
Bethesda Church
Catharpin Run
context: Burning brush trapped many wounded. Unlike previous Union generals, Grant did not retreat after the bloody draw. He marched south and fought again at Spotsylvania.

question: Sherman's September 2, 1864 capture of which city probably saved Lincoln's reelection?
answer: Atlanta
choices: Atlanta
Charleston
Mobile
Wilmington
context: He telegraphed Lincoln: 'Atlanta is ours, and fairly won.' Northern despair turned to confidence within days. McClellan's peace platform collapsed.

question: The last major battle of the age of sail, fought in 1827 to help Greek independence, was at:
answer: Navarino
choices: Navarino
Lepanto
Trafalgar
Algeciras
context: British, French, and Russian fleets destroyed an Ottoman-Egyptian armada in a Greek bay. Greek independence followed. Ironsides and steam were already coming.

question: In September 1870, the Prussian capture of Napoleon III led to the end of the Second French Empire at:
answer: Sedan
choices: Sedan
Metz
Gravelotte
Worth
context: Helmuth von Moltke commanded. 100,000 French surrendered with their emperor. France went on to declare a republic; the Paris Commune followed. German unification was complete.

question: In April 1917, the Bolshevik leader Germany sent to Russia by sealed train to destabilize the war effort was:
answer: Vladimir Lenin
choices: Vladimir Lenin
Leon Trotsky
Lev Kamenev
Grigory Zinoviev
context: Ludendorff approved the move. Lenin arrived at the Finland Station and demanded 'all power to the Soviets.' Eight months later he seized power.

question: The Bolshevik seizure of power in Petrograd happened on what date in the Russian calendar?
answer: October 25, 1917
choices: October 25, 1917
March 8, 1917
November 7, 1918
December 25, 1922
context: Old-style October 25 = new-style November 7. Trotsky organized the coup; Lenin led it. The Winter Palace fell with little resistance. A century of communism began.

question: Lenin's secret police, founded in December 1917 under Felix Dzerzhinsky, was called the:
answer: Cheka
choices: Cheka
NKVD
KGB
GRU
context: Within months it was executing class enemies without trial. The model was set: every later Soviet security service descended from this body. Lenin called for terror; the Cheka delivered.

question: In August 1940, Stalin's agent Ramon Mercader killed Leon Trotsky in Mexico City with what weapon?
answer: An ice axe
choices: An ice axe
A pistol
A garrote
A knife
context: Mercader had infiltrated the household posing as a sympathizer. Trotsky lived a day after the blow. The murder ended Stalin's last major rival from the Revolution era.

question: Starting in 1929, Stalin's campaign to 'liquidate as a class' wealthier peasants targeted the:
answer: Kulaks
choices: Kulaks
Mensheviks
Nepmen
White Russians
context: Roughly 1.8 million deported, hundreds of thousands shot or starved. The word originally meant 'tight-fisted' peasant. Land was collectivized; agriculture collapsed.

question: The Soviet Ukrainian famine of 1932-1933 in which several million peasants starved is known as the:
answer: Holodomor
choices: Holodomor
Velvet Famine
Black Earth Hunger
Great Russian Famine
context: 3.5-7 million dead by serious estimates. Stalin's grain seizures plus sealed borders made it man-made. The word means 'death by hunger' in Ukrainian. Recognized as genocide by many states.

question: The New York Times Moscow correspondent who covered up the Holodomor and never had his Pulitzer revoked was:
answer: Walter Duranty
choices: Walter Duranty
Eugene Lyons
Louis Fischer
Anna Louise Strong
context: Gareth Jones reported the famine; Duranty called him a liar. The Pulitzer board has reviewed the matter twice and declined to revoke. The Times now describes his work as 'discredited.'

question: The Welsh journalist who in 1933 reported the truth of the Ukrainian famine — and was murdered two years later in Mongolia — was:
answer: Gareth Jones
choices: Gareth Jones
Malcolm Muggeridge
Eugene Lyons
Arthur Koestler
context: He had walked rural Ukraine. He named names. He was killed in 1935, possibly by the NKVD. A film, 'Mr. Jones,' was made in 2019. His Pulitzer-winning rival went on lying.

question: Stalin's 1936-1938 purges featured what kind of public proceedings against old Bolsheviks?
answer: Show trials
choices: Show trials
Closed tribunals
Truth commissions
Star chambers
context: Kamenev, Zinoviev, Bukharin: all 'confessed' under torture and threats to family, all shot. About 750,000 executed in 1937-38 alone. Even loyal NKVD chiefs were shot in turn.

question: In 1940 the NKVD murdered about 22,000 Polish officers, intellectuals and clergy in forests at:
answer: Katyn
choices: Katyn
Vinnitsa
Bykivnia
Kuropaty
context: Each victim shot in the back of the head. The Soviets blamed Germany until 1990. Russia has officially admitted it but resists calling it genocide.

question: On August 23, 1939, the foreign ministers who signed a non-aggression pact dividing Eastern Europe between Hitler and Stalin were:
answer: Ribbentrop and Molotov
choices: Ribbentrop and Molotov
Hess and Litvinov
Goering and Mikoyan
Neurath and Litvinov
context: Secret protocols carved up Poland, the Baltics, Romania. Stalin sent congratulatory telegrams. The pact lasted until Hitler invaded in June 1941.

question: From September 1941 to January 1944, the Soviet city besieged by Germany for 872 days was:
answer: Leningrad
choices: Leningrad
Stalingrad
Sevastopol
Murmansk
context: About a million civilians dead, mostly from starvation. Shostakovich composed his Seventh Symphony there. The ice road across Lake Ladoga was the only lifeline.

question: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn's three-volume documentation of the Soviet camp system, smuggled west in 1973, was titled:
answer: The Gulag Archipelago
choices: The Gulag Archipelago
Inside the First Circle
Cancer Ward
Letter to Soviet Leaders
context: Built from 227 prisoners' testimonies plus his own years. Roughly 18 million passed through; many died. The book exiled him in 1974. The Soviet edition could not appear until 1989.

question: Solzhenitsyn was first arrested in 1945 for what?
answer: Letters criticizing Stalin
choices: Letters criticizing Stalin
Religious activity
Counter-revolutionary agitation as a teen
Black-market trading
context: A captain on the front, he had written privately to a friend. Eight years in camps followed, then exile. He returned to Russia after the USSR fell, in 1994.

question: Khrushchev personally allowed the 1962 publication of which Solzhenitsyn novella set in a Stalin-era camp?
answer: One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich
choices: One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich
Matryona's House
The First Circle
An Incident at Krechetovka
context: A single day in the camps, in flat prose. Soviet readers were stunned. Brezhnev's regime later closed the window. The novella made Solzhenitsyn world-famous.

question: The Soviet H-bomb father who turned dissident and won the 1975 Nobel Peace Prize was:
answer: Andrei Sakharov
choices: Andrei Sakharov
Yuri Orlov
Anatoly Marchenko
Vladimir Bukovsky
context: He could not attend Oslo; his wife Yelena Bonner read his speech. He was exiled to Gorky from 1980 to 1986. Gorbachev personally invited him back. He served in the new parliament before dying in 1989.

question: The Soviet Jewish 'refusenik' who spent nine years in the Gulag, traded for spies in 1986, and later served in the Israeli cabinet was:
answer: Natan Sharansky
choices: Natan Sharansky
Anatoly Shcharansky alone
Yuli Edelstein
Edward Kuznetsov
context: Reagan and Thatcher made his case a Cold War symbol. He walked across the Glienicke Bridge to freedom in February 1986. He went on to write Fear No Evil.

question: The 1934-1935 retreat across China that established Mao Zedong's leadership of the Chinese Communist Party covered roughly:
answer: Six thousand miles
choices: Six thousand miles
Six hundred miles
Twenty thousand miles
Sixty thousand miles
context: About 86,000 began; perhaps 7,000 finished. Mao took control along the way at the Zunyi conference. The march entered communist mythology. The base at Yan'an survived to win the civil war.

question: On October 1, 1949 in Tiananmen Square, who proclaimed the People's Republic of China?
answer: Mao Zedong
choices: Mao Zedong
Zhou Enlai
Liu Shaoqi
Zhu De
context: Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists fled to Taiwan. Mao ruled 600 million people. He would launch the Great Leap and the Cultural Revolution in the next two decades.

question: Mao's 1950-1953 'land reform' campaign killed roughly how many Chinese landlords and 'class enemies'?
answer: About 1-2 million
choices: About 1-2 million
About 10,000
About 100,000
Tens of millions
context: Local 'speak bitterness' meetings condemned and killed. Mao himself estimated several million. It was a foretaste of larger horrors to come.

question: Mao's 1956-1957 campaign inviting criticism — and then punishing those who offered it — was the:
answer: Hundred Flowers Campaign
choices: Hundred Flowers Campaign
Great Leap Forward
Cultural Revolution
Four Cleanups
context: 'Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend.' Within months he reversed: 500,000 intellectuals labeled 'rightists' and persecuted in the Anti-Rightist Campaign.

question: Mao's 1958-1962 Great Leap Forward caused a famine that killed roughly:
answer: 30 to 45 million people
choices: 30 to 45 million people
Several hundred thousand
1 to 2 million
A few thousand only
context: Historian Frank Dikotter put the figure near 45 million. Backyard furnaces ruined steel. Quota lies starved the countryside. The worst famine in human history.

question: Mao's 'Four Pests' campaign exterminated rats, flies, mosquitoes — and which bird, leading to ecological collapse?
answer: Sparrows
choices: Sparrows
Crows
Pigeons
Magpies
context: Sparrows ate grain — so they were killed nationwide. Locust populations then exploded; harvests crashed. China had to import sparrows from the Soviet Union.

question: Mao's 1966-1976 campaign of mass purges, Red Guards and destruction of 'old culture' was the:
answer: Cultural Revolution
choices: Cultural Revolution
Great Proletarian Movement
Anti-Bourgeois Drive
Maoist Rectification
context: Up to 2 million dead, many tortured. Schools closed; intellectuals sent to farms. Ancient temples destroyed. Even Liu Shaoqi, the head of state, was tortured and left to die in prison.

question: Lin Biao's collection of Mao quotations, distributed by the billions during the Cultural Revolution, was the:
answer: Little Red Book
choices: Little Red Book
Yellow Compendium
Black Manual
White Almanac
context: Officially the Quotations from Chairman Mao. Estimated print runs of 4-5 billion. Lin himself was killed in 1971 fleeing China after an alleged coup attempt.

question: Henry Kissinger's secret July 1971 trip to Beijing prepared the way for Nixon's February 1972 visit to:
answer: Mao Zedong
choices: Mao Zedong
Deng Xiaoping
Zhou Enlai alone
Jiang Qing
context: Kissinger flew via Pakistan claiming illness. Nixon's visit split the Soviet Union from China and reshaped the Cold War. Mao met Nixon weeks before the dictator's last public year.

question: Within a month of Mao's 1976 death, four radicals including his wife Jiang Qing were arrested. They were the:
answer: Gang of Four
choices: Gang of Four
Shanghai Group
Beijing Five
Wuhan Faction
context: Jiang got a suspended death sentence; she hanged herself in 1991. Deng Xiaoping then opened China. The Cultural Revolution was officially called a catastrophe.

question: On June 4, 1989, the People's Liberation Army cleared protesters from which Beijing square?
answer: Tiananmen
choices: Tiananmen
Wangfujing
Xidan
Qianmen
context: Hundreds to thousands killed; exact toll still hidden. 'Tank Man' faced down a column of T-59s the next day. Deng Xiaoping had ordered the crackdown.

question: The June 5, 1989 photograph of a lone man standing before a column of tanks near Tiananmen Square is called:
answer: Tank Man
choices: Tank Man
Lone Stand
Last Citizen
Brave One
context: Multiple photographers got the shot. His identity has never been confirmed. Inside China the image is still censored. Outside, it became one of the icons of the late 20th century.

question: The Chinese dissident who co-authored Charter 08 and won the 2010 Nobel Peace Prize from a prison cell was:
answer: Liu Xiaobo
choices: Liu Xiaobo
Hu Jia
Wei Jingsheng
Wang Dan
context: He had been jailed in 1989 and again from 2009. The Nobel ceremony in Oslo featured an empty chair. He died in 2017 of liver cancer in state custody.

question: Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge took Phnom Penh in April 1975 and proclaimed which year as the start of history?
answer: Year Zero
choices: Year Zero
Year One
Liberation Year
People's Year
context: Cities emptied at gunpoint. Glasses or soft hands meant death. Up to 2 million died — roughly a quarter of the population — in less than four years. Vietnam invaded and ended the regime in 1979.

question: The Khmer Rouge interrogation prison in Phnom Penh, formerly a high school, was called:
answer: S-21 / Tuol Sleng
choices: S-21 / Tuol Sleng
Anlong Veng
Choeung Ek
Ta Mok
context: At least 14,000 prisoners passed through. Twelve known survivors. Detailed photographs were taken of each victim — the regime's bookkeeping became the evidence against it.

question: After 1975, roughly a million people fled communist Vietnam by sea, becoming known as the:
answer: Boat People
choices: Boat People
Sea Wanderers
Mekong Refugees
Coastal Fleers
context: Tens to hundreds of thousands died at sea or to pirates. Many reached refugee camps in Hong Kong, Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines. The exodus continued into the 1990s.

question: In October 1967, the Argentine revolutionary captured and executed by Bolivian troops was:
answer: Che Guevara
choices: Che Guevara
Camilo Cienfuegos
Tania Bunke
Regis Debray
context: He had tried to start a peasant revolt; the locals refused to join. He was shot in a schoolhouse. His diaries became a youth-rebellion bible — though the rebellion he led had killed thousands of Cubans.

question: After taking Havana in January 1959, Castro's forces executed political opponents at the firing-squad fortress of:
answer: La Cabana
choices: La Cabana
Moncada
Bay of Pigs
Camp Columbia
context: Che Guevara supervised many of the trials. Estimates run from hundreds to several thousand executed. Religious clergy, gay men, dissidents, and former allies all disappeared.

question: In 1980, Castro briefly opened a port through which 125,000 Cubans fled to Florida. The port was:
answer: Mariel
choices: Mariel
Cienfuegos
Santiago
Matanzas
context: Castro emptied prisons and mental hospitals into the boats. The crisis embarrassed Carter and helped Reagan win that fall. Many of the refugees became hard-working Americans.

question: The Venezuelan strongman whose 1999-2013 'Bolivarian Revolution' destroyed the country's oil-fed prosperity was:
answer: Hugo Chavez
choices: Hugo Chavez
Nicolas Maduro alone
Diosdado Cabello
Rafael Caldera
context: His successor Maduro pushed the country into hyperinflation and famine. By the late 2010s some 6 million Venezuelans had fled. The richest economy in South America had been broken.

question: The founder of North Korea, who ruled from 1948 to 1994 and built a hereditary dynasty, was:
answer: Kim Il-sung
choices: Kim Il-sung
Kim Jong-il
Kim Tu-bong
Choe Yong-gon
context: Soviet-installed. Triggered the Korean War in 1950. His grandson Kim Jong-un still rules. Estimates of camp inmates run between 100,000 and 200,000 in any given year.

question: The 1994-1998 famine in North Korea that killed perhaps 600,000 to 2.5 million was officially called the:
answer: Arduous March
choices: Arduous March
Great Hunger
Iron Path
Path of Suffering
context: Hidden from the outside world for years. Children were stunted in a generation. The state preserved missile and nuclear programs through the famine.

question: In 100 days in 1994, perhaps 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were murdered in:
answer: Rwanda
choices: Rwanda
Burundi
Congo
Uganda
context: Machetes were the main weapon. Radio Mille Collines incited it. UN peacekeepers stood down. Bill Clinton later said the failure to intervene was his deepest regret.

answer: House of Wisdom

Mosque of Cordoba
Library of Alexandria
Academy of Athens
context: Funded by Abbasid caliphs. Scholars translated Aristotle, Euclid and Ptolemy into Arabic. The texts later passed to medieval Europe via Spain and Sicily.

question: The 9th-century Persian mathematician who gave us the words 'algebra' and 'algorithm' was:
answer: Al-Khwarizmi
choices: Al-Khwarizmi
Al-Kindi
Al-Razi
Al-Battani
context: His book Al-Kitab al-Mukhtasar fi Hisab al-Jabr wa'l-Muqabala — 'The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing' — gave algebra its name. His Latinized name became 'algorithm.'

question: The 11th-century Persian polymath whose Canon of Medicine was a textbook in European universities for 600 years was:
answer: Ibn Sina (Avicenna)
choices: Ibn Sina (Avicenna)
Ibn Rushd (Averroes)
Al-Razi (Rhazes)
Al-Kindi
context: Born near Bukhara around 980. He memorized the Quran at 10 and Aristotle by 16. His Canon synthesized Greek and Islamic medicine. Latin translations were the standard text into the 1600s.

question: The 14th-century Moroccan traveler who covered some 75,000 miles from Spain to China was:
answer: Ibn Battuta
choices: Ibn Battuta
Ibn Khaldun
Ibn Jubayr
Al-Idrisi
context: 30 years on the road. His Rihla — Travels — describes the Islamic world at its medieval height. He served as a judge in the Maldives, traveled with the Mali emperor, met the Yuan court.

question: The 14th-century king of Mali whose 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca with gold caused inflation in Egypt for years was:
answer: Mansa Musa
choices: Mansa Musa
Sundiata Keita
Askia Muhammad
Sunni Ali
context: His caravan reportedly included 60,000 people and 12,000 slaves. Each carrying gold staffs. He gave away so much gold in Cairo that the Egyptian dinar lost value for a decade.

question: In 1187, Jerusalem was retaken from the Crusaders by the Kurdish-born sultan of Egypt and Syria:
answer: Saladin
choices: Saladin
Baibars
Nur ad-Din
Suleiman
context: He had crushed the Crusader army at Hattin three months earlier. He spared Jerusalem's Christians, in contrast to the 1099 sack. Even Dante put him in Limbo with the virtuous pagans.

question: The 16th-century Ottoman sultan called 'the Magnificent' in the West and 'the Lawgiver' at home was:
answer: Suleiman I
choices: Suleiman I
Selim I
Mehmed II
Murad III
context: Reigned 1520-1566. He took Belgrade, Rhodes, Buda; failed at Vienna 1529. He patronized the architect Sinan. His Russian-born wife Roxelana became the most powerful Ottoman woman in history.

question: The Mongols sacked which great Islamic capital in February 1258, killing the last Abbasid caliph?
answer: Baghdad
choices: Baghdad
Cairo
Damascus
Samarkand
context: Hulagu's army wrapped Caliph Al-Musta'sim in a carpet and trampled him to death by horses (so no royal blood touched the ground). The Tigris ran black with ink from destroyed libraries.

question: The 1923 founder of the modern Turkish Republic, who abolished the caliphate and switched the alphabet to Latin, was:
answer: Mustafa Kemal Ataturk
choices: Mustafa Kemal Ataturk
Ismet Inonu Pasha
Enver Pasha Sultan
Talaat Pasha Bey
context: Hero of Gallipoli. He banned the fez, gave women the vote, secularized education. The reforms turned Ottoman ruins into a modern state. Some Islamists still oppose his legacy.

question: On January 2, 1492, the last Muslim ruler of Granada surrendered the Alhambra to Ferdinand and Isabella. He was:
answer: Boabdil
choices: Boabdil
Yusuf IV
Ismail II
Hassan I
context: Also Muhammad XII. His mother reportedly told him: 'Weep like a woman for what you could not defend like a man.' Reconquista was complete. Columbus sailed the same year.

question: The 3rd-century BC Indian emperor who converted to Buddhism after seeing the carnage of his conquest of Kalinga was:
answer: Ashoka
choices: Ashoka
Chandragupta Maurya
Bindusara
Chandragupta II
context: His pillars carved with edicts of moral law stood across South Asia. He sent missionaries as far as Greece and Sri Lanka. The four-lion capital at Sarnath is India's national emblem.

question: The 5th-century Indian mathematician-astronomer who gave a clear value for pi and worked with the concept of zero was:
answer: Aryabhata
choices: Aryabhata
Brahmagupta
Bhaskara
Madhava
context: Around 499 AD, age 23. He calculated Earth's circumference, proposed it spins on its axis, and modeled eclipses. The Indian zero, transmitted via Arabs, became the modern numerals.

question: The 16th-century Mughal emperor famous for religious tolerance, public dialogues among faiths, and the Din-i-Ilahi was:
answer: Akbar the Great
choices: Akbar the Great
Babur the Tiger
Humayun II
Aurangzeb I
context: Reigned 1556-1605. He abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims, married Hindu princesses, invited Jesuits to court. His grandson Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal.

question: Built 1632-1653 in Agra as a tomb for the emperor's beloved wife Mumtaz, the Taj Mahal was commissioned by:
answer: Shah Jahan
choices: Shah Jahan
Akbar
Babur
Aurangzeb
context: She had died in childbirth. About 20,000 craftsmen worked on it. Shah Jahan was later deposed by his son Aurangzeb and imprisoned for eight years in the Red Fort, with a view of the Taj.

question: On June 23, 1757, the British East India Company victory that began British dominance in India was at:
answer: Plassey
choices: Plassey
Buxar
Wandiwash
Seringapatam
context: Robert Clive's 3,000 men defeated about 50,000 thanks largely to bribery — Mir Jafar held back. A monsoon ruined Bengali powder, not British. A subcontinent changed hands.

question: The 1857 Indian uprising — sparked by rumors of beef and pork grease on rifle cartridges — was led by sepoys in:
answer: Northern India
choices: Northern India
Madras Presidency
Bombay region
Kerala
context: British rule was suspended in Delhi, Lucknow and Kanpur for months. It was suppressed brutally. The East India Company was abolished; the Crown took direct control as the British Raj.

question: In March-April 1930, Gandhi led a 240-mile march to the sea to protest the British salt monopoly. It ended at:
answer: Dandi
choices: Dandi
Bombay
Surat
Porbandar
context: He picked up a lump of natural salt and broke colonial law. Mass civil disobedience followed; 60,000 jailed. The salt march made him a global figure of nonviolent resistance.

question: India's August 1947 independence was accompanied by partition into India and Pakistan, with violence killing roughly:
answer: 1 million people
choices: 1 million people
10,000 people
10 million people
100,000 people
context: Up to 15 million displaced. Lord Mountbatten was last viceroy. The Punjab and Bengal were split with little planning. Kashmir remains disputed to this day.

question: In 1971, East Pakistan won independence after a war with West Pakistan and Indian intervention. The new country was named:
answer: Bangladesh
choices: Bangladesh
East Bengal
Sheikh Mujib's State
Bengali Republic
context: Pakistani forces had massacred perhaps several hundred thousand Bengalis; ten million fled to India. Indira Gandhi committed Indian troops. Sheikh Mujibur Rahman became the first prime minister.

question: In 1206, the Mongol prince Temujin was acclaimed Great Khan and given the title:
answer: Chinggis Khan
choices: Chinggis Khan
Tengri Khan
World Khan
Steppe Khan
context: Also rendered Genghis. He died in 1227. His descendants built the largest contiguous land empire in history, from Korea to Hungary. The Yam postal system tied it together at horse-speed.

question: At its 13th-century height, the Mongol Empire was the largest contiguous:
answer: Land empire in history
choices: Land empire in history
Maritime empire of antiquity
Religious confederation
Commercial trading network
context: About 24 million square kilometers — roughly twice Russia today. The Pax Mongolica let trade and ideas move safely from Beijing to Damascus. Plague traveled the same routes.

question: The Mongol strategist whose 1241 European invasion crushed Hungarian and Polish armies in the same month was:
answer: Subutai
choices: Subutai
Batu Khan
Hulagu
Tolui
context: Mohi destroyed Hungary's army; Liegnitz crushed Polish-German knights two days apart. Mongols withdrew when Great Khan Ogedei died. Europe was spared by a death thousands of miles east.

question: The 14th-century Turco-Mongol conqueror who built pyramids of skulls from Delhi to Damascus was:
answer: Tamerlane
choices: Tamerlane
Babur the Tiger
Hulagu Khan
Ulugh Beg Mirza
context: Also called Timur. Lame from a youthful arrow wound. His capital Samarkand was filled with looted treasures. He died in 1405 preparing to invade China. His tomb's 1941 opening supposedly cursed the USSR.

question: The Aztec capital, founded in 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco, was:
answer: Tenochtitlan
choices: Tenochtitlan
Tula
Teotihuacan
Tlatelolco
context: Reportedly the largest city in the Americas when Cortes arrived. About 200,000 people, with causeways, aqueducts, floating gardens. Mexico City was built on its ruins.

question: When Hernan Cortes arrived in 1519, the Aztec emperor who initially received him as a possible returning god was:
answer: Montezuma II
choices: Montezuma II
Cuitlahuac
Cuauhtemoc
Ahuitzotl
context: He was eventually killed during a Spanish-Aztec battle in 1520 — by what, exactly, remains disputed. Tenochtitlan fell in 1521. Smallpox did much of the conquering.

question: Built around 1450 as a royal retreat for the Inca ruler Pachacuti, the high-Andes citadel rediscovered in 1911 was:
answer: Machu Picchu
choices: Machu Picchu
Cusco
Sacsayhuaman
Ollantaytambo
context: Hiram Bingham of Yale was the academic 'rediscoverer.' Local farmers had always known of it. The Spanish never found it. UNESCO World Heritage since 1983.

question: In 1532, Pizarro captured the Inca emperor at Cajamarca during a meeting that became an ambush. The emperor was:
answer: Atahualpa
choices: Atahualpa
Huayna Capac
Manco Inca
Tupac Amaru
context: Atahualpa filled a room with gold for ransom. Pizarro garroted him anyway in 1533. The Inca empire collapsed despite ten times the Spanish numbers — smallpox had already cut them down.

question: Despite ruling 12 million people across the Andes, the Inca empire had no:
answer: Writing or wheel
choices: Writing or wheel
Roads or aqueducts
Bureaucracy
Mathematics
context: They recorded with knotted strings — quipu. Roads totaled 40,000 km. They never developed iron or the wheel. Llama trains crossed the mountains; runners carried messages in stages.

question: Machu Picchu sits at what elevation above sea level?
answer: Roughly 2,430 meters
choices: Roughly 2,430 meters
Roughly 430 meters
Roughly 4,300 meters
Roughly 9,000 meters
context: About 7,970 feet. Cusco itself sits at 11,000. The Inca built without mortar; stones fit so tightly a knife blade can't pass. Earthquakes have left the citadel essentially intact.

question: The Mayan calendrical system that ran through cycles ending in December 2012 was called the:
answer: Long Count
choices: Long Count
Tzolkin
Haab
Calendar Round
context: 5,125-year cycle. The 'end' meant a calendrical reset, not apocalypse. Mayan astronomy was sophisticated — Venus tables predicted positions over centuries. Their hieroglyphic writing was decoded only in the late 20th century.

question: Pre-modern Polynesians sailed thousands of miles across the Pacific using stars, waves, birds, and what other aid?
answer: Memorized routes
choices: Memorized routes
Brass astrolabes
Magnetic compass
Sand-glass timer
context: Generations passed routes down by chant. Hawaii was settled around 400 AD, New Zealand around 1280. Easter Island, perhaps 1200. The reconstructed canoe Hokule'a relearned the techniques in the 1970s.

question: The Polynesian island whose iconic stone moai were carved between roughly 1250 and 1500 was:
answer: Rapa Nui
choices: Rapa Nui
Tonga
Samoa
Fiji
context: Also known as Easter Island. About 900 statues; the largest weighs 82 tons. The civilization collapsed around 1700. About 90% of the population died in the 1862 Peruvian slave raids.

question: Under Mansa Musa in the 14th century, the Mali Empire built a famed center of Islamic learning at:
answer: Timbuktu
choices: Timbuktu
Djenne
Gao
Niani
context: The Sankore madrasah held thousands of manuscripts. Salt and gold passed through. Ibn Battuta visited in 1352. The Songhai Empire took over later in the 1400s.

question: Between roughly 1100 and 1450 a sophisticated stone-built kingdom flourished in southern Africa, leaving ruins now called:
answer: Great Zimbabwe
choices: Great Zimbabwe
Kilwa Kisiwani
Mapungubwe
Mbanza Kongo
context: Massive dry-stone walls without mortar. Long-distance trade reached the Swahili coast and Chinese porcelain. Colonial-era authorities long pretended Africans could not have built it. They had.

question: The 12th-13th-century churches carved straight down into bedrock in Ethiopia are at:
answer: Lalibela
choices: Lalibela
Aksum
Gondar
Harar
context: Eleven monolithic churches. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church traces its origin to the 4th century. Italy invaded twice; in 1896 Ethiopia famously defeated them at Adwa.

question: In 1896, Ethiopia humiliated Italy and preserved its independence at the Battle of:
answer: Adwa
choices: Adwa
Dogali
Coatit
Amba Alagi
context: Emperor Menelik II won. About 17,000 Italian casualties. The defeat shocked Europe. Only Ethiopia and Liberia escaped European colonization at the height of imperialism.

question: Released on February 11, 1990 after 27 years in prison, the South African leader was:
answer: Nelson Mandela
choices: Nelson Mandela
Walter Sisulu
Oliver Tambo
Govan Mbeki
context: He had refused conditional releases for years. F.W. de Klerk had unbanned the ANC days earlier. They shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize. Mandela was elected president in 1994.

question: In April-July 1994, perhaps 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were murdered over how many days?
answer: About 100 days
choices: About 100 days
About 10 days
About 1,000 days
Several years
context: Machetes were the main weapon. Radio Mille Collines incited it. UN peacekeepers stood down. Romeo Dallaire's plea for 5,000 more troops was refused. Bill Clinton later called inaction his greatest regret.

question: The early 19th-century Zulu king who reorganized warfare with the short stabbing spear and triggered the Mfecane was:
answer: Shaka Zulu
choices: Shaka Zulu
Cetshwayo Zulu
Dingane Zulu
Mpande Zulu
context: His military revolution displaced peoples across southern Africa. The Mfecane — 'crushing' — left millions displaced or dead. He was assassinated by his half-brothers in 1828.
