'Mr. Gorbachev, open this gate!'
'Mr. Gorbachev, dismantle this barrier of fear!'

context: The Wall came down on November 9, 1989 — two years and five months later. Critics had derided the speech as empty bluster; historians have reassessed it as a moment that helped accelerate the collapse of Soviet power in Eastern Europe.

question: On the evening of November 9, 1989, after weeks of growing East German protest and Hungarian and Czech border openings, an East German press spokesman misread instructions at a 6 p.m. press conference and announced — in confused terms — that travel restrictions to the West were lifted 'immediately.' By midnight crowds were dancing atop the Wall. Who was the spokesman?
answer: Günter Schabowski — Politburo member at the fateful press conference
choices: Günter Schabowski — Politburo member at the fateful press conference

Erich Honecker — but Honecker had been deposed weeks earlier in October
Markus Wolf — but Wolf was the East German foreign intelligence chief
context: Schabowski had not read the instructions before walking into the press conference. His confused answers — 'as far as I know, immediately' — opened the floodgates. The East German state collapsed within weeks.

question: On December 25, 1991, Mikhail Gorbachev announced his resignation as president of the Soviet Union and ceded control of nuclear codes to the president of the Russian Federation. The hammer-and-sickle flag was lowered from the Kremlin for the last time. To whom did Gorbachev transfer authority?

Leonid Kravchuk — but Kravchuk was now leading independent Ukraine

context: The fifteen Soviet republics had declared sovereignty over the previous year. Yeltsin had defied the August 1991 coup attempt by standing atop a tank outside the Russian parliament. The Cold War, in any meaningful sense, was over.

question: On the morning of September 11, 2001, 19 hijackers from al-Qaeda flew four passenger airliners. Two struck the World Trade Center in New York; both 110-story towers collapsed within two hours. A third struck the Pentagon. choices: Roughly 2,977 victims plus the 19 hijackers — the deadliest attack on US soil
Roughly 1,500 victims, the lowest range of early estimates that morning
Roughly 4,500 victims, the highest range of early estimates
Roughly 6,000 victims plus the hijackers, an early erroneous figure
context: The attacks triggered the US wars in Afghanistan (October 2001) and Iraq (March 2003). They reshaped American politics, foreign policy, security architecture, and immigration policy for at least two decades.

question: On October 7, 2001, the United States launched air strikes against al-Qaeda training camps and Taliban government positions in Afghanistan. CIA paramilitary teams and US Special Forces, working with the Northern Alliance, captured Kabul on November 13. Where did Osama bin Laden likely escape to in December 2001?

Kandahar — but Kandahar fell to the Northern Alliance in December 2001
Mazar-i-Sharif — but Mazar fell to the Northern Alliance much earlier

context: Bin Laden was killed in a US Navy SEAL raid on his compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan, on May 2, 2011 — nearly ten years later. The Afghanistan war became the longest in US history before the 2021 withdrawal.

question: On September 15, 2008, a 158-year-old Wall Street investment bank filed for bankruptcy after the federal government declined to rescue it — unlike Bear Stearns six months earlier. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 504 points. Within a month, Congress passed a $700 billion bank-rescue program. What was the bank?
answer: Lehman Brothers — largest bankruptcy filing in US history
choices: Lehman Brothers — largest bankruptcy filing in US history
Bear Stearns — but Bear Stearns was rescued by JPMorgan in March 2008
Merrill Lynch — but Merrill was acquired by Bank of America that weekend

context: The 2008 crisis triggered the Great Recession — the deepest US downturn since the Depression. Unemployment hit 10% in 2009. Banks, automakers, and homeowners received hundreds of billions in federal aid; the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 followed.

question: Shortly after midnight local time on May 2, 2011, two Black Hawk helicopters carrying members of US Naval Special Warfare Development Group landed at a compound in the Pakistani city of Abbottabad — 35 miles from the capital, near a major military academy. After a 40-minute operation, the al-Qaeda founder was dead. What group conducted the raid?
answer: SEAL Team Six (formally DEVGRU) — under Joint Special Operations Command
choices: SEAL Team Six (formally DEVGRU) — under Joint Special Operations Command
Delta Force — but Delta is the Army equivalent, not the SEAL raid force
75th Ranger Regiment — but Rangers are conventional special operations
Marine Force Recon — but Force Recon is reconnaissance, not direct action
context: President Obama and his national security team watched the operation live from the White House Situation Room. Bin Laden's body was buried at sea from the USS Carl Vinson within 24 hours to prevent a memorial site forming.

question: On August 2, 216 BC, the Carthaginian general Hannibal Barca faced two Roman consular armies under Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Gaius Terentius Varro — perhaps 86,000 men — at a small village on the Aufidus River in southeastern Italy. Hannibal's crescent-shaped line bent backward; his African veterans on the wings closed the trap. What is this textbook tactic called?
answer: Double envelopment — Hannibal's perfect example studied at staff colleges
choices: Double envelopment — Hannibal's perfect example studied at staff colleges

Echeloned refusal — a different and older Theban tactical innovation
Hammer and anvil — broadly similar but a distinct cavalry-infantry model
context: Roughly 50,000 Romans died — the highest single-day death toll on a Western battlefield until the Somme in 1916. Paullus was killed; Varro escaped. Yet Hannibal could not take Rome itself; Carthage was finished at Zama 14 years later.

question: On October 1, 331 BC, on a plain east of Mosul, Alexander the Great with about 47,000 men defeated Darius III's army of perhaps 100,000 Persians. Alexander led the Companion cavalry in a flanking wedge that broke through to Darius's chariot — Darius fled the field. The Persian empire was effectively finished. What is the battle?
answer: Gaugamela — also called Arbela, on the plain of Gaugamela

Issus — but Issus was the earlier 333 BC clash with Darius, smaller
Granicus — but Granicus was Alexander's 334 BC first major Persian battle
Hydaspes — but Hydaspes was the 326 BC clash with Porus in India
context: Darius was murdered the next year by his own satrap Bessus. Alexander hunted Bessus down and executed him in 329 BC. The successor states — Seleucid, Ptolemaic, Antigonid — divided Alexander's empire after his death in Babylon, 323 BC.

question: In September AD 9, three Roman legions under Publius Quinctilius Varus, marching home from summer campaigns through dense German forest, were ambushed by a coalition of Germanic tribes under a Roman-trained chieftain. Over three days the legions were destroyed. Suetonius records Augustus crying out: 'Quinctili Vare, legiones redde!' — 'Varus, give me back my legions!' Who led the Germans?
answer: Arminius — Cheruscan chief and former Roman auxiliary commander
choices: Arminius — Cheruscan chief and former Roman auxiliary commander
Maroboduus — but Maroboduus was the Marcomanni king, not at Teutoburg
Vercingetorix — but Vercingetorix was Gallic and died decades earlier
Boudica — but Boudica was the British queen of AD 60, much later
context: Three legion eagles were lost. Germanicus retrieved two between AD 15 and 17. The Rhine became Rome's effective northern frontier. Hermann the Cheruscan became a German national symbol in the 19th century.

question: On August 9, AD 378, the Eastern Roman emperor Valens, refusing to wait for his nephew Gratian's reinforcements, attacked a Visigothic encampment north of the city of Adrianople in Thrace. His army was caught by returning Gothic cavalry, and roughly two-thirds of it — including the emperor himself — was destroyed. What is the strategic significance most often given?
answer: The traditional end of dominant Roman infantry, beginning of heavy cavalry
choices: The traditional end of dominant Roman infantry, beginning of heavy cavalry
The end of the Roman Republic (it had ended four centuries earlier)
The end of the Roman senatorial class (it survived for centuries more)
The end of the Latin language as an imperial tongue (it survived intact)
context: Modern historians are more skeptical of the 'cavalry revolution' framing. But the political consequence is clear: Gothic federate communities established themselves inside Roman frontiers, and the Western Empire never recovered military equilibrium.

question: In August AD 636, on the Yarmouk River valley southeast of the Sea of Galilee, an Arab Muslim army under Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated a much larger Byzantine army under the emperor Heraclius's brother Theodore. The defeat ended Byzantine rule in Syria and Palestine for good. Why is the battle so consequential?

choices: It opened the entire Middle East to the rapid Arab Muslim conquests
It restored Byzantine authority over Egypt for the next two centuries
It established the Sasanian Persians as the dominant regional power
It triggered the Crusades centuries later by ending Christian Levant rule
context: Within 25 years of Muhammad's death in AD 632, Arab armies had taken Syria, Iraq, Egypt, Persia, and much of North Africa. The Byzantines held Anatolia and Constantinople; the Sasanian Empire of Persia simply collapsed.

question: In October AD 732, somewhere between Tours and Poitiers in west-central France, a Frankish army under Charles Martel formed a tight phalanx that Arab cavalry could not break. The Arab commander, Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, was killed. The raid was over. What did Edward Gibbon famously argue about the battle?
answer: It saved Christian Europe from Muslim conquest — though modern historians disagree
choices: It saved Christian Europe from Muslim conquest — though modern historians disagree
It opened the Holy Land to Frankish settlers ahead of the actual Crusades
It crushed the Visigothic remnant that had fled into Aquitaine after 711
It ended Charlemagne's grandfather's career, which actually thrived
context: Modern historians regard Tours as one of many Frankish-Arab clashes rather than the singular event Gibbon imagined. But the cultural impact is unambiguous: no Muslim army would penetrate so deep into Western Europe again.

question: On August 10, 955, near the Lech river south of Augsburg in Bavaria, King Otto I of East Francia decisively defeated a Magyar raiding force whose cavalry had terrorized Western Europe for sixty years. The defeat ended Magyar raids west of the Carpathians; the Magyars settled, adopted Christianity, and became Hungary. What is the battle?
answer: Lechfeld — Otto would be crowned Holy Roman Emperor seven years later
choices: Lechfeld — Otto would be crowned Holy Roman Emperor seven years later
Riade — Otto's father Henry I won there in 933, an earlier Magyar defeat
Pressburg — but Pressburg in 907 was a Magyar victory, not defeat
Augsburg — but the engagement is named for the river, not the city
context: Otto was crowned emperor in Rome in 962. Lechfeld is often called the birth of medieval German power and the end of the migration-era nomadic threat to Western Europe.

question: On October 14, 1066, on a low ridge in Sussex, the army of William, Duke of Normandy, defeated the army of Harold Godwinson, King of England, who had just marched 250 miles south from defeating a Norwegian invasion at Stamford Bridge. According to the Bayeux Tapestry, how did Harold die?
answer: Shot in the eye by a Norman arrow during the late afternoon collapse
choices: Shot in the eye by a Norman arrow during the late afternoon collapse
Killed by a Norman knight in single combat early in the battle
Drowned trying to escape after the rout, fleeing west toward Pevensey
Captured and executed publicly by William the next morning at the ridge
context: Tradition associates the arrow with the Tapestry image, though historians dispute exactly which figure is Harold. William was crowned at Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066. Norman French became the language of England's ruling class for centuries.

question: On July 4, 1187, on a hilltop above the Sea of Galilee, the Crusader kingdom's main army under King Guy of Lusignan, marching across a waterless plateau in midsummer, was surrounded and destroyed by Saladin. Guy was captured; the relic of the True Cross was lost. Jerusalem fell three months later. What is the battle?
answer: Hattin — the Horns of Hattin, named for two volcanic hills
choices: Hattin — the Horns of Hattin, named for two volcanic hills
Tiberias — but Tiberias was the city Saladin had besieged to lure Guy
Acre — but Acre was the Crusader port, recovered by the Third Crusade
Arsuf — but Arsuf was Richard the Lionheart's later victory in 1191
context: Hattin broke the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem. The Third Crusade (1189-1192) recovered the coastal cities but never Jerusalem itself. Saladin died at Damascus in 1193.

question: On August 26, 1346, on a slope in northern France, the army of Edward III — perhaps 12,000 men, mostly Welsh and English longbowmen behind defensive pits — destroyed a French chivalric army perhaps three times larger. The French lost perhaps 1,500 knights including the blind King John of Bohemia. What new weapon dominated the field?
answer: The English longbow — yew bow drawing 100+ pounds, lethal at 250 yards
choices: The English longbow — yew bow drawing 100+ pounds, lethal at 250 yards
Plate armor — but heavy plate would not become standard for decades after
Pike and shot — but pike and shot is a 16th-century combined-arms formation
Cannon — primitive cannon were present at Crécy but were not decisive
context: Crécy opened the long English period of dominance in the Hundred Years' War, which ended only in 1453. King John of Bohemia, blind, asked his men to lead him into the press of battle; he was found dead with his guides still strapped to his horse.

question: On October 25, 1415 — St Crispin's Day — Henry V of England, with about 6,000 men (mostly archers) facing perhaps 25,000 French knights and men-at-arms, won a victory in a muddy field bordered by woods in northern France. French heavy cavalry could not maneuver; longbow fire was devastating. What is the battle?
answer: Agincourt — celebrated in Shakespeare's Henry V three centuries later
choices: Agincourt — celebrated in Shakespeare's Henry V three centuries later
Poitiers — but Poitiers was Edward III's earlier 1356 victory
Verneuil — but Verneuil was the later 1424 follow-up to Agincourt
Patay — but Patay was Joan of Arc's 1429 French revenge
context: Henry's St Crispin's Day speech in Shakespeare — 'We few, we happy few, we band of brothers' — is fiction, but Agincourt is fact. Henry married Catherine of Valois and was named heir to the French throne by treaty in 1420 — only to die of dysentery in 1422.

question: In April 1429, a 17-year-old peasant girl from Domrémy in Lorraine, claiming to hear voices from saints, arrived at the besieged French city on the Loire with reinforcements from the dauphin. Within nine days, Joan of Arc had broken the seven-month English siege and turned the tide of the Hundred Years' War. What city?
answer: Orléans — relieved May 8, 1429, the turning point of the war
choices: Orléans — relieved May 8, 1429, the turning point of the war
Reims — the coronation city, recovered later in July 1429 but unbesieged
Paris — Joan's failed September 1429 attack on Paris, not a relief
Rouen — but Rouen was where Joan herself was burned, May 30, 1431
context: Charles VII was crowned king at Reims on July 17, 1429, with Joan present. She was captured at Compiègne in May 1430, sold to the English, tried for heresy and witchcraft, and burned at Rouen on May 30, 1431, at age 19.

question: On May 29, 1453, after a 53-day siege punctuated by the bombardment of Theodosian walls by the Hungarian-cast 27-foot bombard of Orban, a 21-year-old Ottoman sultan took the last fragment of the Eastern Roman Empire. The last Christian emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos died fighting in the breach. Who?
answer: Mehmed II — the Conqueror, who made the city his capital
choices: Mehmed II — the Conqueror, who made the city his capital
Bayezid I — but he had died in 1403, half a century before
Suleiman I — but he was born in 1494, not until decades later
Murad II — Mehmed's father, who had died in 1451, two years before
context: Hagia Sophia was converted to a mosque the same day. Refugee Greek scholars fled west, bringing Greek manuscripts that helped feed the Italian Renaissance. The Ottoman Empire would dominate the eastern Mediterranean for centuries.

question: On October 7, 1571, in the Gulf of Patras off western Greece, a Christian Holy League fleet of perhaps 212 ships under Don John of Austria smashed an Ottoman fleet of similar size. About 30,000 Ottomans died. Spanish writer Miguel de Cervantes, fighting aboard the Marquesa, was permanently maimed in his left hand. What battle?
answer: Lepanto — the last major galley battle in the Mediterranean
choices: Lepanto — the last major galley battle in the Mediterranean
Preveza — but Preveza was the 1538 Ottoman victory, the previous high
Djerba — but Djerba was the 1560 disaster for the Holy League fleet
Tunis — but Tunis 1574 was a later Ottoman counterattack
context: Lepanto did not end Ottoman naval power — the Ottomans rebuilt their fleet within a year. But it broke the myth of Ottoman naval invincibility. Cervantes called his maimed hand 'the lesser to the greater glory of the right.'

question: On September 17, 1631, near a small village outside Leipzig, the Swedish king Gustavus Adolphus led a combined Swedish-Saxon army to victory against the Imperial-Catholic army of Count Tilly. Gustavus's flexible mixed formations of musket and pike, combined with light field artillery, set the pattern for European tactics. What battle?
answer: First Battle of Breitenfeld — the great Swedish victory in 1631
choices: First Battle of Breitenfeld — the great Swedish victory in 1631
Lützen — but Lützen was Gustavus's last battle, in 1632
Nördlingen — but Nördlingen was the 1634 Swedish defeat after Gustavus
Rocroi — but Rocroi was the 1643 French victory ending Spanish dominance
context: Gustavus would be killed the next year at Lützen (November 16, 1632), winning the battle but losing the king. Sweden remained a great power until early in the 18th century, when Charles XII was defeated by Peter the Great at Poltava in 1709.

question: On June 14, 1645, in Northamptonshire, the Royalist army of Charles I and Prince Rupert was decisively defeated by the New Model Army under Sir Thomas Fairfax and Oliver Cromwell. Captured Royalist papers revealed Charles I's plans for an Irish Catholic army. What was the battle?
answer: Naseby — the decisive parliamentary victory of the English Civil War
choices: Naseby — the decisive parliamentary victory of the English Civil War
Edgehill — but Edgehill was the earlier 1642 drawn first battle
Marston Moor — but Marston Moor was the 1644 earlier parliamentary win
Worcester — but Worcester 1651 was the Civil War's final battle
context: After Naseby, Charles I's military position was hopeless. He surrendered to the Scots in 1646, was handed to the English, tried by a special court, and beheaded on January 30, 1649. England became a republic under Cromwell.

question: On September 12, 1683, after a two-month Ottoman siege of Vienna had nearly succeeded, a relief army of roughly 70,000 — including 18,000 Polish hussars and 65,000 Holy League troops — descended from the heights of Kahlenberg. The Polish king led from the front in the largest cavalry charge in history. Who was the king?
answer: Jan III Sobieski of Poland — the relief at Vienna saved Christian Europe
choices: Jan III Sobieski of Poland — the relief at Vienna saved Christian Europe
Leopold I — but he was the Holy Roman Emperor, in flight from the city
Charles V of Lorraine — commander of the imperial forces but not king
John George III of Saxony — present with the German contingent only
context: Sobieski wrote home to his queen: 'Venimus, vidimus, Deus vicit' — 'We came, we saw, God conquered.' The Ottoman tide in Europe broke at Vienna; the high-water mark of Ottoman expansion had passed.

question: On August 13, 1704, on the Danube near the Bavarian village of Blindheim, the Duke of Marlborough and Prince Eugene of Savoy crushed a Franco-Bavarian army under Marshal Tallard. The French lost perhaps 38,000 men; Marshal Tallard was captured. Louis XIV's army of dominance was broken. What did the English call the battle?
answer: Blenheim — anglicizing the German Blindheim
choices: Blenheim — anglicizing the German Blindheim
Höchstädt — but the French called it Second Höchstädt; English called it Blenheim
Donauwörth — but Donauwörth was an earlier July 1704 storm by Marlborough
Ramillies — but Ramillies was Marlborough's later 1706 victory
context: Marlborough received Blenheim Palace at Woodstock from a grateful Queen Anne. Winston Churchill, his descendant, would be born there in 1874.

question: On June 27, 1709 (or July 8 by Western reckoning), on the Ukrainian steppe, Charles XII's Swedish army — having marched far from supply, with the king himself wounded and on a stretcher — was decisively defeated by Peter the Great. Charles fled to Ottoman territory, and Russia replaced Sweden as the dominant northern power. What battle?
answer: Poltava — perhaps the most consequential European battle of the early 18th century
choices: Poltava — perhaps the most consequential European battle of the early 18th century
Narva — but Narva was Charles XII's earlier 1700 spectacular victory
Pultusk — but Pultusk was a much smaller 1703 Swedish-Polish-Russian engagement
Klissów — but Klissów was the 1702 Charles XII victory in Poland
context: Charles XII was killed by a stray bullet at the siege of Fredriksten in Norway in 1718, still trying to recover Swedish greatness. The Treaty of Nystad in 1721 confirmed Russia's gains and the end of the Swedish empire.

question: On April 16, 1746, on a windswept moor east of Inverness in northern Scotland, the Jacobite army of Charles Edward Stuart — 'Bonnie Prince Charlie' — was destroyed in under an hour by a government army under William, Duke of Cumberland. The Highland charge could not penetrate disciplined musket fire. What battle?
answer: Culloden — the last pitched battle fought on British soil
choices: Culloden — the last pitched battle fought on British soil
Falkirk Muir — but Falkirk Muir 1746 was the earlier Jacobite victory
Prestonpans — but Prestonpans 1745 was the earlier Jacobite victory
Sheriffmuir — but Sheriffmuir 1715 was the earlier Jacobite drawn battle
context: Charles Stuart fled to France; Cumberland earned the nickname 'Butcher' for the systematic suppression that followed. The Highland clan system, kilt, and Gaelic language were targeted for suppression for a generation.

question: On September 13, 1759, on the Plains of Abraham above the St. Lawrence River, a British army under Major General James Wolfe — having scaled the cliff at night — caught a French army under the Marquis de Montcalm in the open and broke it in a few minutes. Both generals died of wounds within a day. What city fell?
answer: Quebec — Canada became a British colony at the war's end
choices: Quebec — Canada became a British colony at the war's end
Montreal — but Montreal fell only the next year, September 1760
Louisbourg — but Louisbourg had already fallen to Amherst in 1758
Detroit — but Detroit was a small western post, not the Plains of Abraham
context: The French and Indian War ended with the 1763 Treaty of Paris, transferring French Canada to Britain. The loss helped trigger the French Revolution by ruining the royal finances — and, through American resentment of British post-war taxation, helped trigger the American Revolution.

question: On June 23, 1757, at a mango grove north of Calcutta in Bengal, the British East India Company army under Robert Clive — perhaps 3,000 men — defeated the Nawab of Bengal Siraj ud-Daulah's army of 50,000 with a key general defection negotiated in advance. What did the battle establish?
answer: British East India Company control over Bengal — the springboard for India
choices: British East India Company control over Bengal — the springboard for India
British control over the Carnatic — but the Carnatic Wars were separate
British control over Mysore — but Mysore was conquered only by 1799
British control over the Mughal court — but Delhi fell only in 1803
context: Mir Jafar, the defecting Bengal commander, became the new Nawab — a puppet. Clive returned to Britain rich; Pitt the Elder used the Bengal revenues to finance the rest of the Seven Years' War. The Company became a state within a state.

question: On October 17, 1777, at a battlefield north of Albany on the Hudson, British Major General John Burgoyne — having marched south from Canada hoping to split New England from the rest of the colonies — surrendered nearly 6,000 men to an American army under Horatio Gates. Benedict Arnold provided the tactical brilliance. What did the battle trigger?
answer: The French alliance — Louis XVI recognized American independence in February 1778
choices: The French alliance — Louis XVI recognized American independence in February 1778
British evacuation of Boston — but that had happened a year earlier, in March 1776
American capture of New York City — but New York stayed British until 1783
British surrender at Yorktown — but Yorktown was four years later, in 1781
context: American militia ate Burgoyne's supply lines. The Convention of Saratoga allowed his men to return to Britain, but Congress later refused to honor it. Foreign volunteers — Lafayette, Kosciuszko, von Steuben, de Kalb — soon arrived in numbers.

question: On October 19, 1781, after a three-week siege by combined American and French forces under Washington and Rochambeau — with de Grasse's French fleet sealing Chesapeake Bay against Royal Navy relief — Lord Cornwallis surrendered roughly 7,000 British troops at a Virginia tobacco port. British military will to continue collapsed. What is the port?
answer: Yorktown — the decisive land battle of the American Revolutionary War
choices: Yorktown — the decisive land battle of the American Revolutionary War
Williamsburg — but Williamsburg was the staging ground, not the surrender
Charleston — but Charleston had fallen to the British in 1780
Savannah — but Savannah had fallen earlier in 1778 and held by British
context: Cornwallis claimed illness and sent General O'Hara to surrender his sword. Washington designated Benjamin Lincoln to receive it. The war did not formally end until the Treaty of Paris in 1783.

question: On September 20, 1792, in the rain on a ridge in the Argonne forest of northeastern France, an unstrategic artillery duel between a revolutionary French army and the Prussian-Austrian invasion force ended in Prussian withdrawal. The young French republic had survived. Goethe, present with the Prussians, reportedly told his companions that day what?
answer: 'From this place and from this day forth begins a new era in the world's history'
choices: 'From this place and from this day forth begins a new era in the world's history'
'The age of monarchy is over; the age of nations begins'
'I have seen the future, and it is the Revolution'
'We are looking on the death of one Europe and the birth of another'
context: France declared the Republic the next day, September 21, 1792. Louis XVI was tried in December and beheaded in January 1793. The revolutionary wars would last, with brief interruptions, for the next twenty-three years.

question: On October 21, 1805, off Cape Trafalgar in southwestern Spain, the British Mediterranean fleet under Admiral Horatio Nelson broke the combined French-Spanish fleet of Admiral Villeneuve, sinking or capturing 22 of 33 enemy ships of the line at the cost of none of his own. Nelson himself was shot from his quarterdeck by a sniper. What was his last signal to the fleet?
answer: 'England expects that every man will do his duty'
choices: 'England expects that every man will do his duty'
'Engage the enemy more closely' — but that was the final signal, hoisted later
'Strike the colors of the enemy' — but no such signal was made
'Sail before the wind' — but no such signal was used at Trafalgar
context: Nelson died below decks four hours later, reportedly asking Hardy to kiss him. His body was preserved in brandy and returned to Britain for a state funeral. The Royal Navy controlled the seas for the next century.

question: On December 2, 1805, on the first anniversary of his coronation, Napoleon faced a combined Russian and Austrian army on a frozen plateau in Moravia. He deliberately weakened his right flank to lure the allied attack; then he hit their center on the Pratzen Heights. The Austrians and Russians broke; lakes filled with retreating soldiers cracked under cannon fire. What is the battle?
answer: Austerlitz — the Battle of the Three Emperors, Napoleon's masterpiece

Wagram — but Wagram was Napoleon's later 1809 victory over Austria

context: Austria signed the Treaty of Pressburg ceding Venice, Dalmatia, and parts of Bavaria. The Holy Roman Empire — over 1000 years old — was dissolved the next August. Pitt the Younger looked at a map of Europe and reportedly said: 'Roll up that map; it will not be wanted these ten years.'

question: On September 7, 1812, on a plateau seventy miles west of Moscow, Napoleon's 130,000-strong Grande Armée engaged Kutuzov's roughly 120,000 Russians in the bloodiest single day of the Napoleonic Wars: perhaps 70,000 combined casualties. Tactically Napoleon won; the Russians withdrew. What did the Russians abandon a week later?
answer: Moscow — which the Russians burned rather than leave intact for the French
choices: Moscow — which the Russians burned rather than leave intact for the French

Smolensk — but Smolensk had already fallen earlier in August 1812
Vilnius — but Vilnius had also already fallen earlier in the summer
context: Napoleon entered Moscow on September 14; the city burned around him; the Russians refused to negotiate. The retreat began October 19; by December, the Grande Armée was destroyed by cold and Cossack pursuit.

question: From October 16 to 19, 1813, near the city of Leipzig in Saxony, four allied armies (Russian, Prussian, Austrian, Swedish) totaling over 380,000 men engaged Napoleon's 225,000-strong force in the largest battle in Europe before World War I. Roughly 100,000 combined casualties. Napoleon was forced to retreat into France. What is the battle commonly called?
answer: Battle of the Nations — Völkerschlacht in German
choices: Battle of the Nations — Völkerschlacht in German
Battle of the Three Emperors — but that name belongs to Austerlitz 1805
Battle of the Coalition — a generic name not specifically used

context: Napoleon abdicated in April 1814 and was exiled to Elba. His escape in February 1815 led to the Hundred Days, ending at Waterloo on June 18, 1815.

question: On June 18, 1815, on a ridge south of Brussels, the Duke of Wellington's mixed Anglo-Dutch-German army held against repeated French attacks long enough for the Prussian army under Marshal Blücher to arrive from Wavre and roll up the French right flank. Napoleon was finished. The battle has named more sites than perhaps any other. Wellington's verdict?

'Hard pounding, gentlemen' — but that is a different Waterloo phrase

context: Napoleon was exiled to St Helena and died there in May 1821, probably of stomach cancer at 51. Wellington became prime minister; Blücher became a Prussian national hero. The Congress of Vienna had already redrawn the European map.

question: On October 20, 1827, in the Bay of Navarino off the western coast of the Peloponnese, a combined British-French-Russian fleet under Admiral Sir Edward Codrington — sent ostensibly to monitor an armistice — destroyed an Ottoman-Egyptian fleet of comparable size. It was the last major naval battle of the age of sail. What did it secure?
answer: Greek independence from the Ottoman Empire after centuries of rule
choices: Greek independence from the Ottoman Empire after centuries of rule
Russian access to the Black Sea straits — but that came later, in stages
Ottoman recognition of British control of Egypt — but Britain took Egypt in 1882
Italian independence from Habsburg rule — but that came decades later
context: The Greek War of Independence (1821-1829) inspired European liberals including Lord Byron, who died at Missolonghi in 1824. The Ottoman Empire was thereafter often called 'the sick man of Europe.'

question: On October 25, 1854, in the Crimean War, a confused order to a British cavalry brigade led to a hopeless charge directly into Russian artillery in a valley near a Black Sea port. Of 670 horsemen, 110 died, 161 were wounded, and 60 were captured. Tennyson's poem made it immortal. Who led the charge?
answer: Lord Cardigan — James Brudenell, 7th Earl of Cardigan

Lord Lucan — but Lucan was the cavalry division commander, not the leader

context: Tennyson's poem 'The Charge of the Light Brigade' includes the line: 'Theirs not to reason why, theirs but to do and die.' The Crimean War (1853-1856) modernized military medicine through Florence Nightingale.

question: On March 9, 1862, in Hampton Roads, Virginia, two ironclad warships fought to a tactical draw — the first such battle in history. The Union USS Monitor, with its rotating turret designed by John Ericsson, fought the Confederate CSS Virginia (originally USS Merrimack) for four hours. What was the strategic effect?
answer: Wooden warships were instantly obsolete worldwide
choices: Wooden warships were instantly obsolete worldwide
The Confederacy gained naval parity in Atlantic waters for the war
The Union blockade was broken throughout the eastern theater
European navies refused to alter their wooden-fleet doctrines for decades
context: The Monitor sank in a storm off Cape Hatteras on December 31, 1862. The Virginia was burned by Confederate forces in May 1862 to prevent capture. The era of the battleship had begun.

question: On September 17, 1862, near a creek in western Maryland, the armies of Robert E. Lee and George B. What is the battle called by the Union and the Confederacy?
answer: Antietam by Union usage and Sharpsburg by Confederate usage
choices: Antietam by Union usage and Sharpsburg by Confederate usage
Bull Run (Union) and Manassas (Confederate) — but those are different battles

Pittsburg Landing (Union) and Shiloh (Confederate) — but those are different
context: Union forces, including the African-American 54th Massachusetts later, were inspired by the Emancipation Proclamation that followed. Lee retreated to Virginia; the war continued for two and a half more bloody years.

question: From July 1 to 3, 1863, near a Pennsylvania crossroads town, Robert E. Lee's Army of Northern Virginia engaged George Meade's Army of the Potomac in a battle that left perhaps 51,000 combined casualties. On the third afternoon, 12,500 Confederates under George Pickett, Pettigrew, and Trimble crossed open ground against the Union center. What is the assault called?
answer: Pickett's Charge — though Pickett's was only one of three divisions
choices: Pickett's Charge — though Pickett's was only one of three divisions

The Confederate Wave — but no such phrase was used at the time
Longstreet's Assault — Longstreet commanded but it bears Pickett's name
context: Roughly half the attackers were killed, wounded, or captured. The Confederacy's high-water mark, as recorded by historian Bruce Catton, was somewhere on Cemetery Ridge that afternoon. Lee retreated to Virginia. The war continued for nearly two more years.

question: On September 1-2, 1870, at a town on the Meuse in northeastern France, a French army under Marshal MacMahon — accompanying Emperor Napoleon III himself — was surrounded by Prussian armies under Helmuth von Moltke and forced to surrender. Napoleon III was captured. What was the political consequence in Paris?
answer: The Second Empire fell; the Third Republic was proclaimed September 4
choices: The Second Empire fell; the Third Republic was proclaimed September 4
The Bourbon Restoration — but the Bourbons had already fallen earlier
The Commune of Paris of 1871 — but the Commune came after the war ended

context: Paris was besieged from September 19, 1870, to January 28, 1871 — surviving on cats, dogs, and zoo animals. The German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles on January 18, 1871, with Wilhelm I as Kaiser. France ceded Alsace-Lorraine.

question: On June 25-26, 1876, at a Montana river, a US 7th Cavalry detachment of 210 men under Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer was annihilated by a much larger Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho force under Crazy Horse, Gall, and the spiritual leader Sitting Bull. None of Custer's immediate command survived. What is the battle?

choices: Little Bighorn — 'Custer's Last Stand,' the Indian victory's only celebration
Greasy Grass — the Lakota name for the same battle, in their language

Both Little Bighorn and Greasy Grass — used interchangeably depending on source
context: The Wounded Knee Massacre on December 29, 1890, brought the Indian Wars to a tragic end. The bodies of US troops were buried where they fell at Little Bighorn; later reburied in formal cemetery there.

question: On January 22, 1879, in northeastern Natal in southern Africa, a British central column of about 1,300 troops under Brevet Lieutenant Colonel Henry Pulleine was overwhelmed by a Zulu impi of perhaps 20,000 warriors under Ntshingwayo kaMahole. Roughly 1,300 British and African allies died — the worst defeat of a modern army by a pre-industrial force. What battle?

Nyezane — but Nyezane was a smaller skirmish, not the disaster
context: Survivors fled across the Buffalo River to Rorke's Drift, where a small British garrison held against perhaps 4,000 Zulu warriors that night and into the next day, winning 11 Victoria Crosses — the most ever in a single action.

question: On the evening of January 22 and through January 23, 1879, a British company of about 150 men — many of them sick or convalescing — held a mission station at a Buffalo River crossing against approximately 4,000 Zulu warriors under Prince Dabulamanzi kaMpande. About 17 of the British were killed, with perhaps 600 Zulus dead. The garrison received how many Victoria Crosses?

context: Lieutenant John Chard (Royal Engineers) and Lieutenant Gonville Bromhead (24th Regiment) commanded jointly. The 1964 film Zulu dramatized the action; the battle has become a controversial touchstone of British imperial nostalgia.

question: On September 2, 1898, on the Nile near Khartoum in Sudan, an Anglo-Egyptian army under Major General Herbert Kitchener defeated a Mahdist force under Abdullah al-Taashi with massed Maxim machine guns. Roughly 10,000 Mahdists died; British casualties: 47. A young correspondent named Winston Churchill rode in the cavalry charge. What battle?
answer: Omdurman — Kitchener avenging Gordon's death at Khartoum thirteen years earlier
choices: Omdurman — Kitchener avenging Gordon's death at Khartoum thirteen years earlier

context: Hilaire Belloc captured the imbalance: 'Whatever happens, we have got the Maxim gun, and they have not.' The campaign secured British control of Sudan and produced Kitchener as British imperial hero through the next two decades.

question: On May 27-28, 1905, in the strait between Japan and Korea, Admiral Tōgō Heihachirō's Japanese fleet of 89 modern ships intercepted Admiral Rozhestvensky's Russian Second Pacific Squadron, which had sailed 18,000 miles from the Baltic. The Russians lost 21 of 38 ships; the Japanese lost three torpedo boats. What was the strategic significance?

First decisive battle won by submarines — but submarines were not yet decisive
First test of dreadnought-class battleships — but the Dreadnought launched 1906

context: The Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905) ended in Japanese victory and the Treaty of Portsmouth (signed in New Hampshire) for which Theodore Roosevelt received the 1906 Nobel Peace Prize. The defeat helped trigger the 1905 Russian revolution.

question: From September 6 to 12, 1914, on a 200-mile front along a river east of Paris, the French and British armies stopped the German advance — saving Paris and ending German hopes of swift victory. The French commander General Joffre famously commandeered Paris taxis to rush reinforcements. What battle?

context: Roughly 263,000 French, 81,000 German, and 13,000 British casualties. The German Schlieffen Plan had failed; both sides dug in. Trench warfare on the Western Front would last until November 1918.

question: From August 26 to 30, 1914, in the lake country of East Prussia, the German Eighth Army under Paul von Hindenburg and Erich Ludendorff encircled and destroyed the Russian Second Army under Alexander Samsonov. The Russians lost 92,000 prisoners and perhaps 30,000 dead. Samsonov shot himself in the woods. The name commemorates an earlier battle. What earlier?
