Mixed results — Pasteur revised his vaccine over the following months in response
context: The Pouilly-le-Fort demonstration was one of the founding moments of microbiology and public health. Pasteur went on to develop a rabies vaccine — first used on the boy Joseph Meister in July 1885. Pasteur was buried in the Pasteur Institute he founded in Paris. The germ theory and vaccination he championed underlie modern medicine.

question: Between 1856 and 1863, an Augustinian friar in the monastery of St. Thomas at Brünn (modern Brno) crossed thousands of pea plants, tracking seven characteristics (seed color, seed shape, pod shape, etc.). His results, presented in 1865 and published 1866 in the proceedings of the local natural history society, showed traits passed on as discrete units in predictable ratios — 3:1 for single traits, 9:3:3:1 for two. Who was he?
answer: Gregor Mendel — whose pea experiments founded genetics but were ignored until 1900
choices: Gregor Mendel — whose pea experiments founded genetics but were ignored until 1900
Charles Darwin — whose pangenesis theory of inheritance lacked Mendel's mathematical precision
Hugo de Vries — the Dutch botanist who rediscovered Mendel's work in 1900
August Weismann — the German biologist whose germ-plasm theory complemented Mendel's later
context: Mendel's paper sat unread for 34 years. In 1900, three botanists (de Vries, Correns, Tschermak) working independently rediscovered the same laws and credited Mendel. Mendel had become abbot in 1868 and stopped his research — possibly because his experiments with hawkweed gave inconsistent results (the plant reproduces apomictically). Modern genetics dates from the 1900 rediscovery.

question: From 1787 until his death in 1833, a Yorkshire-born evangelical MP and close friend of William Pitt the Younger devoted his career in Parliament to ending the British slave trade. He introduced abolition bills nearly every year through the 1790s — defeated each time. In 1807, after twenty years of effort and amid wartime concerns, his Slave Trade Act finally passed both houses. Three days before his death in 1833, Parliament passed the bill ending slavery itself in British territories. Who was he?
answer: William Wilberforce — whose evangelical Christian conviction drove parliamentary abolition
choices: William Wilberforce — whose evangelical Christian conviction drove parliamentary abolition
Thomas Clarkson — the abolition movement's tireless researcher and organizer
Granville Sharp — the lawyer whose 1772 case had effectively ended slavery in England
Olaudah Equiano — the formerly enslaved African whose 1789 autobiography mobilized public opinion
context: Wilberforce was a member of the 'Clapham Sect' — wealthy evangelicals committed to social reform. The 1807 act banned the trade; ships still carried slaves to other nations' colonies. The 1833 act emancipated about 800,000 slaves across the British Empire, with £20 million in compensation paid not to the slaves but to their owners. The compensation loan was finally paid off by the British Treasury in 2015.

question: In the 1860s, surgical mortality from post-operative infection was so high that hospital wards in Glasgow had a death rate after compound fractures of about 45 percent. The 38-year-old professor of surgery at Glasgow Royal Infirmary read Pasteur's papers on fermentation and microbes and reasoned that wound infection might be caused by airborne germs. He began spraying his operating theaters with a dilute solution of carbolic acid. The mortality dropped within months. Who was he?
answer: Joseph Lister — whose 1867 paper on antiseptic surgery transformed surgical practice worldwide
choices: Joseph Lister — whose 1867 paper on antiseptic surgery transformed surgical practice worldwide
Ignaz Semmelweis — whose 1847 Vienna chlorine handwashing had cut puerperal fever decades earlier
Robert Koch — whose bacteriological methods isolated specific pathogens beginning in the 1870s
Florence Nightingale — whose Scutari sanitation reforms had cut Crimean War mortality 1854–56
context: Lister published in *The Lancet* in 1867. Acceptance was slow — German surgeons led, American surgeons including J. Marion Sims resisted. Listerine mouthwash (1879) was originally formulated as a surgical antiseptic, then marketed against bad breath in the 1920s. Lister was made a baron in 1897.

question: On the morning of December 17, 1903, two bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio, made four short powered flights on the windswept dunes near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. The first, by Orville at 10:35 a.m., lasted 12 seconds and covered 120 feet. The fourth, by Wilbur, lasted 59 seconds and covered 852 feet. A 5-man local witness list and one photograph (taken by John T. Daniels) survive. What were these flights?
answer: The first sustained, controlled, powered heavier-than-air human flights in history
choices: The first sustained, controlled, powered heavier-than-air human flights in history
The first manned glider flights — the powered engine had not yet been installed in the airframe
The first powered flights only, but uncontrolled — the brothers added control surfaces in 1904
The first lighter-than-air flights, using helium-buoyancy gas in a wingless airframe
context: The Wrights' key innovation was three-axis control via 'wing-warping,' which they had refined in years of glider tests at Kitty Hawk. The 1903 Flyer is at the Smithsonian Air and Space Museum. The brothers spent years in patent disputes that arguably retarded U.S. aviation; the technological lead passed to Europe before WWI. Wilbur died of typhoid 1912; Orville lived until 1948.

question: In February 1869, a 35-year-old Russian chemistry professor at St. Petersburg University, struggling to organize a chemistry textbook, made cards of all 63 then-known elements with their atomic weights and key properties. He claimed later he saw the pattern in a dream. He published the resulting table in March, organizing elements by increasing atomic weight in rows that wrapped to align similar chemical families in columns. What did he predict?
answer: Existence and properties of undiscovered elements — gallium (1875), scandium (1879), germanium (1886) all confirmed his predictions
choices: Existence and properties of undiscovered elements — gallium (1875), scandium (1879), germanium (1886) all confirmed his predictions
Existence of subatomic particles — electrons, protons, and neutrons — discovered decades later
Existence of noble gases — though they were not added to his table until Ramsay's 1894–98 discoveries
Existence of isotopes — atoms with same chemistry but different atomic weights, found 1913
context: Mendeleev's table left gaps that he labeled 'eka-aluminum,' 'eka-boron,' 'eka-silicon' — predicted weights and properties that turned out remarkably accurate. He was nominated for the Nobel in 1906 but lost by one committee vote; he died early 1907. Element 101 (mendelevium, 1955) is named for him.

question: Between 447 and 432 BC, under the direction of the sculptor Phidias and the architect Ictinus, Pericles' Athens built a marble temple to Athena Parthenos atop the Acropolis. The Doric peripteral structure (17×8 columns) was decorated with a continuous Ionic frieze depicting the Panathenaic procession, metopes showing battles of Greeks vs. their mythic enemies, and a 38-foot gold-and-ivory cult statue. What is the temple called?
answer: The Parthenon — built 447–432 BC as the centerpiece of Pericles' Acropolis building program
choices: The Parthenon — built 447–432 BC as the centerpiece of Pericles' Acropolis building program
The Erechtheion — the slightly later temple housing the cult statue of Athena Polias and Poseidon
The Temple of Hephaestus — the contemporary Doric temple in the Agora, the best-preserved Greek temple
The Temple of Olympian Zeus — the colossal Athens project begun by tyrants and completed by Hadrian
context: The Parthenon survived essentially intact for 2,000 years — used as a Christian church (6th century) and then a mosque under the Ottomans. In 1687, a Venetian artillery shell during the siege of Athens hit gunpowder the Ottomans had stored inside, blowing the roof and central walls out. Lord Elgin removed major sculptures 1801–12 (the 'Elgin Marbles' at the British Museum). The Parthenon Marbles are now claimed by Greece.

question: Sometime in the 8th or 7th century BC, oral epic poetry that had been performed by traveling bards for generations was written down in the Greek alphabet, then spreading from Phoenician sources. Two enormous narrative poems emerged — one about a few weeks during the tenth year of the Greek siege of Troy, focused on the wrath of Achilles; the other about the ten-year homeward voyage of Odysseus. Who is the tradition's attributed author?
answer: Homer — though whether he was one poet, several, or a tradition is the 'Homeric Question'
choices: Homer — though whether he was one poet, several, or a tradition is the 'Homeric Question'
Hesiod — author of the *Theogony* and *Works and Days*, Homer's near-contemporary in Boeotia
Pindar — the Theban lyric poet of victory odes a couple of centuries later
Aeschylus — the Athenian tragic playwright drawing on Trojan-cycle material for *Oresteia*
context: The 'Homeric Question' — whether a single poet composed both epics, when, and how the oral tradition relates to the texts we have — has been argued since the Hellenistic Library of Alexandria. Milman Parry's 1930s field work with Bosnian *guslar* singers showed how oral epic composition could work. The Greeks of the classical period treated Homer as foundational education — Plato's *Republic* discusses his moral influence.

question: Between 264 and 146 BC, Rome fought three wars against the Phoenician trading city of Carthage in modern Tunisia. The first (264–241 BC) was fought largely at sea over Sicily. The second (218–201 BC) brought Hannibal across the Alps with elephants and his fifteen-year campaign in Italy. The third (149–146 BC) was the Roman senator Cato the Elder's project — he ended every speech with 'Carthago delenda est.' How did it conclude?
answer: Carthage was besieged, stormed, and razed; survivors enslaved; the site ritually cursed in 146 BC
choices: Carthage was besieged, stormed, and razed; survivors enslaved; the site ritually cursed in 146 BC
Carthage was forced to pay tribute and accept a Roman governor, surviving as a tributary state
Carthage was partitioned between Rome and Numidia, with the city itself preserved as a free port
Carthage successfully repelled the third Roman assault and signed a treaty of friendship in 146 BC
context: Scipio Aemilianus (grandson by adoption of Scipio Africanus) commanded the final siege. After breaching the walls, the Romans fought through the city for six days. Of perhaps 250,000 inhabitants, 50,000 survivors were sold as slaves. The Romans plowed the site — the salt-sowing is later legend. Caesar refounded Carthage as a Roman colony a century later; it became one of the empire's major cities.

question: In 73 BC, a Thracian gladiator named Spartacus and about 70 companions broke out of the gladiator school at Capua armed with kitchen knives. They overpowered guards, seized military weapons, and fled to Mount Vesuvius. Within a year their numbers had grown past 70,000 escaped slaves and farm laborers — defeating multiple Roman armies sent against them. They marched the length of Italy. How did the revolt end?
answer: Crassus defeated Spartacus in Apulia 71 BC; 6,000 captives were crucified along the Via Appia from Capua to Rome
choices: Crassus defeated Spartacus in Apulia 71 BC; 6,000 captives were crucified along the Via Appia from Capua to Rome
Pompey crushed the revolt in Cisalpine Gaul as Spartacus tried to cross the Alps to freedom
Spartacus successfully crossed to Sicily with the help of pirates and held the island for a decade
Spartacus was killed by his own followers after they rejected his plan to escape Italy
context: Plutarch and Appian are the main sources; Spartacus' body was never identified after the final battle. Pompey, returning from Spain, mopped up survivors and stole credit. Crassus and Pompey reconciled long enough to share the consulship of 70 BC. Spartacus became a figure of leftist revolutionary mythology in the 19th–20th centuries; the German *Spartakusbund* (1916) was named for him.

question: In 48 BC, pursuing his defeated rival Pompey to Egypt, Julius Caesar arrived at Alexandria — to be presented with Pompey's severed head by agents of the boy-king Ptolemy XIII. Caesar wept. He stayed in the city and intervened in a Ptolemaic dynastic war between Ptolemy and his sister-wife. According to legend (preserved by Plutarch), how did the 21-year-old queen first reach Caesar inside the palace?
answer: Smuggled in rolled inside a carpet (or sleeping bag) by her servant Apollodorus
choices: Smuggled in rolled inside a carpet (or sleeping bag) by her servant Apollodorus
Brought through the palace cisterns by her brother's defectors during a banquet
Disguised as a Roman soldier among Caesar's own bodyguard at evening assembly
Climbed the palace wall at night with the help of Caesar's centurion Cornelius
context: Plutarch's *Life of Caesar* gives the carpet story — likely it was a sleeping bag (a Greek *stromateus*) rather than the silk-Persian-carpet image of Hollywood. The relationship produced a son, Caesarion (executed by Octavian in 30 BC). Cleopatra became Caesar's lover, then after his assassination Mark Antony's. After Actium (31 BC) and Antony's suicide, she took her own life with what tradition says was an asp.

question: On July 18, AD 64, a fire broke out in shops near the Circus Maximus in Rome. Fanned by summer wind, it burned for six days, then flared again for three more. Ten of the city's fourteen districts were damaged; three completely destroyed. The 26-year-old emperor Nero had been at Antium when it began; he hurried back. Rumors blamed him for the fire — to clear ground for a new palace. According to Tacitus, on whom did Nero shift the blame?
answer: The Christians — many were arrested, crucified, set alight as torches in his gardens, or thrown to dogs
choices: The Christians — many were arrested, crucified, set alight as torches in his gardens, or thrown to dogs
The Senate — Nero accused several leading families and confiscated their estates after their execution
The Jewish community — Nero used the fire as pretext for harsh measures against the Roman synagogue
The Praetorian Guard prefect Tigellinus — though Tacitus considered the charge a transparent fiction
context: Tacitus' *Annals* (15.44) is the chief source for the Neronian persecution and is one of the earliest non-Christian mentions of Christ — describing how the founder of the sect had been executed under Tiberius by Pontius Pilate. Whether Nero fiddled (or sang or played the lyre) is uncertain — fiddles didn't exist yet, but Suetonius reports he sang 'The Sack of Ilium' in stage costume.

question: On November 27, 1095, at the Council of Clermont in central France, Pope Urban II preached a sermon calling on Western Christendom to march east and rescue the Holy Land from Muslim rule. The crowd, according to chroniclers, broke into shouts of 'Deus vult!' ('God wills it!'). Tens of thousands of fighters, mostly French and Norman, marched east through Constantinople and Anatolia. After three years of campaigning, what did they accomplish?
answer: The capture of Jerusalem on July 15, 1099, followed by massacre of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants
choices: The capture of Jerusalem on July 15, 1099, followed by massacre of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants
The defeat of the Seljuks at Antioch with the help of a 'Holy Lance' but failure to reach Jerusalem
The negotiated handover of Jerusalem under terms allowing Muslim and Jewish residents safe departure
The conversion of the Fatimid caliphate to Christianity and joint rule with Crusader lords
context: The First Crusade was unique in succeeding militarily. The four Crusader states (Edessa, Antioch, Tripoli, Jerusalem) lasted nearly two centuries before Acre fell to the Mamluks in 1291. Saladin retook Jerusalem in 1187. Modern Muslim discourse about the Crusades is heavily shaped by 19th-century European debates; medieval Muslim sources mostly treated them as a Frankish invasion of comparable type to many others.

question: Born in 1181 or 1182 to a wealthy cloth-merchant family in the Umbrian hill town of Assisi, the young Giovanni Bernardone (called 'the Frenchman' by his father) experienced a religious conversion around 1205. He stripped naked in the cathedral square, renouncing his inheritance, and embraced absolute poverty. He preached to birds. In 1224, two years before his death, while in retreat on Mount La Verna, he reportedly received what marks?
answer: The stigmata — wounds matching the Five Wounds of Christ, the first recorded case in Christian history
choices: The stigmata — wounds matching the Five Wounds of Christ, the first recorded case in Christian history
The tonsure of poverty — Francis cut his own monastic crown and renounced his abbot's office
The seven-pointed star — a vision of cosmic harmony recorded by his biographer Bonaventure
The crown of thorns — pressed onto his head in a vision and leaving visible marks for days
context: Francis was canonized in 1228, two years after his death. His order — the Franciscans — became one of the great medieval orders, alongside the Dominicans. The current Pope Francis (elected 2013) is the first pope to take that name. Giotto's frescoes at Assisi (c. 1297–1300) shaped Western religious art toward more naturalistic depiction.

question: Founded in 1119 by nine French knights to protect pilgrims to the Holy Land, the Order of the Poor Knights of Christ and the Temple of Solomon had become Europe's most powerful banking institution by 1300. The French king Philip IV ('the Fair'), heavily in debt to them, ordered the simultaneous arrest of all Templars in France on a Friday — October 13, 1307 — on charges of heresy, sodomy, and idolatry. Confessions were extracted under torture. What followed?
answer: Pope Clement V dissolved the order 1312; Grand Master Jacques de Molay was burned at the stake 1314
choices: Pope Clement V dissolved the order 1312; Grand Master Jacques de Molay was burned at the stake 1314
The order was found innocent by an ecclesiastical court and relocated its headquarters to Cyprus
The Templars went underground and reappeared as the original Freemasons in 18th-century Scotland
Philip IV reversed the prosecution after Clement V threatened him with excommunication
context: Whether the 'Friday the 13th' superstition derives from the Templar arrests is doubtful — the unlucky-day association is documented mostly from the 19th century onward. Templar property was largely transferred to the Hospitallers. De Molay reportedly cursed Philip and Clement from the flames; both died within a year. Conspiracy theories about Templar survival fuel novels from Walter Scott to *The Da Vinci Code*.

question: Between May 1508 and October 1512, the Florentine sculptor Michelangelo Buonarroti — reluctantly diverted from his preferred work in marble — painted the ceiling of the Pope's chapel in the Vatican Palace. The 5,800-square-foot fresco depicts nine scenes from Genesis (Creation, Fall, Flood) flanked by prophets, sibyls, and *ignudi*. The central image of the Creation of Adam — God's finger almost touching Adam's — became one of the most famous images in Western art. Who commissioned it?
answer: Pope Julius II — the 'Warrior Pope' whose other commissions included Bramante's new St. Peter's
choices: Pope Julius II — the 'Warrior Pope' whose other commissions included Bramante's new St. Peter's
Pope Leo X — Julius' Medici successor who would later excommunicate Luther
Lorenzo de' Medici 'the Magnificent' — Michelangelo's earlier patron in Florence
Cosimo I de' Medici — Florence's Grand Duke who commissioned later Vasari decorations
context: Michelangelo painted standing, not lying on his back (a common myth). He returned 1535–41 to paint *The Last Judgment* on the altar wall — figures originally nude, later partly draped by Daniele da Volterra under Counter-Reformation pressure. He died in 1564, age 88, and is buried in Santa Croce, Florence. Pope Paul III oversaw the *Last Judgment* unveiling.

question: In 1513, a 44-year-old former Florentine diplomat — recently tortured (the *strappado*) and exiled to his country estate after the Medici returned to power — wrote a short Latin treatise on the art of governing, designed to win back political favor. He dedicated it to Lorenzo de' Medici (grandson of the Magnificent). The treatise argued that a ruler must learn 'not to be good,' that the ends justify cruelties if the prince is to maintain power. Who wrote it?
answer: Niccolò Machiavelli — whose *Il Principe* gave 'Machiavellian' its meaning and founded political realism
choices: Niccolò Machiavelli — whose *Il Principe* gave 'Machiavellian' its meaning and founded political realism
Francesco Guicciardini — Machiavelli's friend whose *Storia d'Italia* offered a parallel realist history
Baldassare Castiglione — whose *Book of the Courtier* (1528) described the cultivated Renaissance courtier
Giovanni Botero — whose *Reason of State* (1589) later refined the realist tradition Machiavelli began
context: *The Prince* was not published until 1532, five years after Machiavelli's death. The Catholic Church placed it on the Index 1559. Machiavelli's longer and more republican *Discourses on Livy* is in some ways his more profound work. He died in 1527 — the year the imperial mutiny that became the Sack of Rome destroyed the city he had served.

question: On the morning of October 12, 1492, after 36 days at sea from the Canaries, a lookout aboard the *Pinta* sighted land. The 41-year-old Genoese navigator commanding three ships in service of Ferdinand and Isabella of Castile believed he had reached the eastern fringe of Asia. He had actually reached an island in the Bahamas (probably San Salvador / Watlings Island). He was wrong about Asia. He made three more voyages 1493, 1498, 1502. What is his name?
answer: Christopher Columbus — the navigator whose voyages opened sustained European-American contact
choices: Christopher Columbus — the navigator whose voyages opened sustained European-American contact
Amerigo Vespucci — the Florentine navigator for whom 'America' was named in 1507
Vasco da Gama — who reached India by the Cape of Good Hope route in 1498
John Cabot — who reached the North American mainland (Newfoundland) for England in 1497
context: Columbus thought he had reached Asia until his death in 1506. The Norse had reached Newfoundland c. 1000 AD (Vinland sagas; Leif Eriksson at L'Anse aux Meadows). The 1492 contact differed because it was sustained and global in consequence — initiating the Columbian Exchange of plants, animals, microbes, and people that reshaped both hemispheres. His treatment of the Taíno was harsh; he was arrested 1500 by his own subordinates.

question: On September 20, 1519, the Portuguese navigator Fernão de Magalhães left Seville in command of 5 Spanish ships and 270 men, seeking a westward passage to the Spice Islands. They crossed the Atlantic, struggled down South America, mutinied at Patagonia (Magellan executed two captains), found and crossed the strait now bearing his name, were the first Europeans to cross the Pacific, and were nearly starved when they reached Guam in March 1521. Magellan was killed in the Philippines in April 1521. What happened next?
answer: Juan Sebastián Elcano led 18 survivors home in one ship (*Victoria*), reaching Seville September 1522
choices: Juan Sebastián Elcano led 18 survivors home in one ship (*Victoria*), reaching Seville September 1522
The Spanish king recalled the survivors and abandoned the route as unprofitable
Pizarro succeeded in commanding the remnant fleet through the Indian Ocean to the Cape
The Portuguese intercepted the survivors at Malacca, claiming the route violated Tordesillas
context: The 18 survivors of the *Victoria* were the first humans to circumnavigate the globe — a voyage of three years, perhaps 60,000 miles. Antonio Pigafetta, an Italian chronicler aboard, kept the diary that is our main source. The voyage confirmed Earth was round and that the world was larger than Columbus had supposed. Magellan's strait is at the southern tip of South America; the Pacific got its name ('Mar Pacífico') from him for its (deceptive) calm.

question: In February 1519, an ambitious Spanish hidalgo from Extremadura landed on the Yucatan coast with 11 ships, 500 men, and 16 horses. Marching inland, he gathered native allies (the Tlaxcala, enemies of the Aztec Empire) and reached the lakeside capital Tenochtitlan in November. The 33-year-old Mexica emperor Moctezuma II welcomed him; the Spaniards took the emperor hostage. After two years of war, smallpox outbreak, and siege, the city fell in August 1521. Who was the Spaniard?
answer: Hernán Cortés — whose conquest of the Aztec Empire was completed 1521
choices: Hernán Cortés — whose conquest of the Aztec Empire was completed 1521
Francisco Pizarro — whose conquest of the Inca Empire began about a decade later
Pedro de Alvarado — Cortés' lieutenant who later conquered the Maya highlands of Guatemala
Hernando de Soto — explorer of southeastern North America in the 1540s
context: Cortés' translator and consort, the Nahua woman La Malinche (Doña Marina), was central to his diplomacy. The smallpox epidemic that arrived in 1520 killed perhaps a quarter of central Mexico's population in two years — including Cuitláhuac, Moctezuma's successor. Bernal Díaz del Castillo, a foot soldier in the expedition, wrote a chronicle (published 1632) that is one of the great firsthand accounts in any language.

question: On May 23, 1618, three Catholic regents in Prague were thrown from a window 70 feet up in Hradčany Castle by Protestant nobles angered by the violation of religious liberties under the new Habsburg king. They survived the fall (a dunghill, according to Catholics; angels, said the Protestants). The 'Defenestration of Prague' triggered a war that consumed central Europe for thirty years. Roughly what percentage of Germany's population died?
answer: About one-third — perhaps 8 million dead from combat, famine, and disease in German lands alone
choices: About one-third — perhaps 8 million dead from combat, famine, and disease in German lands alone
About one-tenth — concentrated in the Saxon and Bohemian provinces of greatest fighting
Roughly half — including the entire male population of military age in central Germany
About one-twentieth — the war was destructive but its demographic effects have been overstated
context: The war began Bohemian, became Calvinist-Lutheran-Catholic, became dynastic (Habsburg vs. Bourbon), and ended at Westphalia 1648 with Habsburg power broken in the Empire and France ascendant. Gustavus Adolphus, Sweden's warrior king, was killed at Lützen 1632. Wallenstein, the imperial generalissimo, was assassinated 1634. Pieter Bruegel-the-Younger paintings and Callot's etchings document the war's horrors.

question: On January 30, 1649, in front of the Banqueting House at Whitehall in London, King Charles I of England was beheaded on a public scaffold — wearing two shirts so the cold would not make him shiver and appear afraid. He had been tried by a special High Court of Justice for treason against the people of England. The court had been engineered by the New Model Army faction of the Long Parliament. Who led that faction?
answer: Oliver Cromwell — whose Commonwealth and Protectorate (1649–1660) replaced the monarchy
choices: Oliver Cromwell — whose Commonwealth and Protectorate (1649–1660) replaced the monarchy
John Pym — the parliamentary leader of the 1640s, but he had died in 1643
Thomas Fairfax — commander of the New Model Army but opposed to the king's execution
John Lambert — Cromwell's deputy who later opposed the restoration of the Stuarts
context: Cromwell was a Huntingdonshire gentleman who emerged as a parliamentary cavalry commander, then a political force after his New Model Army won Naseby (1645). He ruled 1653–58 as Lord Protector. After his death in 1658, his son Richard could not hold the regime; the monarchy was restored under Charles II in 1660. Cromwell's corpse was exhumed and posthumously hanged at Tyburn.

question: In November 1688, after years of growing Protestant anxiety about Catholic King James II's policies, a fleet of about 250 ships and 21,000 troops under the Dutch stadtholder William of Orange landed at Brixham in Devon. James fled to France (after a tense weeks-long collapse of his support). Parliament declared the throne vacant and offered it jointly to William (James' son-in-law and nephew) and Mary (James' eldest Protestant daughter). What document did Parliament require them to accept?
answer: The Bill of Rights (1689) — limiting royal power and guaranteeing parliamentary sovereignty
choices: The Bill of Rights (1689) — limiting royal power and guaranteeing parliamentary sovereignty
The Act of Settlement (1701) — defining the Protestant succession and excluding Catholics
The Petition of Right (1628) — Charles I's earlier acceptance of limits on royal taxation
The Habeas Corpus Act (1679) — the earlier statute against unlawful imprisonment
context: The English Bill of Rights of 1689 banned standing armies in peacetime without parliamentary consent, the prerogative of suspending laws, and cruel and unusual punishment — language echoed verbatim in the U.S. Bill of Rights a century later. The 'Glorious Revolution' became the founding constitutional moment for Whig political thought; Burke wrote in 1790 of preserving 'the old constitution' of 1689 against French innovations.

question: In 1628, the personal physician to James I and Charles I of England published a thin Latin book of 72 pages titled *Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus* (Anatomical Exercise on the Motion of the Heart and Blood in Animals). Through dissection, vivisection, and quantitative reasoning about how much blood the heart pumps per hour, the author overturned 1,500 years of Galenic doctrine. What did he establish?
answer: That blood circulates through the body in a closed loop pumped by the heart
choices: That blood circulates through the body in a closed loop pumped by the heart
That blood is manufactured continuously in the liver and consumed by the tissues
That arteries and veins contain different fluids — arterial blood carrying spirit, venous blood nourishment
That blood ebbs and flows tidally between heart and tissues, never circulating completely
context: Harvey's argument was decisive: if the heart's stroke volume were 60 cc, and the rate 60 per minute, the body would have to manufacture 540 pounds of blood per hour — impossible. So the same blood must return. Marcello Malpighi later (1661) saw the missing piece — capillaries — with the microscope. Harvey served at Edgehill (1642) and survived the Civil War; he died in 1657.

question: Between 1673 and his death in 1723, a Dutch cloth merchant in Delft who ground his own single-lens microscopes (reaching 270×) reported in a long stream of letters to the Royal Society in London his observations of what he called 'animalcules' in pond water, dental plaque, rainwater, and many other materials. He was the first to see bacteria, protozoa, sperm cells, blood capillaries, and many other microscopic structures. Who was he?
answer: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek — Dutch microscopist who founded microbiology with single-lens instruments
choices: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek — Dutch microscopist who founded microbiology with single-lens instruments
Robert Hooke — English Royal Society curator whose *Micrographia* (1665) named the 'cell'
Jan Swammerdam — Dutch contemporary whose insect anatomy was equally pioneering
Marcello Malpighi — Italian whose microscopic anatomy of capillaries completed Harvey's circulation
context: Leeuwenhoek used compound microscopes too but found single tiny beads of glass gave the highest resolution. His letters were translated by the Royal Society secretary Henry Oldenburg. He never trained a successor; the field went quiet for a century after his death. His original observations of bacteria predate the germ theory by two centuries.

question: Born in Clermont-Ferrand 1623, a French mathematician and physicist invented the mechanical calculator at 19 to help his tax-collector father, exchanged founding letters on probability with Fermat in 1654, demonstrated atmospheric pressure with mercury barometer experiments, and after a mystical experience on November 23, 1654 (sewn into his coat, found there after his death) turned to religious writing. His *Pensées* — fragmentary notes for a planned defense of Christianity — were published posthumously 1670. Who was he?
answer: Blaise Pascal — mathematician, physicist, philosopher, and author of the *Pensées*
choices: Blaise Pascal — mathematician, physicist, philosopher, and author of the *Pensées*
René Descartes — author of *Meditations* (1641) and the *cogito ergo sum*
Antoine Arnauld — Pascal's Jansenist mentor and author of the Port-Royal Logic
Pierre de Fermat — Pascal's correspondent and originator of Fermat's Last Theorem
context: Pascal died at 39 in 1662, of a stomach ailment of long standing. The 'wager' argument in the *Pensées* — that betting on God's existence has higher expected value than betting against — is one of the earliest applications of decision theory to religion. The SI pascal (pressure unit) and the Pascal programming language are named for him.

question: On April 26, 1336, the Italian poet and scholar Francesco Petrarca and his brother climbed Mont Ventoux in Provence — a 6,200-foot peak rising starkly above the surrounding plain — apparently for the sheer pleasure of the view, with no practical purpose. At the summit Petrarca opened his pocket copy of Augustine's *Confessions* at random and read about men marveling at mountains while ignoring themselves. Some historians treat the climb as marking what?
answer: The symbolic dawn of the Renaissance — a new attitude of curiosity about the natural world
choices: The symbolic dawn of the Renaissance — a new attitude of curiosity about the natural world
The end of the Avignon papacy and the beginning of the Great Schism
The earliest documented case of recreational mountaineering as alpine sport
The beginning of the Black Death's spread through southern France
context: Petrarca (1304–74) is the great early voice of humanism — the recovery of classical learning, the celebration of individual sensibility, the cultivation of Latin style. His sonnets to Laura (the *Canzoniere*) set the form for the European love-sonnet tradition. The 'Renaissance' as a periodizing term was popularized by Jules Michelet and Jacob Burckhardt in the 19th century.

question: From 1494 to 1498, a Dominican friar from Ferrara dominated republican Florence after the Medici were expelled. He preached against immoral books, music, paintings, lewd clothing, and luxury — culminating in a 'Bonfire of the Vanities' on the Piazza della Signoria on February 7, 1497 (Mardi Gras), in which thousands of objects were burned. He claimed prophetic gifts and excoriated Pope Alexander VI Borgia. The Pope excommunicated him. How did the friar end?
answer: Hanged and burned in the same piazza on May 23, 1498, after torture and a botched ordeal
choices: Hanged and burned in the same piazza on May 23, 1498, after torture and a botched ordeal
Exiled to France where he died in 1505 of fever in a Dominican house at Lyon
Restored to favor by the next pope, Julius II, and made a cardinal in 1503
Killed in the 1499 French invasion of Italy while preaching against Charles VIII
context: Girolamo Savonarola was tortured to confess fraud, then hanged with two fellow friars; their bodies were burned to prevent relics. Botticelli reportedly threw some of his own paintings into the bonfire — a costly conversion. Machiavelli, who watched the friar's career closely, took Savonarola as a case study in the failure of 'unarmed prophets' in *The Prince* chapter 6.

question: In April 1521, summoned by the 21-year-old Holy Roman Emperor Charles V to the imperial diet meeting at Worms (a Rhineland town), the excommunicated Augustinian friar Martin Luther appeared before the assembled princes, bishops, and the emperor. Asked to recant his books, he asked for a day to consider. The next day, on April 18, he gave his answer in German. According to the standard account, what did he say?
answer: 'Here I stand; I can do no other. God help me. Amen.' — refusing to recant against Scripture and conscience
choices: 'Here I stand; I can do no other. God help me. Amen.' — refusing to recant against Scripture and conscience
'I commit my cause to God and to the Emperor.' — a formal submission to imperial judgment
'I shall return to Wittenberg and consult my colleagues.' — buying time for further negotiation
'The Pope has erred and I shall prove it.' — challenging Rome to a public theological dispute
context: The exact 'Here I stand' line is probably a later embellishment; what is reliably recorded is Luther's statement that his conscience was captive to the Word of God and he could not act against it. Charles V issued the Edict of Worms making Luther an outlaw; Frederick the Wise of Saxony staged a fake kidnapping to hide him at the Wartburg, where he translated the New Testament into German.

question: Published in Latin at Louvain in 1516, this short book by an English lawyer, scholar, and friend of Erasmus described a fictional island commonwealth where private property had been abolished, religious toleration was practiced (within limits), and the citizens worked six hours a day, ate in common dining halls, and despised gold. The work's Greek-derived title means 'no-place.' Who was the author?
answer: Thomas More — Henry VIII's Lord Chancellor, executed 1535 for refusing the Act of Supremacy
choices: Thomas More — Henry VIII's Lord Chancellor, executed 1535 for refusing the Act of Supremacy
Erasmus of Rotterdam — More's friend whose *In Praise of Folly* (1511) was dedicated to him
Francis Bacon — whose later *New Atlantis* (1627) described a different scientific utopia
Tommaso Campanella — Italian Dominican whose *City of the Sun* (1602) was another Renaissance utopia
context: More became Henry VIII's Lord Chancellor in 1529 but resigned in 1532 over the king's break with Rome. Refusing the oath of supremacy, he was beheaded on Tower Hill July 6, 1535. His reported scaffold words: 'I die the King's good servant, and God's first.' Canonized 1935. *Utopia* gave a permanent name to a genre — including its opposite, *dystopia*.

question: On January 13, 532, riots broke out at the Constantinople hippodrome by partisans of the Blue and Green chariot teams against the emperor Justinian's taxes. The mob burned much of the city, including the old basilica of Holy Wisdom. After his general Belisarius slaughtered the rioters at the hippodrome (the Nika revolt cost perhaps 30,000 lives), Justinian rebuilt the church on an unprecedented scale — a vast central dome on pendentives. Completed December 27, 537. Who was the architect?
answer: Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus — Greek geometers who pioneered the pendentive-supported dome
choices: Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus — Greek geometers who pioneered the pendentive-supported dome
Justinian himself — he sketched the plans in consultation with his wife Theodora
Apollodorus of Damascus — though Apollodorus had died four centuries earlier under Hadrian
Bramante and Sangallo — a later Latin-speaking team brought in from Rome
context: Hagia Sophia (Holy Wisdom) was the world's largest cathedral for nearly a thousand years. After Constantinople fell in 1453, Mehmed II converted it to a mosque, adding minarets. From 1934 to 2020 it served as a museum; in 2020 Turkey converted it back to a mosque. The pendentive — a curved triangle transitioning a square plan to a round dome — was a Byzantine engineering breakthrough.

question: In May 325 AD, the Emperor Constantine summoned about 300 bishops to the imperial summer residence at Nicaea in northwest Anatolia to settle a doctrinal dispute that had divided eastern Christianity for years. The Alexandrian priest Arius taught that Christ the Son was created by the Father and therefore not co-eternal. His opponents, led by the young deacon Athanasius, insisted Christ was 'of one substance' (*homoousios*) with the Father. What did the council produce?
answer: The Nicene Creed — declaring Christ 'of one substance with the Father,' condemning Arius
choices: The Nicene Creed — declaring Christ 'of one substance with the Father,' condemning Arius
The Edict of Toleration — formally ending state persecution of Christians
The Vulgate Latin Bible — commissioning Jerome to translate from Greek and Hebrew
The Roman Canon — fixing the books of the New Testament in their current form
context: Arius and two bishops were exiled. The creed was extended at the First Council of Constantinople (381) to its modern form. Arianism survived for centuries among the Germanic peoples (Goths, Vandals, Lombards) who had been evangelized by Arian missionaries. Athanasius spent five exiles during his career as patriarch of Alexandria — 'Athanasius contra mundum.'

question: On June 8, 793 AD, longships landed on Holy Island off the Northumbrian coast. Norse raiders sacked the monastery of Lindisfarne — burning buildings, killing monks, carrying off relics and the wealth accumulated since St. Aidan founded the house in 635. The English scholar Alcuin, writing from Charlemagne's court, said 'never before has such terror appeared in Britain as we have now suffered.' What era did this raid open?
answer: The Viking Age — three centuries of Norse raiding, trade, and settlement across Northern Europe
choices: The Viking Age — three centuries of Norse raiding, trade, and settlement across Northern Europe
The Saxon Wars — Charlemagne's thirty-year campaign to convert the continental Saxons
The Anglo-Saxon Heptarchy — the era of seven competing English kingdoms before Alfred
The Carolingian Renaissance — Charlemagne's revival of classical learning at his court
context: The Lindisfarne Gospels (c. 700) survived the raid, eventually finding their way to the British Library. Vikings went on to settle Iceland (870s), Greenland (980s), and briefly Newfoundland (c. 1000). The English king Alfred the Great defeated the Great Heathen Army at Edington (878). The Battle of Stamford Bridge (1066) is conventionally taken to end the Viking Age.

question: In November 1095, Pope Urban II preached at the Council of Clermont in central France. The crowd responded with shouts of 'Deus vult!' Within weeks, an unauthorized 'People's Crusade' under the preacher Peter the Hermit set out east — to be massacred by the Seljuk Turks at Civetot in October 1096. The disciplined armies of the princes (Godfrey of Bouillon, Bohemond, Raymond of Toulouse) followed. Where did they capture in July 1099?
answer: Jerusalem — taken July 15, 1099, after a five-week siege, followed by a slaughter of the inhabitants
choices: Jerusalem — taken July 15, 1099, after a five-week siege, followed by a slaughter of the inhabitants
Antioch — taken June 3, 1098, after a six-month siege, though Jerusalem fell to the Fatimids
Damascus — taken July 1099 as the closer target, with Jerusalem only besieged the following year
Constantinople — Bohemond's faction broke with Byzantium and sacked it before going south
context: The First Crusade was the only crusade to achieve its stated goal in full. Godfrey of Bouillon was named 'Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre,' refusing the title of king. Four Crusader states (the County of Edessa, the Principality of Antioch, the County of Tripoli, the Kingdom of Jerusalem) lasted nearly two centuries until Acre fell to the Mamluks in 1291. Saladin retook Jerusalem in 1187.

question: After Saladin's destruction of the Crusader army at Hattin in July 1187 and his capture of Jerusalem in October, three Western monarchs took the cross: the German emperor Frederick Barbarossa (who drowned in 1190 crossing a river in Anatolia), Philip II of France (who went home), and the English king who stayed on. Over 1191–92 he won battles at Acre and Arsuf, came within sight of Jerusalem, but did not take it. He made a three-year truce. Who was the English king?
answer: Richard I 'Lionheart' — captured by an Austrian duke on his way home, ransomed at enormous cost
choices: Richard I 'Lionheart' — captured by an Austrian duke on his way home, ransomed at enormous cost
Edward I 'Longshanks' — who had crusaded earlier as prince but reigned 1272–1307
Henry II 'Curtmantle' — who had taken the cross but died before he could depart
John 'Lackland' — Richard's brother and successor who lost most of the French territories
context: Richard's capture by Leopold V of Austria on his return (1192) and his ransom of 150,000 marks (perhaps three years of English royal revenue) shaped the late 12th-century European balance. His brother John ruled while Richard was away — a setting reused in *Robin Hood* legend. Saladin died of fever in Damascus in March 1193, leaving (the chroniclers say) one gold coin and 47 silver ones — having given away the rest of his wealth.

question: In 1202, an army gathered in Venice intending to go to Egypt. Unable to pay the agreed price for ship transport, the Crusaders agreed to attack the Hungarian Christian port of Zara as part-payment. Pope Innocent III excommunicated them but the campaign continued. In 1203, diverting again, the army turned on the Byzantine capital, intervened in a dynastic dispute, and in April 1204 stormed the city. What did they do?
answer: Sacked Constantinople for three days; established a Latin Empire 1204–61; the East-West schism deepened irrevocably
choices: Sacked Constantinople for three days; established a Latin Empire 1204–61; the East-West schism deepened irrevocably
Negotiated a treaty restoring Alexios IV and continued to the Holy Land as originally planned
Withdrew at Innocent III's renewed orders and disbanded without reaching the Holy Land
Conquered the Bulgarian Empire to the north and made it a Crusader feudal state for a generation
context: The Fourth Crusade is one of the worst Western moral failures of the Middle Ages. Centuries-old relics, libraries, and artworks were smashed or carried west. The Latin Empire of Constantinople lasted until 1261 when the Byzantines retook the city, weakened beyond recovery. The Ottoman conquest of 1453 was, in a sense, completed in 1204. Pope John Paul II apologized for the sack on its 800th anniversary in 2004.

question: Beginning around 1387, an English diplomat, customs official, and Member of Parliament — friend of John of Gaunt and son of a London wine merchant — began writing a long Middle English poem about pilgrims traveling from Southwark to the shrine of Thomas Becket. Each pilgrim was to tell two tales going and two coming back. He completed only about a quarter of the plan before his death in 1400. Who was he?
answer: Geoffrey Chaucer — whose *Canterbury Tales* shaped the English literary tradition
choices: Geoffrey Chaucer — whose *Canterbury Tales* shaped the English literary tradition
William Langland — whose *Piers Plowman* is the other great Middle English long poem
John Gower — Chaucer's friend whose *Confessio Amantis* used a similar narrative frame
Sir Thomas Malory — whose *Le Morte d'Arthur* compiled the Arthurian tradition c. 1469
context: Chaucer was buried in what became 'Poets' Corner' in Westminster Abbey — the first poet so honored. His pilgrims (the Knight, the Miller, the Wife of Bath, the Pardoner, the Prioress) became archetypes of medieval English life. William Caxton printed the *Tales* in 1476 — among the first books printed in English. Caxton's edition was reset by Caxton's apprentice Wynkyn de Worde.

question: Beginning around 1397 with the banking foundation laid by Giovanni de' Medici, a Florentine family rose over the following century to dominate the politics, art, and intellectual life of one of Europe's wealthiest republics. Cosimo 'il Vecchio' (the Elder, 1389–1464) and his grandson Lorenzo 'il Magnifico' (1449–92) patronized Brunelleschi, Donatello, Botticelli, Leonardo da Vinci, and the young Michelangelo. Two members became Pope (Leo X, Clement VII) and two became queens of France. Which family?
answer: The Medici — Florence's banker-rulers and patrons of the Italian Renaissance
choices: The Medici — Florence's banker-rulers and patrons of the Italian Renaissance
The Sforza — Milan's mercenary-rulers and patrons of Leonardo's Milanese period
The Visconti — Milan's earlier ducal dynasty patronizing Petrarch a century earlier
The Este — Ferrara's dukes whose court included Ariosto and the young Tasso
context: Florence's golden age peaked under Lorenzo. After his death (1492), the Medici were briefly expelled (1494–1512 under Savonarola and the republican government) but returned. The grand-ducal Medici line ran until 1737. Cosimo's bank financed Brunelleschi's dome and the rebuilding of San Lorenzo; Lorenzo employed Botticelli to paint Venus and Primavera.

question: Born in 1452 in a Tuscan village, the illegitimate son of a notary and a peasant woman trained as a painter in Verrocchio's Florentine workshop. He worked for the Sforza of Milan (1482–99), then in Florence (commissions for the *Mona Lisa* and the lost *Battle of Anghiari*), in Milan again under the French, and from 1516 in France at the court of Francis I, where he died at the manor of Cloux in 1519. He left 13,000 pages of notebooks. Who was he?
answer: Leonardo da Vinci — painter, anatomist, engineer, and notebook polymath
choices: Leonardo da Vinci — painter, anatomist, engineer, and notebook polymath
Michelangelo Buonarroti — Leonardo's younger rival, sculptor and Sistine Chapel painter
Raphael Sanzio of Urbino — papal painter whose *School of Athens* synthesized the Roman High Renaissance
Albrecht Dürer — Nuremberg engraver-painter who twice traveled to Italy
context: Leonardo painted perhaps 15–20 surviving works including the *Mona Lisa* (Louvre), *Last Supper* (Milan, badly deteriorated), and *Virgin of the Rocks* (Louvre, London versions). His notebooks include anatomical drawings (from dissections at Santa Maria Nuova hospital), flying-machine designs, military engineering, and the famous 'Vitruvian Man.' He was left-handed and wrote in mirror script.

question: Between 1509 and 1511, a 26-year-old Umbrian painter recently recruited to Rome painted four large frescoes in the papal apartment (the Stanza della Segnatura) on themes of theology, philosophy, poetry, and law. The philosophy fresco depicted classical sages in a vast vaulted hall — Plato (modeled on Leonardo) gesturing upward, Aristotle gesturing outward, Pythagoras writing, Euclid drawing, Diogenes lounging, Heraclitus brooding (modeled on the older Michelangelo). Who painted it?
answer: Raphael Sanzio — whose *School of Athens* synthesizes the High Renaissance ideal
choices: Raphael Sanzio — whose *School of Athens* synthesizes the High Renaissance ideal
Pietro Perugino — Raphael's master whose earlier Sistine fresco *Christ Delivers the Keys* taught him perspective
Pinturicchio — Pope Alexander VI's apartment painter whose stylistic legacy Raphael inherited
Giulio Romano — Raphael's pupil who completed his master's works after Raphael's death in 1520
context: Raphael (1483–1520) died on his 37th birthday, April 6, 1520, supposedly from a fever after a too-vigorous night with his mistress La Fornarina. The unfinished portion of Vatican commissions was completed by his workshop. Pope Leo X wept; Raphael was buried in the Pantheon. *School of Athens* is reproduced and copied more than perhaps any image of philosophy ever made.

question: Between September 1501 and September 1504, the 26-year-old Florentine sculptor Michelangelo Buonarroti carved a 17-foot statue of the young David from a single block of marble that had been quarried decades earlier and abandoned by two previous sculptors. The figure stands tense and watchful, sling over his shoulder, stone in his right hand, head turned to face an unseen Goliath. Where was the statue first placed?
answer: In front of the Palazzo Vecchio — symbol of the Florentine Republic confronting larger powers
choices: In front of the Palazzo Vecchio — symbol of the Florentine Republic confronting larger powers
In the Duomo, on a buttress facing east — where the original commissioning project intended it
In the Bargello courtyard — alongside Donatello's earlier bronze David from the 1440s
In the Boboli Gardens — moved there decades later by Cosimo I as a centerpiece
context: The David was moved to the Galleria dell'Accademia in 1873 to protect it from the elements. A copy stands on the original Palazzo Vecchio site. Donatello's earlier bronze David (c. 1440s) is in the Bargello — naked, young, almost effeminate, with Goliath's head between his feet. Michelangelo's David transformed the meaning — from triumph after to tension before the battle.

question: Born a Protestant prince of Navarre in 1553, this man inherited claims to the French throne in 1589 amid civil war between the Catholic League (backed by Spain) and the Huguenot minority. He won battles at Arques (1589) and Ivry (1590), but Paris held against him under Spanish supply. To end the war and unite the country, he formally converted to Catholicism in 1593 — reportedly saying 'Paris is well worth a Mass.' He was crowned in 1594. Who was he?
answer: Henry IV (Henri IV) — first Bourbon king of France, author of the Edict of Nantes 1598
choices: Henry IV (Henri IV) — first Bourbon king of France, author of the Edict of Nantes 1598
Henry III — last Valois king, assassinated in 1589, opening the succession
Henry of Guise — Catholic League leader, assassinated by Henry III in 1588
Louis XIII — Henry IV's son, who succeeded him after the 1610 assassination
context: Henry IV signed the Edict of Nantes in April 1598, granting Huguenots civil rights and many fortified towns. He rebuilt the wrecked country (the 'chicken in every pot' promise). He was assassinated by François Ravaillac on May 14, 1610, on the rue de la Ferronnerie in Paris — stabbed in his carriage. The Edict was revoked by his grandson Louis XIV in 1685, driving 200,000 Huguenots into exile.

question: Born in 1596, educated by Jesuits at La Flèche, a French mathematician and philosopher served briefly in armies during the Thirty Years' War, then settled in the United Provinces (Holland) for twenty years, partly to escape French scrutiny. In 1637 he published the *Discourse on Method* in French; in 1641 the *Meditations on First Philosophy* in Latin. The *Meditations* used radical doubt to find one undoubtable foundation. What did he conclude?
answer: *Cogito, ergo sum* — I think, therefore I am — the one certain truth amid universal doubt
choices: *Cogito, ergo sum* — I think, therefore I am — the one certain truth amid universal doubt
*Esse est percipi* — to be is to be perceived — the foundation of Berkeley's later immaterialism
*Tabula rasa* — the mind is a blank slate — the empiricist foundation Locke would develop
*Substantia infinita* — there is one infinite substance — Spinoza's later monist conclusion
context: Descartes founded modern philosophy. The mind-body dualism his *Meditations* defended shaped (and troubled) every subsequent thinker. He invented analytic geometry (Cartesian coordinates). He died in Stockholm 1650 — Queen Christina insisted on philosophy lessons at 5 a.m. and pneumonia took him. He was buried in Sweden, dug up, partly lost; most of him is in Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

question: Published in London in 1651 — two years after the execution of Charles I and during the Commonwealth — this work by an Oxford-trained tutor to the future Charles II argued that humans in a state of nature live in 'continual fear, and danger of violent death' with life 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.' To escape this condition, individuals contract to surrender natural rights to a sovereign whose power must be absolute. Who was the author?
answer: Thomas Hobbes — whose *Leviathan* founded modern social-contract theory in its absolutist form
choices: Thomas Hobbes — whose *Leviathan* founded modern social-contract theory in its absolutist form
John Locke — whose *Two Treatises* (1689) gave a contrasting limited-government contract account
James Harrington — whose *Oceana* (1656) offered a republican alternative
Robert Filmer — whose *Patriarcha* (posthumously 1680) defended the divine right of kings
context: Hobbes lived 1588–1679, dying at 91. He had been mathematics tutor to the exiled Charles II in Paris. The *Leviathan* was burned by Oxford University in 1683. Hobbes' materialism, his refusal of clerical authority, and his absolute-sovereign argument disturbed both Royalists (for being too secular) and Parliamentarians (for being too absolutist). The book's title-page engraving — a sovereign composed of tiny citizens — is one of the most famous in political philosophy.

question: Published in 1759 in Geneva and immediately banned in Paris, Vienna, Geneva, and Rome, a short satirical novella by the most famous French writer of the 18th century followed an innocent young man through war, the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, Inquisition floggings, slavery, and lost loves — all while his tutor Pangloss continues to insist 'all is for the best in the best of all possible worlds.' The book ends with the famous resolution 'we must cultivate our garden.' Who was the author?
answer: Voltaire (François-Marie Arouet) — whose *Candide* satirized Leibnizian optimism after Lisbon
choices: Voltaire (François-Marie Arouet) — whose *Candide* satirized Leibnizian optimism after Lisbon
Denis Diderot — whose *Encyclopédie* (1751–72) is the great Enlightenment reference work
Jean-Jacques Rousseau — whose *Émile* and *Social Contract* both appeared 1762
Charles de Montesquieu — whose *Persian Letters* (1721) was an earlier satirical work
context: Voltaire (1694–1778) wrote *Candide* partly in response to the November 1, 1755 Lisbon earthquake — which killed perhaps 30,000–50,000 on All Saints' Day and shook the Enlightenment's confidence in providence. Pangloss is a caricature of Leibniz' *Theodicy* (1710). Voltaire's grave is in the Panthéon in Paris.

question: Published in Amsterdam in April 1762, a treatise by a Geneva-born French-language philosopher opened with the famous line 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.' It argued that legitimate political order rests on the 'general will' of the people. Within months the book was banned in Paris and Geneva; its author fled to Switzerland and eventually to England (where he quarreled with David Hume). Who was the author?
answer: Jean-Jacques Rousseau — whose *Social Contract* shaped French Revolutionary thought
choices: Jean-Jacques Rousseau — whose *Social Contract* shaped French Revolutionary thought
Voltaire — whose feud with Rousseau dominated French intellectual life for two decades
Adam Smith — whose 1776 *Wealth of Nations* offered a contrasting commercial-society vision
Edmund Burke — whose 1790 *Reflections* attacked the Rousseauian inheritance in France
context: Rousseau (1712–78) also published *Émile* (treatise on education) and *Julie* (epistolary novel) the same year. The 'general will' became a slogan of the Jacobins; Robespierre carried Rousseau's portrait. His autobiographical *Confessions* (posthumously 1782) was the founding document of modern self-revealing memoir. He died in 1778; his remains were transferred to the Panthéon in 1794.

question: From a fixed daily schedule in Königsberg (East Prussia) so regular that neighbors set their clocks by his afternoon walks, a Prussian professor of philosophy revolutionized Western thought between 1781 and 1790 with three massive 'Critiques' — of pure reason, of practical reason, of judgment. His moral philosophy demanded that one act only on maxims that one could will to be universal laws. Who was he?
answer: Immanuel Kant — whose 'categorical imperative' grounded duty-based ethics
choices: Immanuel Kant — whose 'categorical imperative' grounded duty-based ethics
Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel — Kant's successor whose dialectical idealism dominated German philosophy after 1800
Johann Gottlieb Fichte — Kant's immediate successor at Jena, then Berlin
Friedrich Schelling — the youngest of the German idealist trio, ranging from Jena to Munich
context: Kant (1724–1804) never married, never traveled more than 100 miles from Königsberg, and lived a life of intellectual revolution from a quiet study. *Critique of Pure Reason* (1781), *Critique of Practical Reason* (1788), *Critique of Judgment* (1790). The Königsberg of Kant is now Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave. He is buried at the cathedral; the tomb survived WWII and Soviet rule.

question: Born in Edinburgh 1711, a Scottish philosopher, historian, and economist published his first work — *A Treatise of Human Nature* — anonymously in 1739 to little notice (it 'fell dead-born from the press'). His *Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding* (1748) restated the same ideas more accessibly. Famous for arguing that we never observe causation, only constant conjunction; that miracles cannot be reasonably believed; and that reason is 'slave of the passions.' Who was he?
answer: David Hume — Scottish empiricist whose skepticism woke Kant from his 'dogmatic slumber'
choices: David Hume — Scottish empiricist whose skepticism woke Kant from his 'dogmatic slumber'
Adam Smith — Hume's close friend and the author of *Wealth of Nations* (1776)
Thomas Reid — Hume's Scottish opponent and founder of 'common sense' philosophy
John Locke — Hume's English empiricist predecessor whose *Essay* (1689) Hume revised
context: Hume (1711–76) was twice denied a university chair on charges of irreligion. He served as librarian of the Faculty of Advocates and earned his living from his *History of England* (six volumes, 1754–61). When he was dying of cancer, Boswell visited and was unsettled that Hume met death with cheerful Stoic composure rather than Christian fear. Adam Smith's published letter on Hume's death sparked a clerical outcry.

question: Published in 1862 in five volumes simultaneously in Paris, Brussels, London, Madrid, and Leipzig, this 1,500-page novel by an exiled French politician and Romantic poet followed the convict Jean Valjean from his bishop's silver candlesticks through the Paris uprising of 1832. The author had been in exile on the Channel Islands since Louis Napoleon's 1851 coup. Who wrote it?
answer: Victor Hugo — whose *Les Misérables* became the great social novel of 19th-century France
choices: Victor Hugo — whose *Les Misérables* became the great social novel of 19th-century France
Honoré de Balzac — whose *Comédie Humaine* (1830s–40s) was a precursor and rival
Émile Zola — whose later naturalist novels (1870s–90s) extended the social-novel tradition
Alexandre Dumas — Hugo's contemporary whose *Three Musketeers* and *Monte Cristo* were popular successes
context: Hugo published *The Hunchback of Notre-Dame* (1831) earlier. Exiled 1851 after writing pamphlets against Napoleon III, he returned to France in 1870. His funeral procession in 1885 reportedly drew two million people. The Broadway musical adaptation (1980 in French, 1985 in English) became one of the most-performed shows in history.

question: Between May 1831 and February 1832, two French aristocratic magistrates traveled the United States ostensibly to study the prison system on a grant from the July Monarchy. The 25-year-old senior author returned and wrote a two-volume study of American mores, institutions, and culture published in 1835 (volume 1) and 1840 (volume 2). Who was the senior author?
answer: Alexis de Tocqueville — whose *Democracy in America* remains the classic outside study of the US
choices: Alexis de Tocqueville — whose *Democracy in America* remains the classic outside study of the US
Gustave de Beaumont — Tocqueville's traveling companion whose own novel *Marie* appeared 1835
François Guizot — the French statesman whose *History of Civilization in Europe* parallels in date
Hippolyte Taine — whose later *Origins of Contemporary France* (1875–93) was a different project
context: Tocqueville (1805–59) sat in the Chamber of Deputies under Louis-Philippe, served briefly as foreign minister 1849, and wrote *The Old Regime and the Revolution* (1856). His warnings about the 'tyranny of the majority,' the role of voluntary association in American civic life, and the soft despotism of bureaucratic states have made him perpetually relevant. He died of tuberculosis at Cannes.

question: Published in February 1848 in London — on the eve of revolutions in Paris, Berlin, Vienna, and elsewhere — a 23-page pamphlet was commissioned by the Communist League. It opened 'A spectre is haunting Europe — the spectre of Communism.' It announced that all history is the history of class struggles, that bourgeois capitalism creates its own gravediggers in the proletariat, and that the proletarians of all countries should unite. Who wrote it?
answer: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels — whose *Communist Manifesto* shaped 20th-century revolutionary movements
choices: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels — whose *Communist Manifesto* shaped 20th-century revolutionary movements
Karl Marx alone — Engels' contribution was confined to *Anti-Dühring* and *Origin of the Family*
Pierre-Joseph Proudhon — whose *What is Property?* (1840) had argued 'property is theft'
Mikhail Bakunin — whose anarchist response to Marx split the First International decades later
context: Marx (1818–83) wrote *Das Kapital* volume 1 in 1867 (volumes 2 and 3 edited by Engels after Marx's death). The Manifesto was originally not widely read; it became canonical after the Paris Commune (1871) and especially after the Bolshevik Revolution (1917). Marx is buried at Highgate Cemetery, London. The Soviet Union published billions of copies of his work in the 20th century.

question: On New Year's Day 1863, President Abraham Lincoln signed an executive proclamation freeing slaves in those territories then in rebellion against the United States — about 3 million of the 4 million slaves. Limits were political and legal: the proclamation was a war measure, applying only to areas outside Union control. Border states (Kentucky, Maryland, Delaware, Missouri) kept slavery. What constitutional change made abolition final?
answer: The Thirteenth Amendment — ratified December 6, 1865, ending slavery throughout the United States
choices: The Thirteenth Amendment — ratified December 6, 1865, ending slavery throughout the United States
The Fourteenth Amendment — 1868, but it concerned citizenship and equal protection, not abolition
The Fifteenth Amendment — 1870, on voting rights regardless of race, color, or prior servitude
The Reconstruction Act — 1867, a statute rather than an amendment, military government of the South
context: The Emancipation Proclamation transformed the war's purpose. Lincoln's address at Gettysburg in November 1863 made this explicit. The Thirteenth Amendment was passed by the Senate (April 1864) and House (January 1865) and was ratified after Lincoln's assassination. The British abolition of 1833 had paid compensation to owners; American emancipation came through war.

question: From May to October 1851, the first international industrial exhibition was held in Hyde Park, London, in a vast iron-and-glass structure designed by the gardener Joseph Paxton — 1,851 feet long, with 300,000 panes of glass, built in less than a year and removed afterward. Six million visitors saw 14,000 exhibits from around the world. The exhibition was promoted by Prince Albert and the Society of Arts. What was the structure called?
answer: The Crystal Palace — disassembled, moved to Sydenham 1854, destroyed by fire 1936
choices: The Crystal Palace — disassembled, moved to Sydenham 1854, destroyed by fire 1936
The Albert Hall — the later concert venue built in Kensington in the 1860s
The Royal Pavilion — Brighton's earlier oriental-style royal residence under George IV
The British Museum — the earlier 1820s neoclassical building in Bloomsbury
context: Profits from the Exhibition funded the South Kensington museum complex (Victoria and Albert, Science, Natural History). The Crystal Palace site at Sydenham became Crystal Palace Park; the football club takes its name from there. Prince Albert died of typhoid 1861. The international exhibition tradition culminated in the great late-19th-century world's fairs at Paris (1889 Eiffel Tower) and Chicago (1893 World's Columbian Exposition).

question: Between 1857 and 1866, the American businessman Cyrus West Field led five attempts to lay a telegraph cable across the floor of the North Atlantic. The first cable (1858) worked for three weeks then failed; the next attempts ended with cable broken on the ocean floor. In July 1866, the steamship *Great Eastern* (designed by Isambard Kingdom Brunel) successfully laid a working cable from Valentia in Ireland to Heart's Content in Newfoundland. What did this enable?
answer: Same-day transatlantic communication — a 10-day journey reduced to minutes
choices: Same-day transatlantic communication — a 10-day journey reduced to minutes
The transatlantic shipping of perishables — refrigerated steamers depended on telegraphic ordering
The Atlantic telephone service — though telephone signals could not span the ocean until the 1920s
The transatlantic financial market — though London and New York markets had already integrated by 1850
context: Field returned to a hero's welcome in New York. The first transatlantic phone service started 1927 (radio relay). Submarine cable telegraphy reshaped journalism, diplomacy, and global finance. The cost per message dropped from £20 (1866) to a few shillings by 1900. The fiber-optic submarine cables of the 21st century still follow many of the same routes Field's people charted.

question: Between April 1859 and November 17, 1869, the Suez Canal — connecting the Mediterranean and Red Sea across 120 miles of Egyptian desert — was constructed under the leadership of a former French diplomat to Egypt. The opening ceremony involved the Empress Eugénie of France, the Khedive of Egypt, and the Austrian emperor Franz Josef. Verdi was commissioned to write an opera (*Aida*, premiered 1871 at the new Cairo Opera House). Who was the canal's builder?
answer: Ferdinand de Lesseps — French diplomat-engineer who later failed at Panama in the 1880s
choices: Ferdinand de Lesseps — French diplomat-engineer who later failed at Panama in the 1880s
Isambard Kingdom Brunel — British engineer of bridges, ships, and the Great Western Railway
Gustave Eiffel — French engineer whose 1889 tower would become Paris' icon
John Stevens — American who later succeeded with the Panama Canal under Theodore Roosevelt
context: The canal cut the London-to-Bombay sea journey from about 11,500 miles (via Cape) to 6,250 miles. Britain bought a controlling interest in 1875 from a financially strapped Khedive (Disraeli to Queen Victoria: 'It is settled; you have it, madam'). Nationalized by Nasser in 1956, triggering the Suez Crisis. Closed during the Arab-Israeli wars 1967–75. Today it carries about 12% of global trade.

question: From November 15, 1884 to February 26, 1885, representatives of fourteen European nations and the United States met at the German chancellor Otto von Bismarck's official residence in Berlin to negotiate the rules for European colonization of Africa. No African representatives attended. The conference established 'effective occupation' as the standard for colonial claims and recognized King Leopold II of Belgium's personal control of the Congo. What did this initiate?
answer: The 'Scramble for Africa' — within 30 years, 90 percent of Africa was under European control
choices: The 'Scramble for Africa' — within 30 years, 90 percent of Africa was under European control
The end of the African slave trade — though the trans-Atlantic trade had ended decades earlier
The Anglo-Boer wars — though those had local roots in Cape Colony rather than Berlin
The Congress System collapse — though Bismarck's diplomatic order held until 1890
context: The Berlin Conference partitioned a continent that European powers had previously controlled mostly along the coasts. Leopold's personal rule in the Congo (1885–1908) produced one of the worst colonial atrocities — millions dead from forced rubber labor, documented by Edmund Morel, Roger Casement, and Joseph Conrad (*Heart of Darkness*, 1899). Most African states gained independence between 1957 (Ghana) and the early 1960s.

question: During the plague years 1665–66, Cambridge University was closed and the 23-year-old Lucasian Professor's predecessor's student returned to his mother's farm at Woolsthorpe in Lincolnshire. In about 18 months he developed the binomial theorem, the method of fluxions (calculus), the theory of colors (with prism experiments), and the basis of universal gravitation. He never published the famous apple-tree story himself. Who is he?
answer: Isaac Newton — whose 'annus mirabilis' at Woolsthorpe laid the foundations of modern physics
choices: Isaac Newton — whose 'annus mirabilis' at Woolsthorpe laid the foundations of modern physics
Robert Hooke — Newton's Royal Society rival whose *Micrographia* appeared in 1665
Edmond Halley — Newton's later patron who financed the publication of the *Principia*
Christiaan Huygens — Dutch contemporary whose pendulum clock and wave theory of light competed with Newton's work
context: The apple story comes from John Conduitt (Newton's nephew-in-law) and William Stukeley, both recording Newton's reminiscences in old age. Whether the apple actually fell on Newton's head is myth; Newton just said he saw one fall and wondered why it fell straight down. The Woolsthorpe tree (a 'Flower of Kent' apple) still stands; cuttings have been planted at universities worldwide.

question: Born in 1546 into Danish nobility, an astronomer who as a 19-year-old student at Rostock in December 1566 quarreled with his cousin Manderup Parsberg over a mathematical problem at a betrothal feast. They fought a duel in the dark; Tycho lost the bridge of his nose. For the rest of his life he wore a prosthetic — variously reported as gold, silver, or copper alloy. King Frederick II later gave him the island of Hven, where he built the observatory Uraniborg. Who was he?
answer: Tycho Brahe — Danish astronomer whose pre-telescope observations enabled Kepler's laws
choices: Tycho Brahe — Danish astronomer whose pre-telescope observations enabled Kepler's laws
Johannes Kepler — Tycho's German assistant who later derived the three laws of planetary motion
Galileo Galilei — Tycho's Italian contemporary who pioneered telescopic astronomy
Nicolaus Copernicus — Tycho's Polish predecessor whose 1543 work proposed heliocentrism
context: Tycho's island observatory operated 1576–97 — the most accurate pre-telescope astronomy ever done, funded by perhaps 1 percent of Denmark's GDP. He died in Prague in 1601 of a bladder problem brought on (the story goes) by reluctance to leave a banquet to relieve himself — etiquette killed him. His tomb was opened in 1901 and again in 2010; analysis showed no obvious poisoning, despite legends about Kepler.

question: The German polymath Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716) was at the same time a diplomat, lawyer, librarian, and inventor of binary arithmetic. He developed his version of the calculus in 1675–76, published in 1684 in *Acta Eruditorum* — fifteen years after Newton had developed (but not published) his 'method of fluxions.' By the 1700s, English and Continental partisans fought a bitter priority dispute. Who chaired the Royal Society committee that judged the case in 1712?
answer: Isaac Newton — who chaired the committee that judged his own claim and ruled against Leibniz
choices: Isaac Newton — who chaired the committee that judged his own claim and ruled against Leibniz
Jakob Bernoulli — Leibniz's Swiss disciple who was actually on the Continental side
Edmond Halley — Newton's friend and astronomer who later edited the report
John Wallis — earlier English mathematician whose work had influenced both men
context: The dispute embittered both men's later years. Leibniz died in Hannover in 1716 — his secretary the only mourner at the funeral, his patron the Elector having left for England as George I. Modern consensus: both developed calculus independently. Leibniz's notation (dx, dy, integral sign) won out over Newton's; we still use it. Voltaire satirized Leibnizian optimism (the 'best of all possible worlds') in *Candide*.

question: Born 1627, the seventh son of the Earl of Cork — one of the richest men in Britain — devoted his life to natural philosophy. His *Sceptical Chymist* (1661) attacked the Aristotelian four elements and the alchemical three principles, arguing for an experimental, atomistic approach. His 1662 law described the inverse relationship of gas pressure and volume at constant temperature. He helped found the Royal Society (1660). Who was he?
answer: Robert Boyle — chemist and natural philosopher, founder of the experimental approach
choices: Robert Boyle — chemist and natural philosopher, founder of the experimental approach
Isaac Newton — whose alchemical and theological writings filled trunks but were mostly unpublished
Robert Hooke — Boyle's curator-assistant whose own work on elasticity was equally pioneering
Joseph Priestley — the 18th-century chemist who isolated oxygen in 1774
context: Boyle had a German assistant, Robert Hooke, who built the air pump for the gas experiments. Boyle was deeply religious — he founded the Boyle Lectures (still running) for the defense of Christianity against atheism. He never married. He died 1691 within a few days of his sister Katherine, with whom he had shared a London house. His will established the lectures and funded translations of the Bible into Irish and Turkish.

question: Beginning in 1751 and continuing for twenty-one years through repeated suppressions, smuggled volumes, and the loss of his chief co-editor Jean d'Alembert in 1759, the chief editor of a 28-volume *Encyclopédie* assembled articles from around 150 contributors. The work aimed to gather all secular knowledge and to teach skepticism toward authority. Subscribers included royal households and serfs' children at the village priest's bookshelf. Who was the chief editor?
answer: Denis Diderot — whose *Encyclopédie* became the great reference work of the Enlightenment
choices: Denis Diderot — whose *Encyclopédie* became the great reference work of the Enlightenment
Voltaire — who contributed entries on philosophy and history but did not edit
Jean-Jacques Rousseau — who contributed entries on music and political economy before quarreling with Diderot
Jean Le Rond d'Alembert — Diderot's co-editor until he withdrew in 1759 under pressure
context: Diderot (1713–84) was imprisoned at Vincennes 1749 for *Letter on the Blind*. Catherine the Great of Russia bought his library while letting him keep the books for life and pay him as 'librarian.' He visited her in St. Petersburg 1773–74.
