Diderot's *Rameau's Nephew* (written 1761, published posthumously in German translation by Goethe 1805, then in French 1821) is one of the strangest and most original dialogues of the century.

question: Around 387 BC, the Athenian philosopher Plato — having spent twelve years traveling after Socrates' execution in 399 BC — bought a grove sacred to the hero Academus on the outskirts of Athens and founded an institution of philosophical inquiry that would survive in some form for over 900 years until Justinian closed it in 529 AD. There he wrote dialogues including the *Republic*, which argued that justice in the city mirrors justice in the soul, and that philosophers should rule. What is the institution called?
answer: The Academy — the first sustained Western philosophical institution
choices: The Academy — the first sustained Western philosophical institution
The Lyceum — the institution Aristotle founded after Plato's death in 347 BC
The Stoa — the painted porch where Zeno would later teach Stoicism
The Garden — Epicurus' commune founded a generation later in 306 BC
context: Plato's pupils included Aristotle (who arrived at 17 and stayed 20 years) and Eudoxus, who developed the theory of proportions used in Euclid Book V. The Academy went through skeptical (Middle Academy) and Neoplatonic phases over its 900-year history. The English word 'academy' descends from it.

question: Born in Stagira in northern Greece in 384 BC, the son of a court physician at the Macedonian court joined Plato's Academy at 17 and stayed twenty years. After Plato's death in 347 BC, he traveled, then in 343 BC was hired by King Philip of Macedon to tutor his 13-year-old son. The pupil would conquer the Persian Empire within twenty years. In 335 BC, the philosopher returned to Athens and founded his own school in a grove sacred to Apollo Lyceios. Who was the tutor?
answer: Aristotle — whose Lyceum founded biology, logic, ethics, politics, and physics as systematic studies
choices: Aristotle — whose Lyceum founded biology, logic, ethics, politics, and physics as systematic studies
Theophrastus — Aristotle's successor as head of the Lyceum and author of *Characters*
Speusippus — Plato's nephew and immediate successor as head of the Academy
Xenocrates — third head of the Academy, contemporary with Aristotle's tutoring of Alexander
context: Aristotle's works as we have them are lecture notes, not finished books — the lost dialogues were considered his polished work in antiquity. After Alexander's death (323 BC), anti-Macedonian feeling drove Aristotle from Athens 'so the Athenians may not sin twice against philosophy' (Socrates had been first). He died in Chalcis 322 BC. His logic dominated Western thought until the 19th century.

question: From 431 to 404 BC, two coalitions of Greek city-states — the Athenian-led Delian League and the Spartan-led Peloponnesian League — fought a war that ended Athens' Golden Age. A failed Athenian expedition to Sicily 415–13 BC was disastrous. An Athenian general exiled for failure at Amphipolis (424 BC) wrote a history of the war — never finished, breaking off mid-sentence in 411 BC. Who was the historian?
answer: Thucydides — whose *History of the Peloponnesian War* founded political history
choices: Thucydides — whose *History of the Peloponnesian War* founded political history
Herodotus — whose *Histories* had covered the earlier Greco-Persian wars
Xenophon — whose *Hellenica* continued Thucydides' history from 411 BC onward
Plutarch — whose *Parallel Lives* gave biographical portraits of Greek and Roman figures
context: Thucydides' funeral oration of Pericles, the plague of Athens (430 BC), and the Melian Dialogue ('the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must') remain canonical texts. The war ended with Athens' walls torn down and the imposition of an oligarchy. Sparta won — but Macedon and Persia profited. Thucydides explicitly distinguished his work from Herodotus' looser narrative method.

question: By 326 BC, the 30-year-old Alexander had defeated Darius III at Issus and Gaugamela, taken Persepolis, marched through Bactria and across the Hindu Kush, and crossed the Indus into the Punjab. At the Hydaspes River (modern Jhelum) he defeated King Porus and his war elephants. He pressed east toward the Ganges. At what river did his exhausted soldiers refuse to continue?
answer: The Hyphasis (modern Beas River) — the easternmost point of his conquests
choices: The Hyphasis (modern Beas River) — the easternmost point of his conquests
The Indus itself — at the city of Multan after the crossing of the river
The Oxus (modern Amu Darya) — back in Bactria before his Indian campaign began
The Ganges — after a final battle against the Nanda Empire of Magadha
context: Alexander's army turned back at the Hyphasis. The retreat through the Gedrosian desert killed thousands. Alexander reached Babylon in 324 BC and died there of fever (or poison, or alcohol — debated) in June 323 BC, age 32. His empire was divided among his generals (the Diadochi) into Hellenistic kingdoms — the Ptolemies in Egypt, the Seleucids in Asia, the Antigonids in Macedon.

question: In October 202 BC, on a plain near the town of Zama in what is now Tunisia, two Roman legions and Numidian cavalry under King Masinissa met Hannibal's army returning from sixteen years' campaign in Italy. Roman cavalry under Masinissa drove off the Carthaginian horse and returned at a critical moment to take Hannibal's infantry in the rear. The battle ended the Second Punic War. Who commanded the Romans?
answer: Scipio Africanus — who had studied Hannibal's tactics in years of campaigning in Spain
choices: Scipio Africanus — who had studied Hannibal's tactics in years of campaigning in Spain
Quintus Fabius Maximus — the 'delayer' whose strategy of avoidance had restored Roman strength
Marcellus — Roman commander who had captured Syracuse in 212 BC
Lucius Aemilius Paullus — the consul killed at Cannae in 216 BC
context: Hannibal escaped Zama and lived another twenty years, eventually advising the Seleucid Antiochus III against Rome. Pursued, he poisoned himself c. 183 BC. Scipio Africanus, accused of corruption later in life by Cato the Elder, withdrew to his country estate. He died in 183 BC, the same year as Hannibal. The Second Punic War made Rome the dominant Mediterranean power for the next 600 years.

question: Roman emperor from 98 to 117 AD, the first emperor born outside Italy (in Spain), this ruler led the empire to its greatest territorial extent. His two Dacian Wars (101–102, 105–106) conquered modern Romania, taking enormous gold and silver from King Decebalus' treasury. Funds paid for a forum, a market, a column, and the relief of Roman debts. His column in Rome shows the war in 155 spiraling reliefs. Who was he?
answer: Trajan — declared *optimus princeps* (best emperor) by a grateful Senate
choices: Trajan — declared *optimus princeps* (best emperor) by a grateful Senate
Hadrian — Trajan's successor who consolidated rather than expanded the frontiers
Antoninus Pius — Hadrian's successor whose reign was famously peaceful
Marcus Aurelius — last of the 'Five Good Emperors,' whose *Meditations* survive
context: Trajan died in Cilicia (modern Turkey) in 117 AD, returning from a Parthian campaign that had briefly added Mesopotamia to the empire (Hadrian abandoned it). His ashes were placed in the base of his column — the only Roman emperor known to have been so honored. Trajan's column survives intact in Rome, its 30-meter spiral relief one of the most extraordinary documents of ancient warfare.

question: On May 11, 330 AD, after six years of construction, the emperor Constantine dedicated a new imperial capital at the ancient Greek colony of Byzantium on the Bosphorus. The site straddled Europe and Asia, controlled the Black Sea trade, was easily defensible, and was free of Rome's pagan associations. The city was provided with its own Senate, churches, fora, and (taking statues from older cities) art treasures. What did Constantine name it?
answer: New Rome — formally — though it came to be called Constantinople ('Constantine's City')
choices: New Rome — formally — though it came to be called Constantinople ('Constantine's City')
Augusta Constantia — a name combining the imperial Augustan tradition with Constantine's family
Byzantium — the city kept its old Greek name throughout the imperial period
Constantia Sacra — a sacral name reflecting the increasingly Christian character of the empire
context: Constantinople became the eastern (and ultimately the only surviving) Roman capital. It fell to Mehmed II in 1453 after 1,123 years from Constantine's founding. The Ottoman Turks renamed it Istanbul (from the Greek *eis tin polin*, 'to the city'); both names were used for centuries. The 'Byzantine Empire' is a modern term — contemporaries called themselves Romans (Romaioi).

question: On July 16, 1054, the cardinal-legate Humbert of Silva Candida — representing Pope Leo IX (recently dead) — placed a bull of excommunication against the patriarch of Constantinople Michael Cerularius on the altar of Hagia Sophia. Cerularius reciprocated. The break followed centuries of growing distance over theological (the *filioque* clause in the Creed), liturgical (leavened vs. unleavened bread), and political (papal supremacy) differences. What is this called?
answer: The Great Schism — the formal split of Eastern Orthodoxy from Roman Catholicism
choices: The Great Schism — the formal split of Eastern Orthodoxy from Roman Catholicism
The Western Schism — though that refers to the rival popes of 1378–1417 in Rome and Avignon
The Investiture Controversy — the parallel papal-imperial conflict of 1075–1122
The Iconoclastic Controversy — earlier 8th-century Byzantine dispute over religious images
context: The 1054 excommunications were technically against individuals — Humbert and Cerularius — but the rupture proved permanent. Each side claimed the other had introduced innovations. Centuries of attempts at reunion (Lyon 1274, Florence 1439) failed. Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras lifted the mutual anathemas in 1965. The Eastern Orthodox communion today numbers about 220 million.

question: In the 1110s, the brilliant scholastic philosopher Pierre Abélard was teaching at the cathedral school of Notre Dame in Paris when he was hired to tutor the 17-year-old niece of Canon Fulbert. The two became lovers; she became pregnant; he secretly married her. When Fulbert discovered the affair, he hired men to attack and castrate Abélard. Both parties entered religious life — he as a monk at Saint-Denis, she as a nun. They later exchanged letters that survive. What was her name?
answer: Heloise — abbess of the Paraclete and one of the great Latin letter-writers of the Middle Ages
choices: Heloise — abbess of the Paraclete and one of the great Latin letter-writers of the Middle Ages
Eleanor of Aquitaine — queen of France then England, contemporary but later
Hildegard of Bingen — the visionary abbess of the Rhineland, contemporary but in Germany
Catherine of Siena — the 14th-century Dominican tertiary and Doctor of the Church
context: Abelard (1079–1142) was condemned for heresy at the Council of Sens (1140), pushed by Bernard of Clairvaux. His autobiography *Historia Calamitatum* (c. 1132) is one of the earliest in the Western tradition. Heloise and Abelard are buried together at Père Lachaise cemetery in Paris — moved there during the 19th-century romanticism that made them lovers' icons.

question: Convened in November 1215 in Rome under Pope Innocent III, the Fourth Lateran Council was attended by perhaps 1,200 prelates and laymen. Its 70 canons defined Catholic doctrine and discipline more comprehensively than any council since Nicaea. It mandated annual confession and communion for the laity, used the term 'transubstantiation' for the Eucharist, called the Fifth Crusade, and required Jews and Muslims to wear distinguishing dress. What was the council's significance?
answer: The high-water mark of medieval papal authority — Innocent III shaped Christendom as no pope before
choices: The high-water mark of medieval papal authority — Innocent III shaped Christendom as no pope before
The split with the Eastern churches — the council formalized the schism with Constantinople
The condemnation of Aristotelianism — the council banned Aristotle's natural philosophy
The reform of the papacy — the council reduced the temporal power Innocent III had built
context: Innocent III (pope 1198–1216) was perhaps the most powerful medieval pope. He launched the Fourth Crusade (which sacked Constantinople), the Albigensian Crusade (against the Cathars), and the Children's Crusade. The annual-confession requirement of Lateran IV created the medieval penitential system. Innocent died seven months after the council and was buried at Perugia.

question: On December 6, 1273, after celebrating Mass at the Dominican priory in Naples, the 48-year-old Thomas Aquinas stopped writing. His secretary Reginald of Piperno begged him to continue the *Summa Theologica*, especially the unfinished section on the sacraments. According to Reginald's testimony, what did Thomas reply?
answer: 'I can do no more. All that I have written seems to me like straw compared to what I have seen.'
choices: 'I can do no more. All that I have written seems to me like straw compared to what I have seen.'
'My health does not permit it. Pray for me that I may finish in heaven what I cannot here.'
'The next age must complete what I have begun. I have set out the questions; let others answer.'
'I have offended the King of Glory by my pride; let the unfinished sections stand as my penance.'
context: Thomas died three months later, on March 7, 1274, on the way to the Council of Lyon. He was 49. What he had 'seen' — whether a mystical vision, a stroke, or simply burnout from twenty years of nonstop work — is uncertain. His writings already filled what would be many thousand modern printed pages. He was canonized in 1323 and declared a Doctor of the Church.

question: On the afternoon of December 29, 1170, four knights of King Henry II's household — Reginald FitzUrse, William de Tracy, Hugh de Morville, and Richard Brito — rode into Canterbury Cathedral and hacked to death the archbishop in front of the altar of St. Benedict. Six years of dispute between king and archbishop over royal courts' jurisdiction over clergy had culminated in Henry's reported outburst: 'Will no one rid me of this turbulent priest?' Who was the murdered archbishop?
answer: Thomas Becket — formerly Henry's chancellor, later canonized as a martyr
choices: Thomas Becket — formerly Henry's chancellor, later canonized as a martyr
Stephen Langton — earlier archbishop and Magna Carta drafter, though he died of natural causes
Anselm of Canterbury — another archbishop-philosopher, but he died in 1109
Theobald of Bec — Becket's predecessor as archbishop who died of natural causes 1161
context: Becket was canonized within three years (1173). His shrine at Canterbury became the most popular medieval English pilgrimage destination — Chaucer's *Canterbury Tales* dramatizes the route. Henry II did public penance in 1174, scourged by the monks. The shrine was destroyed during Henry VIII's break with Rome 1538 and Becket declared a traitor — the church recovered his cult.

question: From the 1130s through the 1150s, the abbot of the Cistercian monastery he had founded in 1115 in the Champagne countryside was the most influential churchman in Europe. His preaching launched the Second Crusade in 1147 (which failed disastrously). His sermons on the Song of Songs and his *On Loving God* shaped Western mystical theology. He opposed Abelard at Sens in 1140 and won. Who was he?
answer: Bernard of Clairvaux — Cistercian abbot, mystic, and the dominant churchman of his generation
choices: Bernard of Clairvaux — Cistercian abbot, mystic, and the dominant churchman of his generation
Anselm of Canterbury — earlier abbot of Bec and archbishop, author of the *Proslogion* ontological argument
Peter the Venerable — abbot of Cluny, Bernard's contemporary and gentler critic of Abelard
Suger of Saint-Denis — abbot whose 1140s rebuilding of his church launched Gothic architecture
context: Bernard was canonized in 1174 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1830. The Cistercian order he reformed and expanded reached perhaps 700 monasteries across Europe by 1200. His mystical theology emphasizing affective union with Christ shaped later devotion (Bonaventure, Bernardino, Teresa of Ávila). The 'Memorare' prayer is sometimes attributed to him.

question: From December 1545 to December 1563, three popes (Paul III, Julius III, Pius IV) convoked sessions of a general council at the imperial city in the southern Tyrolean Alps. The council clarified Catholic doctrine on justification, the Eucharist, the canon of Scripture, original sin, and the seven sacraments — opposing Lutheran positions — while reforming Catholic abuses (clerical residence, episcopal selection, seminary education). The reforming program is called the Counter-Reformation. Where did the council meet?
answer: Trent (Trento) — straddling imperial and Italian territory, accessible to both sides
choices: Trent (Trento) — straddling imperial and Italian territory, accessible to both sides
Mantua — the original site Paul III proposed but moved due to political complications
Bologna — the brief 1547 relocation due to plague at Trent
Rome — the Pope's preferred site but rejected by the imperial side as too partisan
context: Trent's decrees shaped Catholicism for 400 years until the Second Vatican Council (1962–65). The new Roman Missal of 1570 (the 'Tridentine Mass') was used virtually unchanged until 1969. Trent's reforms produced new orders (Jesuits, Capuchins, Theatines), bishop-residence requirements that reformed Italian dioceses, and seminary education for priests.

question: Born to Basque nobility in 1491, a soldier severely wounded by a cannonball at the siege of Pamplona in 1521 spent his convalescence reading saints' lives. Converting, he became a pilgrim, studied at Paris, gathered six companions who took vows together at Montmartre 1534, and in 1540 obtained Pope Paul III's approval for a new religious order. Their *Spiritual Exercises* (1548) and *Constitutions* shaped Catholic spirituality and education for centuries. Who was the founder?
answer: Ignatius of Loyola — first general of the Society of Jesus (Jesuits)
choices: Ignatius of Loyola — first general of the Society of Jesus (Jesuits)
Francis Xavier — Loyola's Paris companion, missionary to India and Japan
Peter Canisius — German Jesuit whose catechisms shaped Catholic education in northern Europe
Roberto Bellarmine — Italian Jesuit cardinal and controversialist, later canonized
context: Loyola's Jesuits became the Church's leading order of missionaries (Francis Xavier to India and Japan, Matteo Ricci to China, Roque González to Paraguay reductions), educators (founding the modern secondary school), and theologians (Suárez, Bellarmine). Loyola was canonized 1622. Pope Francis (elected 2013) is the first Jesuit pope.

question: In January 1077, the German king Henry IV — recently excommunicated by Pope Gregory VII in the dispute over who could appoint bishops (the 'Investiture Controversy') — crossed the Alps in winter and approached the fortress of Canossa in the northern Apennines, where Gregory was staying. He stood barefoot in penitent's garb outside the gates for three days. Gregory eventually absolved him. What did 'going to Canossa' come to mean?
answer: Humiliating capitulation — Bismarck declared in 1872 he would not go to Canossa
choices: Humiliating capitulation — Bismarck declared in 1872 he would not go to Canossa
Triumphal reconciliation — Henry won the political contest by appearing as penitent
Permanent submission — German kings ever after deferred to papal sovereignty
Excommunication's end — the practice ceased after the Concordat of Worms 1122
context: The investiture controversy continued for another 45 years and was only settled at the Concordat of Worms 1122 — a compromise neither side fully won. Henry IV later deposed Gregory, who died in exile 1085 ('I have loved justice and hated iniquity, therefore I die in exile'). Bismarck used the Canossa reference during the Kulturkampf against the Catholic Church.

question: Convened by the emperor Sigismund and Pope John XXIII (later declared an antipope) in 1414, the Council of Constance had two main tasks: ending the Western Schism (rival popes in Rome, Avignon, and Pisa) and dealing with the Bohemian reformer Jan Hus. Hus, granted an imperial safe-conduct, arrived expecting a hearing. The council seized him, charged him with heresy, and on July 6, 1415, burned him at the stake. What was the consequence in Bohemia?
answer: The Hussite Wars — Bohemian rebels defeated five imperial crusades 1419–34
choices: The Hussite Wars — Bohemian rebels defeated five imperial crusades 1419–34
The Bohemian Brethren — Hussite descendants who emigrated to Saxony and became the Moravians
The Catholic restoration — Bohemia returned promptly to Roman obedience
The Polish-Lithuanian alliance — Bohemia merged with the Jagiellonian crown 1419
context: Hus' Czech-language preaching against indulgences and clerical wealth anticipated Luther by a century. His followers, the Hussites, developed a national-religious identity that survived imperial crusades. The Council of Constance also ended the Western Schism by deposing the three rival popes and electing Martin V (1417). Hus has been a Czech national hero ever since; Pope John Paul II expressed regret for his execution in 1999.

question: From 1378 to 1417, the Catholic Church endured a crisis with rival popes elected by the same college of cardinals. The first dispute came when Roman cardinals elected Urban VI (1378), regretted their choice, and elected Clement VII as antipope (returning to Avignon). The 1409 Council of Pisa, trying to depose both, elected a third (Alexander V, then John XXIII). Each of the three lines claimed legitimate succession. How was the crisis ended?
answer: The Council of Constance (1414–18) — deposed all three claimants and elected Martin V in 1417
choices: The Council of Constance (1414–18) — deposed all three claimants and elected Martin V in 1417
The Council of Pisa (1409) — successfully merged the three lines under Alexander V
The Avignon line's victory — Clement VIII recognized as legitimate by all Catholic powers
The Roman line's victory — Gregory XII's resignation under pressure ended the schism
context: The Great Western Schism (1378–1417) is distinct from the East-West Schism (1054). The crisis weakened papal authority and stimulated conciliarist theories — that general councils have ultimate authority over popes. Martin V's election ended the Schism but conciliarism continued to compete with papal sovereignty into the 16th-century Reformation. Lateran V (1512–17) reaffirmed papal supremacy.

question: On October 25, 1415 — St. Crispin's Day — the English king Henry V's exhausted army, perhaps 6,000 strong (mostly longbowmen, the rest dysenteric men-at-arms), faced a French army at least three times its size on a muddy field in northern France near the village of Azincourt. The English had been marching for two weeks toward Calais after taking Harfleur. The battle lasted three hours. What was the result?
answer: An English victory — perhaps 6,000 French dead including much of the nobility, against ~400 English
choices: An English victory — perhaps 6,000 French dead including much of the nobility, against ~400 English
An English defeat — Henry was captured and ransomed, ending the Lancastrian campaign in France
A draw — both armies withdrew with heavy losses and the campaign continued the next year
A French withdrawal under truce — the Duke of Orleans negotiated safe passage to Calais
context: Agincourt was one of the most decisive medieval European battles. The English longbow on muddy ground devastated French knights. Henry V died of dysentery in 1422 — never completing his conquest of France. Shakespeare's *Henry V* (c. 1599), with the St. Crispin's Day speech ('We few, we happy few, we band of brothers'), shaped English national memory of the battle.

question: Working from the meticulous observations Tycho Brahe had made on Hven and in Prague, the German Lutheran mathematician (1571–1630) struggled for nearly a decade with Mars' orbit. Around 1605 he abandoned the assumption that planetary orbits were circular — held even by Copernicus — and tried ellipses. *Astronomia Nova* (1609) published his first two laws; the *Harmonices Mundi* (1619) published the third (the harmonic law). Who was he?
answer: Johannes Kepler — whose three laws of planetary motion provided the empirical base for Newton's gravitation
choices: Johannes Kepler — whose three laws of planetary motion provided the empirical base for Newton's gravitation
Galileo Galilei — Italian contemporary whose telescopic discoveries Kepler championed
Tycho Brahe — Kepler's Danish mentor whose data made the laws possible but who died in 1601
Nicolaus Copernicus — Polish predecessor whose 1543 *De Revolutionibus* had still used circles
context: Kepler's life was hard — his mother was tried for witchcraft in 1620 (he defended her successfully); three of his children died young; he was driven from Prague by the Thirty Years War. His third law (the period squared is proportional to the semi-major axis cubed) is the foundation of celestial mechanics. He died in Regensburg in 1630, pursuing unpaid imperial salary; his grave was lost in the war.

question: After the 1848 revolution that ended Louis-Philippe's July Monarchy and brought Louis-Napoleon's coup d'état of 1851, the magistrate-turned-author of *Democracy in America* withdrew to his Norman estate to write a different kind of book — a history of how the French Revolution had been prepared by centuries of state centralization. The work appeared 1856 (only the first volume completed before his death from tuberculosis). What is the work called?
answer: *The Old Regime and the Revolution* — Tocqueville's continuity thesis between Bourbon centralization and revolutionary state
choices: *The Old Regime and the Revolution* — Tocqueville's continuity thesis between Bourbon centralization and revolutionary state
*Souvenirs* — Tocqueville's memoir of the 1848 revolution, published posthumously
*Democracy in America volume 3* — though Tocqueville never wrote one
*Reflections on the Revolution in France* — though that was Burke's 1790 work
context: Tocqueville (1805–59) argued the revolution accelerated rather than reversed a centralizing trend already developed under Louis XIV and his ministers. The peasantry's grievances were specific privileges, not 'feudalism' as such. Tocqueville died of tuberculosis at Cannes 1859, leaving the second volume unfinished. His critique of revolutionary mythology has remained influential.

question: Published March 9, 1776, in two volumes by William Strahan and Thomas Cadell in London, this 1,000-page work by a Scottish moral philosopher and former Glasgow Professor of Moral Philosophy used the phrase 'invisible hand' only three times — once in the *Wealth of Nations* (Book IV chapter 2), once in *Theory of Moral Sentiments* (Part IV), and once in his unpublished essay on astronomy. What did the phrase describe in the *Wealth of Nations*?
answer: How the merchant pursuing personal gain unwittingly promotes general prosperity through market exchange
choices: How the merchant pursuing personal gain unwittingly promotes general prosperity through market exchange
How the divine providential ordering of the universe maintains the harmony of the spheres
How the state's planning bureaucracy could coordinate production across the economy
How natural selection drives the evolution of human institutions over generations
context: Smith's argument did not deify markets — he wrote at length about market failures, the need for justice, defense, education, and infrastructure as state functions, and his moral philosophy was rooted in sympathy not self-interest. The 'invisible hand' was less central in Smith's own thought than in 20th-century interpretations. He died 1790 at 67, leaving instructions that most of his unpublished manuscripts be burned (some on jurisprudence survived).

question: Published anonymously in Geneva in 1748 after twenty years of work, this 1,000-page treatise by a Bordeaux *parlementaire* and former president of the *parlement* there compared types of government (republic, monarchy, despotism), the relations between law and physical climate, religion, commerce, and customs, and articulated the doctrine of the separation of legislative, executive, and judicial powers later adopted in the U.S. Constitution. Who wrote it?
answer: Charles-Louis de Secondat, Baron de Montesquieu — whose *Spirit of the Laws* shaped modern constitutionalism
choices: Charles-Louis de Secondat, Baron de Montesquieu — whose *Spirit of the Laws* shaped modern constitutionalism
Voltaire — whose *Letters on the English* (1733) had earlier praised English institutions
Jean-Jacques Rousseau — whose *Social Contract* (1762) gave a more radical account of legitimacy
Cesare Beccaria — Italian Enlightenment author whose *Crimes and Punishments* (1764) followed
context: Montesquieu (1689–1755) drew on his observations of England (where he lived 1729–31) to argue that liberty depended on institutional separation of powers. The work was placed on the Catholic Index in 1751. James Madison, John Adams, and the framers of the U.S. Constitution drew heavily on it. The 'climate' argument — that political character is shaped by geography — fell out of favor but the separation-of-powers doctrine became foundational.

question: In October 1761, in the Catholic-majority city of Toulouse, a 64-year-old Huguenot cloth merchant named Jean Calas was arrested after the suicide-by-hanging of his son Marc-Antoine. Local opinion held that Jean had murdered his son to prevent his conversion to Catholicism. The *parlement* of Toulouse tortured and broke Calas on the wheel in March 1762. The case became a cause célèbre when which Enlightenment figure took it up?
answer: Voltaire — whose *Treatise on Tolerance* (1763) defended the Calas family and won posthumous rehabilitation
choices: Voltaire — whose *Treatise on Tolerance* (1763) defended the Calas family and won posthumous rehabilitation
Rousseau — whose *Émile* (1762) attacked religious intolerance in different terms
Diderot — whose *Encyclopédie* article 'Tolerance' came in earlier volumes
Beccaria — whose *Crimes and Punishments* (1764) attacked torture and capital punishment generally
context: Voltaire (1694–1778) lived at Ferney, just over the French border in Geneva territory. The Calas case became his cause for two years; he wrote pamphlets and worked to get the case reopened. The royal council annulled the verdict March 9, 1765; the family was rehabilitated and compensated. The Calas affair became Enlightenment shorthand for religious fanaticism and judicial murder. Voltaire died 1778; his remains were transferred to the Panthéon 1791.

question: On the early morning of September 2, 1666, a fire began in the bakery of Thomas Farriner on Pudding Lane in the City of London. Driven by an east wind through dry timber houses, it burned for four days. By the time it was checked at Pye Corner near Smithfield on September 5, it had destroyed 87 churches (including old St. Paul's), the Royal Exchange, the Guildhall, and roughly 13,200 houses — about 70 percent of the medieval City. What was the death toll?
answer: Officially recorded at 6 — though modern estimates suggest several hundred mostly poor unrecorded victims
choices: Officially recorded at 6 — though modern estimates suggest several hundred mostly poor unrecorded victims
More than 10,000 — comparable to the previous year's Great Plague though concentrated in days
Around 200 — corresponding to the named victims in parish records of the year
Unknown — no death records were kept due to the destruction of parish registers
context: Christopher Wren designed the rebuilding, including 51 new churches and a new St. Paul's Cathedral (completed 1710). Samuel Pepys' diary describes the fire vividly. The Monument to the Great Fire, designed by Wren and Hooke, stands at the spot where the fire began. The fire actually cleansed the city of plague-bearing rats and is sometimes credited with ending the previous year's Great Plague.

question: On the morning of All Saints' Day, November 1, 1755, a massive earthquake (modern estimates Mw 8.5–9.0) struck Lisbon. The shock destroyed perhaps 40 percent of the city; the subsequent fire and tsunami swept the riverside. Tens of thousands died — perhaps 30,000–50,000 in Lisbon, more in southern Portugal, Spain, and Morocco. Enlightenment philosophers wrestled with the theological problem. Whose famous poem and novella respond to it?
answer: Voltaire — *Poem on the Lisbon Disaster* (1756) and *Candide* (1759) both respond directly
choices: Voltaire — *Poem on the Lisbon Disaster* (1756) and *Candide* (1759) both respond directly
Rousseau — whose response to Voltaire's poem provoked the famous epistolary debate
Kant — whose 1755–56 essays on the earthquake were among his earliest publications
Goethe — whose *Sorrows of Young Werther* (1774) was decades later but evoked the disaster's mood
context: Voltaire's poem rejected the 'all is well' theodicy of Leibniz' *Theodicy* (1710). Rousseau replied that cities and stone buildings were human choices and that the earthquake was nature, not God's judgment. Kant (then 31) wrote three essays for a Königsberg paper trying to explain earthquakes through underground gas accumulation. The Lisbon earthquake is often cited as the Enlightenment's break with optimistic theology.

question: In July 1683, an Ottoman army of perhaps 150,000 under Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha besieged Vienna, which was defended by perhaps 15,000 troops under Count Ernst Rüdiger von Starhemberg. The walls were mined and breached repeatedly through summer. On September 12 a relief army of 70,000 — Austrians, Saxons, Bavarians, and 27,000 Polish hussars — arrived on the heights of Kahlenberg above the city. The Polish king led the largest cavalry charge in history. Who was he?
answer: Jan III Sobieski — Polish king whose Winged Hussars broke the Ottoman line
choices: Jan III Sobieski — Polish king whose Winged Hussars broke the Ottoman line
Karl V Leopold of Lorraine — Habsburg commander who coordinated the relief but was not king
Charles V — Holy Roman Emperor, though that name belongs to the 16th-century Habsburg
Frederick William of Brandenburg — the 'Great Elector,' contemporary but not at Vienna
context: The relief of Vienna on September 12, 1683 marked the turn of the Ottoman tide in central Europe. Sobieski wrote to his wife Marysieńka the morning after: 'Veni, vidi, Deus vicit' — I came, I saw, God conquered. Kara Mustafa was executed in Belgrade three months later. Pope Innocent XI declared September 12 the feast of the Holy Name of Mary in thanksgiving. Vienna would never again face an Ottoman siege.

question: Beginning in 1661 with a hunting lodge his father had built, the 23-year-old King Louis XIV expanded the chateau at a swampy village outside Paris through three major building campaigns (under architects Le Vau and Hardouin-Mansart) until by 1682 his court — perhaps 10,000 nobles, courtiers, and servants — was permanently in residence. The Hall of Mirrors was completed 1684. Louis ruled France for 72 years (1643–1715). What was his motto's claim?
answer: *L'état, c'est moi* — 'I am the state' — though Louis may not actually have said it
choices: *L'état, c'est moi* — 'I am the state' — though Louis may not actually have said it
*Après moi, le déluge* — 'After me, the flood' — but that was Louis XV a generation later
*Cogito ergo sum* — Descartes' philosophical motto, not Louis' political one
*Veni, vidi, vici* — Caesar's, sometimes attributed to Louis in apocryphal collections
context: Louis XIV reigned from age 4 (1643) to death (1715). His revocation of the Edict of Nantes (1685) drove 200,000 Huguenots into exile. His wars (Devolution, Dutch, Nine Years, Spanish Succession) exhausted France. His successor was his great-grandson, Louis XV. Versailles was the model for European royal residences (Schönbrunn, the Winter Palace) and the seat of the French government again 1871–79.

question: Born in Amsterdam in 1632 to a Sephardic Jewish family that had fled the Portuguese Inquisition, a young lens grinder developed philosophical views so heterodox that the Talmud Torah congregation excommunicated him in 1656 with the strongest cherem on record. Living quietly in The Hague, supporting himself by grinding optical lenses, he wrote a metaphysics that identified God with Nature (*Deus sive Natura*) and treated ethics geometrically. The *Ethics* was published posthumously in 1677. Who was he?
answer: Baruch (Benedict) Spinoza — whose *Ethics* offered a rationalist monism rejecting personal God and free will
choices: Baruch (Benedict) Spinoza — whose *Ethics* offered a rationalist monism rejecting personal God and free will
Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz — Spinoza's contemporary who visited him in 1676 and partly responded
Pierre Bayle — whose *Historical and Critical Dictionary* (1697) reviewed Spinoza critically
Pierre Gassendi — earlier French philosopher whose atomism Spinoza modified for his metaphysics
context: Spinoza (1632–77) refused offered chairs at Heidelberg and money from Louis XIV's emissaries. He died at 44 of a lung disease worsened by glass dust. His geometry-style *Ethics* — propositions, definitions, axioms, scholia — is one of philosophy's strangest masterpieces. Persecuted in his own time, vindicated centuries later, admired by Goethe, Einstein, Borges, and many others.

question: On the night of December 16, 1773, after a town meeting at Old South Meeting House had failed to persuade Governor Hutchinson to allow three tea ships to return to England, perhaps 50 men disguised as Mohawk Indians boarded the *Dartmouth*, *Eleanor*, and *Beaver* at Griffin's Wharf in Boston Harbor. Over three hours they dumped 342 chests of British East India Company tea — about £9,659 worth (perhaps $1.5 million today) — into the harbor. Who organized the protest?
answer: The Sons of Liberty — Boston's revolutionary organization, with Samuel Adams as a key figure
choices: The Sons of Liberty — Boston's revolutionary organization, with Samuel Adams as a key figure
The Boston Committee of Correspondence — though the Sons of Liberty did the actual destruction
The Massachusetts Provincial Congress — though it would not be formed until 1774
The Continental Congress — though it would not convene until September 1774
context: British retaliation came in 1774 as the 'Intolerable Acts' (or 'Coercive Acts'): closing Boston port, restructuring the Massachusetts government, and quartering troops. The acts unified the colonies against Parliament and led directly to the First Continental Congress. The 'Tea Party' name dates from the 1820s; participants in 1773 called it 'the destruction of the tea.'

question: Before dawn on April 19, 1775, about 700 British regulars from Boston under Lt. Col. Francis Smith marched 17 miles to seize colonial military stores at Concord, Massachusetts. Warned by Paul Revere and others, militiamen assembled on Lexington Green; the British vanguard under Maj. John Pitcairn ordered them to disperse. Someone fired — historians have argued about who, ever since. Eight Lexington militiamen died. What was the day's outcome?
answer: Colonial militia harassed the British retreat to Boston — 73 British and ~49 Americans killed
choices: Colonial militia harassed the British retreat to Boston — 73 British and ~49 Americans killed
British forces returned to Boston unmolested after destroying the Concord stores undetected
Colonial militia trapped the British at Lexington until Pitcairn surrendered with all his men
The British took Concord without a fight and stayed there, occupying the town for a week
context: The 'shot heard round the world' (Emerson's later phrase from 'Concord Hymn,' 1837) opened the Revolutionary War. The Battle of Lexington and Concord turned a political dispute into armed conflict. Within weeks the Second Continental Congress was meeting and Washington was named commander of the new Continental Army (June 15, 1775).

question: On June 17, 1775, two months after Lexington and Concord, about 1,200 Massachusetts militia under Col. William Prescott had built earthworks on Breed's Hill (overlooking Boston) the previous night. About 2,200 British regulars under General William Howe attacked uphill three times. The Americans repulsed the first two assaults with point-blank musket fire — supposedly told 'Don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes.' What was the outcome of the third attack?
answer: The militia ran out of powder and retreated; British took the hill at a cost of 1,054 casualties
choices: The militia ran out of powder and retreated; British took the hill at a cost of 1,054 casualties
The militia held — Howe retreated, leaving the field as an American victory before reinforcements
The battle ended in a draw — both sides exhausted, with the hill abandoned by sunset
Howe's third attack succeeded with light losses after a flanking maneuver around the redoubt
context: The British 'won' the hill but at devastating cost — about 226 dead and 828 wounded out of 2,400 engaged. American losses were about 115 dead. Howe was reportedly never again willing to launch a frontal assault against fortified Americans. Joseph Warren, president of the Massachusetts Provincial Congress, fought as a private soldier and died at Bunker Hill — one of the great early American martyrs.

question: Published anonymously January 9, 1776, in Philadelphia by Robert Bell, a 47-page pamphlet by an English immigrant who had arrived in Philadelphia only fifteen months earlier transformed colonial debate. It argued plainly — without classical references or legal hairsplitting — that hereditary monarchy was absurd, that George III was a 'royal brute,' and that the colonies should declare independence. It sold perhaps 120,000 copies in three months. Who was the author?
answer: Thomas Paine — whose *Common Sense* and later *American Crisis* shaped the Revolution
choices: Thomas Paine — whose *Common Sense* and later *American Crisis* shaped the Revolution
Samuel Adams — Boston revolutionary whose committee letters had earlier shaped colonial unity
John Dickinson — author of *Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania* (1767–68) but he opposed independence
Patrick Henry — Virginia orator whose 'Give me liberty or give me death' (March 1775) was earlier
context: Paine refused royalties so the pamphlet could be widely distributed cheaply. Combined population of the 13 colonies was about 2.5 million; *Common Sense* may have reached one in five adults. Paine later wrote *The American Crisis* (December 1776, opening 'These are the times that try men's souls') read to Washington's troops before crossing the Delaware. Paine died poor in New York 1809.

question: Between June 11 and June 28, 1776, a five-man drafting committee (Thomas Jefferson, John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Roger Sherman, Robert Livingston) of the Second Continental Congress prepared a Declaration of Independence. Jefferson did the principal drafting, working at a portable writing desk in a Philadelphia boarding house. The Congress voted for independence on July 2; debated and edited the text for two days; and adopted the final version July 4. What is the famous second paragraph's claim?
answer: All men are created equal; endowed with unalienable rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness
choices: All men are created equal; endowed with unalienable rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness
Government derives its just powers from the consent of the governed and may be altered or abolished
We pledge to each other our lives, our fortunes, and our sacred honor in support of this declaration
These united colonies are, and of right ought to be, free and independent states
context: All four phrases are from the Declaration; the second paragraph's opening — 'We hold these truths to be self-evident' — is the most famous. Jefferson's draft had attacked the slave trade specifically; the Congress edited it out. John Hancock signed first as Congress president, in large bold script. The 56 signers risked execution for treason; many lost property; none recanted.

question: On June 14, 1775, less than two months after Lexington and Concord, the Second Continental Congress voted to raise a Continental Army. The next day, after John Adams of Massachusetts proposed the southern colony of Virginia provide the commander to unite the regional war effort, Congress unanimously chose a 43-year-old Virginia planter — a French and Indian War veteran who had been attending Congress in his Virginia militia uniform. Who was he?
answer: George Washington — who refused a salary and led the army for the eight years of war
choices: George Washington — who refused a salary and led the army for the eight years of war
Charles Lee — former British officer who served under Washington but disliked him
Horatio Gates — Saratoga's nominal victor, defeated at Camden 1780
Israel Putnam — Connecticut commander at Bunker Hill, too old for overall command
context: Washington was at the time perhaps the most famous American military figure — known for the 1754 Jumonville Glen affair, the 1755 Braddock expedition, and the defense of the Virginia frontier. He served eight years (1775–83) without pay. After Yorktown he resigned his commission December 23, 1783 — an act George III reportedly called the greatest of his life, since most generals would have made themselves king.

question: On Christmas night 1776 — with Continental Army enlistments expiring in a week and morale collapsing after the disastrous loss of New York — George Washington gave his troops the password 'Victory or Death' and led 2,400 men across the ice-choked Delaware River in a sleet storm. The plan involved three columns crossing at different points; only Washington's main column made the crossing in time. At dawn on December 26, they attacked the Hessian garrison at Trenton. What was the result?
answer: American victory — about 900 Hessians captured (including their commander Rall, dying); 2 Americans killed (frozen on march)
choices: American victory — about 900 Hessians captured (including their commander Rall, dying); 2 Americans killed (frozen on march)
American victory but at heavy cost — 900 Hessians killed against 200 Americans dead in fighting
Hessian withdrawal — the garrison fled in good order before Washington's column arrived
American withdrawal — Washington called off the attack after the other two columns failed to cross
context: Eight days later Washington won again at Princeton (January 3, 1777) — wheeling around Cornwallis' pursuit. The Trenton-Princeton campaign saved the Revolution at its lowest point. Washington's crossing has been painted (most famously by Emanuel Leutze 1851) and studied as a model of operational boldness from a position of desperate weakness.

question: From June to October 1777, the British general John Burgoyne marched south from Canada toward Albany with 7,000 men, intending to cut off New England from the rest of the rebellion. Slowed by terrain, harassed by militia, denied promised reinforcements (Howe had gone to Philadelphia instead), Burgoyne fought two costly battles at Saratoga (Freeman's Farm September 19; Bemis Heights October 7). He surrendered on October 17. What was the diplomatic consequence?
answer: France formally entered the war as an American ally — Franklin negotiated the alliance February 1778
choices: France formally entered the war as an American ally — Franklin negotiated the alliance February 1778
Spain entered the war as an American ally — though Spain only declared war on Britain in 1779
The Netherlands declared independence and joined the American side — the Dutch joined in 1780
Russia mediated a peace treaty between Britain and the colonies — though that was the 1783 settlement
context: Saratoga is conventionally cited as the war's turning point. Horatio Gates technically commanded; Benedict Arnold's aggressive battlefield leadership was decisive. French entry brought naval power, the supplies and money the colonies desperately needed, and the credible threat of conflict in the West Indies that overstretched British strategy. Yorktown four years later closed the war.

question: Between December 19, 1777 and June 19, 1778, the Continental Army wintered at a defensive position about 20 miles northwest of Philadelphia (which the British had occupied). About 11,000 men endured cold, starvation, smallpox, typhoid, and dysentery; perhaps 2,000 died. In February 1778 a Prussian officer of dubious credentials arrived with letters from Franklin and began drilling the troops in European tactics and bayonet use. Who was the Prussian?
answer: Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben — whose drill manual transformed the Continentals into a regular army
choices: Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben — whose drill manual transformed the Continentals into a regular army
Marquis de Lafayette — French volunteer who served at Valley Forge but was not the drillmaster
Casimir Pulaski — Polish cavalry commander who organized the Continental cavalry
Johann de Kalb — Bavarian-born French general killed at Camden in 1780
context: Von Steuben's 'Blue Book' (1779) was the army's drill manual. The Battle of Monmouth (June 28, 1778, in New Jersey) showed the difference — Continentals stood up to British regulars in open battle. Lafayette had arrived 1777 at 19, was wounded at Brandywine, became Washington's near-son. Valley Forge entered American myth as the worst moment endured.

question: On October 19, 1781, after a three-week siege, British general Charles Cornwallis surrendered his army of about 7,000 at the small Virginia tobacco port of Yorktown. He had been driven there from the Carolinas, fortified on the assumption of resupply by sea — but the French fleet under de Grasse had defeated the British relief fleet at the Battle of the Chesapeake (September 5). Washington and Rochambeau had marched 450 miles from New York in secrecy. According to legend, what tune did the British band play at the surrender?
answer: 'The World Turned Upside Down' — though contemporary sources do not confirm it specifically
choices: 'The World Turned Upside Down' — though contemporary sources do not confirm it specifically
'Yankee Doodle' — though that was an American tune, not a British surrender choice
'God Save the King' — the British anthem in defiance of defeat
'Rule, Britannia!' — a defiant naval song amid the army's surrender
context: The 'World Turned Upside Down' story comes from 1828 reminiscences and may be myth. Cornwallis sent his deputy Charles O'Hara to surrender his sword (claiming illness); Washington had his own deputy Benjamin Lincoln accept. The Treaty of Paris was signed September 3, 1783; Washington resigned his commission December 23, 1783; the American Revolution was over.

question: On September 21, 1780, the brigadier general commanding the fortress of West Point on the Hudson River met British Major John André at a clandestine meeting near Stony Point. He had been bargaining for a year — through letters in invisible ink and intermediaries in New York — to surrender the fortress to General Henry Clinton for £20,000 and a British commission. André was captured returning to British lines; documents in his boots revealed the plot. What did the conspirator do?
answer: Escaped down the Hudson to a British warship; André was hanged October 2, 1780
choices: Escaped down the Hudson to a British warship; André was hanged October 2, 1780
Was arrested at West Point and executed at Washington's order before André's trial
Negotiated immunity by revealing the plot to French officers attached to Washington's staff
Fled to Spanish Louisiana with the bribe money and was never recovered
context: Benedict Arnold — hero of Saratoga, of Quebec, of the Connecticut coast — became the synonym for American treason. He served as a British brigadier in Virginia (1781), returned to England 1782, and died in London 1801 unwelcomed by either nation. Major André became a tragic figure on the British side. The phrase 'Benedict Arnold' remains in American English for traitor.

question: Between May 25 and September 17, 1787, 55 delegates from 12 states (Rhode Island sent none) met in secret in the Pennsylvania State House (Independence Hall) in Philadelphia. The original mandate was to revise the Articles of Confederation; the actual product was a wholly new Constitution. The 36-year-old James Madison kept the most thorough notes. George Washington presided. The Connecticut Compromise broke the deadlock between large and small states. What did the Compromise establish?
answer: A bicameral Congress — proportional representation in the House, equal representation in the Senate
choices: A bicameral Congress — proportional representation in the House, equal representation in the Senate
A unicameral Congress — based on proportional representation modified by population census
An electoral college — replacing direct election of the president by Congress
A federal judiciary — independent of state courts and ratified by the Senate
context: The 'Connecticut' (or 'Great') Compromise was proposed by Roger Sherman. The Three-Fifths Compromise on slave-counting for representation came alongside it. The Convention finished September 17, 1787; the document was signed by 39 of 42 delegates remaining (Mason, Gerry, and Randolph refused). Ratification required 9 of 13 states; New Hampshire's vote in June 1788 made it effective.

question: Between October 27, 1787 and August 16, 1788, a series of 85 essays defending the proposed Constitution appeared in New York newspapers — most signed 'Publius.' The series, aimed at influencing New York's ratification, covered the structure of the federal government, separation of powers, judicial review, the meaning of 'faction,' the size of the republic, and the necessity of a strong executive. Who were the three authors?
answer: Alexander Hamilton (51 essays), James Madison (29), and John Jay (5)
choices: Alexander Hamilton (51 essays), James Madison (29), and John Jay (5)
Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and Gouverneur Morris of Pennsylvania
Thomas Jefferson, James Madison, and John Marshall of Virginia
James Wilson, James Madison, and Edmund Randolph of the convention
context: The Federalist Papers (collected in book form 1788) are now treated as among the most authoritative interpretations of the Constitution's meaning. Hamilton's contribution focused on executive power and the judiciary; Madison's (Federalist 10 on factions; 51 on separation of powers) are perhaps the most cited essays. Jay wrote on foreign affairs and the Senate. New York ratified July 26, 1788 — barely; the essays mattered.

question: On April 30, 1789, on the balcony of Federal Hall at Wall and Broad streets in New York City, the temporary national capital, the 57-year-old Virginia planter who had commanded the Continental Army took the oath of office as the first President of the United States — administered by Chancellor Robert Livingston of New York. The oath was reportedly extended ad lib with the words 'so help me God.' Who delivered it?
answer: Washington himself — though whether he added 'so help me God' is contested by historians
choices: Washington himself — though whether he added 'so help me God' is contested by historians
John Adams — his Vice President — administered the oath as Senate President
James Madison — the principal drafter of the Constitution and ally of Washington
Roger Sherman — the senior Connecticut framer, present at the inauguration
context: Washington gave his Inaugural Address to a joint session of Congress, written largely with James Madison's help. He wore a brown American-made broadcloth suit (he had ordered it intending it as a symbol of national manufacturing) and a sword. He was elected unanimously by the electoral college (and again in 1792). He declined a third term — establishing the two-term tradition broken only by FDR in 1940.

question: In 1791, Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton's excise tax on distilled spirits had provoked organized resistance from western Pennsylvania farmers — for whom whiskey was both a cash crop and a substitute currency. By summer 1794, 7,000 armed men gathered near Pittsburgh; federal tax collectors had been tarred and feathered. President Washington called out 13,000 militia from four states and personally rode west at their head. What was the outcome?
answer: The rebellion collapsed without a battle — about 150 arrested, 2 convicted (later pardoned)
choices: The rebellion collapsed without a battle — about 150 arrested, 2 convicted (later pardoned)
A pitched battle at Bower Hill ended with federal victory and 50 rebel dead
Washington negotiated a settlement that repealed the whiskey excise within a year
The rebellion spread to Kentucky and Tennessee, requiring a second federal expedition
context: The Whiskey Rebellion was the only time a sitting U.S. president personally commanded troops in the field. The federal demonstration of force established that federal laws had teeth. The whiskey excise was repealed in 1802 under Jefferson — too late to undo the political damage to the Federalist Party. The Pittsburgh region had been settled largely by Scots-Irish who had distilled whiskey for generations.

question: Published in newspapers in September 1796 — drafted with Hamilton's help, but reflecting Washington's longstanding views — the outgoing two-term president's Farewell Address warned the new nation against three dangers. It urged Americans to cultivate national unity over sectional jealousy, to avoid the 'baneful effects of the spirit of party,' and to steer clear of permanent alliances with foreign nations while extending commercial relations as widely as possible. What did the warning about alliances specifically advise?
answer: Avoid 'entangling alliances' — temporary alliances only for extraordinary emergencies
choices: Avoid 'entangling alliances' — temporary alliances only for extraordinary emergencies
Maintain neutrality between Britain and France permanently as a matter of constitutional principle
Pursue alliance with Britain as the natural commercial partner of the United States
Pursue alliance with France in gratitude for Revolutionary War assistance
context: Washington's 'entangling alliances' phrase is actually Jefferson's 1801 paraphrase; Washington said 'permanent alliances' and recommended 'temporary alliances for extraordinary emergencies.' The Farewell Address shaped American foreign policy from Jefferson's Embargo through the Monroe Doctrine to the early 20th century. The phrase 'spirit of party' became a foundational text on the dangers of factionalism in republics.

question: The presidential election of 1800 ended Federalist control of the federal government. The Democratic-Republican electors voted Thomas Jefferson and Aaron Burr equally (the Constitution did not yet distinguish presidential and vice-presidential votes). The tie threw the election into the lame-duck Federalist House of Representatives, which deadlocked through 35 ballots over six days in February 1801. What broke the deadlock?
answer: Hamilton's lobbying — preferring Jefferson over the unprincipled Burr — flipped enough Federalist votes
choices: Hamilton's lobbying — preferring Jefferson over the unprincipled Burr — flipped enough Federalist votes
Burr's withdrawal — Burr formally requested his electors back Jefferson on the 35th ballot
Adams' intervention — the outgoing president personally lobbied Federalists for Jefferson
Federalist resignation — enough Federalist representatives resigned to break the quorum
context: Hamilton hated Burr; he wrote dozens of letters arguing Federalists should choose Jefferson — a 'man of pretensions to character' — over Burr, a man of 'no principles, public or private.' On the 36th ballot enough Federalists abstained to give Jefferson the presidency. The 12th Amendment (1804) fixed the electoral process. Jefferson called his election 'the Revolution of 1800' — a peaceful transfer of power between political parties.

question: In the closing days of John Adams' presidency, his Federalist Congress created new judicial offices and Adams filled them with 'midnight appointments' on his last day in office. Some commissions were left undelivered when Jefferson took over March 4, 1801. One of the unappointed justices of the peace, William Marbury, sued in the Supreme Court to compel delivery. Chief Justice John Marshall (1801–35) decided the case in 1803. What did Marshall establish?
answer: Judicial review — the Supreme Court's authority to invalidate laws contrary to the Constitution
choices: Judicial review — the Supreme Court's authority to invalidate laws contrary to the Constitution
Federal supremacy — that federal law preempts state law on commerce and taxation
Habeas corpus — the right of imprisoned persons to challenge their detention in federal court
Stare decisis — that federal courts must follow Supreme Court precedent absolutely
context: Marshall (1755–1835) wrote the opinion. He held that Marbury was entitled to the commission BUT that the Judiciary Act of 1789, which would have given the Supreme Court jurisdiction to issue the order, was unconstitutional. The cleverness: Marshall declined power in the specific case but established a far greater power in principle. Judicial review of federal legislation was not exercised again until *Dred Scott* (1857).

question: Between January and April 1803, Robert Livingston and James Monroe negotiated in Paris with the French minister Talleyrand and Treasury Minister Marbois. Napoleon had decided — after the loss of Saint-Domingue to Toussaint Louverture's slave revolt and Yellow Fever — to abandon his American empire and fund his European wars. The American negotiators had been instructed to buy New Orleans for $10 million; Napoleon offered the entire territory for $15 million. What did Jefferson buy?
answer: All of Louisiana — about 828,000 square miles, doubling the size of the United States
choices: All of Louisiana — about 828,000 square miles, doubling the size of the United States
New Orleans plus the lower Mississippi valley to Memphis — about 200,000 square miles
All of Louisiana plus East and West Florida — about 1.1 million square miles total
Just New Orleans — the original $10 million target, plus navigation rights to the gulf
context: The purchase price was about 3 cents per acre. Jefferson, a strict constructionist, wrestled with whether the Constitution permitted the acquisition (no explicit power for territorial purchase); he proceeded under his treaty power and asked Congress for retroactive sanction. Lewis and Clark were sent to explore the territory (1804–06). The purchase remains the cheapest large land transfer of modern history.

question: Between May 14, 1804 and September 23, 1806, an American military expedition of perhaps 33 people traveled from St. Louis up the Missouri River, across the Continental Divide via the Lemhi Pass, and down the Columbia to the Pacific. They wintered at Fort Clatsop (modern Oregon) and returned. The expedition mapped vast unknown territory, met dozens of native peoples, and collected hundreds of plant and animal specimens. Who were the leaders?
answer: Meriwether Lewis and William Clark — chosen by President Jefferson; Sacagawea joined at Fort Mandan
choices: Meriwether Lewis and William Clark — chosen by President Jefferson; Sacagawea joined at Fort Mandan
Zebulon Pike and Stephen Long — both explored the Plains but on later separate expeditions
John Colter and Robert Stuart — Colter accompanied Lewis-Clark, Stuart led a return expedition
Manuel Lisa and William Ashley — leading fur traders of the post-expedition years
context: Lewis (1774–1809) and Clark (1770–1838) had been army officers under Anthony Wayne. The 16-year-old Shoshone woman Sacagawea, married to French Canadian trader Charbonneau, was hired with him at Fort Mandan; she helped translate and guide the western part of the journey. Only one expedition member died (apparently of appendicitis). Lewis committed suicide in Tennessee 1809.

question: On the morning of July 11, 1804, the former Treasury Secretary and the sitting Vice President of the United States met on a ledge below the cliffs at Weehawken, New Jersey — the same site where the former Secretary's eldest son had been killed in a duel three years earlier. Pistols were exchanged; the Vice President's shot hit the former Secretary in the abdomen. He died the next afternoon at age 47 or 49. Who were they?
answer: Alexander Hamilton (killed) and Aaron Burr (the killer) — over alleged insults that destroyed Burr's career
choices: Alexander Hamilton (killed) and Aaron Burr (the killer) — over alleged insults that destroyed Burr's career
John C. Calhoun and James Madison — though they never dueled despite political differences
Stephen Decatur and James Barron — actual 1820 naval duel, decades later
Andrew Jackson and Charles Dickinson — actual 1806 duel; Jackson killed Dickinson, was wounded
context: Hamilton, founder of the Federalist Party and architect of American public finance, had spent years opposing Burr — first for the presidency in 1800, then for the New York governorship in 1804. Burr considered specific Hamilton remarks at a dinner unforgivable. The duel destroyed Burr; he was indicted for murder in two states, fled, was later tried for treason after a Mississippi conspiracy (acquitted), and died obscure in 1836. Hamilton's death made him a martyr.

question: From June 1812 to February 1815, the United States fought its second war with Great Britain — partly over impressment of American sailors, partly over British interference with American trade in the Napoleonic Wars, partly over war-hawk ambitions on Canada and the western Indian-British alliance. The war saw the burning of Washington (August 24, 1814), Fort McHenry (September 13, 1814, inspiring Francis Scott Key's lyric), and the Battle of New Orleans (January 8, 1815). Which president signed the war declaration?
answer: James Madison — whose Republican administration faced disaster early and recovery late
choices: James Madison — whose Republican administration faced disaster early and recovery late
Thomas Jefferson — whose Embargo Act had been the previous response to British and French depredations
James Monroe — Madison's Secretary of State and later president (1817–25)
John Quincy Adams — one of the Ghent negotiators but Secretary of State only under Monroe
context: Madison signed the war declaration June 18, 1812 — Congress was divided, the Federalists opposed it as 'Mr. Madison's War.' The Treaty of Ghent was signed December 24, 1814 — but the Battle of New Orleans (January 8, 1815) was fought before the news arrived. The 'Star-Spangled Banner' was written September 14, 1814; it became the U.S. national anthem in 1931. Andrew Jackson emerged as the popular hero of New Orleans.

question: On December 2, 1823, in his seventh annual message to Congress, President James Monroe — guided by Secretary of State John Quincy Adams — declared that the American hemisphere was no longer open to European colonization. The doctrine had three points: no new European colonies in the Americas; no European intervention in independent American republics; no American intervention in existing European colonies in the hemisphere or in European affairs. What was the immediate context?
answer: Spanish American independence movements — the doctrine warned the Holy Alliance against intervention
choices: Spanish American independence movements — the doctrine warned the Holy Alliance against intervention
British-American rivalry — the doctrine asserted U.S. claims against British Canadian expansion
Russian expansion in the Pacific — the doctrine targeted Russian claims to Alaska south of 51°N
All of the above — Spanish, British, and Russian threats combined to provoke the declaration
context: All three motivated the doctrine. The British actually approved it (they wanted Spanish-American markets open); the Russians had been pressing south from Alaska; the Holy Alliance had been intervening in Spain (1823). The doctrine was rarely invoked for half a century, then revived by Theodore Roosevelt (1904 'Roosevelt Corollary'), and re-applied to Soviet missiles in Cuba (1962). Adams largely drafted the language.

question: In the disputed 1824 presidential election, Andrew Jackson had won pluralities of both popular vote and electoral vote but was denied the presidency when the House chose John Quincy Adams under what Jackson called the 'corrupt bargain' with Henry Clay (who became Adams' Secretary of State). In 1828, Jackson ran again — and won decisively, taking 56% of the popular vote. What did his inauguration symbolize?
answer: The rise of the 'common man' in American politics — mass democracy replacing gentry rule
choices: The rise of the 'common man' in American politics — mass democracy replacing gentry rule
The triumph of New England intellectualism — Jackson's son was a Harvard graduate
The shift of political power from agriculture to manufacturing — Jackson's program was protectionist
The reconciliation of North and South — Jackson, a Carolinian, healed sectional rifts of the era
context: Jackson's inauguration crowd reportedly trashed the White House public rooms during the open reception. His presidency (1829–37) featured the spoils system (political appointments as patronage), the Nullification Crisis (1832), the Bank War, the Indian Removal Act (1830), and the Trail of Tears (begun under Jackson, mostly carried out under Van Buren). The Democratic Party as we know it dates from this period.

question: In 1830 Congress passed the Indian Removal Act, authorizing the president to negotiate treaties moving eastern tribes west of the Mississippi. The Cherokee Nation sued in *Worcester v. Georgia* (1832) and won — Chief Justice Marshall ruled that the state of Georgia could not impose its laws on Cherokee territory. President Andrew Jackson reportedly said 'John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it.' What was the outcome by 1838–39?
answer: The forced march of about 15,000 Cherokees from Georgia/Tennessee to Oklahoma — 4,000 died en route
choices: The forced march of about 15,000 Cherokees from Georgia/Tennessee to Oklahoma — 4,000 died en route
The Cherokees successfully resisted removal and remained on their ancestral lands
The Cherokees were assimilated into the white population by mixed-marriage policies
The federal government paid the Cherokees compensation and the relocation was voluntary
context: The Trail of Tears (a Cherokee phrase, *Nunna daul Tsuny*) was carried out under Jackson's successor Martin Van Buren. Other tribes — Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Seminole — were similarly removed. A minority 'Eastern Band of Cherokees' avoided removal by hiding or by claiming North Carolina citizenship; they still live on a reservation in western North Carolina. The Indian Removal era is now broadly recognized as a moral catastrophe.

question: Between August 21 and October 15, 1858, the two candidates for Illinois U.S. Senator held seven public debates in towns across the state — Ottawa, Freeport, Jonesboro, Charleston, Galesburg, Quincy, Alton. The debates focused on slavery — its extension into new territories, the Dred Scott decision, the Kansas-Nebraska Act, the moral and political character of slavery itself. The challenger lost the Senate race but became nationally famous. Who were they?
answer: Abraham Lincoln (challenger) and Stephen Douglas (incumbent) — preparing the 1860 stage
choices: Abraham Lincoln (challenger) and Stephen Douglas (incumbent) — preparing the 1860 stage
Stephen Douglas (incumbent) and John C. Breckinridge (challenger) — also 1860 candidates
Abraham Lincoln (challenger) and Lyman Trumbull (incumbent) — but Trumbull was the other Illinois senator
John C. Frémont (challenger) and Stephen Douglas (incumbent) — but Frémont was the 1856 Republican candidate
context: Senators were chosen by state legislatures until 1913 (17th Amendment); the candidates were really campaigning for legislative seats. Douglas won the Senate seat. Lincoln's national reputation from the debates positioned him for the 1860 Republican presidential nomination. Lincoln's 'House Divided' speech (June 16, 1858) opened the campaign. The Freeport Doctrine that Douglas was forced to articulate hurt him with southern Democrats — opening the 1860 split.

question: On April 12, 1861, at 4:30 a.m., Confederate batteries under General P.G.T. Beauregard opened fire on the federal garrison of Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor. Lincoln had announced he would resupply the fort but not reinforce it; the Confederates demanded surrender before the supply ships arrived. The garrison under Major Robert Anderson — Beauregard's former artillery instructor at West Point — endured 34 hours of bombardment with no fatalities, then surrendered on terms. What followed?
answer: Lincoln called 75,000 volunteers; four more states seceded; the Civil War began
choices: Lincoln called 75,000 volunteers; four more states seceded; the Civil War began
Border states negotiated a peace conference at Washington that failed within weeks
Confederate forces immediately marched on Washington and seized Maryland and Delaware
The British recognized Confederate independence, citing the Anderson surrender as decisive
context: Anderson hauled down the U.S. flag on April 14, 1861 — and four years and one day later, on April 14, 1865 (the day Lincoln was shot), he raised the same flag back over the recaptured fort. Beauregard later commanded Confederate armies through Manassas, Shiloh, and the defense of Petersburg. The 'first shot' was actually fired by Edmund Ruffin, a 67-year-old Virginia secessionist invited to the honor.

question: On July 21, 1861, the first major land battle of the Civil War was fought near a stream called Bull Run, about 30 miles southwest of Washington, near a railroad junction called Manassas. About 30,000 Union troops under General Irvin McDowell faced about 30,000 Confederates under Beauregard. The Confederates were reinforced by Joseph E. Johnston via railroad — the first major rail-troop movement to a battlefield. Civilians from Washington brought picnic baskets to watch. What was the result?
answer: Confederate victory — the Union army collapsed in panic into Washington; 'Stonewall' Jackson got his nickname
choices: Confederate victory — the Union army collapsed in panic into Washington; 'Stonewall' Jackson got his nickname
Drawn battle — both armies withdrew exhausted and the war went into winter quarters early
Union victory — the Confederates retreated south of the Rappahannock by the end of July
Confederate withdrawal — Joseph E. Johnston pulled back to avoid a costly engagement
context: Thomas J. Jackson earned 'Stonewall' from General Bee, who reportedly shouted 'There is Jackson, standing like a stone wall.' (Whether Bee meant it as praise or criticism is debated — Bee was killed minutes later.) The Union rout was complete; the Confederates were too disorganized to pursue. The North realized the war would not be short. McDowell was replaced by McClellan within a week.

question: On September 17, 1862, after Lee's first invasion of the North had moved into Maryland, the two armies met along a creek near Sharpsburg. About 75,000 Union troops under McClellan attacked about 38,000 Confederates under Lee. The fighting moved from the Cornfield to the Sunken Road ('Bloody Lane') to Burnside's Bridge. Lee was outnumbered roughly two to one but held off McClellan's attacks. What was the casualty figure?
answer: About 22,700 total — the bloodiest single day in American military history
choices: About 22,700 total — the bloodiest single day in American military history
About 5,000 total — light casualties compared to later battles like Gettysburg
About 50,000 total — exceeded only by the three-day battle of Gettysburg in 1863
About 100,000 total — including civilian casualties and surrounding skirmishes
context: Antietam was tactically a draw, strategically a Union victory because Lee retreated to Virginia. Five days after the battle, Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation (September 22, 1862); it would have been politically impossible after a defeat. McClellan failed to pursue Lee's wounded army and was relieved of command in November. The battlefield is now a national park.

question: On New Year's Day 1863, President Abraham Lincoln signed an executive proclamation freeing slaves in those territories then in rebellion against the United States. As a war measure, it applied only to areas outside Union control at the moment — about 3 million of the 4 million slaves. Border states (Kentucky, Maryland, Delaware, Missouri) and Union-occupied parts of Confederate states (most of Tennessee, parts of Virginia) were excluded. What was the moral and military significance?
answer: It transformed the war's purpose to abolition; Britain and France could not now recognize the Confederacy
choices: It transformed the war's purpose to abolition; Britain and France could not now recognize the Confederacy
It freed all slaves throughout the Union immediately and ended slavery as a legal institution
It applied retroactively to all slaves ever held in the United States since 1789
It established federal jurisdiction over slave property throughout the Confederate states
context: Frederick Douglass said Lincoln's proclamation made the war a 'sacred effort.' Slaves in Confederate areas heard about it through informal networks; many escaped to Union lines. About 200,000 African American men ultimately served in the U.S. Army and Navy. The Thirteenth Amendment (ratified December 6, 1865) ended slavery throughout the country.

question: From July 1–3, 1863, the largest battle ever fought in the Western Hemisphere took place at a small Pennsylvania crossroads where Lee's Army of Northern Virginia (75,000) met the Army of the Potomac (97,000) under General George Meade (who had taken command only three days earlier). On day three, Lee ordered 12,500 men under General George Pickett to attack the Union center across an open mile of ground. What is the assault called?
answer: Pickett's Charge — Confederate losses ~50%, marking the war's 'high water mark'
choices: Pickett's Charge — Confederate losses ~50%, marking the war's 'high water mark'
Hood's Texas Brigade — Hood served at Gettysburg but Pickett led the famous charge
Stonewall's Last Stand — though Jackson had been killed at Chancellorsville in May
Stuart's Cavalry Raid — Stuart's late arrival prevented his usual reconnaissance
context: Pickett's Charge included Pettigrew's and Trimble's divisions as well. About half the attackers were killed, wounded, or captured. Lee took full responsibility ('It is all my fault'). Lee retreated July 4 — the same day Grant captured Vicksburg, splitting the Confederacy. Gettysburg cost about 51,000 total casualties.
