Joshua Chamberlain's 20th Maine on Little Round Top (Day 2) became a focal point of later commemoration.

question: On the afternoon of November 19, 1863, President Abraham Lincoln spoke for about two minutes at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery on the battlefield. The 'principal speech' was a two-hour oration by the famous orator Edward Everett. Lincoln's remarks ran 272 words — sometimes given as 268 or 269 because of slight variations in the five known manuscript copies. The speech began 'Four score and seven years ago.' What was the year counted back to?
answer: 1776 — the year of the Declaration of Independence ('dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal')
choices: 1776 — the year of the Declaration of Independence ('dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal')
1789 — the year the Constitution went into effect (the Founders' framing of the Union)
1781 — the year of Yorktown and the effective end of Revolutionary War
1773 — the year of the Boston Tea Party and the start of revolutionary crisis
context: Lincoln deliberately dated the nation to the Declaration of Independence and the proposition of human equality, not to the Constitution (which compromised with slavery). Everett wrote Lincoln the next day: 'I should be glad if I could flatter myself that I came as near to the central idea of the occasion in two hours as you did in two minutes.' The 'last best hope of earth' phrase was from Lincoln's 1862 message to Congress.

question: On Palm Sunday, April 9, 1865, in the parlor of a private home in the central Virginia village of Appomattox Court House, the commanders of the Army of Northern Virginia and the Army of the Potomac met. Lee was 58, in his best uniform; Grant was 42, in a mud-spattered private's uniform with his lieutenant general's stars sewn on the shoulders. The terms allowed Confederate officers to keep their sidearms and any private horses. What did Grant reportedly tell his cheering troops afterward?
answer: 'The war is over; the rebels are our countrymen again' — and he stopped the celebratory artillery salute
choices: 'The war is over; the rebels are our countrymen again' — and he stopped the celebratory artillery salute
'Bring me my map — we must finish what we have begun before Johnston can escape with his army'
'Telegraph the President that Lee is taken — he must know within the hour' — though Lincoln had not yet been told
'Strike the colors of the Confederacy and burn them all' — though no such order was given
context: Grant's magnanimity at Appomattox — preserving the rations of Lee's starving men, forbidding triumphant celebration — became a model for postwar reconciliation. Johnston's army surrendered to Sherman in North Carolina April 26. Jefferson Davis was captured May 10. Lincoln was assassinated April 14 — five days after Appomattox. The Civil War cost perhaps 750,000 dead — more than all other American wars combined until Vietnam.

question: On Good Friday, April 14, 1865 — five days after Lee's surrender at Appomattox — President Lincoln and Mrs. Lincoln attended a performance of *Our American Cousin* at Ford's Theatre in Washington. During Act III, around 10:15 p.m., a Confederate sympathizer and well-known actor stepped into the President's box, shot Lincoln once in the back of the head with a single-shot derringer, stabbed Major Henry Rathbone, and jumped to the stage. He shouted 'Sic semper tyrannis!' before escaping. Who was he?
answer: John Wilkes Booth — actor and Confederate sympathizer, killed in a Virginia barn April 26
choices: John Wilkes Booth — actor and Confederate sympathizer, killed in a Virginia barn April 26
George Atzerodt — co-conspirator assigned to kill Vice President Andrew Johnson; he failed
Lewis Powell — co-conspirator who simultaneously attacked Secretary of State Seward
John Surratt — co-conspirator who escaped to Italy and was tried later
context: Lincoln died at 7:22 a.m. on April 15, 1865, at the Petersen House across the street from Ford's. Edwin Stanton: 'Now he belongs to the ages.' Booth was found in a Virginia barn April 26 and killed (either shot by Sergeant Boston Corbett or self-inflicted). Four co-conspirators were hanged July 7, 1865 — including Mary Surratt, the first woman executed by the U.S. federal government. Sic semper tyrannis ('thus always to tyrants') is Virginia's state motto.

question: After failed direct assaults and a winter spent rerouting canals through swamps, General Ulysses S. Grant marched his army down the west bank of the Mississippi River, crossed below Vicksburg on April 30, 1863, defeated Confederate forces in five battles in 17 days, and besieged the city from May 18. Vicksburg, perched on bluffs over a hairpin bend of the river, was the last major Confederate stronghold controlling the Mississippi. On what date did the city surrender?
answer: July 4, 1863 — the day after Pickett's Charge at Gettysburg, splitting the Confederacy in two
choices: July 4, 1863 — the day after Pickett's Charge at Gettysburg, splitting the Confederacy in two
July 7, 1863 — three days after Lee retreated from Gettysburg, in coordinated Union actions
August 14, 1863 — after a six-week siege that exhausted both food supplies and Confederate morale
May 31, 1863 — early surrender after a single week of Union direct assault on the bluffs
context: Grant accepted the surrender of about 30,000 Confederates under John C. Pemberton. The fall of Vicksburg gave the Union control of the entire Mississippi — 'the Father of Waters again goes unvexed to the sea,' Lincoln wrote. Combined with Gettysburg the same week, July 4, 1863 marked the war's strategic turn. Vicksburg would not celebrate Independence Day until 1945.

question: Between November 15 and December 21, 1864, General William Tecumseh Sherman led 62,000 Union troops 285 miles from Atlanta to Savannah, Georgia, living off the land and destroying military and industrial targets. The army cut a swath 60 miles wide through the heart of the Confederacy — burning factories, tearing up railroads, freeing slaves. Sherman wired Lincoln on December 22: 'I beg to present you as a Christmas gift the city of Savannah.' What was the operation's strategic purpose?
answer: Total war — destroying the Confederate economy and will to continue, not just defeating its armies
choices: Total war — destroying the Confederate economy and will to continue, not just defeating its armies
Cutting off Lee — by blocking Confederate supply routes from the Deep South to Virginia
Capturing Confederate gold — believed stored in Savannah's banks for shipment to Britain
Reaching the Atlantic for British peace mediation — though no such mediation was attempted
context: Sherman's march was followed by a similar 'March to the Sea' through the Carolinas (February–April 1865). Atlanta had fallen September 2, 1864 — saving Lincoln's reelection. Sherman's name became synonymous with hard war in the South — Confederate memory hostile, Union memory mostly approving. The Civil War's transformation of warfare toward destruction of economic capacity prefigured the World Wars.

question: On January 31, 1865, the House of Representatives passed by a 119–56 vote (with two votes to spare over the required two-thirds) a constitutional amendment ending slavery throughout the United States. The Senate had passed it in April 1864. Three-fourths of the states (27 of 36, including 8 former Confederate states) had to ratify. Ratification was completed on December 6, 1865 — eight months after Lincoln's death. What did Section 1 say?
answer: 'Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime ... shall exist within the United States'
choices: 'Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime ... shall exist within the United States'
'No state shall make or enforce any law which shall abridge the privileges or immunities of citizens'
'The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged ... on account of race'
'All persons born or naturalized in the United States ... are citizens of the United States and of the State'
context: The Thirteenth Amendment was the first to grant Congress power to enforce its provisions by 'appropriate legislation.' The other three options describe the Fourteenth (citizenship 1868) and Fifteenth (voting 1870) Amendments. The 'except as a punishment for crime' clause was used after Reconstruction to justify convict leasing systems in the South — slavery by another name in some respects.

question: Born around 1820 in Maryland and originally named Araminta Ross, this enslaved woman escaped to Philadelphia in 1849, then made about thirteen trips back to the South over the next decade to lead perhaps 70 enslaved people to freedom — never losing a 'passenger.' During the Civil War she served as a Union scout and led an armed raid in South Carolina (June 1863) freeing 700 slaves. Who was she?
answer: Harriet Tubman — 'Moses' of her people, Underground Railroad conductor and Civil War spy
choices: Harriet Tubman — 'Moses' of her people, Underground Railroad conductor and Civil War spy
Sojourner Truth — abolitionist orator, but not Underground Railroad conductor
Frederick Douglass — escaped slave and orator, but he did not lead rescues back into the South
Mary Edwards Walker — Civil War surgeon and the only woman to receive the Medal of Honor
context: Tubman was small (about 5 feet), illiterate, prone to narcolepsy-like sleep attacks from a youthful head injury, and one of the most courageous figures in American history. She bore a $40,000 dead-or-alive bounty in the South. Frederick Douglass: 'I have wrought in the day; you in the night.' Tubman died 1913 at about 92. The U.S. Treasury announced (2016) plans to put her on the $20 bill; the timing was repeatedly delayed.

question: On July 5, 1852 — Independence Day having fallen on a Sunday — in Rochester, New York, a 34-year-old fugitive slave and abolitionist orator delivered a speech at Corinthian Hall titled 'What to the Slave is the Fourth of July?' Born Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey around 1818 in Maryland, he had escaped slavery in 1838 (disguised as a sailor on a Baltimore train) and published his autobiography in 1845. Who was he?
answer: Frederick Douglass — orator, editor, and the most powerful African American voice of the antebellum era
choices: Frederick Douglass — orator, editor, and the most powerful African American voice of the antebellum era
William Lloyd Garrison — Boston editor of *The Liberator* and Douglass' early mentor
Wendell Phillips — Boston abolitionist orator and Garrison's friend, who lived to fight for women's suffrage
Theodore Parker — Boston Unitarian abolitionist preacher who died in 1860 of tuberculosis
context: Douglass' Rochester speech contained the famous lines: 'What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July? I answer; a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.' Douglass advised Lincoln, advocated for African American troops, championed women's suffrage, served as a U.S. Marshal and minister to Haiti, and died 1895 at about 77.

question: On June 7, 1892, a 30-year-old shoemaker who was 7/8ths of European descent and 1/8th African deliberately violated Louisiana's 1890 Separate Car Act by sitting in a 'whites only' railroad car. He was arrested as planned (the test case was organized by a New Orleans citizens' committee). The case reached the U.S. Supreme Court. On May 18, 1896, the court ruled 7–1 that 'separate but equal' facilities did not violate the Fourteenth Amendment. Who was the plaintiff?
answer: Homer Plessy — whose lost case became the legal basis for sixty years of Jim Crow segregation
choices: Homer Plessy — whose lost case became the legal basis for sixty years of Jim Crow segregation
Booker T. Washington — but Washington was the contemporary Tuskegee educator, not the plaintiff
W.E.B. Du Bois — but Du Bois was a Harvard graduate student in 1896, not the plaintiff
Ida B. Wells — but Wells was a journalist exposing lynchings at this time, not the Plessy plaintiff
context: Justice Henry Billings Brown wrote the majority opinion. Justice John Marshall Harlan filed the lone dissent: 'Our Constitution is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens.' Plessy stood for nearly 58 years until *Brown v. Board of Education* (1954) overturned it. Plessy's grave in New Orleans is now a tourist site; the case site is marked.

question: On May 10, 1869, at a desolate spot in northern Utah, the Union Pacific Railroad (building westward from Omaha) and the Central Pacific Railroad (building eastward from Sacramento) met. About 1,800 miles of new track had been laid in seven years — across deserts, over the Sierra Nevada in winter, through Sioux and Cheyenne territory. The work was done largely by Irish immigrants on the Union Pacific and about 12,000 Chinese laborers on the Central Pacific. What ceremony marked completion?
answer: The Golden Spike — driven by Leland Stanford while a telegraph wire tapped 'DONE' to the nation
choices: The Golden Spike — driven by Leland Stanford while a telegraph wire tapped 'DONE' to the nation
The Silver Spike — driven by Brigham Young, hosting the ceremony in Utah Territory
The Iron Spike — driven by Thomas Durant of the Union Pacific, the senior of the two presidents
The Copper Spike — driven by the Chinese laborers' representative as recognition of their work
context: The Pacific Railroad Acts (1862, 1864) had been signed by Lincoln. The transcontinental cut transit time from New York to San Francisco from months (by ship around Cape Horn) to about a week. The Chinese laborers had been imported from Guangdong; many died on the work. The Promontory spike-driving was famously bungled — Stanford missed his first swing. The original spike is at Stanford University.

question: On January 1, 1892, a new federal immigration receiving station opened on a 27-acre island in New York Harbor, replacing the older state-run Castle Garden facility. Annie Moore, a 17-year-old from County Cork, was the first immigrant processed. Over the next 62 years (1892–1954) about 12 million immigrants would pass through — mostly from southern and eastern Europe (Italians, Poles, Russian and Polish Jews, Greeks, Hungarians, Slovaks). What is this station?
answer: Ellis Island — the eastern equivalent of Angel Island in San Francisco Bay
choices: Ellis Island — the eastern equivalent of Angel Island in San Francisco Bay
Hoffman Island — the smaller New York Harbor quarantine station nearby
The Statue of Liberty pedestal — Bartholdi's statue had been dedicated 1886 but does not include processing
Bedloe's Island — the contemporary name for the Statue of Liberty's home, also called Liberty Island
context: About 40 percent of current Americans have an ancestor who passed through Ellis Island. The processing was usually quick — perhaps a few hours — and about 2 percent were turned away (mostly for medical reasons or 'liable to become a public charge'). Ellis Island closed as an immigration station in 1954 and is now a museum. The Statue of Liberty, on neighboring Liberty Island, had been dedicated October 28, 1886.

question: On the evening of February 15, 1898, the U.S. battleship *Maine* exploded and sank in Havana Harbor — where it had been sent to protect American interests during a Cuban independence struggle against Spain. 266 American sailors died. The cause of the explosion (a Spanish mine, an internal magazine explosion, or sabotage by Cuban revolutionaries) was disputed then and is disputed now. American newspapers — especially Pulitzer's *World* and Hearst's *Journal* — blamed Spain. What slogan rallied the country to war?
answer: 'Remember the Maine, to hell with Spain!' — the war declaration followed in April 1898
choices: 'Remember the Maine, to hell with Spain!' — the war declaration followed in April 1898
'Speak softly and carry a big stick' — though that was Theodore Roosevelt's later 1901 maxim
'Make the world safe for democracy' — though that was Woodrow Wilson's 1917 WWI line
'Don't tread on me' — the Gadsden flag motto from the Revolutionary era, not the 1898 war
context: The Spanish-American War lasted ten weeks (April–August 1898). The U.S. gained Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines; Cuba became a U.S. protectorate. The Filipino insurgency that followed (1899–1902) was bloodier than the war with Spain. The Hearst-Pulitzer 'yellow journalism' that helped drive the country to war became a classic example of media-driven foreign policy.

question: On July 1, 1898, U.S. forces attacked Spanish positions on heights east of Santiago de Cuba. A volunteer cavalry regiment formed three months earlier — recruited from cowboys, Ivy League athletes, Indians, and Plains-trained officers — fought dismounted (their horses had been left in Tampa) up Kettle Hill alongside the regular 9th and 10th Cavalry (African-American 'Buffalo Soldier' regiments). The regiment's lieutenant colonel and effective commander made his political reputation in this fight. Who was he?
answer: Theodore Roosevelt — within three years a vice president, within three months later a president
choices: Theodore Roosevelt — within three years a vice president, within three months later a president
Leonard Wood — the regiment's actual colonel, who later commanded in the Philippines
John J. Pershing — the future WWI commander, though he was on Kettle Hill too as a junior officer
Tasker Bliss — chief of staff during WWI, but not at Kettle Hill
context: TR (1858–1919) had resigned as assistant secretary of the navy to form the regiment. He became governor of New York 1899, vice president March 1901, president September 1901 (after McKinley's assassination), and won the 1904 election. The 'Rough Riders' became one of the iconic American military units of the era. The Buffalo Soldiers' role at San Juan Heights was downplayed in white press accounts.

question: On October 1, 1908, the Detroit-based Ford Motor Company introduced a new automobile designed for mass production at a starting price of $850 (about $25,000 today). The car would be produced — increasingly cheaply, eventually as low as $260 — until 1927. Roughly 15 million were sold. In 1913 the company installed a moving assembly line at its Highland Park plant, cutting chassis assembly time from 12 hours to 90 minutes. Who founded the company and the assembly line?
answer: Henry Ford — whose Model T and $5/day wage (1914) transformed American manufacturing
choices: Henry Ford — whose Model T and $5/day wage (1914) transformed American manufacturing
Ransom Olds — whose Oldsmobile had pioneered assembly-line ideas before Ford
William Durant — whose General Motors competed with Ford by the 1910s
Walter Chrysler — whose own company would not be founded until 1925
context: Ford's $5/day wage (introduced January 1914, more than doubling industry standard) allowed his workers to buy his cars. The Model T came in any color the customer wanted, said Ford, so long as it was black (because black paint dried fastest). Ford was a vocal antisemite — his *Dearborn Independent* published the libelous *International Jew* (1920–22), influencing European fascists. He apologized in 1927 amid lawsuits.

question: On December 17, 1903, on the windswept dunes near a fishing village on North Carolina's Outer Banks, two bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio, made four short powered flights — the first by Orville at 10:35 a.m. (12 seconds, 120 feet) and the longest by Wilbur (59 seconds, 852 feet). The 1903 Flyer was a wood-and-fabric biplane powered by a 12-horsepower gasoline engine they had built themselves. Their key innovation was three-axis control using a technique they had refined in years of glider testing. What was the technique called?
answer: Wing-warping — twisting the wing tips to bank the aircraft, the basis of modern roll control
choices: Wing-warping — twisting the wing tips to bank the aircraft, the basis of modern roll control
Variable pitch — adjusting the propeller blade angle in flight, which they did not actually use
Forward swept wing — anticipating jet-age aerodynamics, but not what the Wrights used
Pulsejet propulsion — a much later 1940s German V-1 technology, not the Wrights'
context: The Wright brothers spent years in patent disputes (especially with Glenn Curtiss) that arguably retarded U.S. aviation. By WWI European designers had moved ahead. The 1903 Flyer is on display at the Smithsonian Air and Space Museum. Wilbur died of typhoid 1912; Orville died 1948 and lived to see jet flight. Their bicycle-shop tools and methods underlay much of their success.

question: In July 1925, in the small town of Dayton, Tennessee, a 24-year-old high school biology teacher named John Scopes was tried for violating a state law (the Butler Act, March 1925) that prohibited teaching that humans had evolved from a 'lower order of animals.' The trial pitted Clarence Darrow (for the defense) against the three-time presidential candidate William Jennings Bryan (for the prosecution). The dramatic climax came when Darrow put Bryan on the stand as an expert on the Bible. What was the verdict?
answer: Scopes was convicted and fined $100 — overturned on appeal due to a technicality
choices: Scopes was convicted and fined $100 — overturned on appeal due to a technicality
Scopes was acquitted by the jury after Darrow's defense overwhelmed Bryan's testimony
The trial was declared a mistrial when Bryan collapsed during his cross-examination by Darrow
Scopes was convicted but the law was struck down on free-speech grounds by the state court
context: The judge instructed the jury that the Butler Act was constitutional; Scopes was the only witness; he was convicted. The Tennessee Supreme Court overturned the conviction in 1927 but upheld the law itself. Bryan died five days after the trial. The Butler Act remained on the books until 1967. The 1955 play (and 1960 film) *Inherit the Wind* dramatized the trial — accurately enough on courtroom scenes, with composite characters.

question: On the morning of May 20, 1927, a 25-year-old American airmail pilot took off from Roosevelt Field on Long Island in a single-engine Ryan monoplane named *Spirit of St. Louis*. Thirty-three hours and 30 minutes later he landed at Le Bourget airfield outside Paris, where 150,000 people swarmed the field. He had flown 3,610 miles alone over the North Atlantic — the first nonstop solo transatlantic flight, winning the $25,000 Orteig Prize. Who was he?
answer: Charles Lindbergh — whose 1927 flight made him the most famous American of his generation
choices: Charles Lindbergh — whose 1927 flight made him the most famous American of his generation
Wiley Post — whose 1933 solo round-the-world flight came six years later
Amelia Earhart — whose 1932 transatlantic solo flight came five years later
Howard Hughes — whose 1938 round-the-world flight in the Lockheed 14 came eleven years later
context: Lindbergh's flight transformed aviation from circus stunt to serious transportation. His son Charles Lindbergh III was kidnapped and murdered in 1932 — the 'crime of the century.' Lindbergh's pre-WWII America First isolationism and reported sympathy for the Third Reich damaged his reputation; he flew combat missions in the Pacific anyway. He died of cancer in Hawaii 1974.

question: After a decade of strong stock-market gains driven by easy credit, optimism, and speculation, the New York Stock Exchange experienced four sharp declines over a two-week period in October 1929. October 24 ('Black Thursday') saw heavy selling; October 28 ('Black Monday') a 13% drop; October 29 ('Black Tuesday') another 12% drop on record volume of 16 million shares. By mid-November the Dow had lost about half its value. What followed?
answer: The Great Depression — unemployment to 25%, deflation, banking failures, lasting through the 1930s
choices: The Great Depression — unemployment to 25%, deflation, banking failures, lasting through the 1930s
A rapid V-shaped recovery — the market returned to peak within 18 months
A regional crisis — the Northeast was affected but the rest of the country was fine
A short-term liquidity crunch — broken by Federal Reserve action within months
context: The 1929 crash was not the cause of the Depression but its trigger and herald. Underlying weaknesses (agricultural debt, industrial overcapacity, the gold standard, banking instability) deepened the downturn. The Dow Jones Industrial Average did not return to its September 1929 peak until November 1954. Roosevelt's 1933 inauguration came at the depth — perhaps 25% unemployment, banks collapsing across the country.

question: On March 4, 1933, Franklin Delano Roosevelt took office at the depth of the Great Depression. Banks were collapsing; unemployment was about 25%; the Dow had lost almost 90% from its 1929 peak. In his Inaugural Address he said 'the only thing we have to fear is fear itself.' On March 5 he declared a national bank holiday. Over the next 100 days, Congress passed 15 major laws he proposed. What was this period called?
answer: The Hundred Days — establishing the New Deal alphabet agencies (FDIC, CCC, AAA, TVA, NIRA, etc.)
choices: The Hundred Days — establishing the New Deal alphabet agencies (FDIC, CCC, AAA, TVA, NIRA, etc.)
The Brain Trust — the term for FDR's advisers, not his legislative program
The First New Deal — though that term usually refers to 1933–34 broadly, not the 100 days
The Court-Packing Period — that came later (1937), not in the first months
context: The Hundred Days included the Emergency Banking Act, the Glass-Steagall Act, the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC), the Federal Emergency Relief Administration, the Agricultural Adjustment Act (AAA), the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA), the National Industrial Recovery Act (NIRA, struck down by the Supreme Court 1935), and others. FDR's 'fireside chats' (first March 12) explained policy in plain language. He was elected four times — the only U.S. president to do so.

question: Signed into law on August 14, 1935, by President Roosevelt, this New Deal legislation created a federal program of old-age insurance funded by payroll taxes on workers and employers — a system in which working generations support retired generations. It also included unemployment insurance and aid to dependent children. Largely drafted by the Committee on Economic Security under Labor Secretary Frances Perkins, the system has been the largest federal program by spending for most of the post-WWII era. What is it called?
answer: Social Security — the cornerstone of America's social safety net since 1935
choices: Social Security — the cornerstone of America's social safety net since 1935
Medicare — though Medicare was added in 1965 under President Johnson
The Civilian Conservation Corps — though the CCC was a New Deal jobs program, not retirement insurance
Aid to Dependent Children — a component of Social Security, not its main feature
context: Frances Perkins (1880–1965) was the first woman to serve in a U.S. cabinet (Secretary of Labor 1933–45). The 1935 Act initially excluded farm laborers and domestic workers — about 65% of African Americans. Subsequent amendments expanded coverage. Social Security currently pays benefits to about 60 million Americans. The 'trust fund' is technically separate from general revenues; its long-term solvency has been a perennial political issue.

question: On the morning of December 7, 1941, two waves of Japanese carrier-based aircraft (353 planes from 6 carriers) attacked the U.S. Pacific Fleet at its base in Hawaii. The attack lasted 90 minutes. 2,403 Americans were killed; 1,178 wounded. Eight battleships were damaged (four sunk); 188 aircraft destroyed. The Japanese lost 29 aircraft and 5 midget submarines. Roosevelt's address to Congress the next day called December 7 what?
answer: 'A date which will live in infamy' — and Congress declared war on Japan that afternoon
choices: 'A date which will live in infamy' — and Congress declared war on Japan that afternoon
'The blackest day in our history' — though that phrase came later in retrospectives
'The dawn of a new American century' — that line is from Henry Luce in 1941 but earlier in the year
'A betrayal beyond the reach of forgiveness' — though Roosevelt did not use those exact words
context: Japan's attack was meant to disable the U.S. Pacific Fleet long enough to consolidate Southeast Asia conquests; instead it united America. The three Pacific Fleet aircraft carriers (Enterprise, Lexington, Saratoga) were at sea and survived — a strategic catastrophe for Japan. Germany and Italy declared war on the United States December 11, bringing America into the European theater as well. The Doolittle Raid (April 18, 1942) was the first counterstrike.

question: Between June 4 and June 7, 1942, a Japanese fleet under Admiral Yamamoto attacked Midway Atoll, intending to draw out and destroy the remaining American aircraft carriers in the Pacific. Thanks to broken Japanese naval code (the 'Magic' intercepts), Admiral Nimitz knew the attack was coming. American dive-bombers from *Enterprise*, *Hornet*, and *Yorktown* caught Japanese carriers (*Akagi*, *Kaga*, *Soryu*, *Hiryu*) refueling and rearming aircraft on deck. What was the outcome?
answer: All four Japanese carriers sunk; the Pacific naval balance permanently shifted to the U.S.
choices: All four Japanese carriers sunk; the Pacific naval balance permanently shifted to the U.S.
Three Japanese carriers and two U.S. carriers sunk in a costly draw battle
Japanese naval victory — Yamamoto captured Midway but lost two carriers in the assault
American pyrrhic victory — Yorktown lost but only one Japanese carrier sunk
context: Midway was the decisive battle of the Pacific war. Japan never recovered its carrier-pilot strength; America's industrial advantage compounded from June 1942 onward. *Yorktown* was lost. The dive-bomber attacks all hit within a few minutes around 10:25 a.m. on June 4 — a moment that decided the war. Wade McClusky and the *Enterprise* dive-bomber group are among the most decorated in U.S. naval history.

question: On June 6, 1944, in the largest amphibious operation in history, about 156,000 Allied troops (American, British, Canadian, Free French, Polish) landed on five beaches along a 50-mile stretch of the Normandy coast (Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno, Sword). The operation had been postponed 24 hours due to weather. Casualties on the first day were perhaps 10,000 — heaviest at Omaha Beach. Who was the Supreme Allied Commander?
answer: Dwight D. Eisenhower — whose decision to launch on June 6 came amid forecast uncertainty
choices: Dwight D. Eisenhower — whose decision to launch on June 6 came amid forecast uncertainty
George C. Marshall — Army Chief of Staff but not the Allied Supreme Commander
Omar Bradley — American First Army commander at Normandy but subordinate to Eisenhower
Bernard Montgomery — British 21st Army Group commander under Eisenhower for D-Day
context: Eisenhower had written but not delivered a statement taking responsibility for failure of the operation — 'If any blame or fault attaches to the attempt it is mine alone.' By August Allied armies had broken out of Normandy. Paris was liberated August 25. Eisenhower became president 1953–61. The 75th anniversary commemoration (June 6, 2019) included the last surviving veterans. The D-Day cemetery at Colleville-sur-Mer is American territory by treaty.

question: From February 19 to March 26, 1945, U.S. Marines fought one of the bloodiest battles of the Pacific war on an 8-square-mile volcanic island 760 miles south of Tokyo. About 70,000 Marines faced about 21,000 dug-in Japanese defenders. American casualties were about 26,000 (6,800 killed); Japanese losses about 18,000 dead, just over 200 captured. On February 23, Joe Rosenthal of AP photographed six Marines raising a second, larger U.S. flag on Mount Suribachi. What is the island called?
answer: Iwo Jima — the volcanic island whose flag-raising image won Rosenthal the 1945 Pulitzer Prize
choices: Iwo Jima — the volcanic island whose flag-raising image won Rosenthal the 1945 Pulitzer Prize
Okinawa — the larger battle (April–June 1945) closer to the Japanese home islands
Saipan — the 1944 Marianas battle that gave U.S. B-29s their first base near Japan
Guadalcanal — the first major American offensive of the Pacific war (August 1942–February 1943)
context: Three of the six flag-raisers were killed in the subsequent fighting. The image became the U.S. Marine Corps War Memorial in Arlington (dedicated 1954). Iwo Jima had two strategic functions: emergency landing field for B-29s and elimination of Japanese radar warning of the bomber raids. Tom Brokaw's *The Greatest Generation* (1998) included Iwo Jima veterans; Clint Eastwood's *Letters from Iwo Jima* (2006) told the battle from the Japanese side.

question: Between 1942 and 1945, the largest secret industrial-scientific project in human history was carried out across some 30 sites — including Los Alamos, New Mexico (the design lab), Hanford, Washington (plutonium production), and Oak Ridge, Tennessee (uranium enrichment). The project employed about 130,000 people at peak and cost about $2 billion (perhaps $30 billion today). The civilian scientific director and the military commander were?
answer: J. Robert Oppenheimer (scientific) and General Leslie Groves (military)
choices: J. Robert Oppenheimer (scientific) and General Leslie Groves (military)
Albert Einstein (scientific) and General George Marshall (military), though neither led Manhattan
Niels Bohr (scientific) and General Curtis LeMay (military), though they had different roles
Enrico Fermi (scientific) and General Henry Arnold (military), though Fermi led only Chicago Met Lab
context: The project produced the Trinity test (July 16, 1945, New Mexico) and the Hiroshima (August 6) and Nagasaki (August 9) bombs. Oppenheimer (1904–67) had his security clearance revoked in 1954 amid McCarthy-era hearings; he was rehabilitated posthumously in 2022. Groves' *Now It Can Be Told* (1962) is the basic insider account. Christopher Nolan's *Oppenheimer* (2023) won Best Picture.

question: At 8:15 a.m. on August 6, 1945, a B-29 Superfortress bomber named *Enola Gay* (after the pilot's mother), commanded by Colonel Paul Tibbets and flying from Tinian in the Mariana Islands, dropped a uranium-235 fission bomb code-named 'Little Boy' on the western Japanese city of Hiroshima. The bomb detonated about 600 meters above ground over a hospital. Perhaps 70,000–80,000 people died instantly; about 140,000 by year's end from injuries and radiation. What was the U.S. military rationale?
answer: Force Japan to surrender quickly, avoiding a costly invasion of the home islands
choices: Force Japan to surrender quickly, avoiding a costly invasion of the home islands
Demonstrate atomic power to the Soviet Union as the Cold War was beginning
Avenge Pearl Harbor specifically — President Truman's view of the bombing's purpose
Test the bomb in real conditions for postwar weapons development
context: Truman's stated reason was avoiding invasion casualties. Whether Japan would have surrendered without the bombings (especially given Soviet entry August 9) has been debated since. The Nagasaki bombing followed August 9 (Fat Man, plutonium implosion, ~70,000 dead). Japan surrendered August 15. The bombings remain the only military use of nuclear weapons in history. Tibbets named the plane after his mother; he died 2007.

question: On March 12, 1947, President Harry Truman addressed a joint session of Congress requesting $400 million in military and economic aid for Greece and Turkey. Greece faced a Communist-led civil war; Turkey was under Soviet pressure for naval bases. Truman declared 'it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures.' What policy did this articulate?
answer: Containment — opposing Soviet expansion globally, the framework of U.S. Cold War policy
choices: Containment — opposing Soviet expansion globally, the framework of U.S. Cold War policy
Rollback — actively reducing existing Soviet control, the right-wing alternative to containment
Détente — reducing tensions through negotiation, the 1970s Nixon-Kissinger approach
Massive retaliation — Eisenhower-Dulles policy of nuclear response to communist aggression
context: George Kennan's 'X' article in *Foreign Affairs* (July 1947) articulated containment more theoretically. The Marshall Plan (June 1947) extended the doctrine to Western European reconstruction — $13 billion in U.S. aid that revived the war-shattered economies. NATO (April 1949) provided collective defense. The Truman Doctrine shaped U.S. foreign policy for 40+ years until the Soviet collapse.

question: In June 1948, the Soviet Union cut off all rail, road, and water access to West Berlin — which lay 100 miles inside the Soviet zone of occupied Germany. The Western allies (US, UK, France) faced a choice: abandon West Berlin's 2 million inhabitants, force the blockade by ground (risking war), or supply the city by air. They chose the third. American C-47s and C-54s, joined by British transports, made about 277,000 flights over 11 months. What did the operation deliver?
answer: About 2.3 million tons of supplies — at peak a plane landed every 30 seconds at Tempelhof
choices: About 2.3 million tons of supplies — at peak a plane landed every 30 seconds at Tempelhof
About 200,000 tons of supplies — a stop-gap until ground access could be negotiated
Mostly raw food only — coal and industrial supplies came via ground after limited concessions
Almost entirely military supplies — civilian needs were met by parallel ground convoys
context: The Berlin Airlift broke the Soviet blockade. Stalin lifted it in May 1949 without achieving anything. The airlift was the first major Cold War victory — won without firing a shot. 'Operation Vittles' (American) and 'Operation Plain Fare' (British) were the operational names. The Royal Australian Air Force, the Royal New Zealand Air Force, and the South African Air Force also participated. The Berlin Wall was not built until 1961.

question: In a Harvard commencement address on June 5, 1947, Secretary of State George Marshall proposed a massive U.S. aid program to rebuild war-shattered European economies. The Economic Cooperation Act of April 1948 authorized $13 billion ($150 billion today) in aid to 16 Western European nations (USSR and Eastern Europe were invited but the Soviets refused). The program ran 1948–52. What were the goals?
answer: Economic recovery to forestall Communist movements and tie Europe to the U.S. politically
choices: Economic recovery to forestall Communist movements and tie Europe to the U.S. politically
Reparations to the war's victims, including substantial sums to Germany and Austria
Military rearmament — though that came later through NATO and the Mutual Defense Assistance Acts
Free trade liberalization only — the program was not primarily about goods transfers
context: The Marshall Plan was extraordinarily successful — European industrial output recovered to 1938 levels by 1951 and exceeded them by 1952. Combined with the Bretton Woods institutions (IMF, World Bank) and GATT, it helped lay the foundation for postwar Western prosperity. Marshall received the Nobel Peace Prize 1953 — the only general so honored. The Soviet refusal accelerated the Iron Curtain's hardening.

question: On June 25, 1950, North Korean forces (about 90,000 troops with Soviet T-34 tanks) crossed the 38th parallel and invaded South Korea, driving south rapidly. By September the Pusan Perimeter (a small enclave around the southeastern port) was all that remained of UN-allied territory. On September 15, in a daring amphibious landing at the western port of Inchon (200 miles behind the front), UN forces under General Douglas MacArthur outflanked the North Koreans. What was the result?
answer: North Korean army shattered; UN forces drove north to the Yalu River by November 1950
choices: North Korean army shattered; UN forces drove north to the Yalu River by November 1950
North Korean army withdrew in good order to defensive positions north of Seoul
A failed landing — Inchon's massive tides made the operation unworkable
A partial success — Seoul recaptured but North Korean forces escaped to mountain bases
context: MacArthur's Inchon landing is studied as a masterpiece of operational deception and risk-taking. But pushing to the Yalu provoked Chinese intervention (October 1950) — about 250,000 troops crossed quietly. The 1st Marine Division's breakout from Chosin Reservoir (November–December 1950) became legendary. The war stalemated around the 38th parallel; armistice signed July 27, 1953. About 36,000 Americans died.

question: On May 17, 1954, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled unanimously (9–0) in a case brought by the NAACP against the Topeka, Kansas, Board of Education that 'separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.' The decision overturned *Plessy v. Ferguson* (1896) and the legal foundation of school segregation. Chief Justice Earl Warren had spent months persuading hostile Southern justices to make the ruling unanimous. What case is this?
answer: *Brown v. Board of Education* — opening the modern civil rights era
choices: *Brown v. Board of Education* — opening the modern civil rights era
*Plessy v. Ferguson* — but that was the 1896 case Brown overturned
*Loving v. Virginia* — but that was the 1967 case ending interracial-marriage bans
*Sweatt v. Painter* — a 1950 precursor on segregated law schools
context: Brown was a consolidation of five cases. Thurgood Marshall (later the first African American Supreme Court Justice, 1967) argued for the NAACP. Implementation was slow — *Brown II* (1955) called for 'all deliberate speed,' which translated to deliberate delay across the South. The Little Rock crisis (1957) and the integration of Ole Miss (1962) and the University of Alabama (1963) tested the ruling. Earl Warren died 1974.

question: On December 1, 1955, in Montgomery, Alabama, a 42-year-old African American seamstress and NAACP secretary refused to give up her seat to a white passenger when ordered by the bus driver. She was arrested. Her arrest prompted a 381-day boycott of the city bus system by African American residents (about 75% of bus ridership). A young Baptist minister recently arrived in the city emerged as the boycott's spokesman. Who was the minister?
answer: Martin Luther King Jr. — 26 years old, recently arrived at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church
choices: Martin Luther King Jr. — 26 years old, recently arrived at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church
Ralph Abernathy — King's close friend and Montgomery colleague
Hosea Williams — later one of King's SCLC lieutenants but not yet in 1955
John Lewis — later civil rights leader and Congressman but in 1955 a teenager
context: The boycott ended on December 20, 1956 when *Browder v. Gayle* (Supreme Court) ordered Montgomery to desegregate its buses. Rosa Parks (1913–2005) had been an NAACP secretary for years; her arrest was not random. King's Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC, 1957) emerged from the Montgomery success. King won the Nobel Peace Prize 1964 and was assassinated in Memphis April 4, 1968.

question: On September 4, 1957, nine African American students attempted to enter Little Rock Central High School in Arkansas under federal court order desegregating the school. The state's governor, Orval Faubus, had ordered the Arkansas National Guard to block them. President Eisenhower, who had moved cautiously on civil rights, took action three weeks later. What did he do?
answer: Sent 1,200 paratroopers of the 101st Airborne Division to escort the students into the school
choices: Sent 1,200 paratroopers of the 101st Airborne Division to escort the students into the school
Indicted Governor Faubus on federal contempt charges; Faubus resigned
Withdrew federal contracts from Arkansas until the state complied with the court order
Requested a constitutional amendment to clarify federal authority over state school systems
context: Eisenhower federalized the Arkansas National Guard (taking it out of Faubus' control) and sent the 101st Airborne. The 'Little Rock Nine' attended Central High for the year under federal protection. Faubus closed Little Rock high schools for the 1958–59 school year ('the Lost Year') rather than integrate; the Supreme Court ruled the closure unconstitutional. The incident was a major Cold War embarrassment — Soviet propaganda exploited it.

question: On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched a 184-pound aluminum sphere with four whip antennas into low Earth orbit using a converted R-7 ICBM. Visible from the ground, audible on the radio as a steady beeping, this satellite orbited for three months. The American reaction was electric — and traumatic. Within months Congress had created NASA (1958), passed the National Defense Education Act (federal funding for science education), and accelerated missile programs. What was the satellite called?
answer: Sputnik 1 — the first artificial Earth satellite, launched October 4, 1957
choices: Sputnik 1 — the first artificial Earth satellite, launched October 4, 1957
Soyuz — the later Russian crew capsule, but not the first satellite
Vostok — the Russian capsule that carried Gagarin in 1961, not a satellite
Luna 1 — the first lunar probe, but launched in 1959, not 1957
context: Sputnik (Russian for 'fellow traveler') triggered the space race. The first U.S. satellite (Explorer 1) followed January 31, 1958. Sputnik 2 carried the dog Laika November 3, 1957 (she died). NASA was established October 1958. Kennedy's commitment to a moon landing (May 1961) was the response. Apollo 11 (July 20, 1969) won the race. The space race produced enormous spillover benefits including microelectronics, GPS, weather satellites, and computer technology.

question: On April 17, 1961, about 1,400 CIA-trained Cuban exiles landed at the Bay of Pigs on Cuba's south coast, intending to spark an anti-Castro uprising. The plan — inherited from the Eisenhower administration and modified by Kennedy — relied on assumed Cuban popular support, U.S. air support, and concealment of U.S. involvement. None of these worked. Within three days the brigade had been destroyed or captured by Castro's forces. What was the consequence?
answer: Kennedy's foreign-policy reputation shaken; Castro publicly proclaimed Cuba a socialist state
choices: Kennedy's foreign-policy reputation shaken; Castro publicly proclaimed Cuba a socialist state
Kennedy's resignation contemplated; CIA Director Dulles' replacement of the State Department
Soviet immediate intervention; missiles installed in Cuba within weeks
Castro overthrown by internal coup; transition government installed within months
context: The Bay of Pigs was Kennedy's worst foreign-policy debacle. He famously said 'How could I have been so stupid?' afterward. The disaster influenced his handling of the Cuban Missile Crisis 18 months later. The brigade prisoners were eventually ransomed (December 1962) for $53 million in food and medicine. Castro emerged strengthened, formally aligned with the Soviet Union. The CIA's reputation took a generation to recover.

question: On October 14, 1962, a U-2 reconnaissance flight over Cuba photographed Soviet medium-range ballistic missile sites under construction. President Kennedy received the news October 16. For thirteen days, the U.S. and USSR teetered on the edge of nuclear war. Kennedy chose a naval 'quarantine' (technically blockade is an act of war) of Cuba rather than airstrikes or invasion. On October 22 he addressed the nation on TV. How was the crisis resolved?
answer: Khrushchev removed the missiles after a secret deal: U.S. would also remove Jupiter missiles from Turkey
choices: Khrushchev removed the missiles after a secret deal: U.S. would also remove Jupiter missiles from Turkey
Kennedy invaded Cuba on October 28 and the Soviets withdrew without confrontation
Khrushchev was overthrown by the Politburo and his successor immediately recalled the missiles
U.S. airstrikes destroyed the missile sites on October 27 before Soviet personnel could complete them
context: October 27 ('Black Saturday') was the closest moment — a U.S. U-2 was shot down over Cuba and a Soviet sub commander considered launching a nuclear torpedo. Khrushchev publicly removed the missiles October 28. The Turkey deal was kept secret for decades. The Moscow-Washington hotline was established 1963. Khrushchev was removed by his colleagues 1964. Robert Kennedy's *Thirteen Days* (1969) is the canonical insider account.

question: On August 28, 1963, about 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial for the 'March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom' — a culmination of the civil rights movement organized by A. Philip Randolph, Bayard Rustin, and others. The day's final speaker was the 34-year-old president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. He had prepared remarks but, encouraged by gospel singer Mahalia Jackson, broke into an extemporaneous passage about a dream. What did the dream describe?
answer: Children judged not by the color of their skin but by the content of their character
choices: Children judged not by the color of their skin but by the content of their character
A country reunited by economic policy after the Depression's racial inequities
Voting rights extended to all citizens regardless of literacy tests or poll taxes
Religious harmony achieved through cooperation among Black and white churches
context: King's full speech included both prepared and extemporaneous material; the famous 'I have a dream' anaphora was largely extemporaneous (he had used similar material at a Detroit rally two months earlier). The Civil Rights Act of 1964 passed Congress less than a year later. King won the Nobel Peace Prize 1964 at age 35 — youngest male laureate at the time. He was assassinated in Memphis April 4, 1968.

question: On July 2, 1964, after a 60-day filibuster in the Senate (broken by 71-29 cloture vote), President Lyndon Johnson signed an act prohibiting discrimination on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin in public accommodations, employment, and federally assisted programs. The act had been proposed by John Kennedy in June 1963; Johnson made passing it a memorial to his predecessor. Republican leader Everett Dirksen of Illinois was critical to breaking the filibuster. What was the act called?
answer: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 — Title VII created the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission
choices: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 — Title VII created the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission
The Voting Rights Act — though that came one year later, in 1965
The Fair Housing Act — though that came in 1968, after King's assassination
The Brown v. Board Act — though that was the 1954 Supreme Court ruling, not a statute
context: Johnson reportedly told an aide 'We have lost the South for a generation' upon signing the act. Six months later (January 1965) he proposed the Voting Rights Act, which became law August 6, 1965. Civil rights legislation transformed American life — public spaces, schools, workplaces. The Republican Party's 'Southern Strategy' under Nixon (1968 onward) responded to the realignment Johnson had set in motion.

question: On March 7, 1965, about 600 civil rights marchers, organized to walk from Selma, Alabama, to Montgomery to demand voting rights, were attacked by state troopers and a sheriff's posse at the Edmund Pettus Bridge. Television cameras filmed the beatings. John Lewis (then 25) suffered a fractured skull. The day became known as 'Bloody Sunday.' What was the immediate political consequence?
answer: President Johnson's voting rights address to Congress March 15 ('we shall overcome')
choices: President Johnson's voting rights address to Congress March 15 ('we shall overcome')
Court orders prohibiting further state interference with the march
International condemnation forcing Alabama Governor George Wallace to resign
FBI federal indictments against the responsible state troopers within a week
context: Johnson's March 15 speech to a joint session of Congress was one of the great political moments of the era: 'And we shall overcome,' he said, deliberately adopting the movement's anthem. The Voting Rights Act passed August 6, 1965. The Selma-to-Montgomery march finally took place March 21–25 under federal protection. John Lewis went on to serve in the U.S. House for 33 years; he died 2020.

question: On July 16, 1969, a Saturn V rocket launched Apollo 11 from Cape Kennedy with three astronauts aboard: Neil Armstrong (commander), Buzz Aldrin (lunar module pilot), and Michael Collins (command module pilot). On July 20, the lunar module *Eagle* landed in the Sea of Tranquility at 4:17 p.m. EDT. At 10:56 p.m. Armstrong stepped onto the surface and spoke the famous line. What did he say?
answer: 'That's one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind' — Armstrong claimed he said the 'a'
choices: 'That's one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind' — Armstrong claimed he said the 'a'
'The Eagle has landed' — but that was at touchdown six hours earlier, not first step
'We came in peace for all mankind' — but that was on the plaque, not Armstrong's first words
'Houston, Tranquility Base, this is Eagle' — radio call, not first step
context: The 'a' before 'man' was either spoken and lost in transmission or genuinely omitted; Armstrong insisted he said it. About 600 million people watched live worldwide. The plaque left on the lunar module's leg read 'We came in peace for all mankind.' Five more Apollo missions landed on the moon (Apollo 12, 14, 15, 16, 17); Apollo 13 (April 1970) was an aborted mission with successful recovery. Armstrong died 2012.

question: On June 17, 1972, five men were arrested at 2:30 a.m. inside the Democratic National Committee headquarters in the Watergate office complex in Washington, D.C. They had been planting wiretaps and photographing documents. One of them, James McCord, was the security chief for President Nixon's re-election committee. Two reporters at the *Washington Post* — Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein — began investigating the connections to the White House. Who was their key inside source?
answer: Mark Felt — FBI Associate Director, called 'Deep Throat,' revealed 2005
choices: Mark Felt — FBI Associate Director, called 'Deep Throat,' revealed 2005
John Dean — White House counsel, later turned witness for the prosecution
Charles Colson — Nixon's special counsel, but he became a born-again Christian, not the source
H.R. Haldeman — White House chief of staff, central to the cover-up but not Woodward's source
context: The Watergate investigation grew through 1973 — the Senate Watergate Committee, the Saturday Night Massacre (October 1973), the secret tapes. Nixon resigned August 9, 1974, the only U.S. president to do so. Gerald Ford pardoned him a month later (September 8). Mark Felt revealed himself as 'Deep Throat' in 2005. The Watergate scandal transformed American politics, the press, and the office of the presidency.

question: On August 5, 1974, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled unanimously in *United States v. Nixon* that President Nixon must surrender White House tape recordings. One tape, from June 23, 1972 — six days after the Watergate break-in — showed Nixon directing his chief of staff to have the CIA intervene to stop the FBI investigation. With impeachment certain in the House and conviction likely in the Senate, what did Nixon do?
answer: Resigned the presidency August 9, 1974 — the first U.S. president ever to do so
choices: Resigned the presidency August 9, 1974 — the first U.S. president ever to do so
Refused to resign and fought impeachment, leading to a Senate trial in October 1974
Pardoned himself and his advisers preemptively before resigning
Negotiated a plea deal allowing him to serve out his term in exchange for cooperation
context: Nixon's August 8 resignation speech announced he would resign effective noon the next day. Gerald Ford, who had been confirmed as vice president just nine months earlier (after Spiro Agnew's October 1973 resignation), became president August 9 — the only U.S. president never elected to either office. Ford pardoned Nixon September 8 — politically costly, possibly the right thing. Nixon died 1994; his rehabilitation as elder statesman was partial.

question: On November 4, 1979 — nine months after Iran's Islamic Revolution overthrew the Shah and brought Ayatollah Khomeini to power — Iranian university students stormed the U.S. embassy in Tehran and took 52 American diplomats hostage. They demanded the U.S. return the Shah (then receiving cancer treatment in New York) for trial. President Carter responded with economic sanctions, a failed military rescue attempt (Operation Eagle Claw, April 1980, ended in a helicopter crash at Desert One), and diplomatic isolation. When did the hostages come home?
answer: January 20, 1981 — released minutes after Reagan's inauguration, ending Carter's presidency
choices: January 20, 1981 — released minutes after Reagan's inauguration, ending Carter's presidency
December 1980 — released after Carter conceded the November 1980 election
April 1980 — rescued by Operation Eagle Claw before the helicopter crash
July 1980 — released during a special U.S.-Iran summit mediated by Algeria
context: The 444-day crisis dominated Carter's last year in office. The Algiers Accords (January 19, 1981) unfroze Iranian assets in exchange for release. The hostages flew out as Reagan was taking the oath of office. Carter lost the 1980 election in a landslide. The crisis ended American post-Vietnam restraint and contributed to the U.S. defense buildup of the Reagan era. Several embassy staff escaped early — the 'Canadian Caper' of January 1980.

question: On March 8, 1983, in a speech to the National Association of Evangelicals in Orlando, Florida, President Ronald Reagan called the Soviet Union 'an evil empire' and 'the focus of evil in the modern world.' Reagan's foreign-policy advisers had urged softer language; he insisted on the formulation. The phrase, controversial in the West (treated as reckless by sophisticated opinion), galvanized Soviet dissidents — including those in the gulag. What was Natan Sharansky's later reaction?
answer: Heard the news in his cell from a guard's slip and tapped the news through the prison walls
choices: Heard the news in his cell from a guard's slip and tapped the news through the prison walls
Met Reagan in 1986 after his release and reported the Soviet officials had panicked at the phrase
Wrote a Soviet samizdat essay celebrating the speech as the first honest American naming
Denounced the speech as American posturing while political prisoners died unmentioned
context: Sharansky's memoir *Fear No Evil* (1988) describes the impact of Reagan's evil-empire framing on dissidents. The speech also articulated the Cold War's moral stakes more clearly than détente-era American leaders. Reagan's Westminster speech (June 1982) had earlier predicted Marxism-Leninism would end on the 'ash heap of history.' By 1989 the Berlin Wall was down; by 1991 the Soviet Union was dissolved.

question: On June 12, 1987, on the western side of the Berlin Wall, President Ronald Reagan stood at the Brandenburg Gate and addressed a German crowd — and, through broadcasts, an East Berlin audience. The State Department and his National Security Council had repeatedly removed a sentence from drafts of the speech; Reagan insisted on keeping it. What did the sentence call for?
answer: 'Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!' — referring to Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev
choices: 'Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!' — referring to Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev
'Mr. Honecker, open this gate!' — referring to East German leader Erich Honecker
'Comrades, choose freedom!' — addressed to East German citizens directly
'Europe, reunite!' — calling for European political unity across the East-West divide
context: The line was nearly cut by speechwriters and the State Department as too provocative. Peter Robinson, Reagan's speechwriter, fought to keep it. The wall fell November 9, 1989, less than 30 months later. Whether Reagan's speech caused the fall or merely captured the moment is debated; the symbolic power is undeniable. Gorbachev's reforms (glasnost, perestroika), Pope John Paul II's Polish visits, and Solidarity's pressure were the immediate proximate causes.

question: On the evening of November 9, 1989, the East German Politburo's communications chief, Günter Schabowski, held a press conference at which he announced new travel regulations. Pressed by an Italian reporter on when the new rules took effect, the unprepared Schabowski stammered 'Effective immediately, as far as I know.' East Berliners rushed to the wall. Guards, lacking clear orders, eventually opened the checkpoints. Crowds danced atop the wall. The wall fell. What was the longer chain of events leading up to it?
answer: Solidarity legalized (April 1989), Hungary opening Austrian border (September), East German exodus, mass protests
choices: Solidarity legalized (April 1989), Hungary opening Austrian border (September), East German exodus, mass protests
Direct U.S.-Soviet negotiations on German reunification through summer 1989
Khrushchev's earlier reforms reaching East Germany after twenty years of delay
Helmut Kohl's election in 1982 as West German chancellor, immediately reuniting the country
context: The wall stood from August 13, 1961 to November 9, 1989 — 28 years. Honecker had been removed in October 1989. German reunification followed within a year (October 3, 1990). The Soviet Union dissolved December 25, 1991. The events of 1989 across Central Europe — Polish elections June, Hungarian border September, Berlin Wall November, Velvet Revolution in Czechoslovakia November–December, Romania December — ranked among the most transformative months of the 20th century.

question: On December 25, 1991, in a televised address from the Kremlin, Mikhail Gorbachev — the last General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union — resigned. The hammer-and-sickle flag was lowered over the Kremlin at 7:32 p.m. Moscow time; the Russian tricolor was raised. The USSR formally dissolved at midnight. What was the immediate sequence of 1991 events leading to this?
answer: August coup against Gorbachev, Yeltsin's defiance on a tank, Baltic independence, Belovezha Accords December
choices: August coup against Gorbachev, Yeltsin's defiance on a tank, Baltic independence, Belovezha Accords December
Direct U.S. military pressure forcing Soviet withdrawal from Eastern Europe in 1991
Polish-Lithuanian secession from the Warsaw Pact forcing Soviet dissolution
Chinese economic pressure on the Soviet Union after Tiananmen Square 1989
context: The August coup (August 19–21, 1991) by hard-liners against Gorbachev failed — Yeltsin's defiance on a tank outside the Russian White House became iconic. The Baltic states (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania) declared independence; Ukraine voted for independence December 1; the Belovezha Accords (December 8) dissolved the Soviet Union by mutual agreement of the Russian, Ukrainian, and Belarusian leaders. The Cold War, which had defined American policy for 45 years, was over.

question: On the morning of September 11, 2001, nineteen al-Qaeda operatives hijacked four American passenger airliners. Two — American 11 and United 175 — struck the World Trade Center's twin towers in New York. A third — American 77 — hit the Pentagon. The fourth — United 93 — crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after passengers attempted to retake the cockpit. About 2,977 people died. Who was the principal organizer behind the attacks?
answer: Osama bin Laden — Saudi exile leading al-Qaeda from Afghanistan, killed by U.S. Navy SEALs 2011
choices: Osama bin Laden — Saudi exile leading al-Qaeda from Afghanistan, killed by U.S. Navy SEALs 2011
Saddam Hussein — Iraqi dictator, but the 9/11 Commission concluded he had no operational role
Mullah Omar — Taliban leader who sheltered bin Laden but did not organize the attacks
Khalid Sheikh Mohammed — operational planner under bin Laden's strategic direction, captured 2003
context: The attacks led to U.S. invasion of Afghanistan (October 2001) and Iraq (March 2003). Bin Laden was killed May 2, 2011, in Abbottabad, Pakistan, by SEAL Team Six under Obama's order. The 9/11 Commission's report (2004) is the canonical investigation. The attacks reshaped American foreign and domestic policy: PATRIOT Act, Department of Homeland Security, two long wars, ongoing debates about civil liberties and surveillance.

question: Late on the night of May 1, 2011 (Pakistan time), about two dozen U.S. Navy SEALs from DEVGRU ('SEAL Team Six') flew two stealth Black Hawk helicopters from Afghanistan into Pakistan, landed at a fortified compound in the garrison town of Abbottabad, killed Osama bin Laden and several others, recovered intelligence material, and departed. The mission lasted about 40 minutes. President Obama and his national-security team watched some of the operation from the White House Situation Room. What was the operation called?
answer: Operation Neptune Spear — based on intelligence developed by CIA over multiple years
choices: Operation Neptune Spear — based on intelligence developed by CIA over multiple years
Operation Enduring Freedom — but that was the broader Afghan war name, not the bin Laden raid
Operation Geronimo — a CIA codename for bin Laden, not the mission name
Operation Anaconda — but that was the March 2002 Afghanistan operation, not the bin Laden raid
context: Neptune Spear was the mission name; Geronimo was bin Laden's codename. Bin Laden's body was buried at sea within 24 hours. The Pakistani government was not informed in advance — bin Laden had been hiding in a compound near Pakistan's military academy for years. One stealth helicopter crashed and was destroyed in place to preserve secrecy. The mission was the culmination of a decade of intelligence work since 9/11.

question: On the evening of March 5, 1770, a single British sentry outside the Customs House on King Street in Boston was harassed by a crowd. Captain Thomas Preston of the 29th Regiment of Foot brought a squad of grenadiers to relieve him. The crowd grew to perhaps 300, throwing snowballs, oyster shells, and ice chunks at the soldiers. After a soldier was knocked down, shots were fired. Five colonists died. Who was the first killed?
answer: Crispus Attucks — a former slave of African and Native American descent, age about 47
choices: Crispus Attucks — a former slave of African and Native American descent, age about 47
Samuel Adams — a Boston revolutionary, but he was not killed at the Massacre
Paul Revere — silversmith and engraver of the famous propaganda print, not a casualty
Patrick Carr — one of the five killed, but the fifth victim, not the first
context: John Adams defended the British soldiers at trial. Six were acquitted; two were convicted of manslaughter, branded on the thumb, and released. Adams later called his defense 'one of the most gallant, generous, manly and disinterested actions of my whole life.' Paul Revere's engraving (published a few weeks later) became revolutionary propaganda. Attucks is sometimes called the first martyr of the American Revolution.

question: On the night of April 18, 1775, Joseph Warren sent two riders to warn the Massachusetts countryside that British regulars were marching from Boston toward Concord. One rider, William Dawes, took the land route via Boston Neck. The other crossed the Charles River by boat and rode to Lexington, then continued toward Concord (where he was briefly captured). His name became famous through Longfellow's 1860 poem. What did he call out?
answer: 'The regulars are coming out!' — not 'the British are coming' (everyone was British then)
choices: 'The regulars are coming out!' — not 'the British are coming' (everyone was British then)
'The Redcoats are coming!' — though Longfellow uses this phrasing in the poem
'To arms! To arms!' — the alarm call but not Revere's specific reported phrase
'Independence or death!' — but that phrase belongs to later Revolutionary rhetoric
context: Paul Revere (1735–1818) was a Boston silversmith. Longfellow's poem 'Paul Revere's Ride' (1860) was historically loose but cemented Revere's fame. Dawes' route through Cambridge was longer and slower. Samuel Prescott, who happened on the riders near Lexington, was the one who actually got through to Concord. Revere was arrested by a British patrol but escaped on foot back to Lexington in time to help Samuel Adams and John Hancock escape.

question: On September 22, 1776, a 21-year-old Yale graduate and Connecticut schoolmaster turned Continental Army captain was hanged by the British in New York City for espionage. He had volunteered for an intelligence mission behind British lines on Long Island following the Continental retreat from Brooklyn Heights. Captured (probably betrayed by a Tory cousin), he was executed without trial the next morning. His last words, according to British accounts, were reported as what?
answer: 'I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country'
choices: 'I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country'
'Give me liberty, or give me death' (Patrick Henry's earlier line, often misattributed)
'I die contented for the cause' (a generic reported version)
'Long live the United States' (anachronistic — the country was not yet 'United')
context: Hale's actual words may have been less polished — the famous version probably edited or composed by witnesses. Nathan Hale became the patron-saint of American patriotic sacrifice. A statue of him stands at CIA headquarters (the unofficial 'patron saint' of American intelligence). He was inducted into the National Spy Museum. His Coventry, Connecticut, schoolhouse is now a historic site.

question: On March 31, 1776, while her husband was at the Second Continental Congress in Philadelphia drafting documents that would soon include the Declaration of Independence, his wife wrote him a letter from their farm in Braintree, Massachusetts. She urged him to 'remember the ladies' when framing the new code of laws, and warned that women would not consider themselves bound by laws in which they had no voice or representation. Who was she?
answer: Abigail Adams — wife of John Adams and one of the most thoughtful letter writers of the era
choices: Abigail Adams — wife of John Adams and one of the most thoughtful letter writers of the era
Martha Washington — Washington's wife, but no comparable correspondence survives
Mercy Otis Warren — Massachusetts historian and playwright, but not the writer of this letter
Phillis Wheatley — African American poet who corresponded with Washington but not John Adams
context: Abigail Adams (1744–1818) wrote about 1,160 letters to John during their long separations. She was the mother of John Quincy Adams (sixth U.S. president). John replied to her 'Remember the Ladies' letter with light teasing, but Abigail's argument anticipated the women's rights movement by 75 years. Her letters are a fundamental source for the period's social and political history.

question: In December 1782, three American commissioners — Benjamin Franklin, John Adams, and John Jay — negotiated the preliminary articles of peace with Great Britain in Paris. Defying their instructions from Congress (which required consultation with the French foreign minister Vergennes), they reached a separate agreement with the British. The final Treaty of Paris was signed September 3, 1783. What did the United States receive?
answer: Independence; boundaries to the Mississippi River; fishing rights off Newfoundland; British evacuation
choices: Independence; boundaries to the Mississippi River; fishing rights off Newfoundland; British evacuation
Independence only; boundaries left to be set by a later joint commission with Britain
Independence and only the original 13 colonies; the Northwest territory remained British
Independence and all of Canada below the St. Lawrence; British recognition of Florida cession to Spain
context: The Treaty's generous boundaries (to the Mississippi) reflected Britain's desire to detach the U.S. from France. The Northwest Territory (north of the Ohio, east of the Mississippi) included what became Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota — a vast addition to the original 13 states. Spain regained Florida from Britain. The Loyalists' property issue caused decades of friction.

question: From August 1786 to February 1787, indebted farmers in western Massachusetts, led by Daniel Shays (a former Continental Army captain), rose up against state debt-collection courts and tax policies. They closed county courts and in January 1787 attempted to seize the federal arsenal at Springfield. Defeated by state militia funded by Boston merchants, the rebellion collapsed. What was the political consequence?
answer: Convinced wavering states the Articles of Confederation were inadequate; helped trigger 1787 Convention
choices: Convinced wavering states the Articles of Confederation were inadequate; helped trigger 1787 Convention
Massachusetts adopted a separate revolutionary constitution dividing the state in two
Continental Congress dispatched federal troops, establishing the principle of federal intervention
Daniel Shays elected to Congress under Massachusetts' new electoral compact of 1788
context: Shays' Rebellion frightened the political class. The Annapolis Convention (September 1786, attended by only five states) had already called for a broader constitutional review; Shays' Rebellion made the case urgent. Washington came out of retirement partly because of it. Shays himself was pardoned and lived quietly until his death in 1825. Madison cited the rebellion in arguing for stronger federal authority in the Federalist Papers.

question: The Constitutional Convention of 1787 faced a fundamental impasse over representation in the new federal legislature. Large states (Virginia, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts) favored proportional representation in both houses (the 'Virginia Plan'). Small states (New Jersey, Delaware) demanded equal representation regardless of size (the 'New Jersey Plan'). The deadlock threatened to dissolve the Convention. Who proposed the resolution?
answer: Roger Sherman of Connecticut — leading to the 'Great Compromise' or 'Connecticut Compromise'
choices: Roger Sherman of Connecticut — leading to the 'Great Compromise' or 'Connecticut Compromise'
James Madison of Virginia — though Madison opposed the compromise
William Paterson of New Jersey — author of the New Jersey Plan, not the Compromise
Edmund Randolph of Virginia — sponsor of the Virginia Plan, not the Compromise
context: Sherman's compromise gave each state two senators (equal representation) and seats in the House proportional to population. Combined with the Three-Fifths Compromise on slave-counting and the agreement on a single executive, it broke the deadlock. The Convention finished its work September 17, 1787. The Constitution required nine state ratifications to take effect; New Hampshire's June 1788 ratification did it.

question: James Madison had opposed adding a bill of rights to the Constitution in 1787, arguing that enumerating specific rights might imply that others not listed were unprotected. But ratification debates made clear that several states would only ratify with a promise of amendments. As a new Member of the House of Representatives, Madison drafted twelve proposed amendments. Ten were ratified by the states by December 15, 1791. What did the First Amendment guarantee?
answer: Freedom of religion, speech, press, peaceable assembly, and petition
choices: Freedom of religion, speech, press, peaceable assembly, and petition
Right to keep and bear arms, with a militia clause
Protection against unreasonable search and seizure
Right to a speedy and public trial by an impartial jury
context: The other three options are real Amendments — the Second, Fourth, and Sixth. The First's specific guarantees come in this order: establishment of religion, free exercise, freedom of speech, freedom of the press, the right to assemble peacefully, the right to petition government. The Bill of Rights initially applied only to the federal government; the Fourteenth Amendment (1868) eventually applied most of it to the states through the doctrine of incorporation.

question: In 1797, President John Adams sent three American commissioners (Charles C. Pinckney, John Marshall, and Elbridge Gerry) to France to negotiate over French seizures of American ships in the Quasi-War. French foreign minister Talleyrand demanded a $250,000 bribe for himself plus a $12 million loan to France as the price for negotiation. The American envoys refused. In Adams' report to Congress, the French agents were called X, Y, and Z. What was the public response?
answer: 'Millions for defense, but not one cent for tribute!' — a wave of anti-French patriotic fervor
choices: 'Millions for defense, but not one cent for tribute!' — a wave of anti-French patriotic fervor
Adams' impeachment, on grounds that he had bungled the negotiation with France
American capitulation — the bribe was paid through indirect channels by Pickering
Diplomatic withdrawal — Adams recalled the commissioners without further response
context: The Quasi-War (1798–1800) was an undeclared naval war with France. Adams resisted the warhawk faction (including Hamilton) that wanted a declared war. The Convention of 1800 ended the conflict and effectively the 1778 alliance. The XYZ Affair boosted Adams' popularity briefly but the subsequent Alien and Sedition Acts (1798) undermined him. He lost reelection 1800 to Jefferson.

question: On October 7, 1780, on a wooded ridge in northern South Carolina, about 900 American backcountry militia (the 'Overmountain Men' from settlements west of the Appalachians) attacked about 1,100 Loyalist provincials under British Major Patrick Ferguson. The Americans, fighting from cover with their long rifles, encircled and destroyed Ferguson's command in about an hour. Ferguson was killed. What was the strategic effect?
answer: Halted Cornwallis' invasion of North Carolina; began the southern campaign's reversal toward Yorktown
choices: Halted Cornwallis' invasion of North Carolina; began the southern campaign's reversal toward Yorktown
Forced British evacuation of Charleston back to New York within weeks
Triggered the French expeditionary force's landing at Newport, Rhode Island
Convinced Loyalist militias in the Carolinas to switch sides immediately to the Patriot cause
context: King's Mountain ended Loyalist recruitment in the Carolinas backcountry. Combined with Daniel Morgan's victory at Cowpens (January 17, 1781), Greene's strategic maneuvers, and the costly British 'victory' at Guilford Courthouse (March 1781), it forced Cornwallis to Virginia — and Yorktown. Thomas Jefferson called King's Mountain 'the turn of the tide of success.' The Overmountain Men's victory is commemorated as a Tennessee/North Carolina cultural touchstone.

question: On January 17, 1781, on rolling pasture in South Carolina, about 1,100 Continentals and militia under Brigadier General Daniel Morgan faced about 1,100 British regulars and Loyalists under the aggressive Lt.
