Col. Banastre Tarleton. Morgan placed his troops in three lines: militia in front with orders to fire two volleys then retreat, Continentals on the main line, and cavalry in reserve. The maneuver looked like retreat to the British. What happened?
answer: Tarleton's force was destroyed in a double envelopment; nine of ten British were killed or captured
choices: Tarleton's force was destroyed in a double envelopment; nine of ten British were killed or captured
Morgan's line collapsed and the Americans retreated to North Carolina with heavy losses
Tarleton broke through the militia and the Continentals retreated in good order
A draw — both armies withdrew, with the British holding the field at day's end
context: Cowpens was a textbook double envelopment — the kind of victory commanders dream of. Tarleton's force was destroyed; Morgan and his army escaped clean. The campaign's combination of Morgan's victories at Cowpens, Greene's strategy of fighting Cornwallis until the British lost too many men to win, and Lafayette's harrying in Virginia, set up Yorktown. Cowpens is studied at staff colleges as a masterpiece of the conditional defensive battle.

question: In late February 1778, a Prussian volunteer arrived at the encampment of Washington's army wintering at Valley Forge, Pennsylvania. Benjamin Franklin had introduced him in Paris with inflated credentials. Within weeks the Prussian — speaking little English but communicating through French interpreters and broken curses — began drilling a model company himself, then sent the trained men to drill others. By spring the Continental Army was a transformed force. Who was he?
answer: Friedrich Wilhelm Augustus, Baron von Steuben — author of the Continental Army's drill manual
choices: Friedrich Wilhelm Augustus, Baron von Steuben — author of the Continental Army's drill manual
Marquis de Lafayette — but Lafayette was a French volunteer aristocrat, not a Prussian drillmaster
Casimir Pulaski — Polish cavalry organizer killed at Savannah 1779
Tadeusz Kościuszko — Polish engineer who fortified Saratoga and West Point
context: Von Steuben's claimed Prussian general's rank was inflated (he had been an aide-de-camp to Frederick the Great as a captain). His drill manual, published 1779 and known as the 'Blue Book,' remained in U.S. Army use through the War of 1812. Lafayette had arrived earlier (1777) and was Washington's adopted protégé; Pulaski organized the cavalry; Kościuszko was an engineer. Von Steuben became inspector general of the Continental Army.

question: In March 1783, with the Continental Army camped at Newburgh, New York, awaiting demobilization and unpaid for months, an anonymous letter circulated among officers proposing a march on Congress to demand back pay — a potential military coup. On March 15, Washington called the officers to a meeting. He arrived to deliver a prepared speech. Beginning to read, he stopped, drew reading glasses from his pocket, and said what?
answer: 'Gentlemen, you will permit me to put on my spectacles — for I have grown gray in your service, and now find myself growing blind'
choices: 'Gentlemen, you will permit me to put on my spectacles — for I have grown gray in your service, and now find myself growing blind'
'I beg your indulgence — these old eyes have seen too much service for plain reading'
'A soldier must adapt — and now I bring out my reading aid as I once brought out a sword'
'You will excuse my hesitation — the press of years upon my brow'
context: The Newburgh moment is one of the great scenes in American history. The officers — many of whom had served years without pay and feared abandonment — broke down. Washington's quiet remark dissolved the conspiracy. He read his speech and left. The army was paid (eventually) and disbanded peacefully. Without Washington's intervention, the United States might have followed the Latin American pattern of military coups against weak civilian government.

question: On December 23, 1783, in the Old Senate Chamber of the Maryland State House in Annapolis (where Congress was then meeting), the 51-year-old victor of the American Revolution stood before the assembled members and surrendered his commission as Commander-in-Chief of the Continental Army. He retired to Mount Vernon. King George III, told of Washington's intention to resign, reportedly said what?
answer: If true, Washington 'will be the greatest man in the world' for declining the power he could have seized
choices: If true, Washington 'will be the greatest man in the world' for declining the power he could have seized
Washington was a fool to leave power that no one would otherwise dispute against him
American independence would not last a year once Washington was no longer in command
Washington's resignation was a tactical move that would not deceive the British government
context: The remark was reported by the American painter Benjamin West, who had been telling George III about Washington's plans. The act of voluntary resignation — comparable to Cincinnatus returning to his plow — became the central symbol of American republican virtue. Washington reluctantly accepted the presidency in 1789 only because the new Constitution had been adopted. He retired again in 1797 — establishing the two-term tradition.

question: On November 1, 1800, John and Abigail Adams became the first occupants of what was then called the 'President's House' (later the White House) in the new city of Washington — moving from Philadelphia, where the federal government had been temporarily located. Construction was not finished; many rooms were unfinished. The East Room — large, prominent, but without function — was used by Abigail for what practical purpose?
answer: Drying the family laundry — though the formal reception room would become an iconic space
choices: Drying the family laundry — though the formal reception room would become an iconic space
Storing the presidential library, which had not yet been transferred from Philadelphia
Practicing harpsichord by the Adams' daughter Nabby during the family's transition
Housing the dozens of unanswered congressional petitions Adams had brought from Philadelphia
context: Abigail's letter to her daughter (November 21, 1800) describing the East Room being used for laundry is a treasure of early American domestic history. John Adams' inscription on a fireplace mantle in the dining room — 'May none but Honest and Wise Men ever rule under this Roof' — was later carved into the mantle on FDR's orders. The Adamses lived in the White House only four months before losing the 1800 election.

question: John Adams' Federalist Congress, in its lame-duck session before Jefferson's inauguration in 1801, passed the Judiciary Act of 1801 creating new federal judgeships. Adams stayed up his last night signing commissions; some were not delivered before March 4. New Secretary of State James Madison refused to deliver them. William Marbury, denied his commission as a justice of the peace for D.C., sued in the Supreme Court. Chief Justice John Marshall faced a political dilemma. How did he resolve it?
answer: Ruled Marbury was entitled to commission but the Court lacked jurisdiction — establishing judicial review
choices: Ruled Marbury was entitled to commission but the Court lacked jurisdiction — establishing judicial review
Ordered Madison to deliver the commission, which Madison promptly did under federal pressure
Dismissed the case as a political question outside the Court's authority to adjudicate
Recused himself due to his earlier service as Secretary of State to Adams
context: Marshall's masterstroke: he gave Jefferson the immediate victory (Marbury never got his commission) but established the far greater principle that the Supreme Court could declare acts of Congress unconstitutional. The case made no immediate stir; it became central to American constitutional thought over the next century. Marshall served as Chief Justice from 1801 to 1835 — 34 years that shaped the federal judiciary.

question: In 1819, Missouri Territory petitioned to join the Union as a slave state, threatening to upset the Senate balance between 11 slave and 11 free states. Congressman James Tallmadge of New York proposed banning slavery there; Southern members protested. After two years of debate, Henry Clay engineered a compromise. What were the three elements?
answer: Missouri as slave state; Maine as free state; no slavery north of 36°30' in remaining Louisiana Purchase
choices: Missouri as slave state; Maine as free state; no slavery north of 36°30' in remaining Louisiana Purchase
Missouri as slave state; gradual abolition program in border states; new federal slave-rendition law
Missouri admitted free; Maine admitted free; existing slave states' representation guaranteed
Missouri admitted under popular sovereignty; Maine as a separate territory; federal acquisition of new western lands
context: The Missouri Compromise preserved the Union for a generation but pleased no one fully. Jefferson called it 'a fire-bell in the night' — terrifying because it signaled how dangerous the slavery question was becoming. The Compromise was effectively repealed by the Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854), which substituted 'popular sovereignty,' and then declared unconstitutional by *Dred Scott* (1857). Henry Clay would be called 'the Great Compromiser' for similar work later.

question: On January 8, 1815, after a series of skirmishes through December, British Major General Sir Edward Pakenham led a frontal assault of about 7,500 men against entrenched American positions south of New Orleans — defended by perhaps 4,500 Americans (regulars, Tennessee and Kentucky militia, Free Men of Color, Choctaw scouts, and Jean Lafitte's pirates). Behind cotton-bale barriers, American riflemen and artillery cut down the British. What was the casualty count?
answer: British 2,000+ casualties (including Pakenham killed); American casualties about 70
choices: British 2,000+ casualties (including Pakenham killed); American casualties about 70
British 500 casualties; American 200 casualties in roughly proportionate fighting
British 7,000 casualties; American 1,500 in a desperate close-run battle
British 100 casualties; American 50 — a small skirmish before withdrawal
context: The Treaty of Ghent had been signed December 24, 1814, but news had not reached America. Andrew Jackson's victory made him a national hero and helped end the war on terms suggesting American honor was vindicated. Pakenham was killed late in the assault. The Battle of New Orleans became the iconic battle of the War of 1812 — Johnny Horton's 1959 song carried the story to a new generation. Jackson rode the victory to the presidency.

question: In February–March 1836, about 200 Texian rebels under William Barret Travis and James Bowie defended a former Spanish mission in San Antonio against the Mexican president-general Antonio López de Santa Anna's army of perhaps 6,000. The defenders held out for 13 days; the final assault on March 6 killed nearly all of them, including the famous Davy Crockett. Six weeks later, on April 21, what did Sam Houston accomplish?
answer: Defeated and captured Santa Anna at the Battle of San Jacinto in 18 minutes
choices: Defeated and captured Santa Anna at the Battle of San Jacinto in 18 minutes
Negotiated with Santa Anna for Texas autonomy within the Mexican federation
Lost the Battle of San Jacinto and retreated to Louisiana before regrouping
Forced Santa Anna to sign a treaty ceding northern Mexico to the U.S.
context: 'Remember the Alamo!' was the Texian battle cry at San Jacinto. The battle lasted 18 minutes; Santa Anna's army was destroyed; Santa Anna himself was captured the next day disguised as a private. He signed the Treaty of Velasco (May 1836) granting Texan independence. The Republic of Texas existed 1836–45 until annexation by the U.S., precipitating the Mexican-American War (1846–48).

question: Between October 1838 and March 1839, about 16,000 Cherokee Indians were forcibly removed from their lands in Georgia, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Alabama to designated 'Indian Territory' (now Oklahoma). Despite their constitution, schools, newspaper, and the Supreme Court ruling in their favor (*Worcester v. Georgia* 1832), they were rounded up by Army units, held in stockades, and marched 1,200 miles. About 4,000 died. What were the major causes of death?
answer: Cold, disease, exhaustion, malnutrition — especially during the winter march
choices: Cold, disease, exhaustion, malnutrition — especially during the winter march
Armed resistance to U.S. troops, fought in small skirmishes throughout the march
Hostile attacks by other Indian tribes whose land the Cherokee crossed in transit
Mass executions by U.S. Army at three separate detention camps along the route
context: President Martin Van Buren (Jackson's successor) implemented the removal Jackson had set in motion. General Winfield Scott commanded the operation. The Cherokee 'Trail of Tears' (*Nunna daul Tsuny*) is one of the deepest injuries in American history. A minority Eastern Band escaped removal by hiding or by claiming North Carolina citizenship. Modern Cherokee Nation, headquartered in Tahlequah, Oklahoma, has about 400,000 enrolled members.

question: On July 19–20, 1848, in a Wesleyan Methodist chapel in the small upstate New York town of Seneca Falls, about 300 women and men attended the first women's rights convention in the United States. Organized by Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Lucretia Mott, and others, the convention adopted a Declaration of Sentiments modeled on the Declaration of Independence: 'all men and women are created equal.' Who attended in support of the suffrage resolution?
answer: Frederick Douglass — whose advocacy helped pass the suffrage demand by a narrow margin
choices: Frederick Douglass — whose advocacy helped pass the suffrage demand by a narrow margin
Susan B. Anthony — though Anthony did not actually attend Seneca Falls; she joined the movement 1851
Sojourner Truth — though Truth's famous 'Ain't I a Woman?' speech was at Akron 1851
Harriet Tubman — but Tubman was still enslaved in 1848, escaping in 1849
context: Stanton's husband Henry doubted the suffrage demand was politically feasible; Stanton insisted. Douglass spoke in support. The convention's resolutions launched the American women's rights movement. Susan B. Anthony joined the movement in the early 1850s; she and Stanton formed the lifelong partnership that would shape suffrage advocacy. The Nineteenth Amendment guaranteeing women's suffrage was ratified August 18, 1920 — 72 years after Seneca Falls.

question: On March 6, 1857, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7–2 in a case brought by an enslaved man who had been taken by his master into free territory and sued for his freedom on that basis. Chief Justice Roger Taney's majority opinion went far beyond the case: it declared that no African American — slave or free — could be a U.S. citizen, that Congress could not prohibit slavery in the territories (overturning the Missouri Compromise), and that slaves were property and thus protected by the Fifth Amendment. Who was the plaintiff?
answer: Dred Scott — whose case galvanized abolitionist opinion and divided the country further
choices: Dred Scott — whose case galvanized abolitionist opinion and divided the country further
Frederick Douglass — but Douglass had escaped slavery in 1838, before any such case
Anthony Burns — Boston fugitive returned to slavery 1854, a different case
James Somerset — but Somerset's was a 1772 British case, not American
context: Taney's opinion was meant to settle the slavery question definitively; it inflamed it. The Republican Party (founded 1854) made overturning *Dred Scott* part of its platform. Lincoln in the 1858 debates argued forcefully against it. Scott was freed by his owner's family three months after the decision; he died of tuberculosis September 1858. *Dred Scott* was effectively reversed by the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Amendments (1865, 1868).

question: In May 1854, Senator Stephen Douglas of Illinois pushed through Congress the Kansas-Nebraska Act, organizing two new territories under 'popular sovereignty' — letting settlers vote on whether to allow slavery. The act effectively repealed the Missouri Compromise of 1820 (which had banned slavery north of 36°30'). The result was guerrilla war between pro-slavery 'Border Ruffians' from Missouri and anti-slavery 'Free-Soilers' from New England. What is this period called?
answer: Bleeding Kansas — 1854–61 violence over slavery; perhaps 100 killed in skirmishes
choices: Bleeding Kansas — 1854–61 violence over slavery; perhaps 100 killed in skirmishes
The Border War — though that term usually applies to later Civil War guerrilla fighting
The Free-Soil Rebellion — though that was a political movement, not the bloody conflict
The Missouri Compromise War — though no such phrase was used at the time
context: John Brown's Pottawatomie massacre (May 1856) — when he and his sons hacked five pro-slavery settlers to death with broadswords — was part of Bleeding Kansas. The Sack of Lawrence (May 1856) had preceded it. The Kansas-Nebraska Act destroyed the Whig Party, drove anti-slavery Democrats out of the party, and helped form the Republican Party. Kansas entered the Union as a free state January 29, 1861 — just before the Civil War.

question: On the night of October 16, 1859, the 59-year-old abolitionist John Brown — already infamous from Bleeding Kansas — led 21 men (16 white, 5 Black) to seize the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, Virginia. He hoped to spark a slave uprising. Within 36 hours, U.S. Marines under Colonel Robert E. Lee (assisted by Lt. J.E.B. Stuart) had stormed the engine house where Brown was holed up. Ten of Brown's men were killed; Brown was captured. What happened next?
answer: Tried for treason against Virginia; hanged December 2, 1859, with national reaction polarized
choices: Tried for treason against Virginia; hanged December 2, 1859, with national reaction polarized
Tried for federal crimes; imprisoned at Fort Sumter for the remainder of his life
Tried for murder under Virginia state law; sentenced to 99 years; freed by Union forces 1861
Escaped during transport and lived in Canada until his death by natural causes 1864
context: Brown's hanging made him a martyr to the abolitionist North and a terrorist to the South. The poet John Greenleaf Whittier and Henry David Thoreau celebrated him; Lincoln distanced himself. Southern fears of insurrection intensified. The 1860 election (Lincoln's victory) and South Carolina's secession (December 20, 1860) followed within 14 months. 'John Brown's Body' became a Union marching song.

question: On November 6, 1860, Abraham Lincoln of Illinois — the Republican candidate — won the four-way presidential election with 39.8% of the popular vote and a clear Electoral College majority. The Democratic Party had split into Northern (Stephen Douglas) and Southern (John C. Breckinridge) wings; John Bell ran for the Constitutional Union Party. Lincoln carried no slave state. What did South Carolina do?
answer: Seceded from the Union on December 20, 1860 — six states followed before Lincoln's inauguration
choices: Seceded from the Union on December 20, 1860 — six states followed before Lincoln's inauguration
Filed a legal challenge to the election in the U.S. Supreme Court that was rejected
Convened a special session of the legislature that affirmed the state's loyalty conditionally
Requested federal mediation between northern abolitionists and southern interests
context: South Carolina's secession was followed by Mississippi (January 9), Florida (January 10), Alabama (January 11), Georgia (January 19), Louisiana (January 26), and Texas (February 1). The Confederate States of America formed February 4 at Montgomery, Alabama. Fort Sumter (April 12, 1861) opened the war. Four more states seceded after Lincoln's call for troops: Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee, North Carolina.

question: After repulsing Lee's first invasion of the North at Antietam (September 17, 1862), President Lincoln issued the Preliminary Emancipation Proclamation on September 22, 1862 — giving Confederate states 100 days to return to the Union or have their slaves declared free. None returned. Lincoln signed the final proclamation on January 1, 1863. The military and moral significance was vast. What was its limitation?
answer: It freed only slaves in Confederate-controlled areas; border states and Union-held South were excluded
choices: It freed only slaves in Confederate-controlled areas; border states and Union-held South were excluded
It freed slaves only after a one-year transitional period of compensated emancipation
It freed only male slaves of military age; female and child slaves were excluded
It freed only slaves whose owners had taken up arms against the Union
context: Lincoln drafted the proclamation as a war measure under his commander-in-chief powers, which limited its constitutional reach. Slavery continued legally in Kentucky, Delaware, Maryland, Missouri, and parts of Tennessee/Louisiana until the Thirteenth Amendment (December 6, 1865). About 200,000 African American men served in the U.S. Army and Navy after the proclamation — turning the war's purpose toward abolition.

question: On the evening of May 2, 1863, after a 12-mile flank march that took Lee's brilliant lieutenant past the Union right wing at Chancellorsville, Virginia, his three divisions crashed out of the woods at dusk in one of the war's great surprise attacks. The Union XI Corps under Howard collapsed. The general rode forward in the dark to scout further attack; his own North Carolina troops fired on what they took to be Union cavalry. Wounded in three places, he died eight days later of pneumonia. Who was he?
answer: Thomas J. 'Stonewall' Jackson — Lee's most aggressive corps commander, lost at Chancellorsville
choices: Thomas J. 'Stonewall' Jackson — Lee's most aggressive corps commander, lost at Chancellorsville
James Longstreet — Lee's 'Old War Horse,' but he was not killed by friendly fire
J.E.B. Stuart — Lee's cavalry chief, killed later at Yellow Tavern May 1864
A.P. Hill — corps commander killed at Petersburg April 1865
context: Lee said on hearing of Jackson's death: 'I have lost my right arm.' Jackson had been Lee's most aggressive subordinate — the Shenandoah Valley campaign (1862), Second Bull Run, the flanking march at Chancellorsville. His left arm was amputated; he died of pneumonia May 10, 1863. The Confederate command structure never fully recovered. Gettysburg (July 1863) was fought without Jackson, who had been killed two months earlier.

question: Born Hiram Ulysses Grant in Ohio 1822, the future commander of all Union armies graduated from West Point 1843 (middle of his class), served in the Mexican War, resigned the army in 1854 amid drinking rumors and a failing personal life, and was struggling in his father's leather store in Galena, Illinois, when war broke out in 1861. Re-entering service, he won early successes — but his great breakthrough victory came in February 1862. What was it?
answer: Fort Donelson — surrender of perhaps 12,000 Confederates; 'unconditional surrender' nickname
choices: Fort Donelson — surrender of perhaps 12,000 Confederates; 'unconditional surrender' nickname
Shiloh — though Grant's near-disaster at Shiloh came two months later, in April 1862
Vicksburg — though Vicksburg came in July 1863, more than a year later
Chattanooga — though Chattanooga came in November 1863
context: Grant's terms to Confederate general Simon Bolivar Buckner at Fort Donelson: 'No terms except an unconditional and immediate surrender can be accepted.' His initials U.S. Grant became 'Unconditional Surrender Grant.' Shiloh (April 1862) nearly ruined him but he survived; Vicksburg (July 1863) and Chattanooga (November 1863) made him the obvious choice for general-in-chief. Lincoln promoted him to lieutenant general March 1864 — only Washington had held that rank.

question: From May 5 to June 12, 1864, Grant's Army of the Potomac fought Lee's Army of Northern Virginia in a continuous series of battles known together as the Overland Campaign — Wilderness, Spotsylvania Court House, North Anna, Cold Harbor — culminating in Grant's crossing of the James River and the siege of Petersburg. Casualties: 55,000 Union, 33,000 Confederate. Lincoln was condemned as a 'butcher.' What was Grant's strategy?
answer: Attrition — forcing Lee into continuous battle to wear down the smaller Confederate army
choices: Attrition — forcing Lee into continuous battle to wear down the smaller Confederate army
Decisive battle — seeking a single climactic engagement to destroy Lee's army outright
Maneuver — flanking Lee out of his fortified positions toward Richmond
Defense — protecting Washington while Sherman's army did the offensive work elsewhere
context: Grant understood that Lee's army could not be allowed to recover; sustained pressure would eventually break it. The Cold Harbor frontal assault (June 3, 1864) was his greatest regret — 7,000 Union casualties in less than an hour. Petersburg held until April 1865 when Lee's lines finally cracked. Lee surrendered at Appomattox April 9. The Overland Campaign's casualty figures were politically damaging in the North but achieved what they had to.

question: Through summer 1864, William Tecumseh Sherman's army of perhaps 100,000 maneuvered against Joseph E. Johnston's smaller Army of Tennessee in north Georgia. Confederate President Jefferson Davis replaced Johnston with the more aggressive John Bell Hood in mid-July; Hood fought Sherman frontally and lost two-thirds of his army in five weeks. On September 2, 1864, the city fell. Sherman wired Lincoln: 'Atlanta is ours and fairly won.' What was the political effect?
answer: Saved Lincoln's reelection — McClellan's peace platform was discredited by the war's apparent imminent end
choices: Saved Lincoln's reelection — McClellan's peace platform was discredited by the war's apparent imminent end
Convinced Britain to formally recognize the Confederacy as a buffer against U.S. expansion
Triggered Lee's surrender within a month, ending the war by October 1864
Caused Grant to relieve Sherman for excessive aggression against Confederate civilians
context: Lincoln won the 1864 election decisively over George McClellan (who had run on a peace platform). Atlanta's fall, combined with Farragut's victory at Mobile Bay (August) and Phil Sheridan's victories in the Shenandoah Valley (September–October), changed the war's perceived trajectory. Sherman's subsequent March to the Sea (November–December 1864) added to Confederate demoralization. The war's outcome was effectively decided in fall 1864 — though the killing went on until April 1865.

question: Born in present-day West Virginia in 1824, the man who would become Lee's most aggressive lieutenant was an orphan raised by an uncle, a graduate of West Point (17th of 59 in his class), a hero of the Mexican War, a professor of artillery and natural philosophy at Virginia Military Institute (where cadets nicknamed him 'Tom Fool Jackson'), and a devout Presbyterian who sucked lemons to relieve dyspepsia. What was his Civil War nickname?
answer: 'Stonewall' — given by General Bee at First Bull Run, July 21, 1861
choices: 'Stonewall' — given by General Bee at First Bull Run, July 21, 1861
'Old Fuss and Feathers' — but that was Winfield Scott, the Mexican War commander
'Old Pete' — but that was James Longstreet, Lee's other corps commander
'Sam' — but that was Ulysses S. Grant's family nickname before his West Point years
context: Jackson's Valley Campaign (March–June 1862) — 17,000 Confederates tying down 60,000+ Union troops with rapid marches and decisive engagements — is studied at staff colleges. His name change from Jonathan to 'Stonewall' was earned at First Bull Run. Killed by friendly fire at Chancellorsville (May 1863); Lee said he had lost his right arm. The death weakened the Confederate command structure decisively going into Gettysburg.

question: Following the Thirteenth Amendment (1865, ending slavery) and the Fourteenth Amendment (1868, citizenship and equal protection), Reconstruction-era Congress proposed and the states ratified a third Reconstruction amendment in 1870. Frederick Douglass had argued for its passage; Susan B. Anthony and Elizabeth Cady Stanton opposed it because it did not include women's suffrage. What did the amendment guarantee?
answer: The right to vote shall not be denied on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude
choices: The right to vote shall not be denied on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude
Federal protection of freedmen's civil rights including travel, marriage, contract, and jury service
Federal jurisdiction over voting rolls, replacing state-controlled voter registration of citizens
Universal adult suffrage including women regardless of race, color, or previous condition of servitude
context: The Fifteenth Amendment was ratified February 3, 1870. Reconstruction-era African American voting in the South was significant: 16 African Americans were elected to Congress 1870–77, including two senators from Mississippi (Hiram Revels, Blanche K. Bruce). After the Compromise of 1877 ended Reconstruction, Southern states used literacy tests, poll taxes, and white primaries to disenfranchise African American voters — circumventions the Voting Rights Act of 1965 finally addressed.

question: The disputed presidential election of 1876 saw Democrat Samuel Tilden win the popular vote and lead in electoral votes, but 20 electors from three Southern states (Florida, Louisiana, South Carolina) plus one from Oregon were contested. An Electoral Commission of 8 Republicans and 7 Democrats voted 8–7 on every contested elector for Republican Rutherford B. Hayes. To prevent Democratic obstruction, a deal was struck. What was the political bargain?
answer: Hayes inaugurated; federal troops withdrawn from the South; Reconstruction ended
choices: Hayes inaugurated; federal troops withdrawn from the South; Reconstruction ended
Hayes inaugurated; Tilden granted Treasury post; Democrats accepted election in exchange
Election rerun in disputed states; Tilden won the rerun and became president
Both candidates withdrew; Congress chose Speaker James Blaine as compromise president
context: The 'Compromise of 1877' (informal, not a formal document) ended the federal presence enforcing Reconstruction. The last federal troops left the South in April 1877. Republican rule in the remaining 'Redeemer' states ended. The Jim Crow era began — segregation, lynching, disenfranchisement. The Hayes-Tilden compromise is regarded as one of the most damaging in American history for African American civil rights — it deferred them for nearly 90 years.

question: When Abraham Lincoln assembled his Cabinet in March 1861, he gave the four most prestigious posts to men who had been his rivals for the 1860 Republican nomination — including the strongest contender, who became Secretary of State and at first thought he should be the real president. The historian Doris Kearns Goodwin gave the strategy a phrase. Who was the Secretary of State?
answer: William H. Seward — who became Lincoln's most loyal supporter after the early friction
choices: William H. Seward — who became Lincoln's most loyal supporter after the early friction
Salmon P. Chase — but Chase became Treasury Secretary, not State
Edward Bates — became Attorney General, not State
Simon Cameron — became Secretary of War, briefly and corruptly
context: Seward had been the front-runner for the 1860 nomination. His 'Thoughts for the President's Consideration' (April 1861) suggested foreign policy diversions to unify the country and proposed himself as policy director — Lincoln gently put him in his place. They became close friends. Seward was attacked the same night Lincoln was shot (April 14, 1865) by a Booth co-conspirator and survived. He served as Secretary of State under Johnson; he negotiated the Alaska purchase (1867). Goodwin's *Team of Rivals* (2005) shaped Obama's Cabinet strategy.

question: The summer of 1898 saw the United States fight a ten-week war with Spain over Cuba, ending Spanish empire in the Western Hemisphere. American victories at sea (Dewey at Manila Bay, May 1; Sampson at Santiago, July 3) and on land (San Juan Heights, July 1) led to the Treaty of Paris (December 10, 1898). The U.S. acquired Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines for $20 million. What was Cuba's status?
answer: Independent republic under U.S. protectorate (Platt Amendment); U.S. retained Guantánamo base
choices: Independent republic under U.S. protectorate (Platt Amendment); U.S. retained Guantánamo base
Annexed directly as a U.S. territory like Puerto Rico
Made a Spanish protectorate under U.S. supervision pending elections
Divided into eastern and western zones under joint U.S.-Spanish administration
context: The Platt Amendment (1901) made Cuba a U.S. protectorate — Cuban constitution required to permit U.S. intervention. Guantánamo Bay was leased in 1903 and remains under U.S. control. The Filipino-American War (1899–1902) was bloodier than the Spanish-American War, with about 4,200 American and 200,000 Filipino dead (most civilian, many from disease). The U.S. emerged as a Pacific power with global ambitions.

question: On January 8, 1918, in a joint session of Congress, President Woodrow Wilson outlined fourteen principles he proposed as the basis for ending World War I and structuring postwar peace. The points included open diplomacy, freedom of the seas, free trade, reduction of armaments, impartial adjustment of colonial claims, evacuation of occupied territories, self-determination for various peoples, and the establishment of a general association of nations. What was the proposed association called?
answer: The League of Nations — central to Wilson's plan; later rejected by the U.S. Senate
choices: The League of Nations — central to Wilson's plan; later rejected by the U.S. Senate
The United Nations — though that name was used in WWII and adopted in 1945
The North Atlantic Treaty Organization — but NATO was formed in 1949
The Concert of Powers — though that phrase referred to the 19th-century European balance
context: Wilson took the Fourteen Points and his League of Nations idea to Versailles 1919; he got the League but not many of the points. The Senate, led by Henry Cabot Lodge, refused to ratify the Versailles Treaty — partly over League membership. The U.S. never joined. Wilson collapsed on a speaking tour (October 1919); his second wife Edith effectively ran his administration for over a year. He died 1924. The League existed 1920–46, weakened by U.S. absence.

question: Ratified January 16, 1919 and effective January 17, 1920, the Eighteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution prohibited 'the manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors' within the United States. The Volstead Act (October 1919) provided enforcement. The amendment was the culmination of decades of advocacy by the Anti-Saloon League, the Women's Christian Temperance Union, and Protestant churches. What were the unintended consequences?
answer: Organized crime expansion, speakeasies, bootlegging, rampant non-enforcement; repealed by 21st Amendment 1933
choices: Organized crime expansion, speakeasies, bootlegging, rampant non-enforcement; repealed by 21st Amendment 1933
Effective elimination of alcohol consumption with strong public compliance throughout the 1920s
Federal-state conflict reducing enforcement to occasional symbolic prosecutions only
Mass exodus of brewers to Canada and Mexico, where they continued legal production
context: Prohibition was famously a failure of social engineering. Al Capone made his fortune as the Chicago bootlegger. Speakeasies flourished. The St. Valentine's Day Massacre (February 14, 1929) symbolized the era. The 21st Amendment (ratified December 5, 1933) repealed the 18th — the only constitutional amendment to repeal another. Some states maintained 'dry' status for years; Mississippi's last 'dry' county went 'wet' only in 2010.

question: After seventy-two years of advocacy beginning at Seneca Falls (1848), an amendment guaranteeing women's right to vote was ratified by the necessary three-fourths of the states on August 18, 1920 — when the Tennessee legislature provided the decisive vote (a 24-year-old representative changed his vote at his mother's urging). What was the amendment's language?
answer: 'The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged ... on account of sex'
choices: 'The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged ... on account of sex'
'Citizens of the United States, including women, shall have the right to vote in all elections'
'The right of every adult citizen of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged'
'No state shall deny the franchise to any person on account of sex, age, or condition of servitude'
context: The 19th Amendment's language deliberately echoed the 15th (which had prohibited race-based denial of suffrage). The Tennessee vote — when 24-year-old Harry Burn changed from 'no' to 'aye' under his mother's urging — gave the amendment the necessary 36 states. Native American women had to wait until 1924 (citizenship) and effectively longer for full suffrage in some states. African American women in the South were largely disenfranchised until the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

question: From 1929 to 1933, the U.S. economy contracted by about a third. Unemployment rose from about 3% to about 25% (perhaps 13 million people). Industrial production halved. About 9,000 banks failed in three years (only one of the major credit-bureaus offered an interbank insurance scheme). 'Hoovervilles' — shantytowns of the unemployed — sprang up. President Hoover's response was inadequate to the scale of the catastrophe. What was the international context?
answer: Worldwide depression — Germany hardest hit, contributing to Hitler's 1933 rise to power
choices: Worldwide depression — Germany hardest hit, contributing to Hitler's 1933 rise to power
U.S.-only — most of Europe was already in recovery from a separate downturn
British-American — France and Germany were economically isolated and unaffected
Western-only — Soviet Union experienced rapid growth and Asia was outside the system
context: The Depression was global. Germany — with hyperinflation history (1923) and now mass unemployment — turned to Hitler in 1933. Britain abandoned the gold standard 1931. Stalin's Soviet Union, isolated from world markets, was running Five-Year Plans and the Holodomor; growth statistics were largely propaganda. The Depression's depth and length had multiple causes including the Smoot-Hawley tariff (1930), banking failures, and Federal Reserve contraction.

question: The Manhattan Project (1942–46) required not just laboratories but entire new cities — designed, populated, and operated in secret. Three sites are the most famous: a New Mexico high desert for design (built around an old boys' school), a Tennessee site for uranium enrichment (in the Cumberland mountains), and a Washington State site for plutonium production (on the Columbia River). Name the three.
answer: Los Alamos (design), Oak Ridge (uranium), Hanford (plutonium)
choices: Los Alamos (design), Oak Ridge (uranium), Hanford (plutonium)
Los Alamos (design), Berkeley (uranium), Pasco (plutonium)
Albuquerque (design), Knoxville (uranium), Seattle (plutonium)
Trinity (design), Manhattan (uranium), Olympia (plutonium)
context: Los Alamos was Oppenheimer's site (he had spent boyhood summers in the area). Oak Ridge separated uranium-235 from uranium-238 (mostly by gaseous diffusion and electromagnetic). Hanford produced plutonium-239 in reactors. About 130,000 people worked at peak. Hanford is now a National Historical Park and Superfund cleanup site (radioactive contamination problems persist). Oak Ridge and Los Alamos remain active national laboratories.

question: On the night of August 12–13, 1961, East German authorities began constructing a barrier between East Berlin and West Berlin — initially barbed wire, soon concrete blocks. The wall would eventually stretch about 96 miles around West Berlin's perimeter, with 302 watchtowers and 20 bunkers. About 5,000 people escaped over the 28 years it stood; about 140 were killed trying. President Kennedy's response was famously stated in Berlin two years later. What did he say?
answer: 'Ich bin ein Berliner' — June 26, 1963, in front of West Berlin's city hall
choices: 'Ich bin ein Berliner' — June 26, 1963, in front of West Berlin's city hall
'Tear down this wall!' — though that was Reagan's 1987 line, not Kennedy's
'Berliner, ich bin frei!' — but that's a German jumble, not what Kennedy said
'Berlin lebe!' — a similar but not exact rendering of the Kennedy speech
context: Kennedy's 'Ich bin ein Berliner' (he was holding a card with the German phonetics) became one of the iconic Cold War moments. (The myth that he had inadvertently called himself a jelly doughnut — *ein Berliner* — is wrong; Berliners themselves don't use 'Berliner' for the pastry.) The wall stood until November 9, 1989. The Brandenburg Gate, where Reagan spoke in 1987, was opened December 22, 1989.

question: On January 30–31, 1968 (during the Vietnamese Tet lunar new year holiday), North Vietnamese and Vietcong forces launched coordinated attacks on more than 100 South Vietnamese cities, towns, and military bases. The U.S. embassy in Saigon was briefly penetrated. Hue, the imperial capital, was held for nearly a month and saw mass executions of civilians. Militarily the offensive was a Vietcong disaster. What was its political effect?
answer: Shattered American public confidence; LBJ withdrew from 1968 reelection in March
choices: Shattered American public confidence; LBJ withdrew from 1968 reelection in March
Forced North Vietnamese surrender within weeks; Paris peace talks opened immediately
Caused immediate U.S. withdrawal from Vietnam; helicopters left Saigon by April
Sparked a Soviet-American diplomatic crisis; nuclear alerts raised on both sides
context: Tet showed the war was not 'almost over' as American officials had suggested. CBS anchor Walter Cronkite's February 27 commentary that the war was 'mired in stalemate' was a turning point. Johnson reportedly said 'if I've lost Cronkite, I've lost middle America.' LBJ withdrew from the 1968 race on March 31. The Vietnam War continued seven more years. About 58,000 Americans died; Vietnam's losses were perhaps 2–3 million.

question: On April 4, 1968, on the second-floor balcony of the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, Tennessee, the 39-year-old president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference was shot in the face by a single rifle round fired from across the street. He had come to Memphis to support striking sanitation workers. He died at 7:05 p.m. The night before, he had given his last speech, ending: 'I may not get there with you, but I want you to know tonight that we as a people will get to the promised land.' Who killed him?
answer: James Earl Ray — escaped convict who pled guilty 1969, later recanted; died in prison 1998
choices: James Earl Ray — escaped convict who pled guilty 1969, later recanted; died in prison 1998
Sirhan Sirhan — but Sirhan killed Robert Kennedy two months later in Los Angeles
Mark Chapman — but Chapman killed John Lennon in 1980 in New York
Lee Harvey Oswald — but Oswald killed JFK in 1963 in Dallas
context: Ray pled guilty (no trial) and was sentenced to 99 years. He later sought to withdraw the plea; the King family came to believe he had not acted alone. Riots followed King's death in over 100 American cities. Robert Kennedy was assassinated in Los Angeles June 6, 1968 — completing one of the most traumatic political years in American history. King won the Nobel Peace Prize 1964 and the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously 1977.

question: On June 5, 1968, just after midnight, Senator Robert F. Kennedy of New York — having just won the California Democratic presidential primary, putting him on track for the nomination — was leaving a victory celebration through a kitchen passageway of the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles. A 24-year-old Palestinian Christian named Sirhan Sirhan stepped from a serving area and fired eight rounds from a .22 revolver. Kennedy was shot three times. What followed?
answer: Kennedy died June 6 at 1:44 a.m.; Hubert Humphrey eventually won the Democratic nomination
choices: Kennedy died June 6 at 1:44 a.m.; Hubert Humphrey eventually won the Democratic nomination
Kennedy survived; Sirhan was executed by California gas chamber within the year
Kennedy died; his wife Ethel ran for his Senate seat and won that fall
Kennedy survived but withdrew from the race for medical reasons
context: Sirhan was convicted; sentenced to death but California's death penalty was overturned (1972) and his sentence commuted. He has been denied parole 15+ times. Robert Kennedy's death — two months after MLK's, in an American year that already included Tet, Lyndon Johnson's withdrawal, and the Czechoslovak invasion that followed in August — added to the period's trauma. Humphrey lost narrowly to Nixon in November.

question: On September 8, 1974 — exactly one month after Richard Nixon's August 9 resignation — President Gerald Ford issued a 'full, free, and absolute pardon' to Nixon for any crimes he might have committed during his presidency. Ford had assured the Senate at his vice-presidential confirmation that he did not contemplate such a pardon. The pardon was politically devastating. What was Ford's rationale?
answer: To spare the country a prolonged trial of a former president and let the nation heal
choices: To spare the country a prolonged trial of a former president and let the nation heal
To allow Nixon to testify openly about Watergate without fear of self-incrimination
To exchange the pardon for Nixon's resignation as part of a secret August deal
To pre-empt similar legal challenges against other Watergate-era officials
context: Ford's approval ratings dropped from 71% to 49% within days. He probably lost the 1976 election to Jimmy Carter partly because of the pardon. In retrospect — particularly given decades of subsequent revelations about Nixon's conduct — many historians now treat the pardon more sympathetically. Ford received the John F. Kennedy Profile in Courage Award (2001) for the pardon. He died 2006 at 93.

question: Between 1985 and 1986, members of the Reagan administration — including National Security Adviser John Poindexter, NSC staffer Oliver North, and CIA Director William Casey — facilitated the secret sale of weapons to Iran (despite an arms embargo) in hope of freeing American hostages in Lebanon. Profits were diverted (via Israeli middlemen) to the Nicaraguan Contras — anti-Sandinista rebels Congress had specifically banned from receiving U.S. government aid. What was the scandal called?
answer: Iran-Contra — exposed November 1986; led to 14 indictments, Reagan's lowest approval ratings
choices: Iran-Contra — exposed November 1986; led to 14 indictments, Reagan's lowest approval ratings
Iran-gate — though the '-gate' suffix derived from Watergate was used informally
The Tower Commission report — but that was the investigative report, not the affair itself
October Surprise — but that referred to a different (alleged) 1980 affair
context: The Iran-Contra Affair was the worst scandal of the Reagan administration. Reagan denied knowing of the diversion; Congress and the Tower Commission concluded he had been inattentive. Oliver North became a TV personality; Poindexter and others were convicted but had convictions overturned on appeal. Pardons by George H.W. Bush in 1992 ended several prosecutions. The affair did not destroy Reagan's presidency the way Watergate had destroyed Nixon's.

question: On January 28, 1986, 73 seconds after liftoff from Cape Canaveral, the Space Shuttle *Challenger* broke apart. All seven crew were killed: Commander Dick Scobee, pilot Michael Smith, mission specialists Ellison Onizuka, Judith Resnik, and Ronald McNair, payload specialist Gregory Jarvis, and teacher Christa McAuliffe (the first 'Teacher in Space'). Live broadcasts to schoolrooms across the country showed the disaster. What was the cause?
answer: O-ring failure on a solid rocket booster, exacerbated by unusually cold launch-day temperatures
choices: O-ring failure on a solid rocket booster, exacerbated by unusually cold launch-day temperatures
Main engine failure caused by metal fatigue in the turbopumps after multiple flights
External tank explosion caused by hydrogen leakage during pre-launch fueling
Pilot error on entry to the prescribed altitude attack-vector for fuel jettison
context: Richard Feynman's televised demonstration of O-ring failure (squeezing a sample in ice water and showing how it lost resilience) made the failure mechanism vivid. The Rogers Commission (1986) concluded NASA's risk management had been compromised by schedule pressure. The shuttle program was grounded for 32 months. *Columbia* would be lost on reentry February 1, 2003 — another seven dead. The shuttle program ended 2011 after 135 missions.

question: On August 2, 216 BC, on a plain in southern Italy near the Aufidus River, two Roman consular armies (about 86,000 men) under Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Gaius Terentius Varro faced Hannibal's Carthaginian army of about 50,000 (Africans, Spaniards, Gauls, Numidian cavalry). Hannibal deployed his weaker center forward in a deliberate convex bulge; the Roman heavy infantry pressed forward, the bulge inverted to concave, and Hannibal's heavy infantry struck both flanks. What did the Numidian cavalry then do?
answer: Wheeled around and attacked the Roman rear, completing a perfect double envelopment
choices: Wheeled around and attacked the Roman rear, completing a perfect double envelopment
Withdrew to defensive positions to prevent Roman cavalry from reaching the supply train
Pursued the Roman cavalry off the field, leaving the infantry battle to play out alone
Held in reserve until dusk and then attacked the retreating Roman columns
context: About 50,000 Romans were killed at Cannae — perhaps the highest single-day Western casualty figure until the Somme (1916). Paullus died fighting; Varro escaped. Cannae remains the model double envelopement and is taught at every staff college. Hannibal failed to follow up with an attack on Rome. Roman recovery from Cannae through Fabian strategy and Scipio's eventual victory at Zama (202 BC) is one of the great institutional resiliences in history.

question: In September AD 9, three Roman legions (XVII, XVIII, XIX) under the governor of Germania, Publius Quinctilius Varus, were marching back to winter quarters when they were ambushed in a wooded defile in northern Germany. Their guide, the Cheruscan chief Arminius (who had served as a Roman auxiliary officer), had betrayed them. Over three days the legions were destroyed. Varus killed himself. What was the strategic consequence?
answer: Roman expansion east of the Rhine was permanently abandoned; the frontier set on the river
choices: Roman expansion east of the Rhine was permanently abandoned; the frontier set on the river
Tiberius led a reconquest within two years that restored Roman rule to the Elbe
The Cheruscan tribes adopted Roman administrative practices voluntarily under Arminius
The legions' eagles were recovered within months, restoring Rome's military honor
context: Augustus reportedly cried out 'Quintili Vare, legiones redde!' ('Varus, give me back my legions!'). The lost legion numbers (XVII, XVIII, XIX) were never reused. The Rhine became the Roman frontier for four centuries. Germanicus recovered some standards in AD 14–16 punitive expeditions. The battlefield was identified in the 1980s at Kalkriese — site contains thousands of artifacts of three Roman legions.

question: On October 14, 1066, on a ridge near the south coast of England, the Norman invader Duke William of Normandy fought the Anglo-Saxon king Harold Godwinson. Harold had marched from Yorkshire (where he had defeated his brother Tostig and the Norwegian king at Stamford Bridge September 25) and his shield wall held the ridge for most of the day. Late in the afternoon, an arrow (according to the Bayeux Tapestry) struck Harold. What happened?
answer: Harold killed; Saxon line broke; William crowned Christmas Day, founding the Norman dynasty
choices: Harold killed; Saxon line broke; William crowned Christmas Day, founding the Norman dynasty
Harold wounded but survived; treaty signed dividing England between Norman and Saxon spheres
William killed; Norman invasion collapsed; Saxon rule continued under Harold's son
Both kings escaped; Norman forces withdrew to Normandy after harsh weather
context: Hastings transformed England. The Norman aristocracy replaced the Saxon; French became the language of the court for three centuries; the legal system, the church administration, the castle landscape were remade. About 7,000 men fought on each side. The Bayeux Tapestry (commissioned by William's half-brother, Bishop Odo of Bayeux) is the great visual narrative — about 230 feet long.

question: On August 26, 1071, the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV Diogenes met Sultan Alp Arslan of the Seljuk Turks near a fortress in eastern Anatolia. The Byzantine army of perhaps 40,000 included unreliable mercenaries (Cuman cavalry, Frankish, Norman). During the battle the Byzantine reserve commander Andronikos Doukas (a political rival) abandoned the emperor and withdrew. Romanos was captured. What was the long-term consequence?
answer: Catastrophic Byzantine loss of Anatolia to Turkish nomads; called Constantinople for help; First Crusade 1095
choices: Catastrophic Byzantine loss of Anatolia to Turkish nomads; called Constantinople for help; First Crusade 1095
Quick Byzantine recovery as Alp Arslan died within a year and Seljuk succession collapsed
Romanos' captivity by Alp Arslan led to a generous peace treaty preserving Byzantine territory
Manzikert's losses were small but psychological; Anatolia held until the 14th-century Ottoman expansion
context: Alp Arslan released Romanos on generous terms — but Doukas faction at Constantinople had already deposed him. Civil war among Byzantines opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement. Within a generation most of the Anatolian heartland — the source of Byzantine soldiery and grain — was lost. Alexios I Komnenos' appeal to the West produced the First Crusade (1095). Manzikert is conventionally cited as the beginning of the end of Byzantine power.

question: On August 26, 1346, Edward III of England with about 12,000 men (including 5,000 English longbowmen) was caught by Philip VI of France's larger army (perhaps 30,000 with up to 6,000 mounted knights and Genoese crossbowmen). The English defended a wooded ridge near Crécy in Picardy. The Genoese crossbows were ineffective in the rain; French knights charged uphill repeatedly through their own men and were cut down by clothyard arrows. What changed in warfare?
answer: The English longbow demonstrated that yeoman archers could destroy mounted knights
choices: The English longbow demonstrated that yeoman archers could destroy mounted knights
The French chivalric class was permanently broken and aristocratic warfare ended in Europe
Crossbows were universally abandoned after the Genoese failure at Crécy in the rain
The English crown ended its claim to the French throne after this initial victory
context: Edward's 16-year-old son, the Black Prince, won his spurs at Crécy. The longbow could be drawn at 100+ pounds and shot 12 arrows per minute; the crossbow shot 2 per minute. The Hundred Years' War continued for 117 years until 1453 (with intervals); the great English victories — Crécy, Poitiers (1356), Agincourt (1415) — relied on the longbow. By 1500 gunpowder was replacing it. The English yeoman archer became a national myth.

question: On St. Crispin's Day, October 25, 1415, Henry V of England with about 6,000 troops (mostly longbowmen, the rest dysentery-afflicted men-at-arms) was caught by a French army at least three times its size on a muddy field in northern France. Henry placed his archers behind sharpened stakes. French knights, on foot in the mud, struggled forward through arrow showers. Many drowned in their armor in the marsh. What was the casualty ratio?
answer: Perhaps 6,000 French dead (including much of the nobility) against about 400 English
choices: Perhaps 6,000 French dead (including much of the nobility) against about 400 English
Perhaps 1,000 French dead against 300 English in roughly proportionate fighting
Perhaps 3,000 French dead and 2,500 English wounded in a closely contested fight
Perhaps 500 French and 100 English casualties — much smaller than legend suggests
context: Henry's controversial order to kill French prisoners during the battle (because he feared a renewed French attack) added to the casualty figure. The English wounded had been ordered to fight on as best they could. Shakespeare's *Henry V* (c. 1599), with the St. Crispin's Day speech, shaped English national memory. Henry died of dysentery 1422; English military prospects in France collapsed after Joan of Arc's intervention at Orleans 1429.

question: On October 7, 1571, off the Greek coast in the Gulf of Patras, the Holy League fleet (Spain, Venice, the Papal States, Genoa, Malta, Savoy) of about 200 galleys under Don John of Austria met the Ottoman fleet of about 230 galleys under Müezzinzade Ali Pasha. The battle was the last major battle fought primarily with galleys. About 30,000 Ottomans died (vs. 7,500 Christians); 117 Ottoman ships were captured; 12,000 Christian galley slaves were freed. What 24-year-old future novelist was wounded there?
answer: Miguel de Cervantes — lost the use of his left hand; later author of *Don Quixote* (1605)
choices: Miguel de Cervantes — lost the use of his left hand; later author of *Don Quixote* (1605)
Christopher Marlowe — but Marlowe was English and not yet born in 1571
Lope de Vega — Spanish dramatist but no record of his presence at Lepanto
Tirso de Molina — Spanish dramatist of later generation, not at Lepanto
context: Cervantes (1547–1616) fought aboard the galley *Marquesa* and was shot three times — twice in the chest and once in the left arm, which he lost use of. He was always proud of his Lepanto wounds. Don John of Austria (illegitimate half-brother of Philip II of Spain) was the celebrated victor. The victory ended Ottoman naval dominance in the central Mediterranean. G.K. Chesterton's poem 'Lepanto' (1911) shaped Anglo-American Catholic memory.

question: On August 13, 1704, in a Bavarian village on the Danube, the English Duke of Marlborough (John Churchill) and the Holy Roman Empire's Prince Eugene of Savoy with about 52,000 troops attacked a Franco-Bavarian army of about 60,000 under Marshal Tallard and Elector Maximilian Emanuel. Marlborough's diversionary attacks pinned the French wings; his decisive cavalry charge in the center broke the French line. About 30,000 French and Bavarians were killed, wounded, or captured. What was the war?
answer: The War of the Spanish Succession (1701–14) — Louis XIV's grandson on the Spanish throne
choices: The War of the Spanish Succession (1701–14) — Louis XIV's grandson on the Spanish throne
The Nine Years' War (1688–97) — earlier conflict, fought before Blenheim
The War of the Austrian Succession (1740–48) — later conflict involving Maria Theresa
The Great Northern War (1700–21) — Sweden vs. Russia/Poland, not Marlborough's war
context: Blenheim saved Vienna and the Habsburg empire from Bourbon dominance. Marlborough was rewarded with Blenheim Palace — Winston Churchill's birthplace (1874) and ancestral home. The campaign showed unprecedented tactical and logistical sophistication — marching 250 miles in 35 days from the Low Countries to the Danube to surprise Tallard. The War of the Spanish Succession was finally settled by the Peace of Utrecht (1713).

question: On July 8, 1709, near the Ukrainian town of Poltava, Tsar Peter I 'the Great' of Russia with about 42,000 troops decisively defeated King Charles XII of Sweden with about 17,000 (Charles having been wounded weeks earlier and forced to direct the battle from a litter). The defeated Swedes retreated to Ottoman territory; about 7,000 were killed and 20,000 captured. What was the strategic consequence?
answer: Russia replaced Sweden as the dominant power of Northern Europe; permanent shift of regional power
choices: Russia replaced Sweden as the dominant power of Northern Europe; permanent shift of regional power
Charles XII regained his throne with Ottoman support and the war continued for decades
Peter's army was so exhausted that Russia paid Sweden tribute in the subsequent treaty
The Russian Imperial Guard was decimated, delaying Russia's wars for a generation
context: Poltava marks the rise of Russia and the decline of Sweden as great powers. Charles XII (the 'Last Viking') spent five years in Ottoman exile, then died fighting in Norway 1718. Peter built St. Petersburg as Russia's window on Europe. The Great Northern War (1700–21) ended at Nystad with Sweden's eastern Baltic provinces (modern Estonia, Latvia) ceded to Russia. Modern Russia dates substantially from Peter's reforms.

question: On October 21, 1805, off Cape Trafalgar on the Spanish Atlantic coast, the British Royal Navy under Admiral Horatio Nelson (27 ships of the line) met the combined Franco-Spanish fleet of Admiral Villeneuve (33 ships). Nelson's signal flew from HMS *Victory*: 'England expects that every man will do his duty.' He attacked in two columns, perpendicular to the enemy line. The British took 22 prize ships; lost none. What was Nelson's fate?
answer: Shot by a French sniper from *Redoutable*; died below decks; last words 'thank God I have done my duty'
choices: Shot by a French sniper from *Redoutable*; died below decks; last words 'thank God I have done my duty'
Mortally wounded but lived to return to England; died in London six weeks later
Wounded but survived; promoted to viscount with national thanksgiving on his return
Captured by the French during the boarding action; ransomed by the British government later
context: Trafalgar ended Napoleon's planned invasion of Britain and gave the Royal Navy command of the sea for the rest of the Napoleonic Wars. Nelson's body was preserved in a cask of brandy for the voyage home and buried in St. Paul's Cathedral, London. The 'Nelson Touch' (his name for his attack plan) became a model of audacious tactics. Trafalgar Day (October 21) is still observed in Britain.

question: On December 2, 1805 — the first anniversary of Napoleon's coronation — the French Grand Armée of about 73,000 met the combined Russian and Austrian army of about 85,000 (commanded by Tsar Alexander I and Emperor Francis II in person) near a Moravian village. Napoleon deliberately weakened his right flank to draw the allies into the attack he wanted, then drove a corps onto the dominating Pratzen Heights through their thinned center. What is the battle called?
answer: Austerlitz — the 'Battle of the Three Emperors,' regarded as Napoleon's tactical masterpiece
choices: Austerlitz — the 'Battle of the Three Emperors,' regarded as Napoleon's tactical masterpiece
Marengo — but Marengo was an earlier 1800 battle in Italy, not 1805
Friedland — a later 1807 battle against Russia alone, not 1805
Eylau — a brutal February 1807 battle in winter, not the 1805 'Three Emperors'
context: Russian and Austrian casualties were about 36,000; French about 9,000. The campaign ended in the Peace of Pressburg (December 1805), which redrew the map of central Europe. The Holy Roman Empire was dissolved 1806. Austerlitz is regularly cited as one of the most perfect tactical victories of European warfare. Tolstoy's *War and Peace* describes the battle through the eyes of Prince Andrei Bolkonsky.

question: On September 7, 1812, about 70 miles west of Moscow, Napoleon's Grand Armée (about 130,000 by this point, reduced from 685,000 who had crossed the Niemen in June) met Kutuzov's Russian army (about 120,000) in the bloodiest single day of the entire Napoleonic Wars. About 70,000 total casualties in twelve hours. The French nominally won the field; the Russians withdrew in order. What did Napoleon enter a week later?
answer: Moscow — which the Russians had set on fire; he found no government to negotiate peace with
choices: Moscow — which the Russians had set on fire; he found no government to negotiate peace with
St. Petersburg — capturing the Russian capital and forcing tsarist negotiation
Kiev — the Ukrainian regional capital, having bypassed Moscow strategically
Smolensk — a major western city, but he had already captured it weeks earlier
context: Tolstoy's *War and Peace* dramatizes Borodino at length. The Russian winter, the long retreat from Moscow (October–December), and Kutuzov's pursuit destroyed Napoleon's army — perhaps 400,000 of the 600,000 invaders died. Borodino was a tactical Napoleonic win but strategic disaster — the kind of victory that does not lead anywhere if the enemy refuses to negotiate. Napoleon's last great battle would be Waterloo (1815).

question: From October 16 to October 19, 1813, the largest battle of the Napoleonic Wars and the largest battle in European history before WWI was fought outside the German city of Leipzig. Napoleon (about 200,000 troops) faced a coalition of Russians, Prussians, Austrians, and Swedes (about 320,000) under Prince Schwarzenberg's general direction. Casualties: 75,000 French, 50,000 allied. The French were driven back across the Rhine. What was this battle called?
answer: The Battle of the Nations (*Völkerschlacht*) — Napoleon's most decisive defeat before Waterloo
choices: The Battle of the Nations (*Völkerschlacht*) — Napoleon's most decisive defeat before Waterloo
The Battle of the Three Emperors — though that was Austerlitz, eight years earlier
The Battle of the Coalition — though no such formal name was used
The Battle of Saxony — though the region's name was not used for the battle
context: Leipzig ended French dominance of central Europe. By April 1814 Napoleon had abdicated and been exiled to Elba. The Hundred Days (1815) and Waterloo (June 1815) were postscripts. Leipzig's monument (*Völkerschlachtdenkmal*, completed 1913 for the centennial) is one of the largest in Europe at 91 meters. The Russian, Austrian, and Prussian alliance dominated European politics for the next four decades.

question: On October 25, 1854, during the Crimean War siege of Sevastopol, a Russian attempt to capture British supply base at Balaklava produced several actions including the famous 'Charge of the Light Brigade.' Through a chain of confused orders involving Lord Raglan's commander-in-chief instructions, Lord Lucan's cavalry division command, and Captain Nolan as messenger, what did the Light Brigade actually do?
answer: Charged about 1.25 miles up the 'Valley of Death' against Russian artillery; ~110 killed, ~160 wounded
choices: Charged about 1.25 miles up the 'Valley of Death' against Russian artillery; ~110 killed, ~160 wounded
Charged successfully against Russian infantry, taking 200 prisoners with light losses
Withdrew under heavy fire after receiving conflicting orders, suffering moderate losses
Captured Russian guns in the South Valley as originally intended without significant loss
context: Tennyson's 'The Charge of the Light Brigade' (December 1854) — written within weeks — fixed the disaster in English memory. The miscommunication chain ended with the Light Brigade attacking 20 Russian artillery pieces at the end of a valley, with more guns and infantry on the flanks. 670 men charged; about 110 returned fit for service. The Crimean War (1853–56) cost about 600,000 lives total — many to cholera and inadequate medicine, addressed by Florence Nightingale at Scutari.

question: On March 9, 1862, in Hampton Roads at the mouth of Chesapeake Bay, two ironclad warships fought the world's first battle between armored steam-powered warships. The Confederate *CSS Virginia* (rebuilt from the captured Union *USS Merrimack*) had destroyed two wooden Union frigates the day before. The new Union ironclad *USS Monitor*, with its revolving gun turret designed by John Ericsson, met *Virginia* at dawn. The four-hour battle ended in a draw. What was the result?
answer: Tactical draw, strategic Union victory — wooden navies obsolete worldwide overnight
choices: Tactical draw, strategic Union victory — wooden navies obsolete worldwide overnight
Tactical Confederate victory — Virginia drove Monitor off but lost too many crew to claim victory
Tactical Union victory — Monitor sank Virginia by penetrating her armored casemate
Both ships sank in the same hour after exchanging close-range broadsides
context: The Hampton Roads battle convinced every major navy that the age of wooden warships was over. Both ironclads were lost in 1862 — *Virginia* burned by her own crew to prevent capture (May), *Monitor* foundered off Cape Hatteras (December). Their armor and turrets shaped naval design for the next 80 years. The Royal Navy's HMS *Warrior* (1860) had been the earlier seagoing ironclad, but Hampton Roads was the first battle.

question: On September 17, 1862, near the Maryland village of Sharpsburg along Antietam Creek, the Union Army of the Potomac under McClellan (~75,000) attacked Lee's Army of Northern Virginia (~38,000) on Lee's first invasion of the North. Three phases (Cornfield, Sunken Road, Burnside's Bridge) and 12 hours produced about 22,700 combined casualties — the bloodiest single day in American military history. What was the political consequence?
answer: Lincoln issued the Preliminary Emancipation Proclamation September 22; Britain reconsidered recognition
choices: Lincoln issued the Preliminary Emancipation Proclamation September 22; Britain reconsidered recognition
McClellan was confirmed in command and given expanded authority over the Eastern theater
Lee surrendered at Sharpsburg, ending the war eight months after Bull Run
The Confederate government collapsed in Richmond, with Davis fleeing to South Carolina
context: Antietam was Lee's first attempt to invade the North; he retreated to Virginia after the battle. The Preliminary Emancipation Proclamation (September 22) — making freeing slaves a war aim — was politically possible only after a Union 'victory' (technically a draw, but a strategic Union win because Lee retreated). McClellan was relieved of command November 7 for failing to pursue Lee's wounded army.

question: On January 22, 1879, during the British invasion of Zululand, a Zulu impi of about 20,000 warriors under Chief Ntshingwayo attacked a British camp at the base of a distinctive sphinx-shaped rock formation. The British force of about 1,800 (mostly the 24th Regiment, plus African auxiliaries) was scattered across a wide perimeter, with ammunition stored too far from the firing line. The British were overwhelmed by ~3 p.m. About 1,300 British and African allies were killed. What is the battle called?
answer: Isandlwana — the worst single British defeat at the hands of an indigenous African force
choices: Isandlwana — the worst single British defeat at the hands of an indigenous African force
Rorke's Drift — but Rorke's Drift was the heroic British defense the same evening, not the disaster
Ulundi — the later British victory in July 1879 that ended the Zulu War
Adwa — but Adwa was 1896, against Italy, and is Ethiopian not Zulu
context: Hours after Isandlwana, about 4,000 Zulus attacked the small British supply depot at Rorke's Drift, defended by 150 men. The defense earned 11 Victoria Crosses — the most ever for a single action. Cetshwayo's army won at Isandlwana but lost the war; Zululand was annexed July 1879. The 1964 film *Zulu* (with Michael Caine) dramatized Rorke's Drift. The British defeat shocked the empire and spurred decades of military reform.

question: On May 27–28, 1905, in the strait between Korea and Japan, Admiral Tōgō Heihachirō's Japanese fleet (4 battleships, 27 cruisers, others) annihilated Admiral Zinovy Rozhestvensky's Russian Baltic Fleet (8 battleships, 3 coastal defense ships) which had sailed 18,000 miles from the Baltic to reinforce Russian forces in the Far East. Of 11 Russian battleships present, 8 were sunk; over 5,000 Russians died vs. 117 Japanese. What was the significance?
answer: First major Asian naval victory over a European power; ended Russo-Japanese War and Russian eastern ambitions
choices: First major Asian naval victory over a European power; ended Russo-Japanese War and Russian eastern ambitions
First use of dreadnought battleships in fleet action, predating HMS *Dreadnought* by a year
First successful Japanese-British alliance against Russia, demonstrating Anglo-Japanese cooperation
First mass loss of Russian sailors leading to revolutionary unrest in the fleet
context: Tsushima ended the Russo-Japanese War. The Treaty of Portsmouth (negotiated by Theodore Roosevelt, September 1905) gave Japan Korea, Liaodong Peninsula, and southern Sakhalin. The war's outcome shook European confidence in racial supremacy assumptions; it also fed Russian revolutionary unrest contributing to the 1905 Revolution. The 'Tsushima syndrome' shaped Russian naval thinking for decades. Tōgō was treated as Japan's Nelson.

question: From February 21 to December 18, 1916, the Imperial German Army attempted to 'bleed France white' by attacking the strategically secondary fortress system of Verdun on the Meuse. About 70 German divisions and 65 French divisions cycled through the meat-grinder. Casualties: 337,000 German, 377,000 French — over 700,000 total. The French commander General Robert Nivelle uttered the defiant phrase. What was it?
answer: 'Ils ne passeront pas!' — 'They shall not pass!' — became the symbol of French resistance
choices: 'Ils ne passeront pas!' — 'They shall not pass!' — became the symbol of French resistance
'Sur le pré, on les aura!' — 'On the meadow, we'll get them!' — actual battlefield exhortation
'Vive la France!' — generic patriotic cry, not Nivelle's signature phrase at Verdun
'En avant, mes braves!' — generic charge command, not the iconic Verdun phrase
context: Verdun became the symbol of French sacrifice in WWI. Pétain's command emphasized rotation of divisions, supply via the 'Sacred Way,' and patient defense. The Battle of the Somme (July 1, 1916, opened to relieve pressure on Verdun) was an even greater disaster — 60,000 British casualties the first day. Verdun's terrain still shows the war: nine villages destroyed completely (*villages détruits*), unexploded ordnance regularly recovered, ossuaries containing remains of 130,000 unknown soldiers.

question: On July 1, 1916, the British Expeditionary Force launched the long-prepared offensive on the Somme — designed to relieve pressure on the French at Verdun. After a seven-day artillery barrage that fired 1.7 million shells but did not destroy the German barbed wire as expected, the infantry walked at 7:30 a.m. across no-man's-land in lines. By nightfall, the British had advanced perhaps a few hundred yards in most places. What were the first-day casualties?
answer: About 57,000 British casualties (19,240 killed) — bloodiest day in British military history
choices: About 57,000 British casualties (19,240 killed) — bloodiest day in British military history
About 15,000 British casualties — heavy but proportionate to the gains made
About 100,000 British casualties — total destruction of the first attack wave
About 5,000 British casualties — light losses given the scale of the offensive
context: Many of the casualties were 'Pals Battalions' — units raised from single towns and friendships. Whole communities lost their young men in a day. The Somme offensive continued until November 1916; total Allied gains were about 6 miles for some 600,000 casualties. The Somme became a foundational image of the futility of WWI warfare. Tanks were first used in combat at Flers-Courcelette (September 15, 1916) during the battle.

question: From May 26 to June 4, 1940, the British Expeditionary Force and French allies — trapped against the English Channel by the German blitzkrieg through the Ardennes — were evacuated from the beaches and harbor of a French Channel port. About 850 vessels (Royal Navy destroyers plus 700 'little ships' — fishing boats, pleasure craft, paddle steamers) shuttled across the Channel through Luftwaffe attacks. How many were evacuated?
answer: About 338,000 Allied troops — far more than the 30,000 the British had initially planned for
choices: About 338,000 Allied troops — far more than the 30,000 the British had initially planned for
About 90,000 troops — losses far exceeded the planned evacuation goal
About 600,000 troops — more than originally believed trapped
About 50,000 troops — most equipment and personnel were lost
context: Most heavy equipment was left behind. Hitler had ordered his panzers halted (the 'Halt Order' May 24) for reasons still debated. Churchill called it 'the miracle of Dunkirk' — but warned in Parliament 'we must be very careful not to assign to this deliverance the attributes of a victory. Wars are not won by evacuations.' Christopher Nolan's *Dunkirk* (2017) won three Oscars. The escape preserved the British army to fight on.

question: From July to October 1940, the Royal Air Force Fighter Command's roughly 1,000 fighters (mostly Spitfires and Hurricanes) defended British airspace against the Luftwaffe's larger force aiming to clear the way for invasion (Operation Sea Lion). Air Chief Marshal Hugh Dowding's careful management of fighter resources, the radar early-warning chain, and the resilience of the pilots ('the Few') wore down the German offensive. What did Churchill say about the pilots?
answer: 'Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few'
choices: 'Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few'
'We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds'
'I have nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears and sweat'
'This was their finest hour'
context: All four are Churchill phrases but only the first refers specifically to the RAF pilots (House of Commons, August 20, 1940). Britain lost about 1,500 pilots in the Battle of Britain; Germany lost about 2,500 aircrew and far more aircraft. By mid-September Hitler had postponed Sea Lion indefinitely. The Battle of Britain was the first major military setback for Germany in WWII and ensured Britain remained in the war until the U.S. entry (December 1941) and the Eastern Front (June 1941) opened.

question: On the morning of December 7, 1941 (Pearl Harbor time), six Japanese aircraft carriers (Akagi, Kaga, Soryu, Hiryu, Shokaku, Zuikaku) launched two waves totaling 353 aircraft against the U.S. Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor. The attack lasted 90 minutes. 2,403 Americans killed; 1,178 wounded. Eight battleships hit (four sunk including USS *Arizona*); 188 aircraft destroyed (most on the ground). Japanese losses: 29 aircraft, 5 midget submarines. What strategic asset escaped?
answer: Three U.S. fleet aircraft carriers (*Enterprise*, *Lexington*, *Saratoga*) were at sea and survived
choices: Three U.S. fleet aircraft carriers (*Enterprise*, *Lexington*, *Saratoga*) were at sea and survived
The U.S. submarine force at Pearl Harbor was undamaged and operational the next day
