context: The August 1991 coup attempt by Soviet hardliners against Gorbachev had failed in three days, partly because Yeltsin (as Russian Federation president) stood on a tank outside the Russian White House and rallied resistance. The Baltic states (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania) declared full independence and were recognized internationally September 1991. Ukraine's December 1 referendum (90% for independence, 84% turnout) made the Union impossible. Belovezha legally killed it.

question: On December 31, 1999, ailing Russian president Boris Yeltsin announced his resignation. He had chosen as his successor (and acting president) a relatively obscure former KGB lieutenant colonel and head of the FSB. Within weeks of the March 26, 2000 election that confirmed him, the new president had launched the Second Chechen War with public approval, consolidated control of major media outlets, and begun restoring elements of Soviet symbolism. Who is he?
answer: Vladimir Putin — whose 20+ years as Russian leader transformed Russia from democratization to autocracy
choices: Vladimir Putin — whose 20+ years as Russian leader transformed Russia from democratization to autocracy
Dmitri Medvedev — Putin's hand-picked successor 2008–12 who returned the post to Putin
Yevgeny Primakov — earlier prime minister whom Yeltsin had dismissed in 1999
Sergei Stepashin — another short-term prime minister displaced by Putin in August 1999
context: Putin (1952–) has served as president 2000–08, prime minister 2008–12, and president 2012–present. His career has included Yukos affair (Khodorkovsky imprisoned 2003), the second Chechen war, war with Georgia (2008), annexation of Crimea (2014), Russian intervention in Syria (2015), invasion of Ukraine (2022). Russian democracy of the 1990s, fragile as it was, has been replaced by personalist rule with limited domestic dissent and aggressive foreign policy.

question: After Chechnya declared independence in 1991, Russia (under Yeltsin) intervened militarily December 1994 to reassert control. The First Chechen War (December 1994–August 1996) was a humiliating Russian defeat; Yeltsin signed the Khasavyurt Accord effectively granting Chechen autonomy. After apartment-block bombings in Moscow and other cities (September 1999, attributed by the Russian government to Chechen terrorists, with persistent allegations of FSB involvement), the Second Chechen War began. What was the outcome of the Second War?
answer: Russian victory; Grozny destroyed; ~100,000 dead; pro-Moscow Kadyrov regime installed
choices: Russian victory; Grozny destroyed; ~100,000 dead; pro-Moscow Kadyrov regime installed
Negotiated Chechen autonomy preserving the 1996 settlement
Chechen independence under international supervision following UN mediation
Stalemate with continuing low-level violence into the 2020s without resolution
context: The Second Chechen War (1999–2009) destroyed Grozny in urban warfare comparable to Stalingrad. Putin came to power partly on the war's success — he had pledged to 'rub out terrorists in the outhouse.' The Kadyrov dynasty (Akhmad until 2004, then his son Ramzan) has ruled Chechnya since under Moscow's direction. Critical voices including Anna Politkovskaya (murdered 2006) documented atrocities. Boris Nemtsov (murdered 2015) opposed the wars.

question: Between 246 and 221 BC, the king of the western Chinese state of Qin (Zhao Zheng, who would become 'First Emperor') unified the warring states of China by conquest, standardized weights and measures, scripts, and axle widths, and ordered the construction of an early version of the Great Wall. He died in 210 BC during an inspection tour. His tomb mound near Xi'an was discovered to contain about 8,000 life-sized clay sculptures of soldiers, horses, and chariots. What is this discovery called?
answer: The Terracotta Army — discovered by farmers digging a well in 1974 near Xi'an
choices: The Terracotta Army — discovered by farmers digging a well in 1974 near Xi'an
The Tomb of the Yellow Emperor — but Huangdi was legendary, predating Qin Shi Huang
The Han Tombs of Mawangdui — but those are in Hunan, from a later dynasty
The Ming Tombs north of Beijing — but those are from the much later Ming dynasty
context: Qin Shi Huang's tomb has not been excavated — the burial chamber itself remains sealed. According to Sima Qian (writing a century later), it contains rivers of mercury (modern mercury readings around the site are unusually high). The Terracotta Army was discovered by farmers in 1974 and has become one of the most famous archaeological sites in the world. The Qin dynasty itself lasted only 15 years; the Han dynasty (206 BC – 220 AD) followed.

question: Around 138 BC, Emperor Wu of Han sent a diplomatic envoy named Zhang Qian westward to seek an alliance against the Xiongnu nomads. Captured and held by the Xiongnu for ten years, Zhang Qian eventually escaped and traveled to the Ferghana Valley (modern Uzbekistan) and Bactria. He returned to Han China in 126 BC with detailed knowledge of Central Asian peoples, kingdoms, and products. What did his travels open?
answer: The Silk Road — sustained Han trade with Central Asia and ultimately the Roman Empire
choices: The Silk Road — sustained Han trade with Central Asia and ultimately the Roman Empire
The Maritime Silk Road — but that became important under the Tang and Song dynasties later
The Tea Horse Road — but that was a later route between Yunnan and Tibet
The Tribute System — but that was a Tang and Ming diplomatic framework
context: Zhang Qian's accounts (preserved in Sima Qian's *Records of the Grand Historian*) are the foundation of Han knowledge of the western regions. The Silk Road carried Chinese silk west and Mediterranean goods east; Buddhism spread along it from India to China; ideas, diseases (probably plague), and people traveled. The Han also exported paper, gunpowder, the compass, and silk weaving. By Roman times, Chinese silk was worn by Roman senators.

question: From 618 to 907 AD, the Tang dynasty ruled China at one of the most cosmopolitan moments in Chinese history. The capital, founded by the Han, drew traders from Persia, India, and Central Asia; Buddhist monks pilgrimaged from there to India; the poetry of Li Bai (701–62) and Du Fu (712–70) flourished. The city's population reached perhaps 1 million during the 8th century, making it the largest in the world. What was the capital called?
answer: Chang'an — modern Xi'an; the eastern terminus of the Silk Road
choices: Chang'an — modern Xi'an; the eastern terminus of the Silk Road
Luoyang — secondary Tang capital, but smaller than Chang'an at peak
Kaifeng — Northern Song dynasty capital, after the Tang
Beijing — but Beijing was not a major capital until the Yuan and Ming dynasties
context: Tang Chang'an's grid layout (rectangular, walled, with broad north-south and east-west avenues) became the model for East Asian capital design — Kyoto (794), Nara, Pyongyang. The Tang were the cosmopolitan height of medieval Chinese civilization. The Tang fell to the An Lushan Rebellion (755–63, devastating) and subsequent crises. Song dynasty (960–1279) followed after the chaos of the Five Dynasties period.

question: Born around 551 BC in the small Chinese state of Lu (modern Shandong province), this philosopher and teacher spent his life trying to find rulers who would adopt his teachings on ethical governance — emphasizing filial piety, ritual propriety, social harmony, and the cultivation of virtue (*ren*, 仁) by the gentleman scholar (*junzi*). He left no writings; his disciples assembled his sayings in a collection. What is the collection called?
answer: The Analects (*Lunyu*) — recorded in conversational form by his disciples
choices: The Analects (*Lunyu*) — recorded in conversational form by his disciples
The Mencius — recorded by Mencius (c. 372–289 BC), a later Confucian
The Tao Te Ching — but that is Daoist, attributed to Laozi
The Art of War — but that is by Sun Tzu, a different 6th-century BC figure
context: Confucius (the Latinized form of Kongzi or Kong Fuzi) became the most influential Chinese thinker; his ideas shaped East Asian civilization. The Confucian classics (Five Classics, Four Books) became the basis of the imperial examination system from the Tang dynasty onward. Mencius developed Confucian ethics; Xunzi offered a stricter version. Han Confucianism (from Dong Zhongshu) became the state ideology. The Communist Cultural Revolution attacked Confucianism; the post-1980s Chinese state has rehabilitated him.

question: Around 500 BC during the Spring and Autumn period of Chinese history, a general probably named Sun Wu served the king of Wu in southern China and reportedly wrote a 13-chapter treatise on military strategy that has been studied for 2,500 years. The work emphasizes deception, the importance of knowing one's enemy and oneself, the value of avoiding battle when possible, and the moral and material conditions of victory. What is the work?
answer: The Art of War (*Bing-fa*) — basis of Chinese military thinking and widely studied worldwide
choices: The Art of War (*Bing-fa*) — basis of Chinese military thinking and widely studied worldwide
The Tao Te Ching — but that's Laozi's philosophical work, not military strategy
The Sun-Tzu Annals — though this is the actual text, the title is wrong
The Records of Wu — but that's an unrelated historical text
context: Sun Tzu's Art of War became influential throughout East Asia. Cao Cao (155–220 AD) wrote a commentary still studied. Mao Zedong drew on it. Western interest grew in the 20th century — Lionel Giles' 1910 English translation; Samuel Griffith's 1963 translation (popular among U.S. Marines). The work is required reading at many military academies and has been read by business strategists. Whether 'Sun Tzu' was one person or several is debated.

question: Around 1206 AD, a man originally named Temüjin united the Mongol tribes of the eastern steppe after years of warfare and political maneuvering. At a *kurultai* (council) at the Onon River, he was acclaimed with a new title. Over the next 21 years he would conquer northern China, Central Asia, and parts of the Caucasus, founding the largest contiguous land empire in human history. What was his new title?
answer: Chinggis Khan ('Universal Ruler') — also rendered Genghis Khan in Western sources
choices: Chinggis Khan ('Universal Ruler') — also rendered Genghis Khan in Western sources
Great Khan (Khaqan) — that title was used by his grandson Kublai for the Yuan dynasty
Khan of Khans — generic Mongol-Turkish title, not Temüjin's specific honorific
Khagan of Mongolia — modern coinage, not the historical 1206 title
context: Chinggis Khan died 1227 during a campaign against the Tanguts. His four sons (Jochi, Chagatai, Ögedei, Tolui) and their descendants ruled the Mongol Empire and its successor khanates. The empire's height under his grandsons (mid-13th century) covered about a quarter of the world's land area. Mongol practices — religious tolerance, the *yam* postal system, commercial standards across the Silk Road — shaped Eurasian history.

question: In 1271, the grandson of Chinggis Khan completed the conquest of the southern Song dynasty's remnants in southern China and proclaimed a new Chinese dynasty with a Chinese name. He moved his capital from Karakorum in Mongolia to Dadu (modern Beijing). His court welcomed the Venetian Marco Polo (probably 1275–92). Who was the Mongol ruler?
answer: Kublai Khan — founder of the Yuan dynasty (1271–1368)
choices: Kublai Khan — founder of the Yuan dynasty (1271–1368)
Mongke Khan — Kublai's brother whom Kublai succeeded as Great Khan
Hulagu Khan — Kublai's brother who founded the Ilkhanate in Persia
Ögedei Khan — Kublai's uncle who led the European invasions of 1241
context: The Yuan dynasty (1271–1368) saw foreign rule over China — Mongols and other non-Han held the highest offices. Marco Polo's *Travels* (dictated in Genoese prison c. 1298) described Kublai's empire to medieval Europe — though some details have been doubted. The Yuan fell to the Ming (founded 1368 by the peasant rebel Zhu Yuanzhang). The Forbidden City in Beijing (1406–20) was built under the Ming Yongle emperor — Beijing remained the Chinese capital under the Yuan, Ming, Qing, and the modern People's Republic.

question: Mughal emperor from 1556 to 1605, the grandson of Babur (founder of the dynasty) consolidated the Mughal Empire over most of the Indian subcontinent. Married to a Hindu Rajput princess (Jodha Bai), he convened religious dialogues at his court at Fatehpur Sikri including Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians, Christian Jesuits, and Muslims. He abolished the *jizya* tax on non-Muslims and proposed a syncretic state cult (*Din-i Ilahi*). Who was he?
answer: Akbar — third Mughal emperor; remembered for tolerance and consolidation of the empire
choices: Akbar — third Mughal emperor; remembered for tolerance and consolidation of the empire
Babur — founder of the Mughal dynasty, but his reign ended in 1530
Aurangzeb — Akbar's great-grandson, but his policies reversed Akbar's tolerance
Shah Jahan — Akbar's grandson, builder of the Taj Mahal but not the tolerance reformer
context: Akbar's grandfather Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat (1526), founding Mughal rule. Akbar's son Jahangir (r. 1605–27), grandson Shah Jahan (r. 1628–58, Taj Mahal), and great-grandson Aurangzeb (r. 1658–1707, more orthodox Islamic policy, expansion to maximum extent) followed. The empire declined through the 18th century; the last emperor Bahadur Shah II was exiled by the British after the 1857 rebellion. Akbar's experiments with religious tolerance have been compared to those of Henry IV of France in the same period.

question: Between 1632 and 1653, the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built a white marble mausoleum in Agra, India, for his beloved third wife who had died in childbirth in 1631. About 20,000 workers and 1,000 elephants were used in construction. The structure became one of the most recognized buildings in the world. What was the wife's name?
answer: Mumtaz Mahal — 'Chosen of the Palace,' Shah Jahan's third wife
choices: Mumtaz Mahal — 'Chosen of the Palace,' Shah Jahan's third wife
Nur Jahan — Jahangir's wife (Shah Jahan's stepmother), powerful in earlier Mughal politics
Jodha Bai — Akbar's Rajput wife (Shah Jahan's great-grandmother)
Roshanara — Shah Jahan's daughter, supporter of his son Aurangzeb
context: Mumtaz Mahal (1593–1631) was the niece of Nur Jahan. She died giving birth to her 14th child. Shah Jahan was deposed by his son Aurangzeb in 1658 and held under house arrest in Agra Fort until his death in 1666 — reportedly able to see the Taj Mahal from his confinement. Aurangzeb buried his father beside Mumtaz in the Taj. The Taj is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1983). Air pollution from nearby industry has been damaging the marble; cleaning efforts continue.

question: From March 12 to April 6, 1930, the 60-year-old Mohandas Gandhi led 78 followers from his Sabarmati Ashram to the coastal village of Dandi — a march of 240 miles in 24 days. At Dandi he picked up a handful of natural salt from the beach, in deliberate violation of the British colonial salt monopoly. The act was illegal but trivial; its symbolic power was enormous. Thousands joined as marchers; perhaps 80,000 were arrested in the months that followed. What did the march demonstrate?
answer: The power of mass nonviolent resistance (*satyagraha*) to challenge British rule
choices: The power of mass nonviolent resistance (*satyagraha*) to challenge British rule
Indian-Pakistani cooperation across religious lines before partition
Communist organization of agricultural workers in Gujarat
British willingness to negotiate immediate Indian independence
context: The Salt March was Gandhi's most famous act of civil disobedience. He had developed *satyagraha* (truth-force) in South Africa (1893–1914); he led several previous campaigns in India (non-cooperation 1920–22). The 1942 Quit India movement followed. India achieved independence August 15, 1947, with partition into India and Pakistan and massive communal violence (perhaps 1 million dead). Gandhi was assassinated January 30, 1948, by a Hindu nationalist who blamed him for accommodating Muslims.

question: On August 15, 1947, two new dominions were born from British India: the Union of India and the new state of Pakistan (East and West, separated by 1,000 miles of Indian territory). The boundary line had been drawn in five weeks by a British lawyer (Sir Cyril Radcliffe) who had never visited India. Hindus and Sikhs in Pakistani areas, and Muslims in Indian areas, moved or fled in massive numbers. What was the human cost?
answer: Perhaps 1 million killed in communal violence; 10–15 million displaced
choices: Perhaps 1 million killed in communal violence; 10–15 million displaced
Limited violence — perhaps 50,000 dead; orderly population exchange
About 5 million killed in widespread atrocities; 50 million displaced
Negligible casualties; partition completed peacefully under UN supervision
context: Partition was one of the largest forced migrations of the 20th century. The Indo-Pakistani Wars of 1947–48 (Kashmir), 1965, 1971 (Bangladesh independence), and 1999 (Kargil) plus the standing nuclear-armed confrontation since 1998 are partition's continuing consequences. Mountbatten's hasty timetable and Radcliffe's rushed boundary award are often blamed. Jawaharlal Nehru's 'tryst with destiny' speech (August 14, 1947) is a landmark of Indian independence rhetoric. Jinnah, Pakistan's founder, died September 1948.

question: About 261 BC, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka (the third Mauryan ruler, grandson of Chandragupta who had founded the dynasty c. 322 BC) launched a war of conquest against the kingdom of Kalinga on the eastern coast of India. The destruction and suffering of the war — perhaps 100,000 dead in battle, 150,000 deported — reportedly produced a moral crisis. Ashoka's response was to convert to a faith he made the kingdom's standard. What was the religion?
answer: Buddhism — Ashoka's pillar edicts spread Buddhist principles across his empire
choices: Buddhism — Ashoka's pillar edicts spread Buddhist principles across his empire
Hinduism — but Hinduism was the existing religion of the region, not a conversion
Jainism — important contemporary religion but not the one Ashoka adopted
Sufism — but Sufism is a later Islamic mystical tradition, not 3rd century BC
context: Ashoka (r. c. 268–232 BC) sent Buddhist missionaries to Sri Lanka (his son Mahinda), to Greek-influenced kingdoms in Bactria, possibly to Egypt and Macedonia. Ashoka's rock and pillar edicts — among the earliest examples of writing in South Asia — survive at sites across India. He is the Mauryan dynasty's most famous ruler. The Ashokan lion capital became the emblem of modern India; the *Dharmacakra* on his pillars appears on the Indian flag.

question: In 1324, the *mansa* (sultan) of the Mali Empire in West Africa undertook the Hajj to Mecca with a caravan of perhaps 60,000 attendants — including 12,000 slaves carrying gold staves, 80 camels carrying 300 pounds of gold each, and a personal retinue of wives, scholars, and merchants. His passage through Cairo (during the reign of the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad) reportedly caused gold prices to plummet for years. Who was the ruler?
answer: Mansa Musa — whose Hajj is one of the great moments in West African history
choices: Mansa Musa — whose Hajj is one of the great moments in West African history
Sundiata Keita — founder of the Mali Empire about a century earlier
Askia Muhammad — ruler of the later Songhai Empire (r. 1493–1528)
Mai Idris Aluma — ruler of Kanem-Bornu, contemporary of Songhai's later rulers
context: Mansa Musa (r. c. 1312–37) put Mali on European maps for the first time — the 1375 Catalan Atlas showed him on a throne with the inscription 'this is the richest king of all the land.' He brought back the Andalusian architect Es-Saheli, who built the great mosques of Timbuktu and Djenné. Sankore University at Timbuktu reached its height in the next century. Mali declined; Songhai rose; Morocco's invasion of 1591 ended the regional empire.

question: Born in Tangier (Morocco) in 1304, a Moroccan-Berber scholar set out at age 21 on what was initially a Hajj pilgrimage and became thirty years of nearly continuous travel — through North Africa, the Middle East, Persia, East Africa (down to modern Tanzania), India, China, the Maldives, Sumatra, Spain, and the Mali Empire. He probably traveled about 75,000 miles. He dictated his observations on his return to Morocco. Who was he?
answer: Ibn Battuta — author of the *Rihla*, the most extensive medieval travel account
choices: Ibn Battuta — author of the *Rihla*, the most extensive medieval travel account
Marco Polo — but Polo was Venetian, traveled earlier (1271–95), and was less far-ranging
Ibn Khaldun — Tunisian historian, contemporary of Ibn Battuta but not the traveler
Al-Idrisi — earlier 12th-century geographer at the Norman court of Sicily
context: Ibn Battuta's *A Gift to Those Who Contemplate the Wonders of Cities and the Marvels of Travelling* (the *Rihla*, 'journey') was dictated to the Andalusian scholar Ibn Juzayy in 1356. The work is a major source for the cultural and political geography of the 14th-century Islamic world — and gives a window on the Mali Empire's eastern Sahel, Delhi Sultanate India, Yuan China, and many other regions. He died 1369.

question: On July 4, 1187, at the Horns of Hattin in northern Palestine, the Ayyubid Sultan Saladin destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem under King Guy of Lusignan and the Templars. The Crusader army had marched out from secure water sources, was harassed by Saladin's cavalry, and broke down in heat and thirst. About 200 Templars and Hospitallers were beheaded after the battle. Saladin freed the captured King Guy. What was the immediate consequence?
answer: Jerusalem surrendered October 2, 1187; most Christian holy sites in Saladin's hands
choices: Jerusalem surrendered October 2, 1187; most Christian holy sites in Saladin's hands
Crusader counterattack from Tyre liberated Jerusalem within months
Stalemate with Saladin unable to capture the city until the next year
Saladin's death in the fighting prevented further conquests in the region
context: Jerusalem's loss triggered the Third Crusade (1189–92) — Richard I 'Lionheart' of England, Philip II of France, Frederick I 'Barbarossa' (drowned crossing a river in Anatolia). Richard recovered the coast (Acre, Jaffa) but not Jerusalem. Saladin died March 1193 in Damascus, leaving (according to chronicles) only one gold coin and 47 silver — he had given away the rest. He has been celebrated in both Muslim and (since the 19th century) Western tradition as a chivalrous opponent.

question: On May 29, 1453, after a 53-day siege, the army of the 21-year-old Ottoman sultan broke through the triple walls of Constantinople. He had commissioned a Hungarian engineer named Orban to build cannons including one massive 27-foot piece that could fire 600-pound stone balls. The Christian Byzantine Empire ended; the Ottoman Empire became a major Mediterranean power. Who was the sultan?
answer: Mehmed II 'the Conqueror' (Fatih) — ruled 1444–46 and 1451–81
choices: Mehmed II 'the Conqueror' (Fatih) — ruled 1444–46 and 1451–81
Suleiman I 'the Magnificent' — later sultan (r. 1520–66) who besieged Vienna
Selim I 'the Grim' — Mehmed's grandson who conquered the Mamluk empire
Bayezid I 'the Thunderbolt' — earlier sultan defeated by Tamerlane at Ankara 1402
context: Mehmed converted Hagia Sophia to a mosque the same day. The Ottoman Empire would last until 1923 (Mustafa Kemal Atatürk's republican revolution). Constantinople (Istanbul) became one of the great Mediterranean cities under Ottoman rule. The fall of the city sent Byzantine scholars and manuscripts west, contributing to the Italian Renaissance. Mehmed's siege artillery marked the gunpowder age's takeover of medieval fortification.

question: Ottoman sultan from 1520 to 1566 — the longest reign in Ottoman history — this ruler took the empire to its territorial peak. He conquered Belgrade (1521), Rhodes (1522), most of Hungary (Mohács 1526), besieged Vienna (1529, unsuccessful), captured Baghdad (1534), and built Ottoman naval supremacy in the eastern Mediterranean (until Lepanto 1571). His architect Mimar Sinan built mosques across the empire. Who was he?
answer: Suleiman I — called 'the Magnificent' in Europe, 'the Lawgiver' (Kanuni) in the empire
choices: Suleiman I — called 'the Magnificent' in Europe, 'the Lawgiver' (Kanuni) in the empire
Selim II — Suleiman's son and successor, whose reign saw Lepanto's defeat
Murad III — late 16th-century sultan during the empire's first signs of decline
Ahmed I — early 17th-century sultan who built the Blue Mosque in Istanbul
context: Suleiman's law codes systematized Ottoman governance for centuries. His Russian-born concubine and (unusually for an Ottoman ruler) legal wife Hürrem (Roxelana) shaped his later reign. Their son Selim II succeeded; his other son Bayezid was strangled. Mimar Sinan (1488–1588) was perhaps the greatest Islamic architect of any era — over 300 surviving works including the Süleymaniye Mosque (Istanbul) and Selimiye Mosque (Edirne).

question: Beginning in the 1630s, after a series of edicts under the third Tokugawa shogun Iemitsu, Japan closed itself to most foreign contact. Japanese citizens were forbidden to leave; foreigners were forbidden to enter; Christianity (which had spread under Portuguese and Spanish missionaries) was suppressed. Some 200,000 to 400,000 Japanese Christians were killed or forced to apostatize. The policy lasted over 200 years. What was the one Western contact point?
answer: Dejima — a small artificial island in Nagasaki harbor where only Dutch traders were allowed
choices: Dejima — a small artificial island in Nagasaki harbor where only Dutch traders were allowed
Hirado — but Dutch trade was moved from Hirado to Dejima in 1641
Yokohama — but Yokohama opened only after the 1854 Treaty of Kanagawa
Osaka — but Osaka was not a foreign trade port under sakoku
context: Dejima was Japan's window on the West during the Edo period. The Dutch alone among Westerners were tolerated — partly because they had supported the shogunate against the 1637–38 Shimabara Rebellion of Catholic peasants. 'Dutch Learning' (*rangaku*) became a recognized intellectual tradition. Commodore Matthew Perry's 'black ships' (1853–54) forced Japan to open. The Meiji Restoration of 1868 ended the Tokugawa shogunate and launched modernization.

question: On July 8, 1853, a U.S. Navy squadron of four black-hulled steam-powered warships under Commodore Matthew C. Perry sailed into Edo (Tokyo) Bay. Perry refused to negotiate at Nagasaki (the designated foreign-trade port) and delivered President Millard Fillmore's letter demanding Japanese ports be opened to American trade. He withdrew with a promise to return; he came back in February 1854 with seven ships. What did the Japanese sign?
answer: The Convention of Kanagawa (March 31, 1854) — opening two ports to American ships
choices: The Convention of Kanagawa (March 31, 1854) — opening two ports to American ships
The Treaty of Shimoda (1858) — though that was later, separate, and broader
Full unconditional surrender of Japanese sovereignty to the U.S.
A military alliance against China, including American basing rights
context: The Convention of Kanagawa opened Shimoda and Hakodate to American shipping. The Harris Treaty (1858) extended trade rights, providing the model for similar 'unequal treaties' with Britain, France, the Netherlands, and Russia. The Meiji Restoration (1868) overthrew the Tokugawa shogunate; modernization (the Charter Oath, abolition of feudal domains, conscript army, industrialization, Constitution 1889) followed within decades. Perry's intervention thus accelerated Japan's transformation into a great power.

question: In January 1868, after years of growing tension between the Tokugawa shogunate (the centuries-old military government) and reformist samurai from the southwestern domains of Satsuma, Choshu, and others, a coup at the imperial court in Kyoto restored direct rule to the 15-year-old Emperor Meiji. A brief civil war (Boshin War, 1868–69) defeated Tokugawa loyalists. The new government launched the most rapid program of state-directed modernization in world history. What was the term for the new regime?
answer: The Meiji Restoration — 'restoration' of imperial rule from the Tokugawa shoguns
choices: The Meiji Restoration — 'restoration' of imperial rule from the Tokugawa shoguns
The Tokugawa Restoration — but Tokugawa was the deposed government, not restored
The Showa Restoration — but Showa refers to Hirohito's reign (1926–89), much later
The Heisei Restoration — but Heisei is Akihito's reign (1989–2019), modern
context: Meiji Japan adopted Western technology, education, military organization, and constitutional government in a generation. The samurai class was abolished (1873); a conscript army replaced them. The 1889 Constitution borrowed heavily from Prussian models. Japan defeated China (1894–95) and Russia (1904–05) — becoming the first non-Western nation to defeat a European power. Meiji died 1912. His grandson Hirohito (Showa, 1926–89) presided over WWII and the postwar reconstruction.

question: From December 13, 1937, when Japanese troops captured the Republic of China's capital, through about February 1938, Japanese forces committed widespread atrocities — mass killings, rapes, looting. Estimates of the death toll vary widely. The Chinese government and most international scholars cite figures around 200,000 to 300,000 killed; Japanese revisionist sources have proposed lower figures. The events remain a flashpoint in Sino-Japanese relations. What is this called?
answer: The Nanjing Massacre (also Rape of Nanking) — central in Chinese memory of WWII
choices: The Nanjing Massacre (also Rape of Nanking) — central in Chinese memory of WWII
The Mukden Incident — but that was Japan's 1931 seizure of Manchuria, not Nanjing
The Shanghai Massacre — but Shanghai's 1937 battle was different in character
The Marco Polo Bridge Incident — but that was the July 1937 spark for full war
context: Iris Chang's *The Rape of Nanking* (1997) brought renewed Western attention to the atrocity. John Rabe — a German businessman and Nazi Party member who organized the Nanjing Safety Zone — saved perhaps 200,000 Chinese; his diaries were a major source. Some Japanese officials, including General Iwane Matsui, were executed at the postwar Tokyo Trials. The Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall opened 1985 (expanded 1995, 2007). Japanese textbook controversies persist.

question: On July 1, 1997, after 156 years of British rule, the colony of Hong Kong was returned to Chinese sovereignty under the Sino-British Joint Declaration (1984). Beijing promised 'one country, two systems' — Hong Kong would retain its capitalist economy, common-law legal system, free press, and civil liberties for 50 years (until 2047). Initial implementation was largely peaceful. What has happened since?
answer: Erosion accelerated 2014 (Umbrella Movement) and 2019 (mass protests); National Security Law June 2020
choices: Erosion accelerated 2014 (Umbrella Movement) and 2019 (mass protests); National Security Law June 2020
Smooth implementation of the agreement throughout the 1997–2047 transition period
Hong Kong full integration into PRC legal system within five years of handover
Negotiated extension of British administration through 2050 after problems emerged
context: The Umbrella Movement (2014) was sparked by Beijing's restrictions on Hong Kong's promised electoral reform. The 2019 protests against the proposed extradition bill grew into mass demonstrations involving millions; the bill was withdrawn but the broader political conflict deepened. The June 2020 National Security Law criminalized broad categories of dissent. Hundreds of activists have been arrested or have fled abroad. The 'one country, two systems' framework is widely considered effectively over.

question: In October 1950, units of the People's Liberation Army crossed the Yangtze River into Tibetan territory. After a brief war, the 15-year-old Dalai Lama's government was forced to sign the 'Seventeen Point Agreement' (May 1951) acknowledging Chinese sovereignty. After years of growing tension and a failed Tibetan uprising in March 1959, what did the Dalai Lama do?
answer: Fled to India where he established a government-in-exile at Dharamshala
choices: Fled to India where he established a government-in-exile at Dharamshala
Negotiated a renewed autonomy agreement with Mao Zedong personally
Remained in Lhasa under Chinese supervision throughout the Cultural Revolution
Died in the uprising along with thousands of Tibetan supporters
context: The 14th Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso (born 1935), has lived in exile in India since 1959. He won the Nobel Peace Prize (1989) and has been a globally recognized advocate for Tibetan autonomy. The Cultural Revolution destroyed about 6,000 Tibetan monasteries. The Chinese government's current policy combines repression of Tibetan religious-cultural distinctiveness with major economic investment. Tibet's population is now substantially Han Chinese in many areas. The Dalai Lama's succession will be a major flashpoint.

question: Between 1405 and 1433, the Yongle Emperor of Ming China commissioned seven voyages of a massive 'treasure fleet' under a Muslim eunuch admiral. The fleets had up to 250 ships, including 'treasure ships' perhaps 400 feet long (the largest wooden ships ever built). They reached Southeast Asia, India, the Persian Gulf, the East African coast (modern Somalia, Kenya), and brought back tribute and exotica including a giraffe. Who was the admiral?
answer: Zheng He — Ming-era eunuch admiral and Muslim from Yunnan
choices: Zheng He — Ming-era eunuch admiral and Muslim from Yunnan
Cheng Ho — same person (older Wade-Giles romanization), so not really another answer
Marco Polo — but Polo was Venetian and traveled by land, not by Chinese fleet
Ibn Battuta — but Battuta was Moroccan, traveled overland and by Arab dhow
context: After the Yongle Emperor's death (1424), the voyages were criticized by Confucian officials as wasteful. The 1433 voyage was the last; the fleet was decommissioned; ship-building records were destroyed; the Ming turned inward. Some have argued (notably Gavin Menzies in *1421* — historically unreliable) that Zheng He reached the Americas, but mainstream historians consider this unfounded. Zheng He's expeditions remain one of the great 'paths not taken' of world history — Chinese naval projection power abandoned just before Iberian voyages launched globalization.

question: From 1839 to 1842 and again 1856 to 1860, Britain (joined by France in the second war) fought two wars with the Qing Empire over British trade in opium (grown in British India, smuggled into China for silver). The Chinese commissioner Lin Zexu's seizure of opium at Canton (1839) was the immediate trigger of the first war. British naval and military forces defeated Chinese forces repeatedly. What were the long-term consequences?
answer: Five treaty ports opened, Hong Kong ceded, extraterritoriality, indemnities — 'Century of Humiliation'
choices: Five treaty ports opened, Hong Kong ceded, extraterritoriality, indemnities — 'Century of Humiliation'
Chinese victory and limited British concessions through negotiated settlement
Establishment of a joint Anglo-Chinese commission to regulate the opium trade
Complete Chinese isolation from foreign trade restored for the next fifty years
context: The 'unequal treaties' of Nanjing (1842), Tianjin (1858), and Beijing (1860) opened China to Western (and Japanese, after 1895) trade and influence under terms that became known in Chinese historiography as the 'Century of Humiliation.' The Taiping Rebellion (1850–64) — perhaps 20 million dead — destabilized the Qing dynasty further. The Boxer Rebellion (1899–1901) and the eight-nation expedition that defeated it deepened humiliation. The Qing fell in 1912.

question: From 1850 to 1864, the largest civil war of the 19th century (and one of the deadliest conflicts in human history) raged across southern and central China. The Taiping rebels followed Hong Xiuquan, a failed scholar who came to believe he was the younger brother of Jesus Christ. They captured Nanjing (1853) and held it as the 'Heavenly Capital' for eleven years. Qing forces (especially the Hunan Army of Zeng Guofan) eventually crushed the rebellion. What was the death toll?
answer: Roughly 20–30 million dead — one of the bloodiest conflicts in human history
choices: Roughly 20–30 million dead — one of the bloodiest conflicts in human history
Roughly 100,000 dead — significant but contained to local areas
Roughly 1 million dead — comparable to other 19th-century civil wars
Roughly 5 million dead — substantial but smaller than the Civil War casualty figures
context: The Taiping Rebellion devastated the Yangtze valley. The Heavenly Kingdom's syncretic theology, its strict moral code, its initial military success, and its eventual destruction make it one of the strangest episodes in world history. Karl Marx wrote about it for the *New-York Daily Tribune*. The Qing dynasty survived but was permanently weakened. The exhausting effects on Qing finances contributed to the unequal-treaty system's deepening over the following decades.

question: In 1899–1900, the 'Boxers United in Righteousness' — a millenarian Chinese movement opposed to foreign influence, Christian missions, and the Qing court's weakness — gained imperial backing under the Empress Dowager Cixi. Foreign diplomats and Chinese Christians were besieged in the Legation Quarter of Beijing for 55 days in summer 1900. An Eight-Nation Alliance expeditionary force (Britain, France, U.S., Germany, Italy, Austria-Hungary, Russia, Japan) relieved the siege August 14, 1900. What were the consequences?
answer: Boxer Protocol indemnity ($333 million silver); further humiliation deepening Qing decline
choices: Boxer Protocol indemnity ($333 million silver); further humiliation deepening Qing decline
Restoration of Chinese sovereignty under reform constitution within months
Quiet stabilization without lasting effects on Qing finances or governance
Western withdrawal from China and acknowledgment of Chinese sovereignty
context: The Boxer Protocol (September 1901) imposed a massive indemnity payable over 39 years. The U.S. eventually returned much of its share for a scholarship program (Tsinghua University, 1911). The Qing dynasty fell in the Xinhai Revolution (October 1911–February 1912); the last emperor Puyi (age 6) abdicated. The Republic of China followed, with Sun Yat-sen briefly as provisional president. Decades of warlordism and civil war followed before the People's Republic in 1949.

question: Between April 7 and July 15, 1994, in 100 days, Hutu militants in the East African country of Rwanda killed approximately 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu. The genocide was triggered by the shooting-down of a plane carrying Rwandan President Juvénal Habyarimana (April 6, 1994). The killings were carried out by ordinary citizens with machetes, often against neighbors, organized by local officials and incited by RTLM radio. The UN peacekeeping force was reduced rather than reinforced. What was the international response?
answer: Massive international failure — the UN, U.S., and others refused to intervene
choices: Massive international failure — the UN, U.S., and others refused to intervene
Rapid French intervention (Operation Turquoise) ended the genocide within two weeks
U.S. military deployment under the Clinton administration ended the killing in May
Effective UN intervention reduced casualties after first week of genocide
context: The UN had peacekeepers (UNAMIR under General Roméo Dallaire) on the ground but with restrictive rules of engagement. The Belgian contingent withdrew after the killing of ten Belgian peacekeepers; UN headquarters refused to authorize broader action. The Rwandan Patriotic Front (Tutsi-led, under Paul Kagame) eventually ended the genocide militarily July 1994. President Clinton's apology (Kigali, March 1998) acknowledged American inaction. *Hotel Rwanda* (2004) dramatized one rescue effort. Kagame has ruled Rwanda since.

question: On February 11, 1990, after 27 years and 6 months in South African prisons (mostly on Robben Island), the leader of the African National Congress walked out of Victor Verster Prison near Paarl as a free man. Nine days earlier President F.W. de Klerk had unbanned the ANC and other opposition organizations. The negotiated transition that followed produced South Africa's first non-racial elections (April 1994), in which his party won. Who was he?
answer: Nelson Mandela — first democratically elected president of South Africa 1994–99
choices: Nelson Mandela — first democratically elected president of South Africa 1994–99
Desmond Tutu — Anglican archbishop and Truth and Reconciliation Commission chair, not Mandela
Steve Biko — Black Consciousness leader but killed in detention 1977
Oliver Tambo — ANC president in exile during Mandela's imprisonment
context: Mandela's release and the peaceful transition to majority rule that followed (helped by his moral authority, F.W. de Klerk's strategic intelligence, and the work of Cyril Ramaphosa, Mac Maharaj, Tutu, and others) was one of the great political achievements of the late 20th century. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (1996–98) under Tutu was a model of transitional justice. Mandela served one term as president (1994–99), refused to seek a second; died December 5, 2013 at 95.

question: On May 30, 1832, in the early morning at a field outside Paris, the 20-year-old French mathematician Évariste Galois was shot in the abdomen during a duel — reportedly over a love affair, though political enemies and an agent provocateur of the police have also been suspected. He spent the previous night writing letters to his friend Auguste Chevalier and scrawling mathematical proofs in the margins of his papers. He repeatedly wrote 'Je n'ai pas le temps' — 'I have not time.' What did he establish in his final night's work?
answer: The conditions for solvability of polynomial equations by radicals — founding group theory
choices: The conditions for solvability of polynomial equations by radicals — founding group theory
The fundamental theorem of algebra — that every polynomial has at least one complex root
The Riemann hypothesis on the distribution of prime numbers
The classification of finite simple groups — completed only in 1983
context: Galois died May 31, 1832 in the Hôpital Cochin. His brother Alfred took the manuscripts; Chevalier preserved them. Liouville recognized the work's importance and published it 1846 — fourteen years after Galois' death. 'Galois theory' is the connection between polynomial solvability and the algebraic structure of permutation groups. Niels Henrik Abel had proved the quintic insolvability earlier (1824, dying himself of TB at 26). Modern algebra dates substantially from Galois' last night.

question: On December 29, 1566, at age 19, the Danish noble astronomy student fought a duel in the dark with his cousin Manderup Parsberg at the home of his professor in Rostock. The quarrel had begun at a betrothal feast and concerned a mathematical problem (whether 21 or 23 was the correct answer to a calculation, depending on sources). The cousin's rapier removed the bridge of his nose. He wore a prosthetic — gold for special occasions, silver for routine — for the rest of his life. Who was the astronomer?
answer: Tycho Brahe — whose Uraniborg observations enabled Kepler's laws of planetary motion
choices: Tycho Brahe — whose Uraniborg observations enabled Kepler's laws of planetary motion
Johannes Kepler — whose German Lutheran calculations rested on Tycho's data
Galileo Galilei — Italian Renaissance astronomer of the next generation
Christoph Clavius — Jesuit Roman calendar reformer of the late 16th century
context: Tycho (1546–1601) built the most accurate pre-telescope observatory in history on the Danish island of Hven (1576–97), with King Frederick II's patronage. He died in Prague in October 1601, supposedly from a bladder rupture caused by etiquette — too polite to leave Rudolf II's banquet table — though arsenic poisoning has been suspected. His meticulous data — 1,000+ stars catalogued, planetary positions to 1 arcminute — enabled Kepler's elliptical-orbit breakthrough.

question: On the evening of November 23, 1654, the 31-year-old French mathematician and physicist Blaise Pascal — already inventor of the mechanical calculator, originator of probability theory (with Fermat), and demonstrator of atmospheric pressure with mercury barometers — had a religious experience lasting about two hours. He recorded the experience on a sheet of parchment and sewed it into the lining of his coat, where it was found after his death. What was the experience?
answer: An intense religious encounter with 'Fire' he recorded as decisive for his life
choices: An intense religious encounter with 'Fire' he recorded as decisive for his life
A philosophical insight that motivated the *Pensées* but not religious in nature
A mathematical demonstration of the geometry he was working on
A premonition of his death that proved accurate exactly seven years later
context: Pascal's 'Memorial' — the parchment — opens 'Fire. God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of philosophers and scholars.' The Jansenist connections at Port-Royal (which the Catholic Church repeatedly attacked) shaped his religious life from this point. The *Pensées* (published posthumously 1670) is the unfinished defense of Christianity he was working on. Pascal died 1662 at 39, of a long stomach ailment. The parchment was lost; transcripts survive.

question: From the 1670s onward, two of the great mathematicians of the 17th century developed the calculus independently. Newton developed his 'method of fluxions' c. 1666 but did not publish; Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz developed his version 1675–76, published 1684 in *Acta Eruditorum*. Charges of plagiarism (most fiercely from Newton's English supporters) escalated. In 1711 the Royal Society — chaired by Newton — appointed a 'committee of inquiry.' What did the committee find?
answer: Ruled for Newton's priority — Newton secretly wrote much of the committee report himself
choices: Ruled for Newton's priority — Newton secretly wrote much of the committee report himself
Ruled for Leibniz's priority — embarrassing the English mathematical establishment
Ruled both had developed calculus independently and acknowledged shared priority
Ruled the matter inconclusive — both should receive credit until further evidence
context: Modern consensus: both developed calculus independently. Leibniz' notation (dx, dy, the integral sign) was superior and is what we still use; the term 'calculus' itself came from him. Newton's *Principia* (1687) used geometric arguments rather than calculus directly. Leibniz died alone in Hannover 1716; his secretary was the only mourner at the funeral. The bitter dispute set back English mathematics for a century — Continental mathematicians using Leibniz' methods leaped ahead.

question: In early 1913, a 25-year-old Indian clerk in Madras — who had failed his university examinations because he neglected non-mathematical subjects — sent a letter to the Cambridge mathematician G.H. Hardy. The letter contained about 120 theorems, many in pure number theory. Hardy and his collaborator J.E. Littlewood reportedly worked through the letter into the night. Some theorems were known; some were wrong; some Hardy could not even understand. What was Hardy's conclusion?
answer: The theorems must be true — 'because if they were not true, no one would have the imagination to invent them'
choices: The theorems must be true — 'because if they were not true, no one would have the imagination to invent them'
The letter was a hoax produced by Cambridge undergraduates to test Hardy
The author had clearly studied Cambridge syllabus material in detail
The work was promising but lacked the rigor needed for serious publication
context: Hardy arranged for Srinivasa Ramanujan (1887–1920) to come to Cambridge. He arrived April 1914. Over five years they collaborated on partitions, modular forms, and other deep number-theoretic results. Ramanujan, a strict vegetarian, suffered from poor health in wartime England. He returned to India 1919 and died of (probably) tuberculosis or hepatic amoebiasis 1920 at 32. The 'lost notebook' of his last year's work was rediscovered 1976 and is still being mined for new mathematics.

question: From 1939 to 1945 at Bletchley Park, a country estate in Buckinghamshire, a team of British codebreakers led from the start by a 27-year-old Cambridge mathematician developed mechanical and electromechanical machines (the 'bombe' and the later 'Colossus') that broke German Enigma and Lorenz cipher traffic in nearly real time. The intelligence (codenamed Ultra) was central to the Battle of the Atlantic, North Africa, and D-Day. Who was the mathematician?
answer: Alan Turing — whose 1936 paper on universal computing machines founded computer science
choices: Alan Turing — whose 1936 paper on universal computing machines founded computer science
Tommy Flowers — Post Office engineer who built Colossus but did not lead the cryptanalytic group
Max Newman — head of the Newmanry section but Turing was the broader leader
Gordon Welchman — Turing's Hut 6 colleague who improved the bombe but Turing was the lead
context: Turing (1912–54) had foreshadowed the digital computer in his 1936 paper 'On Computable Numbers' (the Turing machine). After the war his work continued at the National Physical Laboratory and Manchester. He was prosecuted for homosexual offenses 1952 under the Labouchère Amendment; chose chemical castration (estrogen injections) over prison; died June 7, 1954 of cyanide poisoning, age 41 — a half-eaten apple beside him. Officially suicide; some have suggested accident or murder. Posthumously pardoned 2013.

question: From the late 1860s, a German mathematician working in Halle (then a provincial university) developed the foundations of modern set theory. He proved that the real numbers are uncountably infinite (the 'diagonal argument'), that there are different infinite cardinalities, and that the continuum hypothesis (between aleph-0 and aleph-1) might be unprovable. His former teacher Leopold Kronecker — who held that 'God made the integers; all else is the work of man' — opposed his work bitterly. What was his fate?
answer: Repeated nervous breakdowns from the 1880s; died in a sanatorium in Halle 1918
choices: Repeated nervous breakdowns from the 1880s; died in a sanatorium in Halle 1918
Honored throughout his career; died wealthy and admired by 19th-century mathematicians
Suicide at the height of his career; influenced by Boltzmann's similar end
Returned to Russia where he was celebrated under Tsar Alexander III
context: Georg Cantor (1845–1918) said 'No one shall expel us from the paradise Cantor has created' — David Hilbert's 1925 defense of set theory. Cantor's mental health was fragile from the 1880s; he was hospitalized repeatedly. The Continuum Hypothesis was shown by Gödel (1940) and Cohen (1963) to be independent of standard set-theory axioms. Cantor's modern reputation is enormous; his work shaped 20th-century mathematics fundamentally. Kronecker's hostility was probably one factor in his breakdowns.

question: On September 5, 1906, in the Italian seaside town of Duino (near Trieste), the Austrian theoretical physicist who had founded statistical mechanics — connecting the macroscopic laws of thermodynamics to the statistical behavior of atoms — hanged himself in his hotel room while his family was at the beach. He had been depressed; his work had been opposed by influential continental physicists (Mach, Ostwald) who doubted the reality of atoms. His tombstone in Vienna's Zentralfriedhof bears what inscription?
answer: S = k log W — the relation between entropy and the number of microstates
choices: S = k log W — the relation between entropy and the number of microstates
E = mc² — Einstein's later mass-energy relation
F = ma — Newton's second law of motion
PV = nRT — the ideal gas law from chemistry
context: Ludwig Boltzmann's (1844–1906) statistical mechanics turned out to be correct. Within years of his suicide, Einstein's papers on Brownian motion (1905), Perrin's experiments (1908), and the development of quantum mechanics had vindicated his atomism. The 'Boltzmann constant' k (~1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K) bears his name. His final years had been clouded by depression, eye problems, and the resistance of the Vienna anti-atomist school. His monument is now one of the most-visited grave sites for physicists.

question: On May 8, 1794, during the Reign of Terror in Paris, the 50-year-old founder of modern chemistry — who had named oxygen and hydrogen, demonstrated the conservation of mass in chemical reactions, and developed the modern system of chemical nomenclature — was guillotined along with 27 fellow tax-collectors (the Ferme Générale he had served). The judge reportedly said 'the Republic has no need of savants.' Mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange later wrote what?
answer: 'It took only an instant to cut off his head, and a hundred years may not produce another like it'
choices: 'It took only an instant to cut off his head, and a hundred years may not produce another like it'
'Justice has been done for the people he taxed' — a hostile contemporary view
'His chemistry will outlast his politics' — a balanced retrospective
'He died for science as he had lived for it' — a romanticized memorial
context: Antoine-Laurent Lavoisier had overturned the phlogiston theory in the 1780s. His textbook *Traité Élémentaire de Chimie* (1789) is the founding work of modern chemistry. He was a member of the *Ferme Générale* — the private tax-collecting corporation that was deeply unpopular — and was executed for that, not for his science. His widow Marie-Anne preserved his papers and edited his memoirs. The Republic indeed had no immediate need of savants but produced quite a few later.

question: Born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw (then Russian Poland) 1867, she went to Paris (then under the Sorbonne's still-restrictive rules for women) to study physics. She and her husband Pierre isolated polonium and radium (named after her homeland) from tons of pitchblende ore in a shed. She won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics (shared with Pierre and Becquerel) for the discovery of radioactivity. After Pierre's death in a Paris street accident (1906), she carried on alone. What was her second Nobel?
answer: Chemistry 1911 — first person to win Nobels in two different scientific disciplines
choices: Chemistry 1911 — first person to win Nobels in two different scientific disciplines
Physics 1911 — for further work on radioactivity at the Sorbonne
Peace 1916 — for her wartime radiology work for the French army
Medicine 1937 — but she died in 1934, before any medical award
context: Marie Curie (1867–1934) died of aplastic anemia, almost certainly induced by lifelong radiation exposure. Her notebooks remain so radioactive they are kept in lead-lined boxes; researchers wear protective gear. Her daughter Irène Joliot-Curie won the 1935 Chemistry Nobel for artificial radioactivity (with her husband Frédéric). Marie Curie was the first woman to win a Nobel, the first person to win two, and remains the only person to win Nobels in two different sciences.

question: In 1905, a 26-year-old patent clerk at the Swiss Federal Patent Office in Bern published four papers in *Annalen der Physik* that transformed physics. The first explained the photoelectric effect by treating light as quanta — laying foundations for quantum mechanics. The second explained Brownian motion in terms of molecular collisions — confirming atoms exist. The third presented special relativity. The fourth proposed mass-energy equivalence (E = mc²). Who was the clerk?
answer: Albert Einstein — whose 'miracle year' established modern physics' foundational lines
choices: Albert Einstein — whose 'miracle year' established modern physics' foundational lines
Niels Bohr — but Bohr's atomic model came later, in 1913, and Bohr was Danish
Werner Heisenberg — Heisenberg's career was much later (uncertainty principle 1927)
Max Planck — Planck's quantum constant work was 1900, separate from 1905
context: Einstein (1879–1955) won the 1921 Nobel Prize for the photoelectric effect (the committee found special relativity still too controversial). General relativity (1915) extended the special theory to gravitation. Eddington's 1919 solar eclipse expedition confirmed the bending of starlight. Einstein left Germany 1933 when Hitler came to power; he settled at Princeton's Institute for Advanced Study. He warned Roosevelt of the possibility of atomic weapons (Einstein-Szilárd letter 1939). His grave was not marked at his request.

question: On February 28, 1953, two researchers at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge announced at a local pub (the Eagle, on Bene't Street) that they had 'discovered the secret of life.' They had built a model of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) using X-ray diffraction data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins at King's College London. Their April 1953 *Nature* paper described the double helix structure. Who were they?
answer: James Watson (American) and Francis Crick (English) — Nobel 1962 with Maurice Wilkins
choices: James Watson (American) and Francis Crick (English) — Nobel 1962 with Maurice Wilkins
James Watson and Linus Pauling — but Pauling proposed a different (incorrect) triple helix
Francis Crick and Erwin Schrödinger — but Schrödinger's *What Is Life?* (1944) preceded
Watson and Maurice Wilkins — but the central insight came from Crick's collaboration with Watson
context: Rosalind Franklin's 'Photograph 51' (X-ray diffraction of DNA fibers) was shown to Watson without her knowledge by Wilkins; the data was crucial. Franklin (1920–58) died of ovarian cancer at 37 — before the 1962 Nobel was awarded; the prize cannot go to the deceased. Her contribution has been recognized more clearly in recent decades. Watson's *The Double Helix* (1968) describes the story with frankness that has not always reflected well on its author. The structure suggested replication, mutation, evolution all at once.

question: In May 1952, a 31-year-old crystallographer at King's College London — using a fine-collimated X-ray apparatus she had built up over years — captured an X-ray diffraction photograph of the B-form of crystalline DNA. The photograph showed an unmistakable helix pattern (specifically the characteristic X-shape of cross-hairs that a regular helix produces). Her colleague Maurice Wilkins, without her knowledge, showed the photograph to James Watson. What is the photograph called?
answer: Photograph 51 — perhaps the single most important X-ray image in molecular biology
choices: Photograph 51 — perhaps the single most important X-ray image in molecular biology
Photograph 12 — but that's a different photograph in the same series
Photograph A — but no photograph has that designation
Photograph X — but that's a generic name not the specific famous image
context: Rosalind Franklin (1920–58) had been recruited to King's College in 1951. Her relationship with Wilkins was poor; the lab politics made her position untenable. She moved to Birkbeck College 1953 to work on the tobacco mosaic virus structure. She died of ovarian cancer April 1958 at 37, before any Nobel could be awarded for DNA work. Watson, Crick, and Wilkins shared the 1962 Nobel; Franklin's contribution has been increasingly recognized since Brenda Maddox's biography (2002).

question: In March 415 AD, in the streets of Alexandria, Egypt — then a great center of learning under the patriarchal authority of Cyril — a 50- or 60-year-old Greek mathematician and Neoplatonist philosopher was dragged from her carriage by a Christian mob (probably the *parabalani*, anti-pagan paramilitaries). She was murdered in a church, reportedly flayed with oyster shells or roof tiles. Her name is associated with the symbolic end of antique scholarly tradition in Alexandria. Who was she?
answer: Hypatia — daughter of Theon of Alexandria, last famous Greek mathematician of the city
choices: Hypatia — daughter of Theon of Alexandria, last famous Greek mathematician of the city
Aspasia — but Aspasia was a 5th-century BC Athenian, not 5th-century AD Alexandrian
Sosigenes — but Sosigenes designed the Julian calendar for Caesar, not Alexandria's end
Galen — but Galen was male and from Pergamum, not Hypatia
context: Hypatia's death is one of the most-discussed events in late antiquity — variously interpreted as the start of religious intolerance, the political conflict between Patriarch Cyril and Prefect Orestes (her patron), or as a regrettable incident. The Library of Alexandria, the Mouseion, and other institutions had already declined by 415; she did not represent a still-vibrant intellectual life. Edward Gibbon's *Decline and Fall* (1776–88) and Charles Kingsley's *Hypatia* (1853) made her famous in modern Western culture.

question: Cambridge University was closed by plague from summer 1665 through 1666, and the 23-year-old Lucasian Professor's predecessor's student returned to his mother's farm at Woolsthorpe in Lincolnshire. In about 18 months he developed the binomial theorem, the method of fluxions (calculus), the theory of colors (with prism experiments demonstrating that white light contains all colors), and the basis of universal gravitation. His own account in old age included the apple story. Who recorded it?
answer: John Conduitt and William Stukeley — Newton's nephew-in-law and biographer
choices: John Conduitt and William Stukeley — Newton's nephew-in-law and biographer
Edmond Halley — Newton's astronomer-patron who financed the *Principia*'s publication
Christopher Wren — astronomer and architect, Newton's Royal Society contemporary
Robert Hooke — Newton's bitter rival whose own account would have been hostile
context: The apple story comes from Stukeley's *Memoirs of Sir Isaac Newton's Life* (written 1752, published 1936) and Conduitt's manuscript notes. Newton told them he saw an apple fall and wondered why it fell straight down — not toward any side. The Woolsthorpe tree (a 'Flower of Kent' apple) still stands; cuttings have been planted at universities worldwide. The *Principia* (1687) was published two decades after the 1666 'annus mirabilis.' Newton became Master of the Mint, was knighted 1705, died 1727.

question: Between 1615 and 1621, while the great astronomer was working on his planetary laws, his 70-year-old mother Katharina Kepler was tried in her hometown of Leonberg in Württemberg on charges of witchcraft. Forty-nine accusations included causing illnesses, brewing potions, and the death of a neighbor by witchcraft. The astronomer interrupted his work to defend her. The trial dragged on for years. What was the outcome?
answer: Acquittal in October 1621 after fourteen months in prison; she died six months later
choices: Acquittal in October 1621 after fourteen months in prison; she died six months later
Conviction and burning at the stake in late 1620 despite her son's defense
Conviction and life imprisonment; she died of starvation in prison 1622
Forced exile to Saxony; she died there in 1624 of natural causes
context: Johannes Kepler (1571–1630) brought his mother's case all the way through the Württemberg legal system. The defense documents he prepared are extraordinary documents combining legal argument, character witness, and scientific debunking. Katharina was released in autumn 1621 after about 14 months' imprisonment and died six months later. Kepler's *Astronomia Nova* (1609) and *Harmonices Mundi* (1619) had been completed; the *Rudolphine Tables* (1627) came after the trial.

question: In 1959, at age 30, a brilliant young mathematician at Princeton — recipient of a 1958 *Fortune* magazine profile naming him among 'most brilliant of the younger generation' — began to develop paranoid schizophrenia. He believed he was being persecuted by Communists, that newspapers contained secret messages, that he was a divine messenger. The next three decades saw repeated hospitalizations and apparent recovery without medication. In 1994 he shared the Nobel Prize in Economics for early work in game theory. Who is he?
answer: John Forbes Nash Jr. — Nobel 1994; killed in NJ taxi crash 2015 with his wife Alicia
choices: John Forbes Nash Jr. — Nobel 1994; killed in NJ taxi crash 2015 with his wife Alicia
Norbert Wiener — but Wiener was the founder of cybernetics, different career
John von Neumann — but von Neumann developed game theory contemporaneously and died 1957
Alonzo Church — Princeton mathematician, but in logic not game theory
context: Nash (1928–2015) developed the 'Nash equilibrium' concept in his 28-page Princeton PhD thesis (1950). Sylvia Nasar's biography *A Beautiful Mind* (1998) and Ron Howard's 2001 film adaptation made him famous. Nash and his wife Alicia were killed when their taxi crashed in New Jersey, May 23, 2015 — just days after he had received the Abel Prize for his work in geometric analysis (the *other* major math prize, less famous than the Fields).

question: In 2002–03, a Russian mathematician at the Steklov Institute in St. Petersburg posted three preprints on arXiv proving the Poincaré conjecture — a 99-year-old conjecture about the topological characterization of the three-sphere. He had worked for seven years alone, without grant support or publications. The Fields Medal was awarded to him at the 2006 International Congress of Mathematicians in Madrid. What did he do?
answer: Refused the Fields Medal; refused the $1 million Millennium Prize 2010; withdrew from mathematics
choices: Refused the Fields Medal; refused the $1 million Millennium Prize 2010; withdrew from mathematics
Accepted the Fields Medal and continued his work on topology and dynamical systems
Accepted both prizes and donated the money to the St. Petersburg mathematical community
Refused only the prize money but accepted the medal as a symbolic honor
context: Grigori Perelman (born 1966) lives quietly in St. Petersburg with his mother. He refused all subsequent prizes (Millennium Prize 2010, $1 million from Clay Mathematics Institute). He has cited dissatisfaction with the ethics of the mathematical community — including ethics issues around credit-sharing (the Yau group's claims). Perelman's proof was the second Millennium Prize problem to be solved (none others have been claimed since). He may be the only Fields Medal refusenik in history.

question: Around 1784, in a one-room schoolhouse in the small German town of Braunschweig, a 7-year-old boy in mathematics class was set by his teacher the task of summing the integers from 1 to 100 — a task expected to take perhaps an hour. The boy wrote the answer on his slate in seconds: 5,050. He had noticed that 1+100, 2+99, 3+98, etc. — fifty pairs each summing to 101 — gave 50 × 101 = 5,050. Who was he?
answer: Carl Friedrich Gauss — became one of the greatest mathematicians in history
choices: Carl Friedrich Gauss — became one of the greatest mathematicians in history
Leonhard Euler — but Euler was Swiss, lived 1707–83, and was already dead by 1784
Pierre-Simon Laplace — but Laplace was French and an adult by 1784
Joseph-Louis Lagrange — but Lagrange was Italian-French and an adult by 1784
context: Gauss (1777–1855) showed exceptional mathematical talent from childhood; the Duke of Braunschweig supported his education at the local *Collegium Carolinum* and then at Göttingen. His *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* (1801, age 24) is a foundational text of number theory. He held the chair at Göttingen 1807 until his death; he discovered the asteroid Ceres' orbit (1801) and made fundamental contributions to astronomy, geodesy, and electromagnetism. He kept many results secret for years through perfectionism — losing priority on non-Euclidean geometry, the geometric interpretation of complex numbers, and other areas.

question: In 1915, a 33-year-old German Jewish mathematician moved to Göttingen at David Hilbert's invitation. Although Hilbert lobbied repeatedly, university rules excluded women from holding faculty positions until 1919. She lectured under Hilbert's name; her work on the symmetries of physical systems and conservation laws (Noether's theorem, 1918) is one of the deepest results in modern theoretical physics. She was dismissed from her unpaid position in 1933. Who was she?
answer: Emmy Noether — fled to Bryn Mawr College PA in 1933; died of complications from surgery 1935
choices: Emmy Noether — fled to Bryn Mawr College PA in 1933; died of complications from surgery 1935
Sofia Kovalevskaya — but Kovalevskaya was Russian, died 1891, decades before Noether
Hertha Sponer — German physicist who also fled Nazi Germany but not the same career
Lise Meitner — Austrian physicist who collaborated with Otto Hahn on fission but different field
context: Emmy Noether (1882–1935) is widely considered one of the most important mathematicians of the early 20th century. Her work on abstract algebra (rings, ideals, modules) shaped much of modern algebra. Noether's theorem (every continuous symmetry corresponds to a conservation law) is foundational to modern physics. Einstein wrote a tribute when she died: 'the most significant creative mathematical genius thus far produced since the higher education of women began.' She is buried at Bryn Mawr.

question: On Christmas 1938, in the Swedish town of Kungälv, the 60-year-old Austrian-Jewish physicist — who had fled Nazi Germany earlier that year — was visited by her nephew Otto Frisch. They walked in the snow discussing a recent letter from her former Berlin collaborator Otto Hahn describing puzzling chemistry experiments showing barium when uranium was bombarded with neutrons. Walking in the snow, she and Frisch worked out what had happened. What did they propose?
answer: Nuclear fission — the uranium nucleus had split, releasing enormous energy per event
choices: Nuclear fission — the uranium nucleus had split, releasing enormous energy per event
Nuclear fusion — the uranium had combined with a neutron to form a heavier element
Beta decay — but beta decay is a separate process, not what was happening here
Alpha emission — but alpha emission is also a separate process, not what was happening
context: Meitner and Frisch published the fission interpretation in *Nature* (February 11, 1939). Otto Hahn won the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; the Nobel Committee's exclusion of Meitner is now treated as one of the major missed-Nobel cases. She declined to join the Manhattan Project; she said 'I will have nothing to do with a bomb!' Meitnerium (element 109) was named for her 1997. She died in Cambridge 1968, age 89.

question: On February 11, 1986, before the Rogers Commission investigating the *Challenger* space shuttle disaster, Caltech physicist Richard Feynman performed a simple demonstration with a piece of an O-ring rubber seal, ice water, and a clamp. The clamp compressed the rubber; the ice water reduced its temperature; when Feynman released the clamp, the rubber failed to spring back. The audience saw why an O-ring on a freezing Florida morning could fail. What had Feynman uncovered?
answer: The mechanical failure mechanism of the Challenger O-ring under cold conditions
choices: The mechanical failure mechanism of the Challenger O-ring under cold conditions
A simulation error in NASA's pre-flight risk-assessment software
A previously unknown chemical reaction in solid rocket booster fuel
A latent failure mode in the shuttle main engine turbopumps
context: Feynman (1918–88) had been recruited reluctantly to the commission. His Appendix F to the Rogers Commission report — 'Personal Observations on the Reliability of the Shuttle' — was a withering critique of NASA's organizational culture, the management's optimism, and the gap between engineering and management estimates of risk. He died of cancer 1988. The shuttle program was grounded 32 months. The Columbia accident (February 1, 2003) involved different mechanical issues but similar organizational pathologies.

question: On December 17, 1903, two bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio, made four short powered flights on the windswept dunes near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. The first, by Orville at 10:35 a.m., lasted 12 seconds and covered 120 feet. The fourth, by Wilbur, lasted 59 seconds and covered 852 feet. The 1903 Flyer was a wood-and-fabric biplane powered by a 12-horsepower gasoline engine they had built themselves. What was the key innovation?
answer: Three-axis control via 'wing-warping' — banking the wings for roll, alongside yaw and pitch control
choices: Three-axis control via 'wing-warping' — banking the wings for roll, alongside yaw and pitch control
A revolutionary new airfoil shape developed in their bicycle-shop wind tunnel
A lightweight engine purchased from a French manufacturer at the last minute
A take-off catapult system developed for use on naval surface ships
context: The Wrights' three-axis control was the breakthrough. They had spent four years at Kitty Hawk testing gliders (1900–02) and had built their own wind tunnel to test airfoils. The 1903 Flyer is at the Smithsonian Air and Space Museum. By WWI European designers had moved ahead — partly due to Wright patent litigation that retarded U.S. aviation. Wilbur died of typhoid 1912. Orville lived to 1948 and saw jet flight.

question: On December 6, 1877, in his Menlo Park, New Jersey laboratory, the 30-year-old inventor Thomas Edison and his assistants finished assembling a hand-cranked device with a tinfoil-wrapped cylinder and two diaphragm-and-stylus assemblies. Speaking into one, Edison recorded a short rhyme; turning the cylinder back and playing through the other diaphragm, the recording was audible. What did he say?
answer: 'Mary had a little lamb' — the first words ever recorded for later playback
choices: 'Mary had a little lamb' — the first words ever recorded for later playback
'Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you' — but that was Bell's phone call, March 1876
'There is no there there' — Gertrude Stein's later phrase, irrelevant to 1877
'In the beginning was the Word' — too literary for Edison's pragmatic style
context: Edison (1847–1931) called his device the phonograph. The patent (filed December 24, 1877) was granted within months. Edison founded the Edison Phonograph Company (1887) and the modern recording industry. He also developed the practical incandescent electric light (October 21, 1879 demonstrated), the kinetoscope (1891, motion pictures), and many other technologies. His Menlo Park 'invention factory' was the world's first industrial research laboratory. He held 1,093 U.S. patents.

question: On March 10, 1876, in his Boston laboratory at 5 Exeter Place, a 29-year-old elocution teacher and inventor accidentally spilled battery acid on his clothing. He spoke into the experimental transmitter to summon his assistant in the next room: 'Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.' His assistant heard him through the receiver. What had he developed?
answer: The telephone — the first words transmitted electrically by speech were a call for help
choices: The telephone — the first words transmitted electrically by speech were a call for help
The telegraph — but the telegraph had been around for decades (Morse's 1844 'What hath God wrought')
The radio — but radio (Marconi) came two decades later, 1895–1901
The phonograph — but that was Edison, December 1877, not Bell in 1876
context: Alexander Graham Bell (1847–1922) was Scottish-born, living in Boston. His patent (March 7, 1876, three days before the famous transmission) was one of the most valuable in history. The Bell Telephone Company (1877) became the basis of the eventual AT&T. Bell continued inventing — multiple deaf-education projects, hydrofoils, aircraft — for the rest of his life. The unit of sound intensity (decibel, 1/10 bel) is named for him. The legal disputes around his patent (against Elisha Gray) lasted years.

question: On July 20, 1969, at 10:56 p.m. EDT, 38 minutes after the lunar module *Eagle* had landed in the Sea of Tranquility, the 38-year-old commander climbed down the ladder and stepped onto the lunar surface. He spoke to about 600 million television viewers worldwide. Who was he?
answer: Neil Armstrong — first human to walk on the Moon; commander of Apollo 11
choices: Neil Armstrong — first human to walk on the Moon; commander of Apollo 11
Buzz Aldrin — second human to walk on the Moon; followed Armstrong by 19 minutes
Michael Collins — Apollo 11 command module pilot, remained in lunar orbit
Pete Conrad — Apollo 12 commander, fourth human on the Moon (November 1969)
context: Armstrong (1930–2012) said 'That's one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind' — the 'a' is heard inconsistently in the recording. He insisted he had said it. The plaque on the lunar module's leg reads 'We came in peace for all mankind.' Five more Apollo missions landed on the Moon (12, 14, 15, 16, 17); Apollo 13 (April 1970) was an aborted mission with successful recovery. Armstrong was famously private after the mission; he resented being treated as a national resource.

question: On April 13, 1970, about 56 hours into the mission, an oxygen tank in the Apollo 13 service module exploded — crippling the spacecraft 200,000 miles from Earth. Commander Jim Lovell radioed Houston with what became one of the most famous understatements in history. What did he say?
answer: 'Houston, we've had a problem' — often misquoted as 'Houston, we have a problem'
choices: 'Houston, we've had a problem' — often misquoted as 'Houston, we have a problem'
'Houston, we've lost an engine' — but the problem was more serious than engine loss
'Houston, please advise' — but the actual call was more specific than that
'Houston, oxygen has been compromised' — but Lovell's call was less technical than this
context: The Apollo 13 mission failed to land on the moon but succeeded in returning all three astronauts (Lovell, Fred Haise, Jack Swigert) safely to Earth on April 17, 1970. The lunar module *Aquarius*, designed for two people on the lunar surface, served as a lifeboat for three for four days. Flight director Gene Kranz's 'failure is not an option' became iconic. The Ron Howard film *Apollo 13* (1995) with Tom Hanks dramatized the rescue. NASA called the mission a 'successful failure.'

question: On May 6, 1954, at Iffley Road track in Oxford, a 25-year-old British medical student paced by two Oxford friends ran one mile in 3 minutes, 59.4 seconds — the first time the four-minute barrier had been broken in athletic history. The track announcer Norris McWhirter began reading the time, drawing out 'three minutes...' to let the crowd realize the record had been set. Who was the runner?
answer: Roger Bannister — broke the 4-minute mile barrier on a windy Oxford afternoon
choices: Roger Bannister — broke the 4-minute mile barrier on a windy Oxford afternoon
John Landy — Australian who broke Bannister's record 46 days later, June 21, 1954
Wes Santee — American runner of the era but did not break four minutes
Herb Elliott — Australian middle-distance star but later (1958 record at 3:54.5)
